  new move. (The packet's own two unwinds still discard on a failed packet; see
  `docs/ROADMAP.md`.) The
  pre-affine RESUME shape is different in kind: the restored record already carried
  shared QoS 2 memberships, restore loaded them before the provisioning attempt,
  and they survive the settlement — so the path is owed to a LIVE subscription and
  must not be removed at all. The provisioning save therefore registers a landed
  continuation (`unwindProvisionedQ2AffineOnLanded`) that runs the ordinary
  three-arm unwind under the resolver's token, and `hasSharedQoS2Sub()` is what
  tells those two apart: eligible, never automatic. The guard is mandatory rather
  than defensive, and
  `TestQ2AffineAmbiguousProvisioningKeepsAPathAMembershipOwns` is the resume shape
  it exists for. Only a MINTED generation qualifies at all: a resume that
  re-establishes a path the record already named reaches the same save, and its
  generation may owe assignments to a delivery already started to it. After a crash
  inside that window nothing removes the path at settlement, because there is no
  longer a continuation to run: a later shared QoS 2 SUBSCRIBE REUSES it — making
  it useful again without deleting it or releasing its cost — and session teardown
  is what removes it.
  Its unwind is prepared with `disposeNow` FALSE, so ownership is arbitrated before
  anything irreversible: the cleanup record is CASed first, and only once that write
  is confirmed are the generation's assignments discarded, its delivery subscription
  and MaxAckPending charge released, and its consumer deleted. A remote winner that
  took the session over and preserved the
  generation therefore wins the CAS and keeps its started deliveries, and the
  definite arm restores a path whose claims were never touched. This is the order
  `claimTeardown` already uses, and it is safe to dispose late because
  `materializeQ2AffOnBehalf` terminates a claim whose record no longer names its
  generation. The packet's own two unwinds still dispose first; see
  `docs/CONFORMANCE.md` and `docs/ROADMAP.md`.
- The **claim-cleanup-failure abort** and the path retained after UNSUBSCRIBE of
  the last shared QoS 2 filter are deliberately KEPT: the path may still owe
  outstanding assignments or started deliveries. A later SUBSCRIBE reuses them;
  session teardown is the only thing that removes them.

**A persisted qos-2 shared membership implies an affine generation.** No writer
here can separate them: the path is provisioned in the SUBSCRIBE's first filter
loop, before the membership is persisted, and the record builder writes
`SharedSubs`, `Q2Aff` and `Q2AffGen` as one record. A record that does separate
them predates the affine path, so it is **refused** rather than interpreted —
at CONNECT, in the startup expiry sweep, at a fired expiry timer, and in
`mqttValidateRecordAffinePair`, which the reference walk and teardown adoption
share.

Refusing it is not bookkeeping. `Q2AffGen` is what a contender compares a claim
against to conclude its winner is gone, and an **empty** one mismatches every
claim: read rather than refused, such a record turns a malformed shape into proof
of absence and discards an assignment owed to a delivery already started — the
redistribution [MQTT-4.8.2-5] forbids. `materializeQ2AffOnBehalf` therefore
validates the winner's record **before the comparison**, not inside one of its arms,
because the record is used in both directions: a mismatch discards the assignment,
and a match materializes the copy and **acknowledges the group source**, which is
irreversible and would strand the delivery on a session that can never resume. A
record can match a claim's generation and still be uninterpretable. Its sibling
`discardAbsentWinnerClaim` already validated before the same decision.

The rule is deliberately narrow:
shared QoS 0 and QoS 1 memberships provision no affine path, and a generation with
no consumer config — the shape the `minted` gate is built around — is one the
validator deliberately continues to permit.

It is narrow but not literal, and the difference matters. A persisted shared QoS
byte outside 0..2 is **also refused**, because `processSubs` CLAMPS a filter above
QoS 2 down to 2 while restoring and the resume feeds these values in verbatim: a
record carrying 3 becomes a live shared QoS 2 membership, so a rule matching only
the literal 2 would pass it straight through to the destructive readers the refusal
exists to stop. Every writer stores the value after that clamp has already bounded
it, so no record here can carry one. Whether any writer originates that
second shape is a pre-existing question about the affine design; it is not settled
here, and refusing it would be a new refusal of a shape whose non-existence is
unproven.

The four enforcement points call `mqttValidateRecordAffinePair` **whole** rather
than the new rule alone, which deliberately widens them: the three malformed
pairings it already refused for the sweep — a consumer config with no generation, a
malformed generation, and a config whose names do not match its generation — now
refuse a CONNECT and an expiry too, where before they resumed and were rewritten.
Splitting the predicate is the failure the validator's own comment records
("splitting them once let adoption delete a consumer the reference walk would have
refused to interpret"), and a record uninterpretable to the sweep is not one a
resume may rewrite.

Sharing the validator also means the refusal reaches `buildSessionRefs`, and there
the consequence is scoped **by resource class**. Such a record contributes no affine
reference while the qos-2 memberships it carries mean the session may own an affine
consumer and outstanding claims. The consequence is **exactly one pass**, and stating it
more broadly would be false: the reference
walk reports the affine half indeterminate and the caller suppresses
`reconcileOrphanQ2AffClaims` for the whole account, permanently, since nothing rewrites
the record and expiry will not remove it either. It is not a gate over "every affine
resource" — the retired affine **register** arm sits outside it and can still mutate
claims, and affine consumer deletion is gone entirely (F-036 course E). Its identity
and generation are sound, so the inbound, in-flight and PUBREL references it
contributes are complete and **those classes keep being reclaimed**.

That partition is the rule the affine claim inventory already follows, for the
reason stated at its own call site: otherwise one bad record disables every other
class account-wide, forever, on evidence about a different resource class. A record
whose *identity* cannot be established is the stronger case — the inbound and PUBREL
references are derived from the id hash and the generation, so nothing about it is
trustworthy — and that still aborts the pass outright. Both are logged as warnings;
only a record-shaped failure carries the recreate-the-streams guidance, because a
scan that failed on a timeout or a leader change resolves itself. The cost is stated
in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`.

**Stream prerequisites.** `$MQTT_qos2assign` must be `LimitsPolicy` +
`DiscardOld` + `MaxMsgsPer: 1` — permanent retention is as load-bearing as the
per-subject singleton, because claims are read by direct subject lookup and are
never consumed, so interest or work-queue retention would drop them. `$MQTT_out`
must stay `InterestPolicy`: that is how a discarded session's undelivered copies
disappear with its consumer, and it is why a copy must never be stored before its
consumer exists (a store with no interest returns success and keeps nothing). Both
have validators (`validateQoS2AssignStream`, `validateOutStream`) that **fail
broker startup** rather than update a non-conforming stream in place, and the two
lists differ deliberately: each is derived from what that stream's owner actually
does.

**Scope.** Affinity is a property of the brokers that consult `$MQTT_qos2assign`,
which is every broker serving the account — they all run this tree (see the
Compatibility boundary). It is stated as scope rather than as a rollout condition: a
broker serving the same shared group without consulting the claims would redistribute
a started delivery another broker had claimed, and there is no runtime capability gate
that would stop it. See `docs/CONFORMANCE.md` for this and for the residual that does
remain: a consumer deleted between the copy proof and the source ack (F-063).
Packet-identifier continuity is **not** among them — the in-flight register closed it on
every outbound path.

### On-behalf restoration of a destroyed affine consumer

`$MQTT_out` is interest-retained and `CONSUMER.DELETE` carries no precondition, so
a winner's affine durable can be destroyed out of band while it is away — taking
every copy it held. Nothing owner-independent used to RESOLVE such an assignment:
the dispatcher rereads the claim on every redelivery, the sweep skips any claim of
a referenced generation, and `recoverQ2AffClaims` runs only from the owner's own
resume. Since MQTT permits a session that never expires, "the owner comes back" is
not a reconciler, and the group consumer sets no `MaxDeliver`, so the source is
re-offered forever while holding a `MaxAckPending` slot.

A contender taking such a redelivery now restores the durable from the winner's
record and materializes onto it. **Presence and authoritative absence are not two
paths**: the same create-or-update runs either way, differing only in which
`MemoryStorage` it carries.

- **Replayability is whole-struct equality, not a field list.** The canonical
  configuration has a single constructor, `buildQ2AffineConsumerConfig`, and the
  record's `Q2Aff` is accepted only when it `reflect.DeepEqual`s what that
  constructor returns for the same names plus the record's own three variable
  fields (`AckWait`, `MaxAckPending`, `MemoryStorage`). A list cannot close a
  struct a dependency bump can extend, and `MaxDeliver` alone — outside every list
  an earlier design wrote — reopens the stall. This is not defensive padding:
  `mqttValidateRecordAffinePair` permits `Q2AffGen` with a nil `Q2Aff`, and
  `restoreQ2AffineUnwind` produces a real names-only record whose zero values are
  actively wrong (`AckPolicy` zero is `AckNone`, `DeliverPolicy` zero is
  `DeliverAll`). The comparison is against the persisted REQUEST, which is what
  the record holds.
- **The three variable fields are bounded** at the provisionable domain: `AckWait`
  positive, `MaxAckPending` within `1..mqttMaxAckTotalLimit` and within
  `$MQTT_out`'s live `ConsumerLimits.MaxAckPending` when that is positive.
- **`ConsumerLimits.InactiveThreshold` is read BEFORE the create and refused when
  it is nonzero**, with no create attempted. nats-server substitutes the stream's
  limit whenever the request field is zero, and this configuration deliberately
  sends zero — so for an already-present durable a create-or-update would apply
  the substitution and restart the deletion timer, and refusing afterwards would
  refuse a durable the refusal itself had just made reapable. The predicate is
  `!= 0`, not `> 0`: the field is a signed duration, and the server's own limit
  rejection fires only for a positive limit, so a negative one would slip past and
  mutate the durable anyway. The returned-config check stays, because the
  pre-check is not atomic with the create.
- **A storage type is immutable, so the contender adopts rather than imposes.** It
  builds with the actual durable's `MemoryStorage` where one exists and the
  record's where none does, never its own local option — the owner will meet this
  durable later. On a create refused for that exact cause it looks up **once** and
  retries; a second conflict refuses. Where the relookup finds the durable
  **authoritatively gone**, the retry is issued even though it carries the same
  value the refused request did: the obstacle has been removed, so the identical
  request is exactly what now succeeds, and stopping on that equality would defer
  restoration to another redelivery for no reason. One attempt is a bounded
  fail-closed policy, not a proof the conflict cannot recur, and it is safe
  because no copy has been stored and no source acknowledged at that point.
- **An indeterminate lookup is not an absence.** Only `JSConsumerNotFoundErr`
  authorizes the absent branch; a transport error, a `nil` `ConsumerInfo` and a
  non-nil one carrying a `nil` `Config` all refuse with no create attempted.

**Every refusal above is on the CONTENDER's path only, and that asymmetry is
deliberate.** A refusal costs different things on the two paths. On the contender
it is free: nothing is stored, no source is acked, and no client is connected to
notice. On the owner it costs a live connection — a refusal while a saved shared
filter is being restored at CONNECT is silently skipped, because there is no SUBACK
on that path, and the only remedy that removes the silence closes the connection,
publishing the client's Will and, at a zero Session Expiry Interval, deleting the
session. `ensureQ2AffineConsumerSubscription` therefore gains **no** new refusal:
its initial create is unchanged and it performs no lookup and no stream preflight.

It gains exactly one thing, and it can only turn a current failure into a success:
**a post-failure recovery on a storage-type conflict**. `MemoryStorage` is
immutable, and the owner rebuilds its request from the CURRENT local option while
the durable keeps whatever it was made with — so an operator who reloads
`consumer_memory_storage` breaks affine resume for every session whose durable
predates the reload, permanently, with no contender involved. On that exact
flattened cause the owner looks the durable up once and retries with the storage it
actually has. On a failed lookup or a failed retry the caller-visible outcome and
the reported error are unchanged from today; the lookup's own error is never
substituted for the create's.

**Why this path has that defect and its siblings do not** — which is also the
route that would remove the residual below, if it is ever worth taking.
`ensurePubRelConsumerSubscription` verifies before it creates: it looks the
durable up, marks it verified and RETURNS when it is there, and reaches its
current-option create only when the durable is confirmed absent. An absent
durable cannot conflict on an immutable field, so a reload never reaches one. The
per-subscription consumers escape for the SAME reason, not because of their
names: a persisted `sess.cons[sid]` is verified by the resume reconciliation
phase and then adopted IN PLACE at CONNECT, with no create-or-update carrying
current options. Their `nuid`-bearing identities are minted only where there is
no present consumer to conflict with — a genuinely new subscription, or repair
after the old durable was found authoritatively absent — so the `nuid` protects
those cases rather than the reload. The affine path is the
deviant: it issues an unconditional create-or-update, deliberately, because that
create doubles as the verification that a persisted config still describes a
consumer which exists and still looks like this. That is what puts the current
local option in front of an existing durable, and it is the whole origin of the
conflict this recovery absorbs.

It first reads the live stream and **declines to retry at all** while
`ConsumerLimits.InactiveThreshold` is nonzero. The refused create mutated nothing,
because JetStream checks convergence before it applies anything; the retry is
accepted and would therefore have the stream's limit substituted into it, arming a
deletion timer on a durable the failure had left alone. A retry whose response is
then lost would report failure while leaving that durable due to be reaped with the
session's interest-retained copies — an unresumable session turned into a losing
one. Monotonicity is about state as well as about the caller's outcome, and this is
where the two could have diverged.

The read is **not atomic** with the retry, so a limit landing between them still
reaches it. That window is stated in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md` with the three
conditions it needs, rather than narrowed a third time: consumer create carries no
precondition, so nothing here can fence the update against a concurrent stream
change, and the debris it leaves is the same one an ordinary owner create already
produces under the same mutation.

### What the write audit established, and the gaps it found

*`docs/findings/ha-arbitration.md` F-033, F-063, F-064, F-065 and F-066 are
authoritative for these mechanisms, arms, directions and remedies. This section
summarises and references them, as the compatibility boundary's precedent prescribes; it
is not a second authority.*

F-033 audited every mutation this protocol makes against `test/depproof/`'s route
inventory. **Every claim write carries its per-subject expectation**, because they are all
funnelled through one CAS helper that emits `JSExpectedLastSubjSeq` unconditionally: the
election is create-only (expectation `0`), every later transition CASes at the sequence its
own attempt loaded, and the reap deletes an exact sequence. Seven of the ten transitions
additionally assert the winner's identity. Of the three that do not, the **two
`SourceAcked` writes** rest on the per-subject CAS alone — a fact about the source MESSAGE
applies to whichever incarnation holds the subject — while **`AffineDone` is
owner-independent but incarnation- and copy-fenced**: it states something about ONE
incarnation's own copy, so it asserts the claim's `Nonce` and requires the record to still
name the copy the delivery carried (F-065). Owner-independent is therefore not the same as
unfenced, and removing that fence would not be consistent with this audit. The server-side
contract for those writes is **inherited from F-030 rather than
re-proved here**, per "Trusting the backend"; no lineage is carried on this stream and none
is needed, because a create has no base to descend from and a transition that CASes at a
base it read already answers "is this record still mine?" more strongly than a parent
pointer would. Nothing purges this stream, and the startup validators refuse every
configuration that would evict a claim with no writer at all.

**The gaps are on the other side of the protocol — the copies, not the claims.** The one
operation that carries no condition is `CONSUMER.DELETE` on `$MQTT_out`: the API has no
precondition field, so it removes whatever consumer holds that name when it applies, and
because the stream is interest-retained that destroys every copy the consumer still held.
Three defects follow, each resting on a premise of its own:

- **F-063 — fixed 2026-08-19, guarantee re-scoped.** Nothing bound evidence that a copy was
  RETAINED to the irreversible source acknowledgement that follows it: a store onto a
  deleted consumer succeeds and keeps nothing, and the only re-read was on the
  CAS-rejection path, so the claim reached `materialized` and the group source was released
  for a message that no longer existed. Every route now proves the copy with a presence
  check and releases the source only on
  `copyPresent ∨ AffineDone ∨ Discarded ∨ Lost ∨ SourceAcked`. Because `CONSUMER.DELETE`
  carries no precondition, the guarantee is conditioned on a fresh but **non-atomic**
  observation. The residual spans the final copy lookup through any intervening claim
  load or CAS retry to the confirmed source ack — no bound narrower than that is
  claimed — and is stated in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`.
- **F-064** — a live generation reference makes the sweep skip every claim of that
  generation. The sweep still does, deliberately: it carries no payload, so it could only
  resolve such a claim by asserting a fact it cannot prove. What has changed is that the
  STALL no longer waits for the owner — a group redelivery does carry the payload, and
  restores the winner's consumer on its behalf. Two things remain: settled claims of a live
  generation are still not reaped (**F-065**'s fence), and a `materialized` claim whose copy
  is gone is still owner-dependent, which is why the `Lost` narrative in
  `docs/CONFORMANCE.md` still holds only for a session that comes back.
- **F-065 — fixed.** The reaper evaluated its two-sided predicate on a copy-absence
  reading taken BEFORE its own `SourceAcked` transition, so a copy stored during that
  round trip was invisible and the claim was deleted out from under it — leaving a copy
  the delivery gate can only NAK, forever, holding a `MaxAckPending` slot. Three routes
  reached that state and all three are closed: the reaper now takes its copy reading
  AFTER its own last write and immediately before the delete; a materialization attempt
  WITHDRAWS the exact copy sequence it proved present once it proves no claim of that
  copy's incarnation remains; and the claim now carries an INCARNATION, so a replacement
  election can neither adopt a superseded copy nor be written to by a superseded actor.
  A PUBREC that leaves the affine side unproven additionally RETIRES its source, so the
  register it retains is read as "past PUBREC" rather than as a live PUBLISH — gated on a
  SUCCESSFUL PUBREC, because a rejected delivery stores no PUBREL and therefore has no
  PUBCOMP at which an unlanded durable mark could be retried.
  The stated guarantee is **re-scoped**, as F-063's was: the
  withdrawal is a compensation rather than an arbitration — claim and copy are on
  separate streams and JetStream cannot commit to both together — so a copy stranded by
  an attempt that crashed, whose delete was unconfirmed, or whose final claim reading was
  indeterminate is bounded by ordinary teardown, or by the gate disposing it once a later
  incarnation holds the subject, and is otherwise retained. (A later orphan-sweep consumer
  deletion used to be a third bound; F-036 course E removed it.) See `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`.
- **F-066** — a `stopAll`-instructed recreation of ONE stream is treated as a
  self-contained procedure, but durable records persist identities other streams issue. A
  verified sample of such identities — explicitly not a census, since four enumeration
  attempts were falsified and the census was deferred to F-034, which landed it on
  2026-08-22 — shows **three** epoch
  couplings, all against `$MQTT_sess` and all ad hoc, with every confirmed reference to
  `$MQTT_msgs`, `$MQTT_out`, `$MQTT_qos2assign` and `$MQTT_inflight` uncoupled, and one
  `$MQTT_sess` reference uncoupled too. On this
  path the VERIFIED AFFECTED SUBSET — not a proven closed unit; F-034's census enumerates
  the population but is a drift GUARD over the interpretation surface rather than a closure
  proof, so it does not settle that either — is those four
  streams; recreating a proper subset loses accepted messages, delivers an OLD payload for
  a new message, or NAK-loops orphaned copies forever.

Two consequences on this path are **F-036's** rather than ours. The contender's discard arm
firing on an absent winner record rests on F-036's own falsified premise; the
different-generation reading is settled on the clean-start route, where teardown marks every
assignment of the retiring generation `Discarded` before deleting its consumer. And the
orphan sweep's affine consumer delete — by name, past a `Created` fingerprint that a
resuming session's ADOPTION left unchanged — reached its window only when a session was
resident with that generation while its record was absent, which is F-036's premise
exactly. **It was REMOVED by F-036 course E**: every positive authorization for it was
sought and refused, so the route is gone rather than guarded, and the accepted price is
the correlated leak in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`.

## UNSUBSCRIBE drain

A drain has **two entry points**, and the section keeps its name because the
UNSUBSCRIBE one came first and every cross-reference cites it.

[MQTT-3.10.4-3] requires the server to complete the delivery of any QoS 1/2
message it has already **started** sending, even after the client unsubscribes.
UNSUBSCRIBE used to tear the plain consumer down immediately, and since
`$MQTT_msgs` is interest-retained, deleting the durable deleted the messages it
still held: the started PUBLISH was simply lost.

**A QoS 1/2 → QoS 0 re-SUBSCRIBE owes the same completion**, under a different rule.
[MQTT-3.8.4-3] requires a SUBSCRIBE on an identical topic filter to *replace* the
existing subscription, and [MQTT-3.8.4-4] forbids interrupting the flow of
publications — so the broker may neither refuse the packet nor wait for the exchange,
and the started PUBLISH must still complete. That path used to close delivery, purge
the pending exchanges and delete the durable, losing every outstanding exchange
including a QoS 2 one already past PUBREC. It now converts the consumer into a drain
instead, and the QoS 0 filter is served by the raw subscription. The two entry points
differ only in *when* the conversion happens; see "Where each entry point converts"
below.

A **drain** is what that teardown becomes when started deliveries remain
(`internal/mqtt/unsub_drain.go`). The durable and its delivery subscription
survive; already-started deliveries keep being redelivered and completed; fresh
messages on the filter are discarded. The drain is a field on the session record
(`Drains`), so it survives disconnect, restart and failover, and it lives until
every started delivery completes or the session ends. It is deliberately kept
**out** of the record's `Cons` map, because in this tree `Cons` restores straight
into `sess.cons`, and single ownership (I7 below) requires a drained consumer to live
in exactly one place. Drains restore through their own path instead, and a
re-SUBSCRIBE reclaims one by adopting it explicitly.

The invariants, in the order they matter:

- **Persist before ack.** A delivery of a claimed sequence is acked only after a
  *confirmed* save in which the drain no longer claims it. One helper owns every
  such ack; a refused fence or failed save acks nothing and the message is simply
  redelivered.
- **The commit points.** QoS 1 has one phase. For QoS 2 the durable **PUBREL
  intent** — written *before* the PUBREL is stored — commits the exit from the
  PUBLISH phase, and only a **confirmed** PUBREL (stored *and* in delivery)
  authorizes removing and acking the source claim. The phase is three-valued, not
  a boolean, because "a PUBREL exists" and "the store outcome is unknown" must not
  authorize the same actions.
- **Only transmitted deliveries drain.** A message withheld by the in-flight cap
  was never sent, so it is discarded rather than enrolled.
- **Single ownership.** From the moment it is staged, a drained consumer lives
  exclusively in `sess.drains` and its `cons[sid]` entry is gone, so nothing can reach
  it through `cons` and create a second durable on the same filter. A re-SUBSCRIBE
  therefore **adopts** the drain explicitly. For a QoS 0 downgrade the *staging moment*
  is the packet's final-update boundary rather than the filter's own staging, and the
  invariant that keeps the two mechanisms apart there is **temporal**: the downgrade
  holds its `cons` entry for the whole filter loop, the conversion runs after the last
  occurrence, and no revocation can follow it.
- **A live SUBSCRIBE adopts only what can deliver.** A resume can leave a drain with
  no delivery subscription — the blanket QoS 2 withholding when PUBREL setup fails,
  and a restore whose own `processQOS12Sub` failed. Adoption would then move that
  durable into `cons`, and `processJSConsumer`'s existing-consumer arm reads the entry
  as proof a subscription exists: the filter is SUBACKed **successfully** and delivers
  nothing for the rest of the connection. So a live SUBSCRIBE **reclaims** such a drain
  first — installing its delivery subscription and adopting it in one `sess.mu`
  section — or fails the filter with `0x80`. Four things about how, each of which a
  review round established:
  - It installs with the **SUBSCRIBE's own** terms, not the drain's. The
    existing-consumer arm's metadata refresh runs after that lock is released, so
    installing the drain's terms leaves a window in which the callback selects with
    them — a drain with No Local set, against a backlog the install just made
    available, acks away a message the client is owed.
  - It **adopts inside the same critical section**, so nothing observes the durable as
    neither a drain nor a consumer.
  - It does **not** register `drainByDur` first, as `restoreDrains` does. That
    registration is right where the drain stays a drain; here it is never observable
    before the adoption removes it, and a mechanism whose presence and absence are
    indistinguishable is one too many.
  - It decides "already delivering" from the **subscription**, never from the reverse
    index. `restoreDrainLocked` registers `drainByDur` when the record is restored,
    before any subscription exists, and the blanket withholding leaves that entry in
    place while installing nothing — so an index-keyed test reads a withheld drain as
    healthy and repairs nothing. The index says a drain is known; only the
    subscription says it can deliver.

  The reclaim is recorded into the packet's restore snapshot, because it is a state a
  rollback must **restore** rather than undo: the drain was entitled to its delivery
  subscription and the resume failed to install one. That is also what keeps
  `rollbackSubscribePacket` unchanged — its adopted-drain exclusion asks whether the
  durable was a drain's before the packet, and after the reclaim the honest answer is
  yes.

  What the reclaim does **not** establish is stated in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`. Two of the
  three residuals it once named are now **closed**: an already-started QoS 2 exchange
  reclaimed by a QoS 1 re-SUBSCRIBE (an exchange's QoS is carried, not recomputed), and the
  durable a filter failing *after* adopting used to strand (see "An adopted durable is named
  continuously" below). What remains is the **CONNECT restore** route, on a sid a QoS 0
  re-SUBSCRIBE already gave a key.

### An adopted durable is named continuously (I8)

**The invariant.** *While a durable that was a drain's is held under a sid whose membership
key is absent, every record written names it — in `Cons` where the membership survives, in
`Drains` where it does not.*

What it prevents is loss, not untidiness, and it needs no crash and no failure. Between
`adoptDrainLocked` and the packet's final `sess.update` the sid has a consumer and no
membership, and the record builder drops a `cons` entry whose membership key is absent — so
the record named the durable **nowhere**. `sweepOrphanedConsumers` deletes any `$MQTT_msgs`
consumer no record references, protects only sessions resident on the **sweeping** broker,
and keys eligibility on the consumer's **creation** time, so adoption starts no new
grace: a
sibling deletes a live session's durable, with its started deliveries, on an
interest-retained stream. A later shared filter's early persist inside that window is enough
to write such a record.

The scope of the claim is exact: what is closed is *this omission-induced sweep race*, by
preserving a reference the sweep's own contract already reads. That is **preservation of a
reference, not distributed ownership arbitration**, and it is not a general claim that
concurrent deletion is harmless. Switching a durable between `Cons` and `Drains` inside one
continuously referenced record needs no agreement with the sweep.

- **The adoption retains the drain object** in `sess.adoptedDrains`, keyed by sid. It still
  leaves `drains` and `drainByDur`, so **nothing on the delivery path changes**: the callback
  finds no drain for that durable and the consumer behaves as the ordinary consumer the
  client subscribed to. The map is read by the record builder and by settlement, never by
  delivery.
- **The builder names it where it drops the `cons` entry**, on the **exact consumer
  identity** — a retention whose `cc` is no longer what `cons[sid]` holds describes a
  consumer that has been replaced or deleted. The predicate is **current state, never packet
   history**, which is what makes duplicate occurrences of one filter, the QoS 0
   exclusion and
  fork repair's adoption resolve with no special case.
- **A QoS 0 membership needs nothing.** Its `subs` key survives, so the `cons` entry is
  retained and the durable is already named — two references to one fact would be one too
  many.
- **Release is by SETTLEMENT, never by a cleanup pass.** A retention is released only
  where a
  confirmed outcome accounts for it: the sid gained ordinary membership, responsibility moved
  to an active drain, or the consumer's deletion or replacement is committed. A changed
  pointer alone is **not** evidence that disposal was authorized, and staging legitimately
  removes `cons[sid]` for a while — releasing there is what would let a definite UNSUBSCRIBE
  failure restore the consumer and the membership with the retention already gone. The last
  step is incarnation disposal: a completed `clear()` drops them, an aborted one does not.

#### Omission is owned by the retirement transition

`Drains` omission used to be read off the claim count. It is now authorized by one
thing: an
owned retirement transition has **marked** that exact object.

I3 is unchanged by that — the save that omits the entry is still the save the retirement
rides on, so the durable is unreferenced **before** it is deleted. What moved is who decides.
Reading the count let *any* writer un-name a durable whose obligations were not yet
established, and let an omission land while an unresolved reservation could still belong to
it, which a sibling sweep then acts on.

- **The mark goes on before an EXISTING owned save**, wherever one exists — ordinary
  finalization's claim-clearing save, recovery's pruning save, the PUBREL barrier's
  completion — so one save both clears the last claim and omits the entry, and
  `finishDrainIfEmpty` issues **no save at all**. Adding a second, later save instead would
  destroy a property this tree has: a failed *claim-removal* save keeps the claim and its
  redelivery retry, whereas a save after the source is already acked has no fallback, and
  nothing else revisits the drain for the life of the connection.
- **Marking is gated on retirement ELIGIBILITY, not on emptiness.** The known claim set
  emptying is not the same as nothing being owed. The gate discounts **this attempt's own
  removals** — the transition has already set `unclaimUnconfirmed` on the claim it is
  removing, which the plain predicate rejects, so asking it would never open the gate — and
  keeps every other guard.
- **An already-empty, still-referenced drain gets its own transaction**, because it has no
  claim-clearing save to ride on: a definite failure clears the mark and leaves the reference
  to the next resume; an ambiguous one **keeps** the mark and defers the delete to the landed
  continuation; only a confirmed removal deletes.
- **While marked, the sid refuses through the shared hold.** In the ambiguous window the
  omission may already be durable, so reusing the durable would leave a live consumer no
  record names. The property is that the old durable is never **reused** — deliberately not
  that the record still names it, since after an ambiguous omission it may not.

### A restored drain's claim set is a floor

A persisted `Started` set records what was owed **when it was written**. Absence from it is
not evidence that a delivery never started, and treating it as if it were is a loss with an
identifier leak attached.

After an adoption the consumer is ordinary, so a delivery it starts is tracked by the
ordinary in-flight machinery and nothing adds it to the retained drain's claims. On the next
resume the restored drain does not claim that sequence: the callback's unclaimed arm
acks the
**source** away on an interest-retained stream, while the recovered register is installed
holding its identifier with **no future delivery that could ever discharge it** — released
only by the client's terminal ack, which can never come, or by session destruction.

What licenses adding a claim is F-072's durable discriminator, not an inference. A
possibly-attempted entry may have reached the client, so the delivery is owed; a
proven-unsent one demonstrably was not, and claiming it would make the drain redeliver,
as a
started delivery, a payload the client has never seen. That is the same three-way
classification UNSUBSCRIBE staging applies, and it has **one home**:

- **enrol** — transmitted, or possibly attempted;
- **cancel** — allocated with its register store still in flight, so nothing was transmitted;
- **withdraw** — confirmed and provably never transmitted.

**Eligibility is the caller's, not the classifier's.** No single pending entry can carry the
phase: a recovered PUBREL reserves its **source** under the same `cpending` map while
`pendingPublish` holds nothing for that identifier, and a recovered PUBREL entry may
carry a
nonzero QoS. So each caller first sorts a mapping into a positively identified non-PUBLISH
obligation, which restricts nothing and whose own machinery owns its completion, or an
unresolved one, which fails closed.

**Recovery only READS the classification**; staging and rollback also perform its side
effects. That asymmetry is deliberate — recovery is reconstructing obligations, while the
other two change live delivery ownership.

The floor is keyed on the **installed source mapping**, never on the register scan: a
possibly-attempted register over a *finished* source is deliberately retained with no
mapping, because the payload can never be re-offered while the receiver may still hold the
identifier, and enrolling it would manufacture a claim for a delivery that can never happen.
Walking `cpending` is what keeps those out without a second exclusion rule to keep in step.

It runs at the end of register recovery's apply phase — before any destructive drain
reconciliation, and before any drain can deliver, since a record-restored drain has no
delivery subscription until `restoreDrains` installs one.

#### A SUBSCRIBE rollback completes the same transition

`rollbackSubscribePacket` restores both drain maps from a shallow snapshot, so the
reactivated object is the **pre-adoption** drain and claims nothing started since. Enrolling
is not enough on its own: a callback parked in its register write (the admission ladder
`runInflightAdmission`, behind both `admitInflightPublish` and the affine `storeInflightRegister`)
confirms against the
pending **entry's** identity, not against drain membership, so an allocation merely *skipped*
would confirm and transmit a sequence the reactivated drain does not claim. The cancel half
therefore untracks the entry as well as recording its verdict.

A reactivated drain is not *staged*, so `commitDrains` would never collect its withdrawals
and the rollback's own cancellation list is built from the packet's newly created consumers,
which excludes the adopted ones. Its withdrawn pairs are carried explicitly instead, and
settled on the rollback save's classified outcome: deleted on a confirmed one, kept on a
definite failure because nothing durably says the withdrawal happened, and deferred to the
landed continuation on an ambiguous one.

### Uncertainty is attributed per source

Two readers act on a claim's **absence**, and both are destructive if the view is
incomplete: the delivery callback's unclaimed arm, which acks an interest-retained message
away, and retirement eligibility, which deletes a consumer. They decline while a restriction
covers what they are about.

Everything with **positive per-exchange evidence** is never restricted, whatever else is
uncertain — a recovered PUBREL's own completion, a confirmed PUBREL transition, a client's
terminal acknowledgement, an authorized expiry or packet-size discard, and recovery's
pruning of a claim whose consumer ack floor has advanced or whose message is confirmed
absent. Withholding those blocks progress for no safety gained: an exchange recovery has
fully classified must be allowed to finish.

The restriction itself is **derived, never latched on the drain**:

- an unresolved reservation whose source identity survives — an opaque recovered register
  keeps its durable and sequence even though its `cpending` mapping is gone — restricts
  **its own source**, and retirement aggregates those by durable;
- a **failed or incomplete reconstruction**, or a reservation with no source identity to
  attribute, restricts the **session**.

Missing `cpending` is **not** the discriminator, and one durable's opacity says nothing about
another durable or about a different sequence on its own.

#### The apply-completion provenance

Telling those two rows apart needs a fact `piSpaceIncomplete` cannot carry, because it
is set
in both histories: whether the latest recovery attempt **applied** at all. An enumeration
failure returns before the apply phase and exhausted reclassification never reaches it, so
`inflightApplyCompletedWalk` is stamped only at that boundary — and **unconditionally there,
including when opacity remains**.

Equality with `inflightWalks` means one of exactly two things, and both authorize per-source
attribution: the incarnation's initial baseline, or a completed latest apply. Inequality
means an unknown population may have been missed entirely, so an apparently attributable
reservation proves nothing about the rest.

It is **incarnation-scoped**, and `setIncarnationLocked` rebases it. `clear()` preserves the
walk counter while discarding the pending maps and re-minting the generation, and the fresh
session does not run recovery at all — so without the rebase a failed predecessor's mismatch
would impose its session-wide restriction on an incarnation that never ran a walk, and a new
attributable reservation, which sets `piSpaceIncomplete` without advancing either counter,
would be misread as that same failure. The walk counter is deliberately **not** reset: the
opaque reservations' own walk stamp reads it. An aborted clear never reaches the
re-mint, and
an ordinary resident reconnect never calls it, so both correctly preserve the existing
provenance.

### Staging has a third disposition

`stageDrain` reports "staged" or "nothing owed", and its callers destroy the consumer on the
second. That is only sound when the emptiness is a **fact**: an opaque recovered reservation
loses its `cpending` mapping while keeping its source identity, so an empty mapping set can
equally mean *an obligation exists and recovery could not place it*.

So there is a third answer — **no demonstrated claim, completeness unknown** — and its
disposition adds no mechanism. It installs an **empty** drain through the ordinary
construction, hold check and map installation: the builder already names an empty drain, so
the durable stays referenced and no sibling sweep can take it, and the restriction that made
this path fire already declines to ack its unclaimed sources or retire it. The next resume,
with the identifier space reconstructed, enrols the real claims or retires the drain through
its owned transition. It is reported as staged, which is what stops the destructive teardown,
and the membership removal persists alongside it in one record (I4).

Where the stream forbids draining at all, the existing immediate teardown stands and
says so.

### Where each entry point converts

UNSUBSCRIBE stages its drains **before** its record write and commits them after: the
membership removal and the drain that replaces it are one record (I4).

A QoS 0 downgrade cannot do that, and the reason is the shape of a SUBSCRIBE packet.
`sess.subs` is mutated only inside `update`, which for a SUBSCRIBE runs at the **final**
save — so a downgrade that moved `cons[sid]` into `drains[sid]` at its filter's own
staging would leave any mid-packet write (a later shared filter's early membership
persist) describing a positive-QoS membership with no consumer and a drain, a shape that
does not otherwise exist. Resume reconciliation collects every positive-QoS membership
and mints a fresh durable for one whose `cons` entry is absent, so restarting from such a
record would put a **second** durable on the filter alongside the restored drain.

So the conversion runs at the **final-update boundary**, inside the same `sess.mu`
section that applies the membership and before the save that carries both. Four things
about it, and each is load-bearing:

- **The not-yet-transmitted allocations are cancelled at the filter's staging**, not at
  the conversion. The delivery barrier does not stop a callback that is already past it:
  the send gate tests the pending entry's registration state and never `sub.mqtt.closed`,
  so an allocation whose register store is still in flight would otherwise confirm and
  transmit under a membership the packet has removed.
- **The transmitted registers are NOT voided** for a consumer that will convert. A void
  says "never transmitted", and those exchanges are the ones being preserved — any save
  in the packet would make the lie durable, and unvoiding afterwards cannot retract what
  a save already stored. Where the conversion is refused instead, the void runs at the
  boundary so its verdicts ride the same record.
- **The durable's live withheld markers are transferred around `stageDrain`.** It owns
  `sess.deferred` for its durable: it drops every entry and re-installs only the
  cancellations it discovered itself, so a marker whose sequence the earlier cancellation
  already removed — and a marker for a delivery withheld at the in-flight **cap**, which
  never had a registration at all — would be destroyed. A marker is what makes a later
  *first* transmission carry DUP=0, so the boundary snapshots the durable's live set
  before the call and re-installs it after, merging it into the drain's own set so a
  commit retires it and a rollback keeps it. The **live map** is the source, never a
  packet descriptor's history: history is neither complete nor attributable to the
  occurrence that converts, and a marker already consumed is absent from the live map and
  so cannot be wrongly resurrected.
- **A definite save failure un-converts before the rollback enumerates.** The rollback
  discovers the consumers the packet created by walking `sess.cons`, so a converted one
  has left that map; putting it back first is what lets the existing classification see
  it as pre-packet, as packet-created, or as an adopted drain and act correctly for each.

The confirmation is one operation, reached inline or from the resolver: it commits the
drains, reopens the delivery the staging closed — the delivery callback tests
`sub.mqtt.closed` *before* it looks for a drain, so a drain whose subscription stays
closed can never retransmit. (It used to clear the per-consumer inactivity timers too; F-105
creates these consumers with none.) An ambiguous
write keeps the drain **staged** and its barrier **closed** until those exact bytes are
proven durable, with the operation registered as a landed continuation; a forked verdict
discards it, because a continuation's premise is that its write landed. A **detached**
client at that point reopens nothing and is normal, not an anomaly: an ambiguous write can
stay unresolved while its connection closes, and the surviving drain takes its source
interest from the ordinary resume instead.

**A downgrade that is NOT converted gives up its `cons` entry at the same boundary**, and
for the same reason the conversion is there: the membership and the consumer reference are
one fact, so the record that carries `Subs` at QoS 0 must not still name a durable the same
packet is about to delete. `releaseDowngradedConsumersLocked` runs one step after the
conversion, over the same descriptors, and it deliberately does **not** require
`dd.convert` — a stream inactivity limit stops a descriptor from ever being offered to the
conversion, and that is precisely the route that must be released. It skips a converted,
revoked or replaced descriptor, and a membership that is **absent** rather than zero, which
is UNSUBSCRIBE's path. `dd.cc` already carries the config the teardown needs, so nothing
is re-homed and no third map exists.

Three things make it safe, and each is the counterpart of a conversion rule:

- **A mid-packet write still carries the pre-packet pair.** `sess.subs` moves only inside
  `update`, so a save issued before the final one sees the positive QoS *and* the consumer,
  which is the honest state until the membership changes.
- **The `inLock` hook reports the release**, so the record is written even when the
  membership did not change — a QoS 0 re-SUBSCRIBE over a filter already at QoS 0 that still
  holds a `cons` entry changes nothing else, and without this the entry would leave memory
  while the record kept naming it.
- **A definite save failure un-releases before the rollback enumerates.** The rollback
  restores `sess.cons` wholesale from the pre-packet snapshot, which covers every entry that
  predates the packet; what it cannot recover is a consumer this packet **created** and then
  downgraded, because it finds those by walking `sess.cons`. The un-release fills only an
  absent sid, since recording that we removed an entry does not prove nothing was installed
  there since.

**A released durable's `MaxAckPending` charge comes back at the resolution**, on the one arm
where nothing else gives it: an ambiguous save that proves landed runs a refund-only
continuation for every durable the boundary released. The teardown is what normally refunds,
and that arm never reaches it; the retirement that eventually deletes the durable
(below) is not this packet's and refunds nothing. Refund and nothing else — no `Cons`
entry returns, because re-persisting one under the QoS 0 membership is this item's defect,
and the delete stays the retirement owner's because it needs a disposal decision, a
JetStream round trip and a classified result while the refund is memory-only and
idempotent. The charge is honest to give back: the delivery subscription stayed closed on
that arm, so the orphaned durable holds no in-flight budget the client could spend.

**What this gives up is stated in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`, not claimed away.** Between the
confirmed save and the teardown the durable is named by neither the record nor `sess.cons`,
but its name still stands LIVE: nothing has decided its end. No orphan sweep — on this
broker or on a peer, whose sparing pass cannot see another broker's residents — deletes a
durable whose name is not RETIRED, so the window is withheld rather than raced. The pending
teardown records the disposal decision and the retirement owner retires the name and
deletes the durable; a delayed CREATE after that is a RETIRED-name orphan the sweep reaps.
The safety criterion is a descriptor's **current disposition, not its ancestry** — an
adopted durable downgraded again later reaches the release like any other — and a
*drained* or *adopted* durable must stay NAMED, because a consumer nothing names is what a
later tenure's settlement decides to retire, and its started exchanges would go with it.
That is what keeps `Drains` in the record and why the builder's `Cons` predicate is
membership **presence** rather than positive QoS. A positive-QoS predicate would omit a
durable an adoption has just moved into `cons` while the membership is still at the
pre-packet QoS 0, leaving it named nowhere with a started exchange inside it.

On the ambiguous-landed arm no teardown runs, so nothing decides the consumer's end and its
name stays LIVE: no sweep reaps it. Convergence is the session's **next accepted tenure**,
on any broker (`outbound_tenure_settle.go`): its settlement decides a source consumer
provisioned under a tenure that no longer serves and named by nothing the serving tenure
holds, and the retirement owner retires it. That is demonstrated as far as a broker that is
gone: the cross-broker fixtures stop the owning broker, await its shutdown lifecycle to
completion, and resume on the peer. A session that never resumes keeps the durable until
its end discards the generation. The owner's own shutdown does not delete the durable
either, and the reason is narrow rather than flattering — its drain walks live *clients*
(`drainClients`), and the periodic passes over `as.sessions` stop with `quitCh`, so an
**unbound** session's consumers are reached by nothing in that lifecycle. The assertion
is a regression barrier over that fact, not evidence about the release. An abrupt
process death is not constructible in the harness and nothing is claimed for it.

Recovery is positive, never an inference from absence. Because the phase is
memory-only, a restart would otherwise establish source interest and resend the
payload of an exchange already past PUBREC — before the correlated PUBREL callback
ever ran. So a barrier runs **before any source interest exists**: it reads the
persisted intent, indexes the PUBREL records still on the session's subject (they
are unacked, hence incomplete), and resolves each claim. Intent with a record →
confirmed. Intent without one → recreate it under the *original* identifier,
having first verified the PUBREL durable exists and then checking **presence at
the returned sequence** rather than trusting the store response. A missing record
can never mean "already completed", because the callback removes claim and intent
before forwarding. No intent → the client provably never PUBREC'd durably, so the
payload is redelivered with DUP and the exchange completes. Any failure withholds
that drain's source interest for the connection rather than denying the CONNECT.

A stored PUBREL names its source (`Nmqtt-Q2SrcDur` / `Nmqtt-Q2SrcSeq`), which is
what links it back after a restart — `cpending` is memory-only. A **drained**
PUBREL additionally carries a deduplication identity scoped by an attempt counter,
so a superseded broker's late store collapses into it; the ordinary path
deliberately carries none, because there the only legitimate re-store is the
post-restart one after a redelivery, and a surviving dedupe entry would silently
swallow it.

### A CONNECT restore is the third entry point

A session record can carry `Subs[f]` at **QoS 0** while `Cons[f]` still names a durable
holding unacknowledged QoS 1/2 exchanges — the pair a failed drain adoption leaves behind.
Resume reconciliation collects **positive-QoS** memberships only, so such an entry is never
verified and no phase-owned delivery subscription is installed for it; the restore therefore
reached `processJSConsumer`'s existing-consumer arm and deleted the durable **inline**,
taking its started deliveries with it on an interest-retained stream. Neither of the other
two entry points reaches this: UNSUBSCRIBE and the QoS 0 downgrade both run inside a
SUBSCRIBE-shaped packet, and the restore has no packet transaction, no membership change and
no final update to convert at.

So the restore has a boundary of its own, `settleRestoredDowngrades`, and three things about
it are load-bearing:

- **The deferral moved into `processJSConsumer` for both paths.** Its QoS 0 arm no longer
  branches on `fromSubProto`; it returns the descriptor and deletes nothing, because there
  is no point inside that function at which the conversion could be made durable first.
  `processSubs`' staging call was already path-independent, so the restore inherits the
  whole descriptor machinery — the delivery barrier, the cancellations, the per-packet
  `drainingAllowed` check and the per-filter cancellation — rather than growing a parallel
  one.
- **The save exists solely to move the durable from `Cons` to `Drains`.** The record already
  says QoS 0, so `updateWithDetailConverting` is called with no filters and the `inLock`
  hook's return is the only thing that decides whether anything is written. It writes
  whenever any descriptor reached the boundary: a *destructive* one still needs the record
  to stop naming a durable the restore is about to delete.
- **The conversion is atomic under `sess.mu`, and the record transaction spans the rest.**
  The hook moves the entry between the maps in one critical section, so no reader sees the
  durable in neither; `sess.mu` is then released before the save, but the accept
  transaction is still held, so no other local writer can serialize the session. The
  staging step before it leaves `cons[sid]` in place, so anything serialized there names the
  durable in `Cons`. That continuity is the whole protection against a peer's orphan sweep,
  which spares only sessions resident on the sweeping broker and keys eligibility on the
  consumer's creation time.

The three save outcomes mirror the live path's, with one difference: the confirmed arm does
**not** reopen a delivery, because this path closed none. `restoreDrains` installs the
converted drain's source interest later, after the accept transaction is released, treating
it exactly as it treats a record-restored drain. An ambiguous save keeps the drains
**staged** and registers the completion as a landed continuation — which matters more here
than on the live path, because a refused CONNECT does **not** evict a persistent
session, so the resolver may settle the attempt on the very object that stays resident.

**A conversion already proven durable is never rolled back by a later step's failure.** The
restore can still refuse after this boundary — a cleanup write's CAS rejection, the shared
ownership arbitration, the requested-lifetime save, the CONNACK write, the 3.1.1 forced
leave — and none of them undoes it, because the conversion is a fact about the record rather
than about this connection and the client's exchanges are owed either way. What this does
*not* claim is that the exchange therefore always completes later: a foreign or forked
disposal, ordinary expiry, a granted zero lifetime or a legitimate sibling teardown are all
subsequent authoritative transitions, and none is compensated for here.

The restore now also **reads** its own `recordCASRejected`, which nothing on that path did
before it wrote records. A rejection says this broker may no longer speak for the record —
not that a successor exists, which neither `10071` nor `10164` establishes alone — so the
disposition is to refuse the resume, not to dispose of anything.

#### A drain whose membership is QoS 0 still has to retransmit

The converted drain keeps `d.qos == 0`, which is the honest value: it has no subscription,
because its membership is QoS 0. Nothing is derived and nothing invented — a drain-wide
maximum would apply one exchange's QoS to another, and persisting it leaves a value no later
resume revisits. Three per-exchange rules replace it.

- **The first-transmission gate does not apply to a claimed drained sequence.**
  `min(published, granted)` decides whether *this* callback owns a first delivery at
  all; a claimed sequence completes one already on the wire, which [MQTT-3.10.4-3] owes.
  The wire QoS comes from the entry in the send section, as it does for every other
  retransmission.
- **No exchange QoS, no retransmission — refused before allocation.** Where a claimed
  sequence on such a drain has no identity-matched pending entry carrying a nonzero QoS,
  the callback withholds without acknowledging, releasing or unclaiming anything. The send
  section's existing zero-QoS arm would refuse it anyway; refusing earlier costs no packet
  identifier and stores no QoS-0 register. It is confined to `qos == 0`: a positive-QoS
  drain reaching the same state has its own grant to register at, and withholding there
  would strand a claim nothing can rebuild.
- **No Local does not suppress a claimed drained sequence.** That arm *acknowledges the
  source*, so applying a grant the exchange did not start under destroys the message and
  leaves the claim standing. Two grants can differ: a converted drain has no original value,
  and a live re-SUBSCRIBE can turn the option on before a later UNSUBSCRIBE stages a drain
  over exchanges started without it.

Missing evidence is deliberately **not** read as proof that the exchange completed. Two
states produce it with no client acknowledgement at all — the window in which PUBREC has
removed the PUBLISH entry but not yet recorded the drain intent, and a marker-opaque
reservation recovery installed without a `cpending` mapping — so settling there would
destroy an unfinished exchange. The retention this leaves is stated in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`
and has no automatic repair.

**A drain's `subject` is its durable's filter subject, not its delivery inbox.** All three
stagers derive it from `cc.FilterSubject`. They used to copy `sub.subject`, which for a
QoS 1/2 delivery subscription is the `$MQTT.sub.<nuid>` inbox, so
`isMQTTReservedSubscription` was computed over an inbox and a resumed drain of a `#`, `*`
or `*.>` filter lost its reserved marking ([MQTT-4.7.2-1]). The restore's conversion has no
subscription to copy from at all, which is what surfaced it.

### Retirement and disposal

Retirement is what ends a drain once it claims nothing, and it is deliberately two
halves: a critical section that issues nothing, and a request that is *classified*
rather than assumed.

**One critical section, and the delivery barrier goes on WITH the map drop.** Under a
single `sess.mu` hold, `retireDrainLocked` proves the drain still owns its sid, marks
the object retired, sets `sub.mqtt.closed` on its delivery subscription, and drops
both drain maps. The ordering is the repair, not decoration: a delivery callback
dispatched before retirement re-checks `closed` and only *then* looks its drain up,
both under one acquisition of that same lock, so no interleaving can observe
`closed == false` together with an absent drain. Unsubscribing alone does not reach
such a callback — it removes the subscription from `c.subs` while the `*subscription`
the callback already holds stays valid — which is why the deferred consumer delete
and the shared-group teardown both set that flag *in addition to* unsubscribing.
Without the barrier the callback falls through to ordinary PUBLISH processing and
retransmits a past-PUBREC source under a fresh packet identifier.

**A terminal per-object flag, at the insertion boundaries.** `retired` is never
cleared: clearing it once a delete looked slow is the design in which a late delete
destroys a consumer that has come back into service. Four routes could otherwise
hand the same `*mqttDrain` back to the session, and each consults the flag under
`sess.mu`: the SUBSCRIBE rollback (which restores from a **shallow** snapshot, so a
flag set after the snapshot is visible through it — the property a post-hoc ownership
check cannot have, because the resurrection arrives through a snapshot taken
*earlier*), the resume's per-item restore, and the two-map re-insertion helper (a
fourth, the inactivity-timer clear, was deleted with the timers). The rollback restores
**each map's own entries** and does not
derive one from the other: the two legitimately disagree, because a failed
delivery-subscription restore deletes the reverse entry while the sid mapping
survives, and that absence is a deliberate rollback rather than a gap to fill.
Adoption and the delivery reclaim need no guard — both read `sess.drains[sid]`, which
retirement empties under the same lock — and a fresh SUBSCRIBE mints a new nuid
durable, so it can never name a retired one.

**A disposal decision, not a delete (F-105 7c-lc).** The drain is out of both maps, out
of the record and terminally retired, and its confirmed omission is the decision that its
consumer is ended. It no longer deletes the consumer: an obligation it no longer claims
may still hold it, and the drain hands the decision to the session's retirement owner
(see "The source consumer's lifecycle" in the outbound obligation authority chapter),
which retires the name and performs the classified delete once nothing holds it. The
decision is recorded under the entitlement of the connection whose transaction set the
removal mark, carried on the drain beside the mark; a decision with no accepted
entitlement is not recorded and the consumer is left for recovery, never deleted raw. A
crash anywhere after the omission leaves an unreferenced durable whose resource the
recovery executor retires once its generation is discarded (7d), and which a still-serving
generation's next accepted tenure decides `tenure-superseded` (7f) — the plain orphan sweep
no longer deletes a consumer on the strength of no record naming it.

**Where the hand-off runs.** The hand-off issues no request, but the retained
continuations, which run under the uncertain-write resolver's open transaction, still
queue it, carrying `{durable, entitlement}`, so the order of decisions and the release
boundary stay what they were. The queue is **detached
inside** `endRecordTxLocked`'s critical section and executed after the unlock, on the
releasing goroutine — detaching after the unlock would let one releaser issue a later
transaction's work and strand its own. It runs after the void-verdict handoff, so a
persistence attempt a stager is already owed is not delayed by a timeout per queued
drain. A refused release — an invalid token, or a non-owner — returns before the
detach, so the batch is carried to the next successful release rather than dropped,
and `clear()` discards it with the rest of the generation's state.

**The charge follows the proof.** A drain removed by reconciliation's consumer-absent
arm never reaches retirement, so its local consumer charge is refunded when the
save is *proven landed* — in the immediate arm and in the retained continuation
alike, through one helper. Not at the drop: a definitely failed save restores the
object still charged, so there would be nothing to re-charge.

**What the guarantee covers.** Once retirement has run, this drain **object** can
never again deliver to this session and can never be handed back to it, for the
lifetime of this **resident session object**. Not "one incarnation": a record restore
builds a new session object while preserving the generation, so a fork sibling's
record that still names the drain can rebuild it on a fresh object, which no
per-object flag reaches. `docs/CONFORMANCE.md` states that residual; the two others it
used to carry — an indeterminate delete and an inactivity-clear create in flight — went
with the inline delete and the timers.

## Plain QoS 1/2 consumer reconciliation on resume

The session record persists each plain QoS 1/2 subscription's JetStream consumer
config (`Cons`), and the CONNECT restore path used to trust it verbatim: a
durable reaped by an inactivity threshold — a stream-forced
`ConsumerLimits.InactiveThreshold` on `$MQTT_msgs`, which reaches consumers
requesting 0 (since F-105 the broker itself requests none for these consumers) — or
deleted out of band was silently restored, and the client got
Session
Present = 1 with a subscription that never delivered again until a clean start.

The fix is a dedicated resume phase (`sess_resume_reconcile.go`), run inside the
CONNECT's accept transaction **after** register recovery (so every in-flight
register is classified against the *old* durable names before any repair
exists) and **before** the CONNACK (so a failure refuses the CONNECT and
nothing has been transmitted when it fails). It is deliberately CONNECT-only:
repairing inside SUBSCRIBE processing would make every record-write site in
that thicket replacement-aware, and the packet's final update may legitimately
not write at all. Placing the repair before the CONNACK makes its save the
first record write after the accept save *by construction* — no general
subscription-processing write can observe a half-committed replacement.

The pass:

1. **Collect.** Every plain (non-shared) QoS 1/2 filter's `(subject, sid)`
   pairs from the restored subscriptions — the level-up companion of a
   multi-level filter included, since it is an independent consumer. A QoS 1/2
   sid with **no** `Cons` entry at all is classified *absent identity* and
   minted here (left alone, restoration would create its consumer later in the
   resume and never persist it: the restore path runs no final subscription
   save). No filter here can be in the reserved `$MQTT.>` namespace: such a
   record is refused at restore, and a resident session could never have
   subscribed to one. A stale `Cons` entry with **no** matching subscription is not an active
   delivery entry and is deliberately not verified (a stated residual in
   `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`). A membership at **QoS 0** carries no `Cons` entry where its
   consumer was *destroyed*, because the downgrade releases the reference at its packet's
   final-update boundary — so this pass's QoS 0 skip and the record agree by construction
   rather than by coincidence. Where such a membership *does* carry an entry the durable is
   **live and owed** — an adoption mid-packet, or one a failed filter left behind — and it
   is named on purpose.
2. **Subscribe everything closed, then batch-verify.** Before any lookup, a
   **closed, flushed** delivery subscription is installed on every recorded
   deliver subject, marked *phase-owned* — for present consumers too, because a
   consumer that is present at lookup can be reaped a moment later (the lookup
   does not stop the inactivity timer), and its dead recorded deliver subject
   would then be restored: the original bug, reproduced. The flush is what
   makes the interest authoritative before the lookup result means anything.
   It **narrows** that window rather than closing it outright: JetStream checks
   a consumer's activity, releases its lock, and only then performs the
   deletion, so interest that registers after the decision cannot revoke it
   while `ConsumerInfo` still reports the consumer present. A consumer reaped
   inside that last gap is trusted for this connection and repaired at the next
   CONNECT — the same disposition as any other out-of-band deletion, and a
   bounded fraction of the original defect, which persisted until a clean
   start.
   Installing interest this early means JetStream immediately pushes the
   session's whole **offline backlog** into a window in which nothing may be
   transmitted yet, so a QoS 1/2 delivery arriving there **waits** on the
   subscription's *phase gate* rather than being dropped: dropping it would
   hold every queued message until AckWait (30s by default) — turning an
   immediate resume delivery into a half-minute stall — and then re-send it
   with DUP set on its **first** transmission to the client. Waiting keeps the
   backlog first deliveries, in order, at adoption speed. The wait is bounded
   by the connection's effective **AckWait** (capped by
   `mqttPhaseGateWaitMax`), which is the deadline past which waiting buys
   nothing because JetStream re-pushes the message anyway, and which also stops
   a CONNECT that died without releasing — every ordinary exit releases, so
   that means a panic — from parking a delivery goroutine. A delivery that does
   run out its wait, or that belongs to a filter the sweep reclaims unadopted,
   is **recorded as withheld** exactly as an in-flight-cap deferral is, so the
   attempt that finally goes out is still marked a first transmission
   ([MQTT-3.3.1-1]) and a freed slot can NAK it forward instead of waiting out
   AckWait. Its position in the stream's order is not preserved, which is the
   ordinary consequence of any redelivery and is recorded as a residual.
   Then one bounded, batched `lookupConsumersMulti` pass resolves every
   collected durable: **present** (the closed subscription holds its interest),
   **absent** (authoritatively gone → repair), or **indeterminate** (a
   transport failure or unreadable entry → **refuse the CONNECT**; a session
   resumed with silently dead subscriptions is the bug this phase exists to
   fix, and nothing is ever recreated over a consumer that may still exist).
3. **Repair, under a fresh identity.** Recreation never reuses the recorded
   durable name, because that name is an identity to two mechanisms: an
   in-flight register naming `(dur X, seq N)` classifies *Lost* while X is
   authoritatively absent (a POSSIBLY-ATTEMPTED identifier is then reserved —
   the safe direction; a proven-unsent one is released on its marker, which is
   safe in either classification) but flips to a false *Complete* if a new
   instance of X reaches `AckFloor.Stream >= N`, freeing identifiers the client
   may still hold; and recorded `$JS.ACK`/NAK
   subjects embed the consumer name with per-instance counters. So the repair
   mints a fresh nuid durable and deliver subject, subscribes it closed
   **first** (interest exists before the consumer, so the replacement cannot be
   reaped in the create-to-subscribe gap), retires the stale charge
   (`refundConsumerChargeLocked` — permanently: it named a consumer that no
   longer exists, so no failure path re-adds it), creates the durable
   `DeliverNew`, charges the replacement, and replaces the session's `cons`
   entry. Any failure undoes exactly the phase's own work — phase subscriptions
   removed, created durables deleted (refunded exactly once), replaced entries
   restored **uncharged** — and refuses the CONNECT.
4. **One repair save, still pre-CONNACK.** Ownership is revalidated by the CAS
   at that instant — there is no lease. The two wrong-last-sequence kinds are
   deliberately not equivalent, and the raw store error is captured at the
   store boundary (`saveWithDetail`) because `save()`'s formatting destroys the
   kind: **10071** (the single-writer check) means the subject MOVED after our
   accept save — which is weaker than a takeover, and F-084 owns the gap — and is disposed
   through `disposeForeignSessionLocked` in a DISCONNECT-suppressing mode (no
   success CONNACK was written, so no packet may precede one). **10164**
   (clustered contention) is a rejection, never a verdict: a bounded re-read
   loop retries the **identical** base sequence and body bytes while the record
   provably has not moved, adopts the landed sequence when the re-read finds
   our exact bytes at a newer one (the response was lost to contention), turns
   a moved record into the foreign disposition, and turns an unreadable re-read
   into an explicitly established pending-write state — a CAS rejection is
   definite, so `save()` deliberately does not mark it uncertain, and the phase
   must do so itself for the deferred settlement to classify or re-attempt anything. An
   **ambiguous** save refuses the CONNECT with the replacements KEPT: the
   settlement re-attempts the phase's own bytes, so the record ends up naming
   them and the next resume verifies them present — nothing further is owed, so
   no continuation is registered. Resolution is
   necessarily deferred — the accept transaction is still open — and no traffic
   is served meanwhile: no SUCCESS CONNACK was sent — a failure CONNACK carrying
   0x83 and the phase's own diagnostic is, which opens nothing — and every phase
   subscription is closed.
5. **Adopt in place.** Subscription restoration — which runs BEFORE the CONNACK
   (F-050) and after this phase — reaches each
   collected filter through `processJSConsumer`'s restore exists-branch, which
   — on finding a phase-owned delivery subscription — refreshes the MQTT
   metadata and clears the closed flag and the marker **on the same
   subscription object**, under the same dual-lock write the re-SUBSCRIBE
   refresh uses. Re-issuing it through `processSub` would unsubscribe the old
   subscription and install a new one, putting a no-interest gap right back
   into the flow — the exact stream-forced inactivity race the subscribe-first
   rule closes. The phase gate is released last, in the same critical section,
   so every delivery parked on it wakes, re-reads the fields just written, and
   goes out under this filter's live options.
6. **Sweep what restoration did not adopt** — and note that F-050 emptied this
   step's population. It was written for a filter restoration skipped *after* the
   CONNACK while the connection stayed live, which nothing else would ever
   reclaim: the subscription would sit closed forever holding consumer interest,
   and a later re-SUBSCRIBE's metadata refresh does not clear `closed`. **That
   state is no longer reachable for a supported record.** Restoration now runs
   before the CONNACK and a filter it cannot install refuses the CONNECT, so an
   unadopted collected filter always ends in a refusal and a teardown rather than
   a live connection. The sweep is retained as the reclaimer of last resort — it
   still runs immediately after `processSubs`, before its error is tested, with an
   idempotent deferred fallback for the exits that never reach it — but it is now
   belt-and-braces rather than the only thing standing between a skipped filter
   and permanent dead interest. The phase's own `undo` is unaffected and remains
   live. Every reclamation path releases the gate **before** unsubscribing, so a
   parked delivery wakes, finds the subscription still closed, and skips instead
   of waiting out the bound.

## Shared group durables are verified on resume, not assumed

The plain reconciliation above deliberately covers only plain filters. Its collect step
says shared subscriptions "live in `SharedSubs` and their group durables have their own
machinery" — and until F-076 that machinery did not exist. This section is it.

`processSharedJSConsumer` has three arms. A re-SUBSCRIBE with a live delivery subscription
refreshes the mutable per-subscription fields. A filter with **no resident `cons` entry**
joins: it creates the group durable, which proves it. Between them sat a fall-through for
a resident entry with no live subscription — a session resume on a new connection — which
subscribed to the recorded deliver subject on the strength of a configuration remembered
from an earlier connection, and proved nothing.

That is the ordinary same-broker reconnect, not an edge case. Shared consumer configs are
**never persisted** (`buildPersistedSessionLocked` skips every entry whose `DeliverGroup`
is non-empty, because `SharedSubs` is the sole authority), so a session rebuilt from its
record has no shared `cons` entry at all and takes the join path. A resident `cons` entry
therefore means the session object survived in this process. If the group durable had been
deleted meanwhile — the orphan sweep's grace window, an operator — the client was told
Session Present = 1 and handed a live subscription on a subject nothing publishes to,
silently.

**Two batched passes, around `processSubs`.** A pre-pass collects exactly the shared sids
with a resident entry — derivable before restoration runs, since the sid is the filter's
session key and the level-up companion follows the same rule `processSubs` applies — and
resolves them through `lookupConsumersMulti` in **bounded chunks** of
`mqttInflightLoadBatch`, the same cap every other resume-time batch here uses. The bound is
a correctness property, not tuning: a session's shared filter count is client-controlled,
each lookup carries its own timeout, and an indeterminate verdict refuses — so one
unbounded request would let a single lost response fail a large session closed on every
reconnect. For the same reason the **first** chunk-level failure stops the pass and marks
every unresolved target indeterminate rather than paying a timeout per remaining chunk:
one indeterminate filter already refuses the CONNECT, so continuing cannot rescue it, and
in the post-pass the stall would run while this connection's queue interest is already
