installed and dropping QoS 0 deliveries. The resume arm then acts on its verdict
**before** subscribing, which keeps the join path's own rule that a group durable must not
deliver to a member until the join is proven.

A post-pass runs after `processSubs` returns, after its phase-sub sweep, and immediately
before the per-filter aggregation. It repeats the **full** classification rather than a
presence check, because a consumer can be deleted *or altered* between the two readings,
and it adopts the second one — a member-variable field may legitimately have moved. A
filter that regresses is marked failed and refused by the restore gate's existing
aggregation, so there is one refusal path rather than two.

**Four outcomes, and the distinctions are the mechanism.** *Present and canonical* adopts
a clone of the live configuration in place of the remembered one. *Present and not canonical*
refuses, and neither updates nor deletes: the durable may be serving other members, and a
configuration this broker would not have built is not one it may normalize on their behalf.
*Authoritatively absent* is **repairable** — the durable provably is not there, so the next
section recreates it and arbitrates the membership it is recreated into. *Indeterminate* —
a failed read, a reply carrying no consumer, a consumer carrying no configuration — refuses,
and is kept distinct from absence precisely because recreating on an unproven absence turns
one broker's transient error into a group-wide change. That distinction was the reason to
keep the two verdicts apart before anything acted on either, and it is what now decides
which one may be acted on.

**Validation is whole-struct and closed by construction.** Every `ConsumerConfig` field
carries exactly one disposition, enforced by a reflection bijection, because a list of
fields worth checking cannot close a struct a dependency bump can extend — the same
reasoning the affine path records. Three fields are legitimately variable across members
and are bounded rather than ignored; two are server-normalized and compared against an
**expected value** rather than accepted from the live consumer, since copying `MaxDeliver`
would admit a durable that discards a delivery after one attempt; one, `Metadata`, is
server-**owned**, its content moving with the dependency, and is constrained instead by
requiring it to carry nothing but the three named server keys. A test measures the
normalized set against a real create, so the expected values are observed rather than
remembered.

**What this establishes is CONFIGURATION evidence, never OWNERSHIP evidence.** A present
canonical durable does not prove this broker still owns the membership the restore is keyed
on. That is a separate fact needing a separate instrument, and the next section is it: on
the CONNECT path every restoration of shared interest — whether it created, repaired or
merely adopted — now proves ownership with a classified record write before the CONNACK. On
the **live SUBSCRIBE** path is arbitrated by its own packet-scoped gate and the same
classified proof (F-078, below).

The window is narrowed, not closed: `CONSUMER.DELETE` and `CONSUMER.CREATE` are
unconditioned, so a durable deleted or altered after the post-pass gets no further check on
that CONNECT. Self-repair now exists for exactly one verdict — an authoritative absence is
recreated — while a non-canonical or unreadable durable still goes on refusing until the
condition clears by any means. All of it is recorded in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`.

A record carrying a shared group consumer configuration in `Cons` is a shape this broker
never writes, and is **refused** at every ingress that reads one rather than accommodated:
the CONNECT restore prologue, record-driven expiry, the session-expiry sweep, the
orphan-consumer sweep, and the shared record validator. The same refusal meets a record whose
`shared_subs` values are the pre-transfer numeric QoS rather than a membership carrying
acquisition references. The refusals divide by what each one protects. The two **expiry**
paths would claim, rewrite and delete the record, normalizing a format nothing here
understands, so they refuse to act on it — the session-expiry sweep only once the record is
otherwise eligible for expiry processing, since a zero or never-expiring interval ends that
pass before the shape is reached. The **delete-by-absence** reader decides what to destroy
from the absence of a reference across the whole record set, so for it a partial view must
never be reported as a complete one: the orphan-consumer sweep **aborts** its pass rather
than skipping. (The last-holder scan, which used to be the second such reader, no longer
exists: a group durable's deletion is now authorized by the group record's arbitrated count,
"A group durable is held by arbitration, not counted by a scan", below.)

## A restored shared membership is arbitrated against the record

The verification above establishes what a group durable *is*. It establishes nothing about
whether this broker still *owns* the membership being restored into it, and those are
different facts needing different instruments. This section is the second one, for the
CONNECT/resume path.

**The finding (F-077).** Broker A holds a resident session with a shared membership. B
accepts a newer CONNECT for the same client ID, its path removes the membership — a 3.1.1
forced leave, an UNSUBSCRIBE, or `clear()` — and B's release retires the group durable (at
the time, by the last-holder scan; now by releasing the group's last acquisition). A restores
that membership anyway and serves the group. "Serves" includes
**acknowledging**: the QoS 1/2 delivery callback acks and drops on a reserved-subject
violation, on No Local suppression, and delivers-and-acks a shared QoS 0 member. (A
subscribe deny used to belong on that list and no longer does — on the ordinary
shared group consumer it now hands the message back rather than acking it, for the
reason given under the delivery guards below. It stays terminal on the affine
shared QoS 2 route, where the copy is already one session's and no other member
can take it. The remaining entries still destroy a group message for the members
that legitimately hold the membership, which is what this section arbitrates.)

**Three routes reach it, and only two of them create anything.** A resume whose durables
all verify present-and-canonical adopts and creates nothing, yet installs delivery interest
under a membership it never revalidated. A resume whose durable is authoritatively absent
now recreates it (below). A record-sourced filter — every shared filter of a session
rebuilt from its record, since shared configs are never persisted — takes the join path and
creates. All three are arbitrated; a create-scoped rule would have covered only the last
two.

**The instrument is a classified record write, and it has to be a write.** A read cannot
arbitrate: JetStream returns 10164 from the clustered pre-proposal check while a write for
the subject is in process, so "the record did not move" is not provable from a load — the
contender's proposal can commit a moment later. `proveSharedMembershipOwnership` performs
the ordinary record write under its per-subject CAS at `sess.seq`, inside the CONNECT's
still-open accept transaction, and classifies the outcome. On a resume the body is normally
the same membership that was read, so it looks like a no-op rewrite and is not one: every
write stamps a fresh `WID` and parents it to the current lineage, and the CAS is what no
read could be.

Five outcomes, and the two rejection kinds are deliberately not equivalent:

- **landed** — this broker owned the record at the write's linearization point. The only
  outcome that permits the CONNACK.
- **10071**, the single-writer check, means the subject moved after the accept save — not
  that another broker owns the session, which is the stronger claim F-084 owns. It
  disposes *without* consulting the contention resolver, so this is the only place a
  sibling lineage can be recognised on that arm: the record is read once and classified,
  which distinguishes a proven sibling from an unclassifiable stranger and mints the fork
  grant for the first only. Both classes now report `0x89`; what separates them is the
  Reason String and, decisively, the mint.
- **10164** is clustered contention rather than a lost race, and gets the bounded
  re-read/retry treatment, whose verdicts map onto the same five.
- **ambiguous** — the mutation is KEPT, no further write is permitted, and the resolver
  settles it. No SUCCESS CONNACK is written, so nothing is served meanwhile; the
  refusal itself carries 0x83 and the step's own diagnostic.
- **definite local failure** — nothing was stored; refuse.

Every refusal reuses the pre-CONNACK abort discipline, which already discards the Will and
leaves the lifetime ungranted. **No `0x8E` reaches the client**: the displacement's
DISCONNECT is gated on the CONNACK having been written, which is false for every refusal
inside the CONNECT, so no DISCONNECT is sent at all. The refusal is not silent, though —
it goes through `refuseDisposing` and carries a **failure CONNACK** whose reason code and
Reason String say what the evidence supports and no more. See "The pre-CONNACK refusal
signal", and "Only a held successor licenses a takeover claim".

**Why this path needs no transmission gate.** The restore gate is armed before the first
subscription the CONNECT installs and opens only after a confirmed success CONNACK, and
every delivery callback consults it — the QoS 0 raw subscription, the QoS 1/2 deliver
subject, and the PUBREL and affine subscriptions a shared QoS 2 filter provisions before
the group consumer exists. So nothing this connection could transmit or acknowledge escapes
the window. One caveat, which is a claim about this connection's outputs rather than about
the group: the gate stops transmission and acknowledgement but cannot undo *queue
selection*, so a shared QoS 0 message selected for this member while the gate is closed is
dropped and reaches no member at all. That is the restore gate's existing residual.

**The trigger is restored interest, and it is stack-local.** The fact that a restore
installed, repaired or adopted shared interest is raised at the sites that do it and
aggregated on the caller's stack — committed per filter only once the whole filter succeeds,
its level-up companion included. It is deliberately not a field on the session: a fact
parked there outlives the operation that raised it and would govern the next one. It is also
kept apart from two accounting facts it used to be inferred from, because each inference
was wrong in a different way. The repair creates a durable this session already holds the
`MaxAckPending` charge for, so it creates while charging nothing; a verify create gated on
the charge would skip exactly the population that just recreated a durable, and a refund
keyed on anything but this invocation's own charge would erase an earlier connection's.

**Absence is repairable; nothing else is.** The verification's four outcomes are re-cut into
one predicate — *terminal unless repairable* — with the authoritative absence as the only
repairable verdict. That is stated as a class rather than as a special case at each decision
site, because the batching seam it touches closed only when the special cases were deleted.
Repairability has to move three decisions together, and moving fewer leaves the repair
unreachable: the batch's termination, the pre-pass's filter-failure, and the resume arm's
own return. A chunk-level transport failure is not a per-target verdict and stays terminal
whatever sits around it.

The asymmetry between the two passes is the mechanism. The **pre-pass** treats absence as
repairable, so the join path recreates the durable and the ownership write then proves the
membership is still ours. The **post-pass** treats absence as terminal: a durable absent
again *after* the repair is not one this broker may create, it is one something is deleting
underneath this CONNECT.

**A durable this broker created and then lost the arbitration for is left in place**, and
that is a decision rather than an omission. Every available deletion is refuted — the
acquisition the repair materialized is the RECORD's, and after a takeover the new owner's
record names it, so releasing it here would retire an incarnation the new owner holds;
and the shared release helper refunds a historic charge and purges through an
already-rejected transaction. If the new owner does hold the membership, the durable is
what it needs. It is not inert, though: the messages stream is interest-retained so the
durable keeps interest, it can accumulate pending across the orphan sweep's grace window,
and a later joiner may receive messages published while no authoritative membership
existed. `docs/CONFORMANCE.md` states that rather than implying it away.

**What this establishes, and what it does not.** Ownership of the *record*, at the write's
linearization point — not continuously, and not the presence of the *consumer*.
`CONSUMER.CREATE` and `CONSUMER.DELETE` carry no precondition field at all, so no finite
check binds the durable's existence to the record's ownership: the durable may vanish at any
point after the last verification or write, this write included, and only the next resume
detects it. A takeover *after* a landed write is the session-record watch's and its
committed-read backstop's to converge.

**The live SUBSCRIBE path is arbitrated by the section below** (F-078). It reaches the same
interest by different routes and needs a packet-scoped transmission gate this path does not,
because the restore gate is already open on a live connection.

## A SUBSCRIBE rollback restores the shared state it attempted

`rollbackSubscribePacket` undoes a SUBSCRIBE whose final record save failed. On its
**definite-failure** arm it puts back `sess.cons`, the delivery subscriptions it closed,
the register nonces it voided and the affine QoS 2 path it unwound — and now also
`sess.sharedSubs`, `sess.rapSubs` and `sess.subIDs` for the shared keys it dropped. (The
drain maps are not part of that arm: they are put back at the reset itself, on every arm,
before the rollback's own save.)

**Why the pre-packet snapshot is not the right value.** A shared filter's membership is
persisted **eagerly, per filter, before its group consumer is created**, carrying the
acquisition references its J1 reserved, so a crash finds what to repair and a rollback finds
what to release. That means the packet has already made a separate durable attempt at the
membership under its own record CAS, and the final save's failure did not undo it. Replacing
the live map with the pre-packet snapshot therefore discards state nothing reverted, and the
next routine save from the session — the disconnect stamp, or `clear()`'s teardown — rewrites
the record **without** a member whose acquisition is still listed. Since the shared-group
lifecycle transfer that acquisition is no longer lost: the packet rollback's own record write
carries a release verdict for every acquisition the attempted membership holds outside the
pre-packet one, and the resume's reconciliation cancels any the ledger lists that the record
does not name. What the restoration below still buys is the in-memory truth on the arm where
the compensating write DEFINITELY failed.

The invariant is therefore **the local shared state as it stood immediately before the
packet's compensation** — the same sample `rollbackSharedSub` takes for a single filter,
taken for the packet. It is deliberately **not** a claim that the map equals the record's
`SharedSubs`: a CAS-rejected eager write leaves the session continuing against a record
another broker moved, which is the arbitration question and not this one's. This change
improves membership bookkeeping and **binds nothing atomically**.

**Three things are load-bearing.**

- **The capture is filtered by membership and copied.** `rapSubs` and `subIDs` are keyed by
  session key and carry plain filters too, whose state the pre-packet snapshot owns — so
  only the keys the membership names are carried. Copying a whole option map would let a
  plain filter's identifier survive a rollback that removed its subscription.
- **The restoration writes through an alias, and that is safe for a reason.** The reset
  assigns `snap.shared` into `sess.sharedSubs` **by reference**, so the restoration mutates
  the snapshot object. The survivor set is copied off `snap.shared` *before* the reset, and
  the only other reader of it — the "existed before this packet" test inside
  `finishSubscribeRollback` — is reachable only on the confirmed arm and the landed
  continuation, never on the arm that writes. The exclusion is structural, not a matter of
  timing. Do not "simplify" the survivor set to read the live map.
- **The definite arm only.** On an ambiguous rollback the rolled-back record may be exactly
  what is stored and the resolver settles it forward by re-attempting those bytes, so the
  rolled-back view must stand. Restoring there would also write into the map that the
  "existed before" test consults from the resolver, and could leave a raw subscription the
  packet *added* installed as though it predated the packet.

**Ordering.** The restoration runs last in the definite arm, after the affine unwind, so a
shared QoS 2 membership is never in memory without its affine generation — the pairing a
record-shape validator refuses. Both restorations are synchronous and neither saves.

**What it does not fix, and what has since been fixed elsewhere.** At the time this
landed, group durables stayed unreclaimable across every crash window: the release ran
after record removal, an indeterminate last-holder scan failed closed, and the scan and
the delete were separate operations. The shared-group lifecycle transfer closed all three
— a release is a verdict in the record executed against the group record's count, the
closing seals before it releases and releases before the record goes, and there is no
scan. What this section removes is the one window where the broker *itself* destroyed the
membership evidence with a routine save.

## A live SUBSCRIBE arbitrates its shared interest before it serves

The section above proves ownership for the CONNECT/resume path. A live SUBSCRIBE reaches the
same interest and, until F-078, revalidated nothing — so the consequence above was reachable
on a connection that was never restoring at all. Three routes get there: the `!exists`
create and its post-subscribe verify `CreateOrUpdate`; the resume fall-through, reached with
nil verdicts on a live SUBSCRIBE, so it subscribes on a remembered config having verified
nothing; and the **refresh** arm,
which revives delivery interest on an existing subscription by updating its mutable fields.
All three are the same fact — *interest was touched* — which is why the trigger is that
rather than "a durable was created".

**The instrument is the same classified record write**, reused unchanged, under the packet's
own record transaction and placed after the packet's final save and its optional affine
unwind, so it is the last record write of the packet and its CAS linearizes where the packet
left the record.

**When it runs is a wider question than the trigger.** The gate opens without a proof only
for a packet that committed no trigger **and** none of whose record writes was rejected by
its per-subject CAS. The second half is load-bearing and not obvious: the early per-filter
membership save converts a definite rejection into a per-filter failure code and
continues, so a record that demonstrably *moved* leaves both the trigger and the returned
error empty. Three further writes lose the same evidence — the affine provisioning save,
the affine unwind, and the void-register verdict store, the last reached through two
chains and through the failed-filter cleanup as well. A packet-local fact records them;
the rejection marker they arm is only consulted before the *next* inbound packet, which is
far too late for a delivery callback already running.

**A CAS rejection, and nothing else, raises the question.** The distinction is evidential,
and not cosmetic: a CAS rejection means the expected-sequence write was *refused*, which
is positive evidence the subject moved; a definite local failure moved nothing and
re-authorised nothing; and an ambiguous write is this broker's own bytes maybe-landing,
which if they landed landed under its own CAS. Treating any failure as evidence turns an
ordinary per-filter failure into a connection-level refusal, which is a contract the
affine paths own rather than this one. The fact is read from the store-boundary detail,
because the outward error is reformatted and loses its identity, and because the
definite-failure classification deliberately merges a CAS rejection with a local failure
and a refused transaction.

**An AMBIGUOUS write does not withhold the gate either, and that ordering is deliberate.**
The quiet check precedes the unresolved-write check, so a packet whose ancillary save went
ambiguous opens the gate while the session still carries that write — and an unresolved
write is an outcome nobody *read*, so it includes "CAS-rejected, response lost". It stands
because a quiet packet installed **nothing**: with no trigger, no shared interest was
created or revived, so the open releases only traffic backed by interest that *predates* the
packet.
Withholding it would give one packet type a stronger delivery guarantee than this broker
provides for any other ambiguous record write, and it would turn an ambiguous affine
provisioning failure into a connection-level refusal — the contract the affine paths own,
which the wider trigger predicate already broke once. The read loop does attempt resolution
synchronously before the failure SUBACK is enqueued, but that attempt can itself return
unresolved, so the exposure is stated as a residual rather than as a bounded window.

**The transmission gate.** Armed before the packet installs anything — before the PUBREL and
affine subscriptions a shared QoS 2 filter provisions — and resolved exactly once through
a defer, so an error path or an abnormal unwind cannot leave it pending. It is scoped to the
connection that armed it *and* to a per-session generation: the first stops an abandoned
verdict crossing into the next connection, the second stops a waiter that watched one packet's
gate from escaping the next packet's — **up to that waiter's final read**, which is the
honest boundary: a gate published before the read is observed by it, and a waiter past it
is the final-check residual the generation does not reach. Its terminal state is a single
CAS, unlike the restore
gate's store-then-CAS pair, because this gate has more terminal paths and a losing opener
must not be able to flip a withheld verdict to open.

All four delivery callbacks consult **both** gates, and the three that can wait — QoS 1/2
delivery, PUBREL and the affine copy — do it through **one** wait under **one absolute
deadline**, re-reading the current generation on each pass; two sequential waits would permit
nearly twice the intended cap. The fourth, shared QoS 0, consults the same two verdicts
without waiting on either and **drops**, as it does for the restore gate. Plain QoS 0
stays ungated: it acknowledges nothing on the group's behalf.

**The disposition follows the two existing precedents rather than inventing a third.** The
FOREIGN outcome disposes — the record is not ours, so this connection may not serve the
group — then notifies and closes, and the packet returns *nothing* to the parser, because
speaking again would race the displacer for the reason the client is left with. Every other
non-owning outcome — a sibling that erased our write, a definite local failure, an
unresolvable ambiguity — does not dispose: the session is left intact.

**Since F-084 the Will is treated the same on ALL of them**, Foreign included, and the
client is told `0x89` on all of them too. This section used to call the Foreign outcome a
"demonstrated takeover" that discarded the Will and notified `0x8E`; it demonstrates no
such thing — a rejected ownership CAS establishes that the subject moved and nothing about
who moved it — and suppressing a Will on it was silent loss. What still separates Foreign
from the rest is the DISPOSAL, not the claim and not the Will.

**Every close here consumes the Will while the ownership gate is still held**, rather
than leaving it to the ordinary close. A record-observation eviction can detach the session
in between, and the detached path publishes only an already-owed *immediate* Will — so a
delayed one would never reach the durable outbox. The Will disposition is consumed exactly
once, so the later close's own attempt is inert; nothing else about that close changes.

**An ambiguous proof is resolved by the packet itself, under the gate it already holds.**
Releasing first would let the periodic pass — which resolves *bound* uncertain sessions —
classify it first and apply the generic policy, which disposes on a forked verdict. A forked
resolution therefore retires the uncertainty *without* disposing: it clears the pending write
and discards the continuations that were owed only if those bytes had landed, leaves the
void-register revision uncredited, and leaves the sequence, lineage and record body at the
acknowledged base, because at forked those bytes demonstrably are not the record. Without
that retirement the close would park a teardown that a later generic disposal consumes,
losing the Will.

## A group durable is held by arbitration, not counted by a scan

The two sections above establish that a group durable is *present and canonical* and that
this broker still *owns* the membership. Neither says when a durable may be
**destroyed**. Until the shared-group lifecycle transfer that decision was a read: a walk
over every session record (`sharedDurablesHeldByOthers`) that reported "no other holder"
out of a record set it had to read in full, and five release paths deleted the group
consumer on that answer. A read is not an arbitration. It could not see a joiner whose
membership save had not landed, its answer merged "another session holds this" with "the
walk could not read a record", a record it could not read spared every later group's
durables for as long as it stood, and the delete it authorized was unconditioned — a
leaver could complete its walk before a join record landed and delete after the joiner's
own verification. Every one of those was a stated residual. This section is the mechanism
that replaced the walk; the release paths are below.

**Two record classes on `$MQTT_shared`, one verdict list in the session record.**

| fact | instrument |
|---|---|
| which PHYSICAL consumer a logical group uses, how many acquisitions hold it, which retired incarnations still owe a deletion | one **group record** per group, `$MQTT.shared.grp.<qkey>`, CAS-arbitrated, never deleted |
| which acquisitions THIS session generation holds, and whether the generation is closed to new ones | one **acquisition ledger** per session generation, `$MQTT.shared.shl.<idHash>.<gen>`, sealed by the closing, permanent |
| which acquisitions this session has durably decided to RELEASE and not yet confirmed released | `AcqReleases` in the session record, written by the record transaction that removes the membership or cancels an uncommitted join |

A JetStream atomic batch is per stream, so a join or a leave commits its group member and
its ledger member together and the session record can never be in that batch. The answer
to that is a division of authority: **the record CAS on `$MQTT_sess` arbitrates every
DISPOSITION** — the commit of an acquisition to a session, its removal, its cancellation —
while **the ledger CAS arbitrates every ACQUISITION and its release**, and the two are joined
by identity (the acquisition nonce) rather than by atomicity. Both classes live under the
F-105 prefix (`MaxMsgsPer: 1`, `AllowAtomicPublish`), so every register walk already skips
them; their class tokens `grp` and `shl` are not obligation classes, so an authority
transition carrying one is refused as a class this broker does not write.

The **group record** is `{epoch, group, live: {inc, holders} | null, retiring: [...],
next}`. `live` names the incarnation currently served and how many acquisitions hold it,
and `live != null ⇔ live.holders ≥ 1` is a validator rule. `retiring` lists incarnations
whose consumer deletion is OWED; an entry is removed only by the CAS that follows a
classified deletion outcome (removed or gone), and the list is bounded at
`mqttSharedRetiringMax`. `next` is a monotone ordinal counter: incarnations are `1, 2, 3,
…` per group and never reused, so **retirement is a derivation from one record's
contents** — `k < next`, `k != live.inc`, `k ∉ retiring` means `k` passed through live →
retiring → deleted, because no other path advances `next` past `k` — and never an
inference from a consumer not being found. `live` is the one legal null in this
mechanism's records: "nobody holds an incarnation" is a positive state the record has to
be able to say. An empty `retiring` is written as `[]`; a null list is refused by the
decoder and by the write boundary, because a nil slice marshals as null and the two must
not be conflated.

The **acquisition ledger** is `{epoch, id, gen, state: open | sealed, tenure: {seq, id},
acqs: [{group, inc, acq}, ...], closed: [acq, ...]}`. `closed` names the listed acquisitions
closed to new dependencies, the first step of an open ledger's release (7e, "The release
fence"); it is a subset of `acqs`, written as `[]` when empty. `acqs` are exactly the
acquisitions the generation currently holds, no history: a join appends one and a release
removes one, each in the batch that moves the group count, which is what makes the count
exact by construction (**count discipline**: the group's `holders` delta equals the
ledger's entry delta in the same batch, +1 for a join, −1 for a release, 0 otherwise). "A
COUNT WAS NOT ENOUGH" above refuted a count stepped by transitions that ended nothing;
here the count can only move together with the entry that IS the thing counted.

**The tenure is which CONNECT of this generation may acquire, and it is ordered.** A resume
preserves the generation, so two brokers may legitimately hold one generation at once; the
record CAS decides which of them owns the SESSION, and no `$MQTT_sess` write reaches
`$MQTT_shared`. The tenure carries that decision onto the ledger, and it is the acceptance's
ONE tenure (F-105 8b): `id` is the outbound authority tenure the acceptance was finalized
under, and `seq` is the `$MQTT_sess` stream sequence of the acceptance's own create-only
FACT, read back by the fact's subject — never derived from the batch acknowledgement, and
never the session record's sequence, a slot every later save advances, so that after a lost
response nothing could say which of its sequences was this acceptance's. A later
acceptance's fact lands higher on the same stream, which is the order the rule below needs.
EVERY acceptance — a fresh generation's and a clean start's included — installs its tenure
after its accept batch and authority finalization and before it reconciles or serves, under
the **non-regression rule**, enforced at the write boundary against the prior ledger:

| prior ledger | installation of `T` |
|---|---|
| absent | create-only `open(G, T, [])` |
| `open(G, T')`, `T'.seq < T.seq` | CAS: `tenure = T`, `acqs` preserved verbatim |
| `open(G, T)` | already installed; nothing written |
| `open(G, T'')`, `T''.seq > T.seq` | REFUSED: this CONNECT is superseded and is refused before its CONNACK; a tenure never downgrades |
| `sealed(G)` | REFUSED: the generation is closing and is never reopened |

The installation over absence is the ONLY creator of a ledger: a JOIN over an absent
ledger is refused by the composer and by the write boundary, and an exhausted
acquisition's abort fences only an existing ledger (it reads an absent one as unresolved
and never recreates it). A connection that never installed — an acceptance that crashed
or was refused before its installation — therefore cannot create a ledger behind a
successor's back, and a delayed acceptance whose successor already installed learns at
its own installation that it is superseded. Every JOIN and every FENCE is composed under
a tenure and names it, and the boundary refuses composing one whose prior ledger carries
a different tenure. An acquisition attempt and every retry of it keep their original
`(gen, tenure, acq)`; a successor tenure preserves committed acquisitions and executes
their release verdicts but never reissues an old acquisition under its own tenure — a
future acquisition of the same key mints a fresh nonce. RELEASES are exempt from tenure
equality: their authority is a committed verdict or the seal, they remove exactly the
named entry and preserve the standing tenure, and concurrent executors converge through
the CAS. The SEAL is authorized by the teardown claim, not by tenure, and no join, fence
or installation undoes it. Cost, stated: one acceptance-fact read on `$MQTT_sess` and
one `$MQTT_shared` transition on the critical path of EVERY CONNECT, whether or not the
session has shared subscriptions, and one permanent ledger subject per generation of
every client within the recovery epoch.

**`sealed` is the generation fence, and it is permanent.** A ledger reads `open` while
its generation is live and `sealed` once its closing has begun; after the closing has
released every entry it reads `sealed` with `acqs == []` and stays there for the recovery
epoch. A stale actor of the generation composing a join against any earlier sequence, or
against absence, is refused for ever, because the subject is occupied and has moved.
Nothing reclaims it, on the ground "Storage this mechanism accepts" gives for closures
and outcomes: there is no proof that every delayed caller has stopped referring to it,
and an expiry would rebuild the inference from absence this mechanism removes.

**Names carry the physical incarnation; the queue keeps the logical group.** The durable
is `$MQTT_SHARED_<qkey>_<inc>` and its deliver subject `$MQTT.qsub.<qkey>_<inc>` — one
token, because `$MQTT.qsub.*` is what the reserved-namespace table and the
service-connection ACL carry, and a two-token suffix would be denied under a `.*`
permission. The queue group stays `$mqttshare.<qkey>`, the LOGICAL identity an
authorization decision recovers from a group durable by parsing `<qkey>_<inc>` and
deriving the queue from `<qkey>` alone. Members of one logical group are always on the
same live incarnation, because `live` changes only when `holders` reaches zero, so the
queue group still load-balances exactly one physical consumer's deliveries.
`mqttSharedGroupNamesFor(key, membership)` is the ONE derivation of the names a key
reaches, from the membership's own acquisition references; `mqttSharedDurablesFor` and
`mqttSharedOwnsDurable` project off it, and nothing else derives a name.

**Invariant I-NAME, the protected interval: while an acquisition on incarnation `X` is
listed by any ledger, no retirement authorization for `X` can exist, and an authorized
delete of an older incarnation can never target `X`'s successor.** A delete is issued
only for an incarnation in `retiring` or derived retired; `X` enters `retiring` only by
the release batch that takes `live.holders` from 1 to 0, which count discipline binds to
the removal of the last listed entry; a join names the incarnation from the group record
it CASes against, so it never joins a retiring or retired one; and a delete for `X`
issued before a join means the join saw `live = null` or `live = Y` and mounted or joined
a fresh incarnation with its own name and deliver subject. This is not perpetual immunity
— `X` is deleted when its last holder leaves, and a disposition by another tenure of the
same generation or by its closing can release a freshly listed acquisition between the
membership save and the consumer create; then the session record has moved, the joiner's
own save or the F-077/F-078 ownership write that follows every join is refused, and
nothing is served on that connection. What the interval buys is what the verify-create
that used to follow the subscribe tried to buy after the fact: a delete racing our own
live join cannot reach our consumer. The verify-create is gone.

**The membership stops being a holder registry.** `SharedSubs` carries, per key, `{qos,
main: {inc, acq}[, up: {inc, acq}]}` — the session's own configuration plus its acquisition
references, `up` being the level-up companion a `foo.>` filter acquires on the parent group.
A session entry alone authorizes neither serving nor recreating; its absence authorizes no
release; a ledger entry may exist before the session entry commits; release requires durable
settlement of the acquisition, never a comparison of two snapshots. A record whose
`shared_subs` values are the old numeric QoS is a shape this broker no longer writes and is
**refused** at every ingress that reads a record — the CONNECT restore, both expiry paths,
the orphan sweeps, the shared record validator — and `mqttValidateRecordAffinePair` refuses
a membership whose references are malformed, a `foo.>` key without `up` or a `foo` key with
one. No migration, no legacy reader (compatibility boundary).

**An acquisition is made once per key and reused thereafter.** Three arms, decided by the
session's in-memory membership for the key, which the record mirrors:

| arm | when | acquisition |
|---|---|---|
| acquire | the key has no membership — a fresh SUBSCRIBE, or the first occurrence of a key in a packet | J1 mints the nonce, J2 writes the membership |
| refresh | the key has a membership and a live delivery subscription — a re-SUBSCRIBE, a QoS or option change, a duplicate filter later in one packet | none: the membership is rewritten with the packet's QoS and options and its references verbatim |
| restore | the key has a membership and no live subscription — a CONNECT resume | none: the resume validates the references (below); recreating an absent consumer materializes the SAME incarnation and adds no acquisition |

**The join protocol** (`processSubs`, acquire arm): **J0** admits the WHOLE filter ahead of
any reservation — the charge ceiling `tmaxack + Σ maxAckPending` over every consumer the
filter needs and the session is not already charged for, so one remaining charge refuses a
`foo.>` filter before either of its acquisitions, and the ledger bound. **J1** acquires on
`$MQTT_shared`, once per consumer the filter needs, composed under this CONNECT's tenure:
one batch that appends the acquisition to the ledger (create-only over absence, CAS at the
read sequence otherwise, requiring `open(G, T)`) and moves the group (`holders+1` on the live
incarnation, or `live = {next, 1}, next+1` when nobody holds one, finishing `retiring`
entries inline first when the list is full). **J2** is today's eager membership save under
the record CAS, carrying the references; it still PRECEDES the consumer create, so a restore
after a crash here finds an authoritatively absent consumer and repairs it, and a rollback
finds the acquisition it must release. **J2 is the DISPOSITION of the acquisition**: it
commits it to this session under the record CAS, which is what arbitrates it against a
cancellation by another tenure — the two contend for the same record sequence and exactly
one lands. **J3** creates `$MQTT_SHARED_<qkey>_<inc>` idempotently after the
`InactiveThreshold` check, reached only through a landed J2. **J4** subscribes the deliver
subject in the logical queue. The F-077/F-078 classified ownership write and the transmission
gate are unchanged.

**J1's settlement loop keeps ONE acquisition identity throughout, and acquisition and
disposition never interleave.** A CAS rejection or a lost acknowledgement re-reads both
records: listed under our tenure ⇒ landed, continue; `open(G, T)` at a sequence past
every one an attempt was composed against and unlisted ⇒ every issued attempt is
excluded, re-attempt the IDENTICAL batch (the only branch that re-appends, reached only
while no disposition of the acquisition has begun); sequence unchanged, or absent after a
first-ever attempt ⇒ the batch may still be in flight, re-attempt at the same expectation
so at most one lands; another tenure ⇒ this CONNECT is superseded on `$MQTT_shared`,
the filter fails, no fence and no retry (a stale tenure never acquires again); `sealed` ⇒
the generation is closing, the filter fails. Bounded at `mqttSharedAcquireAttempts`.
**Exhausting it fails the filter and enters abort settlement, after which no attempt of
that acquisition is ever issued again.** The abort needs a fence that EXISTS ("An
ambiguous transition is decided by a record that EXISTS"): over a present ledger under
our tenure a **bump**, a byte-identical body CASed at the observed sequence; over absence
the **init fence**, create-only `open(G, T, [])`; under another tenure or a seal no
fence, because the successor's installation or the seal already excludes every attempt of
ours. Then the abort table over the re-read ledger: unlisted past every issued attempt ⇒
settled, the filter fails; listed under our tenure ⇒ an attempt landed after all, so a
release verdict is written into the session record and executed, exactly as a failed
membership save is compensated; another tenure or a seal ⇒ the successor or the closing
owns the release, nothing written here. A refused fence is not settlement: it means the
subject moved or exists, and only the re-read decides.

**The release protocol is a VERDICT, then an EXECUTION, and the order is the
recoverability.** The record transaction that removes a membership — UNSUBSCRIBE's
removal, the 3.1.1 forced leave's aggregate write, a failed filter's compensation, a
SUBSCRIBE rollback's restoration of the pre-packet membership, a resume's cancellation of
an uncommitted join — writes the released acquisitions into `AcqReleases` under the
record CAS. That is what makes the release RECOVERABLE (a crash after it leaves a verdict
any later reader executes) and ARBITRATED (a tenure that has lost the record cannot write
it). The execution, **L1**, is one batch per acquisition: ledger CAS removing exactly
that entry, group CAS `holders−1`, and when that reaches zero `live = null` and `retiring
+= [inc]`. Every member carries a nonzero expectation, so an ambiguous or rejected L1 is
settled by re-attempting at the observed sequences and is SETTLED when the re-read ledger
no longer lists the acquisition — sound because the only writers that remove an entry are
executors of its own verdict and the closing after it sealed. **L2** follows when L1
moved the incarnation into `retiring`: `CONSUMER.DELETE $MQTT_SHARED_<qkey>_<inc>`,
classified removed / gone / ambiguous exactly as the affine executor classifies a delete,
then the group CAS removing the entry; ambiguous stops there and leaves the entry
standing for the sweep. The entry is the durable marker of unfinished reclamation, and
`retiring(X)`'s duty survives the move to `live(Y)` because it is a member of a record a
later join mutates but never clears. Once settled, the next record save drops the
verdict, on the positive fact that the ledger no longer lists it — never on a failure to
find it. Any broker that reads a record may EXECUTE its verdicts, because L1's CAS on the
exact entry makes concurrent executors converge (one lands, the others read it unlisted
and stop); only the record's owner may WRITE or CLEAR one.

**Three settlement questions, three answers, and an unreadable ledger is inconclusive for
all of them.** Is a release settled? — the ledger, read after our batch or its refusal, does
not list the acquisition. Did a join attempt land? — the settlement table above, which never
reads "unlisted" as landed and never re-appends once disposition has begun. Is a closing
complete? — the ledger reads `sealed` with `acqs == []`. A listed entry for incarnation `inc`
while the group reads `live == null || live.inc != inc` is a contradiction count discipline
forbids, and is REFUSED with a diagnostic; nothing is released or deleted on it.

**The closing fence is a production write in the teardown, on both routes, through ONE
closing driver** (`closeRetiringGeneration`, F-105 8b) — and, for a clean-start handoff,
which has no teardown of its predecessor, in the recovery executor under the discarding
closure (7e; "A discarded generation retires through its recovery owner"). A T3 release
from a sealed ledger runs no release fence ("The release fence"). Between
`recordGenRetirement` and `deleteTeardownTargets`, composed from the RETIRING generation
captured before the reset (`clear()` re-mints `sess.gen` before its deletions), the
teardown runs **T2 — seal**: create-only `sealed(G, [])` over absence, or CAS `open(G,
·) → sealed(G)` preserving `acqs` and whatever tenure stands; a standing seal reads as
already sealed. From here no join for the generation can land and no installation can
reopen it. **T3** releases every listed acquisition (L1 and L2 per entry, skipping none;
an entry whose group record cannot be read is skipped and reported). **T4**, the shared
closing gate, requires the ledger to read `sealed` with `acqs == []` and withholds
`releaseTeardown` on anything else — a gate of its own, evaluated independently of the
F-105 release gate's vacuous arm. Seal versus a concurrent tenure installation, both
orders: the seal lands first ⇒ the installation and its CONNECT are refused; the
installation lands first ⇒ the seal's CAS is refused, the closing re-reads and seals
what the installation preserved, and T3 releases it. A crash anywhere in T2–T3 leaves
the record MARKED and the adoption repeats T2–T3 from the ledger; a join whose save
races the teardown claim on `$MQTT_sess` is refused by the claim's CAS, its compensation
is refused too, and it then finds the seal and discharges its local state only, the
closing owning the release of whatever the ledger lists. The former enrolment of shared
durables into the closure, the retirement descriptor's shared field, the shared resource
kind and the release gate's target-enumeration inputs are deleted with the walk;
`mqttSealGenLedgerMember` survives because the closure's own sealed-ledger member never
depended on shared state. The driver runs the generation's discarding closure (the
ADMISSION fence) first and the seal (the JOIN fence) second, and the seal runs only
under the licence described in "One tenure and one closing driver (F-105 8b)": the seal
stays its own record, so the exclusion of delayed writes to the ledger subject is
preserved and is never replaced by a lookup of the closure.

**CONNECT restore and resume run every destructive act from a VERDICT, never from a
snapshot**, because two brokers may legitimately resume one generation. After the accept
batch lands and the authority is finalized (the tenure is minted from the acceptance fact,
F-105 8b), the resume (1) installs its tenure per
the table above, refusing the CONNECT before the CONNACK when superseded or sealed; (2)
executes the verdicts the record carries; (3) reconciles the ledger AS THE INSTALLATION
LEFT IT: an acquisition listed that neither `SharedSubs` nor `AcqReleases` names is an
uncommitted join — a crash between J1 and J2, or a stale tenure's J1 whose J2 cannot land
now — and is CANCELLED by a record write, not a ledger write: since the installation
follows the accept save, the cancellation cannot ride that save, so it is a SUBSEQUENT
record CAS writing the acquisition into `AcqReleases`, and it precedes any execution;
exactly one of that cancellation and the originator's J2 lands, both being CASes on one
record sequence, and a record acquisition the ledger does not list is impossible by
construction and refuses the CONNECT; (4) checks group consistency — every committed
acquisition's `inc` equals its group's `live.inc`, anything else refusing the CONNECT —
and keeps the REPAIRABLE arm for a committed acquisition whose consumer is
authoritatively absent: recreate by idempotent create, after the `InactiveThreshold`
check that guards every materialization. Release authority is the committed verdict,
never "the broker that minted the nonce": a restored membership may carry an acquisition
another broker minted, and it is this session's by the record that names it.

**The orphan sweep obtains retirement AUTHORITY from the group record, and executes
verdicts.** For each `$MQTT_SHARED_` consumer older than the grace window it reads the
group record and classifies the ordinal: the old shape without an ordinal is REFUSED and
retained with a warning (a persisted shape this broker no longer writes, never migrated);
a group record unreadable or absent RETAINS the consumer (a consumer is created only
after its J1 landed, so an absent record attributes nothing and licenses nothing); the
live incarnation is retained; a retiring one gets L2; a derived-retired one — the delayed
`CONSUMER.CREATE` that landed after retirement — is deleted under the record's authority.
A second pass walks the group records and finishes any `retiring` entry a leaver's crash
left inside L2. A **third pass of its own** — not an arm of the consumer sweep, whose "no
candidates" early exit must not suppress it — walks the session records and executes the
release verdicts they carry, connected or not (`DisconnectedAt` is irrelevant: the
verdict IS the release authority, and a hard crash leaves `DisconnectedAt == 0` on a
record nothing else revisits when the session never expires), once a verdict has been
STABLY OBSERVED, the same verdicts on two consecutive passes whatever the record's
sequence did meanwhile (7e: a connected session's unrelated saves move it on every pass,
and keying on it left a verdict whose owner's run failed with no executor at all). The
sweep never writes the record; the owner clears the verdict on its next save. All passes
act only on records they read, exhaustion of a walk authorizes nothing, and neither
`$MQTT_shared` class is ever deleted.

**One writer, seven batch shapes, every rule at the write boundary.**
`commitSharedLifecycleBatch` frames every batch through `newAtomicBatchRequest` and
validates it first against the PRIOR records it was composed from, compared with the
store before sending, so every rule is about stored state: **join** (group + ledger,
under a tenure, exactly one entry added, the group moved by one on the live incarnation
or mounted at `next`), **release** (group + ledger, any tenure, exactly one entry
removed, the count down one, `live = null` and `retiring += inc` at zero), **tenure
installation** (ledger alone, the non-regression table), **seal** (ledger alone, `acqs`
and tenure preserved verbatim, or `sealed(G, [])` over absence), **retirement
completion** (group alone, exactly one `retiring` entry removed), **bump** (ledger alone,
our tenure only, body byte-identical at the observed sequence), **init fence** (ledger
alone, create-only `open(G, T, [])`); a join that would mount with a full `retiring` list
is refused before anything is sent. Common rules: `tenure.seq` never decreases and
changes only by an installation; stream confinement to the two class prefixes; each
subject once; count discipline; `live != null ⇔ holders ≥ 1`; `next` monotone; a ledger's
`gen` equals its subject's; both bounds; every body carries the account's recovery epoch
and agrees with its subject; a nonzero expectation wherever a prior record exists and
create-only only over absence; no null list in either class. Decoders follow the F-105
closed-schema rule, and the ledger state enum numbers from 1 so a missing member never
decodes as the permissive value.

**Storage this mechanism accepts.** One fixed-size group record per logical group ever
created in the epoch; one ledger per session generation that ever acquires, closes or is
resumed — every teardown writes an empty seal for a generation that never acquired, and
every resume installs its tenure — proportional to generations, the closure record's own
cardinality; and one `$MQTT_shared` transition on the critical path of every RESUME
CONNECT. Neither class is deleted within the recovery epoch, for the reason given under the
seal.

**What remains, stated in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`.** A delayed `CONSUMER.CREATE` for a
retired incarnation exists until the orphan sweep's grace window; a `retiring` entry
whose delete was ambiguous waits for the sweep; a release verdict left by a crash is
executed by the next resume or by the verdict pass after two stable observations, during
which the consumer stays alive; and ONE client-visible refusal — a join that must mount a
new incarnation while the group's `retiring` list is full fails its filter (retryable),
reachable only after sixteen consecutive ambiguous retirements of one group.

## A release separates the acquisition from the local durable state

A release has two different targets with two different rules, because "this acquisition is
released" and "this session still reaches the consumer" are different facts. Every removed
ACQUISITION gets a verdict and exactly one execution, whether or not another of this
session's keys still reaches the same consumer: `$share/g/foo.>` and `$share/g/foo` hold TWO
acquisitions on the parent group, and unsubscribing either releases its own and leaves the
count at 1. LOCAL DURABLE STATE — this session's delivery subscription, pending state and
ack-budget charge for a physical consumer — is released only when no SURVIVING key reaches
that consumer, the F-082/F-083 surviving-membership property, unchanged in meaning: it decides
the close/purge/refund/unsubscribe half and decides nothing about acquisitions.

**Three dispositions per group consumer, therefore, not two.** Own-held: discharge
nothing locally and delete nothing — the pending purge, the ack-budget refund and the
unsubscribe are all whole-durable, so acting would silently stop a live subscription
delivering — while the leaving key's acquisition on it is released all the same. Held by
another session's acquisition, or the release withheld (a group record that cannot be
read leaves the verdict standing for a later executor): discharge this session's own
state, the consumer stands. Sole holder: both, the incarnation retiring and its consumer
deleted. The overlap that makes this real is deterministic rather than exotic — a
multi-level key acquires a second group consumer for its level-up parent, and that parent
IS the consumer of the plain filter one level up, so `$share/g/foo.>` and `$share/g/foo`
share a durable.

**`sess.cons` is not the authority for what a failed filter must release.**
`addJSConsToSess` runs only once a whole filter has succeeded, so the join a FAILING
filter made has no resident config — while its `MaxAckPending` charge, its pending
deliveries and its deliver-subject subscription are all already real. Everything a shared
key joins is derived instead from the key's membership — its own acquisition references —
through the one derivation `mqttSharedGroupNamesFor`, which is also what
`mqttSharedDurablesFor` and `mqttSharedOwnsDurable` project rather than re-deriving. The
release then takes `(durable, deliverSubject)` for the local half, and the consumer's
fate is the group record's count, executed from the verdicts the compensating write made
durable, so no path can reach a `CONSUMER.DELETE` except through a released acquisition.

**The same keying applies to the pre-save delivery barrier**, and there the ownership test
must
EXCLUDE the key being released: the barrier is lowered before the membership removal, so the
doomed key is still present and counting it would make every closure suppress itself. Two
independent fences protect a live membership from a release it never owed — that
exclusion, and
the rule that a rollback which RESTORES a membership registers no landed release at all.

**The fence is a PROPERTY over the membership that survives the operation, not a rule per
caller.** F-082 fenced two sites and F-083 then found two more by enumerating the
callers, so
the enumeration was the defect rather than the sites. The question is always the same — *does
a membership that SURVIVES this operation still reach this durable?* — and only the membership
it is asked of differs. `mqttSharedSurvivors` is that membership, and every operation supplies
its own as an explicit immutable set of keys:

| Operation | Its surviving membership |
|---|---|
| UNSUBSCRIBE, staging half | the live map **minus the packet's whole doomed set** — the removals have not been applied yet, and one packet can leave BOTH overlapping filters, so excluding only the key in hand lets each protect the other |
| UNSUBSCRIBE, commit half | the live map as it stands: `sess.update` has already applied the removals, so it IS the surviving membership |
| a failed shared filter's release, both halves | the live map; the compensating removal is already durable |
| a SUBSCRIBE packet's rollback, both halves | the **pre-packet snapshot** — a historical value, because the live map still names the very key being rolled back |

Passing the membership is what keeps the last row honest. An exclusion-list API would encode
the UNSUBSCRIBE's ordering rather than the invariant, and would misdescribe a rollback whose
authority is a snapshot. The set is built under `sess.mu` and immutable thereafter; what keeps
it TRUE once the lock is released is the session's **ownership gate**, which every production
route holds. That truth is LOCAL to this session — it says nothing about another broker, and
the non-snapshot join/delete race and the same-client-ID skip are untouched by it.

**Two sites are vacuous rather than exempt**, and the difference matters because only
one of
them owes anything. The 3.1.1 forced leave removes EVERY shared membership and teardown runs
after `sharedSubs` is niled, so no key survives at either and the whole-durable release is
always owed. Teardown carries nothing further.

**The forced leave's own target derivation.** It used to purge over `es.cons` while
voiding over
the membership keys, so the two halves of one operation disagreed about what they were acting
on. It now uses **two authorities, for two different obligations**:

| Obligation | Authority | What only it can see |
|---|---|---|
| the doomed configs, and the CANDIDATES for a consumer release | the membership keys **plus** the `cons` entries | a membership with no config (every record-restored resume), and a config no surviving key names |
| the pending-state purge | the **pending maps** — `cpending`, `deferred`, `srcAckOwed`, filtered by the shared durable prefix | pending state named by *neither* structural view |

For this caller the two questions F-083 separates — is this config doomed, is this
durable owed
a release — **collapse**, because every membership is going, so nothing local survives
to hold
anything. That is what licenses one candidate set here where UNSUBSCRIBE needs a
surviving-key fence. But a target found **only** through the pending maps is purged and
**never deleted**: pending state is not an acquisition, and only the release of a group's
last acquisition — the group record's count reaching zero — authorizes a `CONSUMER.DELETE`.

The pending derivation runs at **both** halves, not just the commit. The write that
removes the
membership is the write that must also say "these allocations were never transmitted",
so a
pending-only durable's verdict has to be staged with the rest; left to the commit, a
crash in
between would leave a live register with no cancellation recorded and **no membership
able to
trigger another leave**, and recovery would reserve its identifier indefinitely. `srcAckOwed`
retirements stay exempt from voiding, for the reason `voidRegistrationsLocked` already
gives: the source-side retirement suppresses a completed payload, while F-092's associated
slot remains the packet identifier's whole-life owner until PUBCOMP. Voiding either fact
would re-offer a completed payload as a QoS 2 duplicate or free an identifier the client
still holds.

This closes F-045's forced-leave instance. It does not alter or re-own the UNSUBSCRIBE
transaction; F-083 already closed the no-`cons` UNSUBSCRIBE instance.

**"This config is doomed" and "this durable is owed a release" are different
questions**, and
the second does not imply the first. A multi-level key's level-up companion has its own
`sess.cons` entry but shares its durable with the plain filter one level up: when the
multi-level key leaves alone, that durable is NOT owed, yet the companion's config must still
go or it outlives the membership with nothing left to reach it by. So an UNSUBSCRIBE's commit
half is three operations — remove the doomed keys' configs unconditionally, compute the owed
targets, then sweep every remaining config naming an owed durable and release it.

**Nothing may discriminate a shared sid from a plain one lexically**, and that includes a
rollback deciding whether a raw subscription predates its packet: both membership snapshots
are consulted, because the two keyspaces are disjoint by construction and a prefix test
misfiles a plain filter that merely looks shared.

`mqttToNATSSubjectConversion` encodes a literal `.` as `//`, so the ordinary plain filter
`$share.foo` has the sid `$share//foo` and satisfies a `$share/` prefix test. The authorities
are `f.shared`, set at parse time, and `cc.DeliverGroup` on a resident config. A plain
UNSUBSCRIBE therefore routes through the same deferred plain-consumer teardown a QoS downgrade
uses; the separate UNSUBSCRIBE-only teardown that used to exist was deleted, having duplicated
that machinery while mutating `sess.cons` without `sess.mu` and never unsubscribing the
deliver subject.

**An ungated `CONSUMER.DELETE` on a shared durable is prevented three times over, and the
three are REDUNDANT WITH EACH OTHER.** The commit half removes the doomed shared configs
before the plain loop runs, so a shared sid reaching that loop finds no config; `f.shared`
dispatches away from it; and the plain accessor refuses a config carrying a `DeliverGroup`.
Removing any ONE changes no observable behaviour, so none of the three is individually pinned
by a test; only removing all three together produces the failure, which is what the paired
mutation demonstrates. That establishes the conjunction and nothing finer — **it does not
license removing any one of them**, and a change that drops one would be invisible to this
suite rather than proven harmless.

## A deferred QoS downgrade is revocable within its packet

One SUBSCRIBE packet may carry the same topic filter more than once. MQTT 5.0 3.8.4
requires the server to handle it "as if it had received a sequence of multiple SUBSCRIBE
packets ... except that it combines their responses into a single SUBACK"
[MQTT-3.8.4-4], and [MQTT-3.8.4-3] makes a later entry replace an earlier one. So a packet
carrying `foo` at QoS 0 and then at QoS 1 must end with **one** subscription at QoS 1,
its consumer intact and delivering.

The QoS 0 occurrence stages a **deferred teardown**: the delivery barrier goes down, the
consumer's not-yet-transmitted registrations are withdrawn into the packet's own
transaction, and the `CONSUMER.DELETE` waits for the confirmed save — or, where the
consumer still holds started deliveries, never happens at all, because the packet converts
it into a drain instead (see "Where each entry point converts"). The `sess.cons` entry
deliberately stays, so a mid-packet save serializes a record consistent with a durable that
still exists. The QoS 1 occurrence then reached the existing-consumer refresh arm, which
sees that entry, refreshes four fields and returns success — knowing nothing about the
pending teardown. The client was granted QoS 1, received nothing for the rest of the
connection, and the record named a durable the packet went on to delete.

**The staging is therefore revocable, and the later occurrence revokes it.**

- **The packet's deferred-delete list is the single authority** on "this consumer is being
  torn down by this packet". Each entry carries the barrier it lowered and the verdicts it
  recorded; the two parallel stack slices that used to hold those facts are gone. They had
  three per-filter boundaries over three different cardinalities — one staging contributes
  at most one closed subscription and zero or more nonces — so a mid-slice removal for one
  sid invalidated the later filters' boundaries, and "withdraw the staging for this sid"
  could not be expressed at all.
- **At most one LIVE entry per sid**, and it needs two proofs rather than one. The staging
  site enforces it by looking the sid up first; that is what makes it hold. The barrier is
  a separate fact: with the subscription closed no *fresh* allocation can accrue, so the
  skip loses no new work — but a second `voidRegistrationsLocked` would still find the
  transmitted entries and re-record verdicts already recorded, so the barrier alone would
  be too weak an argument. The same invariant removes a pre-existing double
  `CONSUMER.DELETE` for `[{foo,0},{foo,0}]`.
- **The barrier, the terms and the un-void move in ONE critical section.** It is the
  *split* that is forbidden, not any particular order inside it: the delivery
  subscription's QoS is still the PRE-PACKET one until the terms are applied, so a delivery
  dispatched between a reopen and a later refresh goes out under the old grant — a QoS 2
  PUBLISH under a QoS 1 subscription for a packet that downgrades 2 -> 1
  [MQTT-3.8.4-8]. Every reader holds one of the two locks the section takes, so the order
  of the assignments within it is unobservable and no correctness claim rests on it.
- **Readiness is proved, not assumed.** The saved subscription pointer says only what was
  true at staging time, so the revocation re-checks that `sess.cons[sid]` is still the
  staged config and that the installed delivery subscription is still the one whose barrier
  it holds. Failing that it REFUSES — the filter fails `0x80` and the deferral stands.
  Granting a QoS the broker cannot serve is the defect this repair removes, not a lesser
  form of it.
- **The reviver's own failure re-stages, through the same helper.** `sess.update` skips a
  failed filter, so the earlier QoS 0 occurrence's membership stands and the downgrade is
  owed again. Re-staging restores neither the saved barrier nor the saved verdicts: between
  the revocation and the failure the barrier was OPEN and the durable live, so new
  deliveries may have been tracked and new identifiers allocated, and only a fresh snapshot
  withdraws them — into **the packet's own membership-removal write**, which is where a
  cancellation has to be.
- **What the revocation deliberately does NOT undo is the staged cancellations.** The
  not-yet-transmitted allocations were destroyed outright, so their tombstones still owe the
  packet's write, or a register store still in flight lands with nothing to explain it and
  holds an identifier and a Receive Maximum slot. Those messages are untransmitted and
  unacknowledged in JetStream, so they are re-offered through the restored subscription and
  allocate fresh identifiers.

**A revoked entry stays in the list.** The execution loop skips it, and nothing else reads
the flag; keeping it is what lets a later per-filter cancellation find it again. That loop
runs after the confirmed save, on the read loop, so the flag needs no lock of its own.

**Population.** Live SUBSCRIBE only, plain filters only. A shared filter routes to the
group-consumer path and never touches `sess.cons[sid]` or the deferral; the CONNECT restore
path executes the teardown inline with no deferral, and a restored record's filters are map
keys, so duplicates cannot occur there. A multi-level wildcard owns two sids and reproduces
the case twice, once per half.

**What it does not do.** It does not make duplicate occurrences of one filter atomic: the
earlier occurrence's raw subscription is still displaced by the later one's, and a
per-filter failure of the later occurrence still leaves the earlier membership standing.
Deliveries the barrier skipped are not NAKed either, so each waits out `AckWait` and can be
overtaken while it waits, and its first transmission carries `DUP=0` because F-072 moved
that derivation off the JetStream delivery count onto the unsent marker. Both are stated in
`docs/CONFORMANCE.md`.

## The restore gate: the CONNACK follows a complete restoration

A resuming CONNECT used to acknowledge the session with Session Present = 1 and
only **then** restore the subscriptions its record names. On that path there is no
SUBACK, `sess.update` is skipped, and a per-filter failure only sets a local
result and continues — so the failure reached nobody. The record kept the
membership, no queue subscription and no group consumer existed, and a client that
is not required to re-subscribe waited forever (F-050).

**Restoration therefore runs BEFORE the CONNACK, and a filter it cannot install
refuses the CONNECT** through the same abort discipline the section below
describes. Five exits are reachable while restoring a saved filter — the PUBREL
consumer, the session-affine QoS 2 consumer, the raw subject subscription, the
plain or group JetStream consumer, and the level-up companion of the last two —
and `processSubs` already records each outcome in the filter itself, because on a
SUBSCRIBE those bytes become the SUBACK. `mqttFirstUnrestoredFilter` reads that
value; it is **local failure aggregation and nothing more**. It does not arbitrate
ownership, does not prove this broker still owns the record, does not prove a
group durable exists, and does not prove an installed subscription yields
end-to-end delivery. What it proves is that no step of this restoration reported
failure, which is what the CONNACK is about to claim.

One unrestored filter refuses the whole CONNECT: there is no packet on this path
that could say *which* filter died, which is the finding. A v5 connection is told
the reason (0x83, with the filter named) because that refusal is the first packet
and a filter that can never be restored — a subscribe permission revoked since it
was saved is the reachable case — would otherwise be an endless silent close with
no hint that a clean start is the recovery. A 3.1.1 connection has no reason code
above 5 and gets the bare close. Every other refusal **in the post-accept-save,
pre-success-CONNACK window** now carries a reason too: that generalisation has
landed, and inside that window only the failed success-CONNACK write is still
silent. Exits earlier in the CONNECT remain silent and are a stated residual. See
"The pre-CONNACK refusal signal".

**The reorder needs one new fact, and it is a property of the CONNECTION.**
[MQTT-3.2.0-1] makes the CONNACK the first packet a client sees, and restoration
installs live delivery interest, so something must withhold transmission until the
CONNACK is written. That something cannot be per-subscription, for two structural
reasons: a per-subscription flag cannot be armed before the subscription exists —
`ensurePubRelConsumerSubscription` uses a bare `c.processSub`, whose NATS handler
goes live *before* `processSub` returns, so a stored PUBREL can enter its callback
with no metadata attached at all — and a per-subscription gate that has been
released is indistinguishable from one that never existed, so a refusal cannot
express "woken, and still not allowed out" that way.

So the fact is one atomically-published verdict on the session
(`sess_restore_gate.go`), consulted by every delivery callback **before** it
touches `sub.mqtt`:

- **armed**, unconditionally on every accepted CONNECT — clean start, cleared
  session and zero-filter resume included — before the first subscription the
  CONNECT installs, which is before the reconciliation phase rather than merely
  before restoration. **Both the earliness and the unconditionality are defence in
  depth**, and neither is a proved behaviour: the phase's own subscriptions are
  installed closed behind their own gate, and a mutation making the arm conditional
  on the record naming a filter survives, because a refusal leaves the record's
  filters exactly as it found them so the CONNECT after one always has some. They
  are kept so no future path has to re-derive either argument.
- **opened** after a confirmed success CONNACK — but **not immediately**, and the gap is
  deliberate. `[MQTT-3.2.0-1]` forbids opening it any earlier; what pushes it later is the
  3.1.1 forced leave, which can still refuse the connection after the CONNACK is
  written. An
  opened verdict is *immediate* permission for the delivery callbacks, which run on
  their own
  goroutines, and a transmission cannot be retracted by a refusal that follows it — so the
  verdict opens only once that leave has settled. `opened` is stored strictly before the
  channel closes, so a waiter released by that close reads the final value rather than racing
  it.
- **abandoned** on every refusal, before the client detaches. Two shapes, and the difference
  is the acknowledgement: a **pre-CONNACK** refusal abandons through the abort helper, which
  also discards the Will and clears acceptance; a **post-CONNACK** refusal — only the forced
  leave's settlement arms — calls `abandonRestoreGate` **alone**, because the CONNACK is
  already written and neither the Will ([MQTT-3.1.2-8]) nor the acceptance may be taken back.
  Both shapes owe the wake for the same reason. The verdict is
  **not cleared**: a delivery arriving after the abandon must still be blocked,
  and the abort helper deliberately leaves `c.mqtt.sess` in place, so `sess.c`
  still names this connection. Waking the waiters is what lets a withheld QoS 1/2
  delivery record itself as never transmitted instead of waiting out its whole
  bound — but that recording is **best-effort across a rebind, deliberately**. The
  marker is scoped to the connection that withheld the delivery, and the refusal
  returns and releases the ownership gate, so a reconnect can bind first and leave
  the woken callback stale. Two remedies were built and withdrawn (a drain, which
  cannot be an admission barrier, and a durable-scoped predicate, which removes the
  race but not the lateness); HEAD already treats this boundary the same way. The
  consequence is a **lost prompt NAK**, stated in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`. The race itself
  still stands; its DUP half no longer follows from it, because F-072 (CLOSED 2026-09-09)
  moved the derivation onto the durable unsent marker, so a stale woken callback cannot
  make a first transmission carry DUP.

Both terminal transitions are CAS-guarded. They are exclusive today; the guard is
what keeps that from being an invariant a later caller can break with a
double close, which panics the process.

The four delivery callbacks, and why they differ:

| Callback | Disposition while the verdict is armed and not opened |
|---|---|
| `mqttDeliverMsgCbQoS12` | **waits**, bounded by the same deadline the reconciliation gate uses; a withheld delivery is recorded — **when the connection that withheld it is still the session's**, which is best-effort across a rebind (above) — so the attempt that finally goes out is a first transmission ([MQTT-3.3.1-1]) and a freed slot can NAK it forward. The recording is shared with the reconciliation phase's own gate through one helper, because both owe the client the same thing, and it is written only for a delivery still OWED (`!closed \|\| phaseOwned`), never for a durable being torn down |
| `mqttDeliverMsgCbQoS0` | **drops.** QoS 0 has no redelivery, so parking a NATS delivery goroutine on an MQTT handshake would buy nothing |
| `mqttDeliverPubRelCb` | **waits**, then disposes by WHY the wait ended. A refusal returns silently, so JetStream redelivers on its own schedule and nothing spins against a session with no client. A TIMEOUT **NAKs**: the bound is min(AckWait, cap), so with AckWait above the cap the wait ends long before any redelivery would, and a PUBREL carries no withheld marker — without the NAK an owed one sits unsent for the rest of that AckWait on a resume that SUCCEEDED. PUBREL carries no DUP ([MQTT-3.6.1-1] fixed-header flags are 0010), so nothing further is owed |
| `mqttDeliverQ2AffineCb` | **waits**, then disposes by why the wait ended, exactly as PUBREL does above: silent on a refusal, **NAK** on a timeout. The NAK matters most for a copy that was materialized and never delivered — absent from the resume's pending snapshot, so nothing else re-drives it. No withheld bookkeeping: DUP is the entry's own `transmitted` bit, seeded on resume from the unsent marker (F-072), so a copy refused here before `trackPublish` writes no marker and its next offer is a first transmission. Waiting is what keeps the ordinary case out of it |

Two orderings around it are load-bearing. The **grant point** moves after
restoration, because its own rule is that the requested Session Expiry Interval
and Clean flag are applied only once everything that can refuse the CONNECT has
passed — restoration is now one of those things, and a granted interval of 0 on a
CONNECT that is then refused would have the close path discard a persistent
session. And the **3.1.1 forced leave** stays *after* the CONNACK, so the
pre-CONNACK restore must exclude shared filters for a non-v5 connection
explicitly; the old code achieved that by ordering alone. Provisioning an affine
consumer, a PUBREL consumer and a group join for memberships the forced leave then
removes is what that exclusion prevents.

One thing does move *before* the CONNACK: the leave's memberships are **parsed** there.
A key `mqttSharedDurablesFor` cannot expand names no durable, so a leave that met one would
remove the membership and release nothing — and retaining just that key would not help,
because a key that names no durable holds no acquisition the group record could count.
Corrupt or unsupported persisted state is therefore **refused pre-CONNACK**, where the abort
discards the Will and leaves the lifetime ungranted, rather than discovered after the
acknowledgement.

**What a restore-path failure no longer destroys.** A per-filter failure used to
reach `cleanupFailedSub`, which for a plain filter whose level-up companion failed
after the main half succeeded deleted a durable the session record still names.
That was survivable while the CONNECT was accepted anyway — the next resume's
reconciliation repaired it — and it is the wrong disposition for a refused
CONNECT, whose record still references that durable and whose backlog is retained
by its interest. On the restore path the cleanup is now the connection-local
subscriptions alone. What the connection did add to `tmaxack` is refunded per
filter, from the amount each group join **reported**: the config comes back
whether a call charged it or reused a resident entry, so refunding by durable
would erase an earlier connection's charge and leave the accounting permanently
short.

The reconciliation phase below needs **no** change for any of this, which is worth
stating: its `phaseOwned`/`closed`/`phaseGate` triple keeps its own meaning, its
adoption still clears `closed` and releases its own gate, and
`sweepUnadoptedPhaseSubs` still keys on `phaseOwned` alone. A delivery that wakes
from the phase's gate simply meets the connection's verdict next.

**Pre-CONNACK abort discipline.** Every post-bind failure exit before a
confirmed success CONNACK — the register-recovery error, the reconciliation
