refusals, **the restoration refusals above**, the lifetime-grant failure below,
the CONNACK size/write failure
(`sendConnAck` now surfaces its write error, so "a success CONNACK was written"
is a checked fact) — goes through one abort helper that discards this
connection's Will and clears the parser's pre-CONNACK connected flag. Without
it, the readLoop would send a v5 DISCONNECT as the **first** packet
([MQTT-3.2.0-1]) and close handling could publish the new connection's Will for
a session that was never granted. The helper deliberately preserves
`c.mqtt.sess`/`c.mqtt.cp`: for a **local** refusal the ordinary close
bookkeeping must still run — it is what detaches the client and
persists/schedules the expiry.

**The requested lifetime is applied only when the resume is granted.** A
resuming CONNECT does **not** overwrite the session's Session Expiry Interval or
Clean flag at rebind, because the accept save that follows would persist them —
and this CONNECT can still be refused. A record describing terms the client was
never told it has is not harmless: with a requested interval of 0 the close path
would discard a persistent session outright (`doClean`), and the client's retry
would find Session Present 0 with its state gone. So the accept save carries the
lifetime the session already had, which is truthful until something is granted,
and the requested values are applied — and persisted, in the same breath — at
the **grant point**, once everything that could refuse the CONNECT has passed
and immediately before the CONNACK. The write happens only when the terms
actually changed, so an ordinary reconnect adds none, and it owes the ordinary
outcome discipline (`applyRequestedLifetime`): a definite failure puts the two
fields back; an ambiguous one puts them back **immediately** and re-applies the
grant only once a readback proves the write landed — because a close happening
while the write is unresolved snapshots the lifetime into its deferred
teardown, so speculative terms there would let a grant that never landed
discard the session, and the landed continuation correspondingly retargets that
snapshot; a 10071 hands the session over — to whoever holds the record, which the
rejection alone does not establish (see "Only a held successor licenses a takeover
claim") — with 10164
resolved by the same bounded re-read the repair save uses. A resume
refused before this point therefore leaves the session exactly as it found it,
in memory and in the record, with no repair machinery at all. A session that
was CLEARED rather than resumed — clean start, a legacy clean session, an
overdue record — takes the requested terms at rebind instead: it has no prior
lifetime to protect and its record is created fresh by the accept save.

### The DISCONNECT lifetime override is a connection's OBLIGATION

A v5 DISCONNECT may replace the Session Expiry Interval (Spec5 [3.14.2.2.2]),
and the same helper persists it — under `mqttLifetimeFinal` rather than
`mqttLifetimeSpeculative`, which is the whole of the difference between the two
callers.

**Three facts have to stay apart, and conflating any two of them was what made
this hard.**

| Fact | Where it lives | Who may act on it |
|---|---|---|
| the session's **confirmed** terms | `sess.expiryInterval` / `sess.clean`, moved only under the ownership gate | anything reading the session |
| a CONNECT's **requested** terms — speculative, still refusable | local to `mqttProcessConnect` | the grant above, and only once it proves durable |
| an accepted connection's **DISCONNECT override** — explicit, unrefusable | `mqtt.lifetimeOverride` | the close, and every park the close can take |

The packet handler writes only the third: it records `mqtt.lifetimeOverride`
under `c.mu` and **no longer touches the session at all**, which is why it needs
no ownership test. A late DISCONNECT from a displaced connection records an
obligation on its own client struct, and its close then finds the session
rebound and does nothing with it. The requested terms must never reach the close
— `mqttAbortAcceptedConnect` exists to guarantee that — and because
`lifetimeOverride` is written only by this packet, a connection whose CONNECT
was refused never has one.

**`clean` and the interval are ONE fact**, derived by
`mqttSessionIsCleanForExpiry`. Persisting the interval alone would be strictly
worse than persisting nothing: the resume decision reads `Clean`, `overdue`
requires a positive interval, and the expiry sweep skips zero — so the record
would be both resumable and unreapable.

**The close applies it**, after the entry uncertainty check and before the
never-expire stamp block, in its **own** record transaction (the fence is not
re-entrant) and re-checking uncertainty **with the fence held**, because the
entry check is a check-then-act. The five classifier outcomes are handled per
outcome, not by one shared fall-through: `Proceed` continues on the applied
terms, `Local` keeps them and reports the lost durability, `Unresolved` parks,
and both disposing verdicts terminate through the existing disposal — an
ownership verdict, not a persistence failure, so continuing would run
`purgeSharedPending` and a second finite save against a record that is no longer
ours.

Under `Final` a definite failure does **not** restore the pre-override terms.
No refusal is possible and the client has already been told nothing further, so
putting them back would silently ignore the instruction — which is the deviation
this exists to fix. The terms stand and only the durable backstop is lost.

**Every park carries the obligation, and every discharge applies it.** A park is
not a refusal, so `mqttDeferDisconnectEx` builds the action's `expiryInterval`
from the override when the connection has one. That also decides the Will at no
extra cost: `mqttWillFireAt`'s cap and `mqttWillIsDelayed`'s classification both
read the action's interval, so an override to zero reclassifies a delayed Will
as due now and a shrink caps the delay at park time. Because the action is built
from the override rather than from the confirmed terms, there is nothing stale
for `retargetDeferredLifetime` to fix — which is why it is called under
`Speculative` only.

`applyDeferredDisconnect` then has exactly two operational branches and **both**
apply the action's lifetime before anything fallible — but only when that
interval **is** a lifetime. `action.expiryInterval` carries two different facts
in one representation: the terms this close ends on, for a park built from a
connection, and a bare discard **instruction**, for the action
`reparkRefusedDiscard` synthesises. That path retries ordinary expiry recovery
for a session whose real lifetime is **finite**, so persisting its zero as
`Clean = true` with `ExpiryInterval = 0` would write over the finite record —
and `sweepSessionExpiries` skips interval-zero records, so a subsequently
refused `clear()` would leave the session unreapable where before it had a
deadline the sweep could retry. `mqttDeferredDisconnect.lifetimeOverridden` is the
distinction, and it is deliberately narrower than "carries a lifetime": it is set
only when the connection actually carried an **override**. An ordinary park with
no override carries the session's own confirmed terms, which the session and its
record already hold — so writing them would add a record store to every parked
close and, worse, let an **ambiguous** store repark a discard that today is simply
attempted, which is behaviour change on a path this item does not own. Only an
override creates an obligation, and only an obligation is written; a synthetic
discard and a no-override park both keep their historical behaviour. The surviving branch
writes
the pair beside its disconnect stamp, in one save: carrying the override in the
action is not enough, because that branch used to persist the session's retained
lifetime and a never-expire override therefore left a finite record for a
restart to expire. The discard branch writes the pair **and the action's stamp**
in a transaction of its own before `clear(true)`, because `clear()` can fail
without deleting anything — a drain timeout reopens the tracker and reparks,
arming no uncertainty, so a CONNECT would find neither `clean` nor `overdue` and
resume a session the DISCONNECT ended. The stamp is not optional there: both
resume checks need a **positive** timestamp to recognise expiry, so a backstop
that writes the lifetime and leaves it at zero leaves an already-expired finite
session resumable — which is the `expiredBy` half of that same case clause. It is
the **action's** stamp, never a fresh sample: the discharge stands in for a close
that happened earlier.

**What this does not do.** It changes no clock source, converts no unit and
rewrites no deadline formula; the expiry-timing residuals are in
`docs/CONFORMANCE.md`. It gives `Clean` no cross-broker ownership semantics —
that predicate is a **resume** predicate, and destructive arbitration stays in
`claimTeardown`. And it does not make the override survive a crash before its
first write, which no durable state can.

**Crash windows.** A crash after a create but before the repair save leaves a
durable with a closed subscription that never transmitted and that no record
names: the next resume repairs again, and the orphan sweep reclaims the
abandoned durable after its grace (the sweep's `Created`-age guard covers the
in-flight construction window). A crash after the confirmed save but before
the CONNACK leaves the record naming the new durable; the next resume verifies
it present. A cross-broker takeover between the accept save and the repair
save CAS-rejects definitively (the later broker accepted *on top of* our
accept sequence) — our consumer never transmitted and is swept; the winner's
own resume verified whatever record it read. Register identity is invariant
throughout: recovery precedes the phase in the same CONNECT, and the old name
stays absent forever, so *Lost* verdicts stay *Lost*.

**Why re-SUBSCRIBE needs no verification.** After this phase, every `cons`
entry on a live connection was verified or repaired at its CONNECT — an
indeterminate verification refused the CONNECT, so no connection carries an
unverified entry — and a successfully adopted filter's consumer cannot be
inactivity-reaped mid-connection, because its delivery subscription holds
interest. The qualification matters: a filter restoration skipped (and the
sweep reclaimed) holds no interest and stays unavailable until the next
CONNECT — a live re-SUBSCRIBE cannot recover it, because the exists-branch
never recreates missing interest. Live re-SUBSCRIBE is **not** a recovery
mechanism; the recovery for anything that slips through is to reconnect. Drain
adoption is untouched: a re-SUBSCRIBE that adopts a drain whose durable was
reaped inherits a dead entry — as today — and the **next CONNECT** repairs it
(the adopted entry is back in `cons` and its filter in the subscriptions),
while `recoverDrains` keeps owning drain-side loss reporting. Both stated in
`docs/CONFORMANCE.md`, together with the delivery-start policy: a replacement
is `DeliverNew`, and no backlog is guaranteed recoverable across a reap.

## The 3.1.1 forced leave is a convergence obligation, not a CONNECT exit

Force-leaving a resuming 3.1.1 client's shared memberships is **broker-side hygiene the client
neither asked for nor can observe**. Its failure therefore owes the client nothing, and the
connection is refused only where refusing is the right answer — never merely because a write
did not succeed. Previously both failure arms returned an error from `mqttProcessConnect`,
which closes: the client held Session Present = 1 and a dead socket, and its Will was published
because the broker could not persist its own bookkeeping.

**The definite bucket cannot contain a transient store failure**, and that fact is what shapes
the whole mechanism. `persistRecord` arms *uncertainty* for every non-CAS-rejection store
error, so an ordinary "JetStream was briefly unavailable" classifies as **ambiguous**, not
definite. What is left definite is exactly: 10071, 10164, and refusals that never reached
JetStream at all.

| Outcome | Disposition |
|---|---|
| landed | commit the leave |
| **ambiguous** | register the landed continuation **first**, then resolve **in line under the CONNECT's own transaction**; continue only on *ours* |
| **10164** (contention) | the bounded re-read/retry classifies it; continue only on *landed*. An unclassifiable outcome parks the continuation **before** returning |
| **10071** (the subject moved) | classify the lineage, dispose with the fork or the ownership-unsettled vocabulary (takeover-or-fork before F-084), refuse |
| any other definite | roll the removal back inside the still-open transaction, and refuse |

Two properties hold the design together. **Continue only on proof**: no arm proceeds
with an
ownership question outstanding, which is why the restore gate can wait for the settlement
rather than needing a second admission barrier. And **one property, not an
enumeration**: the
commit's own register cleanup performs record writes, so rather than threading classified
results back through three helpers, the caller asks the *session* whether anything it did
leaves the connection unable to serve — `recordStateBlocksServing`, one lock-safe
accessor over
"unresolved write **or** armed rejection". That covers writes this code never named, including
ones a later change adds; it does not cover a pre-store refusal, and does not need to, because
none of those is evidence about ownership.

The CONNECT may resolve inside its own transaction where a SUBSCRIBE or UNSUBSCRIBE
defers to
the readLoop, and the difference is structural: `mqttResolveAfterPacket` runs *after*
`mqttProcessConnect` returns, but the resume work inside it needs a resolved session
first. The
CONNECT already resolves once for that reason before its accept transaction is opened; this
ambiguity arises *inside* that transaction, so the in-transaction resolver body is the form
that fits. The old call at this site could never work — it took the ownership gate the CONNECT
already holds and needed a fence the frame already owned, so it reported "unresolved" without
attempting anything.

Every refusing arm owes the restore verdict its terminal, and owes it as
`abandonRestoreGate` **alone**: post-CONNACK there is no licence to discard the Will or clear
acceptance. Waking the withheld deliveries is the point — parked, they wait out their bound,
find the session detached, and can no longer record themselves as never transmitted, so their
redelivery reaches the client marked DUP.

### The pre-CONNACK refusal signal

A v5 client is told **why** its resume was refused, at every refusal in the
**post-accept-save, pre-success-CONNACK window** — which is the scope of this claim, and
exits earlier in the CONNECT are a stated residual in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`. In that window
the sites are: register recovery, the shared-ownership disposing, unresolved
and
local arms, the **plain QoS 1/2 reconciliation verdicts**, the **lifetime grant**, and the
restore path that started this. Without it a permanently unrestorable session is an endless
silent close, and a clean start — the recovery — is a choice the client can only make if it
knows there is something to recover from.

Two limits are structural rather than chosen. It is **v5 only**: a 3.1.1 CONNACK has no reason
code above 5, so that connection gets a bare close. And the code must be one a CONNACK may
legally carry — `0x89` "Server busy" is permitted and keeps "reconnect and resolve this"
exactly, but `0x8E` "Session taken over" is DISCONNECT-only, so nothing here can tell a client
"stop reconnecting".

**What the client is told is NOT the disposal vocabulary, and that separation is the
mechanism.** The vocabulary's bundled contract — reason code, Reason String, log line, close
state — governs the **DISCONNECT**. The CONNACK is a separate projection, and it has its own
two-value vocabulary (`mqttPreConnackRefusal`):

| Outcome | CONNACK | Reason String |
|---|---|---|
| a body claiming our parent | `0x89` | "session ownership could not be established; try again" |
| any other disposing verdict | `0x83` | "session ownership could not be confirmed" |
| local, unresolved | `0x83` | the step's own diagnostic |

The reason the projection exists rather than forwarding `mqttDisposalTakenOver.reasonStr`
is
that most arms reaching a disposing verdict never established a takeover: the rejection is
also reached when the record could not be read, was absent, did not decode, was released,
or
sat at or below our own base. Sending that text would make this mechanism's whole purpose
false. `preConnackRefusalFor` is exhaustive with no `default`, because a default is exactly
how a new outcome would inherit an ownership claim it has no evidence for; an unlisted
outcome reaches a loud log and a bare close instead.

**One exit stays silent, deliberately**: the **failed success-CONNACK write** has no channel
left to explain itself on — the channel is what failed.

The two sites that used to be silent were silent for a reason about their own code, and both
are closed. `reconcileResumedConsumers` and `applyRequestedLifetime` each **disposed the
session internally before returning**, so a CONNACK the caller enqueued had already lost the
race with the `closeConnection` that disposal schedules; and each collapsed a takeover and
a
fork into one verdict, so the caller could not project the right code even with the ordering
fixed. Both now **report** an outcome and a vocabulary, and one caller-side sequence —
`refuseDisposing` — runs **abort, then signal, then dispose**, in that order, for all three
disposing pre-CONNACK sites (the shared-membership ownership write included). The order is
load-bearing at every step: the abort discards this connection's Will before the close it
schedules can publish it, the signal precedes any scheduled close, and the disposal is last.

**The asymmetry that used to sit here is gone.** The CONNACK still deliberately
**under-claims** — it says ownership could not be confirmed even where a child-shaped body
was observed — and the DISCONNECT and log paths no longer over-claim in the other
direction. F-084 closed that: see "Only a held successor licenses a takeover claim".

The classification behind those two sites is one function, `classifyGatedRecordSave`,
shared by
the reconciliation phase and the lifetime grant: both split 10071 from 10164 identically,
and
written twice a new CAS kind would have to be found twice.
`proveSharedMembershipOwnership` deliberately keeps its own copy — unifying that third
consumer is what let an unclassifiable rejection reach F-078's live-SUBSCRIBE Foreign arm
and
change **Will disposition**, which is a different question and F-084's.

## Only a held successor licenses a takeover claim

`0x8E` "session taken over by a new connection" is the one DISCONNECT reason that tells a
client to **stop reconnecting under this session**. The broker used to send it wherever a
record-derived verdict concluded "not ours" — a record that could not be read, was absent,
did not decode, sat at or below our base, or moved to a body that is merely valid-shaped.
`classifyRecordLineage`'s negative verdict says of exactly those cases that *nothing is
established*, and the broker reported the strongest claim it had.

**The rule.** `mqttDisposalTakenOver` and `mqttDiscardWillOnTakeover` are licensed only by
an in-process, causal, same-client-ID replacement in which this broker holds **both** the
connecting client and a **non-nil** displaced client, under the client-ID ownership gate.
That is `discardTakenOverClient`, whose two callers are the ordinary `processConnect`
takeover and the re-drive's T1b. No persisted record shape is positive successor evidence.

The rule is structural rather than asserted: `mqttDisposalTakenOver` has one reader,
`mqttNotifyTakenOver`, which has one caller.

**Why no predicate over the record works.** The obvious candidate is a usable record above
our base whose digest differs, whose `WID` is non-empty and differs from `ackWID`, and
whose `PWID` names `ackWID`. That identifies a **child-shaped body**, not proven ownership:
`createOrRestoreSession` adopts `WID`/`PWID` without validating provenance, valid-shaped
bodies arrive through unconditional publication, and `storeFramedSessionMsg` replays
acknowledged bytes verbatim. So the claim is not narrowed by a better classifier; it is
withdrawn from every route that cannot hold the successor.

**The fourth vocabulary.** `mqttDisposalOwnershipUnsettled` carries `0x89` and
`mqttReasonStrOwnershipUnsettled`, and says what those routes actually know: this broker
may no longer write the record, and nothing established who may. It is a separate value
from `mqttDisposalForked` on the `mqttDisposalTeardownIncomplete` precedent — same code and
text, different name, because the name is read at the call site as the claim being made —
and it **mints nothing**, because a fork grant is a repair anchored to a record proven to
claim our parent.

Both `0x89` vocabularies therefore share a reason code, which makes two things load-bearing.
The fork bit travels **explicitly** from the classification to the mint rather than being
recovered from `voc.reason`; recovering it would mint a grant for every unsettled record.
And a test that asserts only the reason code can no longer tell them apart, so the claim
assertions read the Reason String too.

**The Will follows the licence, not the vocabulary.** A displacement that cannot prove a
successor may not suppress a Will either — that is the same rule the shared-membership
Forked and Local arms already stated ("neither demonstrates another owner, so neither
disposes and neither discards the Will: suppressing it here would be silent loss"), applied
to the classes that were wrongly excluded from it.

Every disposal that goes through the prepared disposition now chooses exactly one typed
`mqttWillAction` and executes it in a second phase. Two rows of the table below are reached
WITHOUT one and are marked as such: the licensed takeover discards through
`discardTakenOverClient`, and the pre-CONNACK refusal discards in
`mqttAbortAcceptedConnect`. A third route, the remote-persist eviction, takes the
record-derived row's actions from its own tail rather than from a disposition. What the
table states is the ACTION each class owes, not the mechanism it reaches it by:

| Disposal class | Live bound Will | Parked deferred action | Reached through |
|---|---|---|---|
| Licensed takeover | discard, keeping the already-owed-now exception | dropped — the takeover owns it | `discardTakenOverClient`, not a disposition |
| Record-derived: unsettled or forked | consume normally | discharge against its ORIGINAL deadline | the prepared disposition, or the eviction tail |
| Teardown-incomplete | consume normally | discharge | the prepared disposition |
| Pre-CONNACK refusal of the ARRIVING connection | discard — no session was granted | n/a | `mqttAbortAcceptedConnect`, not a disposition |

**Phase 1 / phase 2, and why.** `disposeForeignStateLocked` runs the identity check first,
then extracts the stale client and any parked action and chooses the action — all inside
one `sess.mu` critical section, so a competing disposal cannot observe a half-prepared
object and claim the same Will. Nothing irreversible happens there. Phase 2 executes the
action **outside** `sess.mu`, with the caller's record transaction already closed and the
ownership gate still held: the consume does JetStream work, and the discharge would
self-deadlock on a fence its caller holds. A disposition whose identity check refused
carries `mqttWillActionNone` and discharges nothing.

The ordering at every caller **that holds an ownership gate** is `phase 1 → end record
transaction → Will action → release the ownership gate → notify and close`. Inside
`mqttProcessConnect` that is two defers rather than one tail: the notify/close tail is
registered before the gate-release defer and the Will phase after it but before
`defer endAcceptTx()`, so LIFO produces exactly that sequence.

The remote-persist eviction is the one record-derived route where that ordering does not
apply, and its contract is the **inverse**. It decides under `as.mu`, detaches inside that
section, and runs its Will action from a tail that executes once the record token and every
lock are released — so no ownership gate is held there at all, and asserting one would
assert something false. What it shares with the gated callers is the fence: the record
transaction is CLOSED before the action, because both the discharge and the consume do
JetStream work. Two oracles pin the two contracts, and each would fail if given the other's
route.

**The five Will-loss routes this closed.** Four were real losses and one is correct:

- `disposeForeignStateLocked` took the parked deferred action and dropped it.
- A detached client's ordinary close publishes only an **immediate** Will
  (`mqttPublishOwedWill`), so an owed-delayed one was dropped.
- The remote-persist eviction detached, notified and closed while performing **no** Will
  action at all.
- The takeover discard reached classes that had demonstrated no takeover.
- `mqttAbortAcceptedConnect` discards the **arriving** connection's Will. Correct and
  unchanged: no session was granted to it. This is why the rule above is scoped to the
  *displaced* session's Will — on a pre-CONNACK disposing arm both are in play and they
  take opposite actions.

`dischargeDeferredWill` is extracted from `applyDeferredDisconnect`'s lower half and is
Will-only: no clear, no save, no purge, no re-park, and no record fence.
`applyDeferredDisconnect` calls it too, so the discharge exists once. Re-park is
deliberately absent — phase 1 has already deresidented the session, so putting the action
back would strand it where no pass can reach it.

**What this costs, and it is a real cost.** A genuine remote takeover — another broker
really did take the session, and this broker sees its record — is now reported `0x89` and
its old connection's Will is **published** rather than suppressed. The client is invited to
reconnect against permanently unclassifiable state. That is accepted deliberately: this
broker cannot tell that case apart from a forged, replayed, unrelated or malformed record,
and telling a live client to stop reconnecting on evidence that establishes nothing is
worse. Stated in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`.

## Outbound in-flight registers

`pendingPublish`, `pendingPubRel`, `cpending` and the packet-identifier allocator
were memory-only. A same-process reconnect therefore re-sent a started QoS 1/2
delivery under its original packet identifier, but a broker restart, a failover, or a
resume on another broker did not: the tracking maps came back empty, the delivery
looked unstarted, and the redelivery went out with DUP set under a **freshly
allocated** identifier — which a client is entitled to read as a new message.
[MQTT-4.4.0-1] requires both sides to re-send unacknowledged PUBLISH *and* PUBREL
packets under their **original** identifiers, so this bounded the broker's
exactly-once guarantee to one process lifetime, for QoS 1 as much as QoS 2.

An **in-flight register** supplies the missing durable fact
(`internal/mqtt/inflight_register.go`): one small record per started PUBLISH-phase
delivery on `$MQTT_inflight`, at `$MQTT.inflight.<idHash>.<gen>.<PI>`, naming the
source durable and stream sequence it came from.

The register records that an identifier is ALLOCATED; whether a PUBLISH was ever put
on the client's socket is a second fact, and the **outgoing DUP flag** is derived from
it and nothing else ([MQTT-3.3.1-1] requires DUP=0 on a first delivery; deriving it
from the JetStream delivery count was the defect F-072 closed, because a copy offered
and refused before tracking raises that count without any PUBLISH reaching the client).
The register is created BEFORE its PUBLISH, so it cannot itself carry that fact. So the
PUBLISH phase is a **pair**: the same atomic batch that creates the register also
creates a sibling **unsent marker** on `$MQTT.inflight.<idHash>.<gen>.<PI>.unsent`,
whose body names the register's nonce (`inflight_marker.go`). The marker is consumed —
deleted at its exact stream sequence, **with confirmation** — as the durable record of
**send intent**, issued after the frame is admitted and BEFORE the first byte is written;
nothing rewrites either record, and nothing durable happens after the write. That order is
the whole mechanism, and it exists because no protocol can commit a storage write and a
socket write atomically: a record made AFTER the write is exactly the one a crash in
between loses, and the same identifier then retransmits with DUP=0 (holistic finding, F-072).

The pair therefore has two durable states and the DUP flag follows them. **Proven-unsent**
— register and marker both present, the marker naming the register's nonce, and no output
token outstanding on the register (since F-088 a recovered `ActionToken` beside a standing
marker reads possibly attempted, with the marker kept as deletion debt; see "A late
acknowledgement is bound before it arrives") — means no
transmission was ever attempted: a resumed entry is a first transmission, sends DUP=0, and
may be discarded as never sent by Message Expiry or an UNSUBSCRIBE drain's withdrawal.
**Possibly-attempted** — register present, marker authoritatively absent (or standing
beside a recovered output token) — means a
transmission was intended and MAY have happened; recovery cannot tell "intent recorded,
write not begun" from "written, not acknowledged", because the durable state is identical,
so it treats the two as one: DUP=1 on the next send, the identifier HELD, expiry and
withdrawal REFUSED (`provenUnsentReleasableLocked`), and release only by the client's own
terminal acknowledgement or by the session's destruction. The durable record proves intent,
never a physical write, and is never described as proving one. A crash between intent
confirmation and the write is thus answered DUP=1 — the accepted conservative reading: a
spurious DUP=1 is harmless to a conforming receiver (§3.3.1.1, DUP is not a receiver-side
dedup signal), while DUP=0 on a genuine retransmission is the wire-visible error this item
removes. The binding acceptance seam (a crash after the pair confirms and before the send,
T2) sits BEFORE intent and still yields DUP=0.

Three consequences follow. **Admission precedes intent**: the sender frames and size-checks
the PUBLISH first (`mqttPreparePublishMsgTo`), after the Sparkplug and Subscription
Identifier rewrites and against the Topic Alias table — an established alias can make a
packet fit where the full-topic frame would not — and only an admitted frame records
intent, so a Maximum Packet Size refusal never leaves a transmitted-looking register for a
PUBLISH that never left. The verdict is monotone (a binding is never reassigned, a fresh
binding frame is always larger than plain), which is what lets the alias commit and the
`queueOutbound` stay atomic under `cc.mu` at transmission (`mqttEnqueuePreparedPublishMsgTo`)
without holding that lock across the JetStream round-trip between them. **An intent delete
is classified, never read back**: confirmed (including already-gone) proceeds; a definite
refusal writes nothing and leaves the entry proven-unsent; an ambiguous result writes
nothing, releases nothing, and holds the entry **unresolved** with its captured sequence
until the next offer re-attempts the same exact delete (`intentUnresolved`). The
classification is of the WHOLE confirmed operation, and ambiguity dominates within it: an
attempt that got no answer may have landed, and no later attempt's definite refusal proves
it did not, so "lost, refused, refused" is ambiguous, never definite. And "definite" is
narrow by construction (`mqttDeleteRefusedBeforeMutation`): only an explicit refusal the
server makes before touching the store — no JetStream, no such stream, a malformed request
— proves the delete changed nothing. A generic delete failure does not, because the file
store can record the deletion and then fail (a compaction error persists as its write error
and is reported on every later attempt too), so `JSStreamMsgDeleteFailedF` is ambiguous.
**Six routes release an outbound identifier as never transmitted, and all six ask the
same `provenUnsentReleasableLocked`**: Message Expiry on the plain callback, Message Expiry
on the shared-QoS 2 affine callback, an UNSUBSCRIBE drain's withdrawal, the **resume reap**
(F-100), and — since F-101 — a consumer teardown's **purge** and the **void staging** that
runs before it. A teardown establishes what the TEARDOWN owes; it never establishes that
the client completed, so `purgeConsumerPendingLocked` RESERVES a possibly-attempted entry
rather than deleting it: identifier and Receive Maximum slot held, its register left
uncollected so the ladder cannot destroy the owner slot the exchange still needs, and no
settle parked, because every parked continuation frees the identifier. Only the source
mapping goes, with the consumer being destroyed — the `regForeign` arm's shape, and
deliberately unlike the resume reap, which keeps its mapping because a live callback may
still hold the payload. `voidRegistrationsLocked` records its never-transmitted verdict
only for a register that is actually proven unsent.

**A staged verdict FENCES its own register**, which is what makes it true rather than
merely recorded first. `beginSendLocked` refuses a send under a register whose nonce carries
one. Staging decides before a send, so without the refusal a delivery callback already past
the subscription barrier could open a section, delete the marker and transmit — leaving the
membership-removal save carrying a known-false verdict for an exchange the client now holds,
and recovery reads such a verdict as licence to free the identifier. It is keyed on the
NONCE, so a verdict restored from the record cannot fence a fresh allocation, and a
rollback's existing `unvoidRegNonces` restores admission in the same step that withdraws
the verdict — which is why the fence is keyed on the verdict rather than on the
subscription's closure. The fence is unconditional; what lifts it for a register recovery
restores as possibly attempted is the verdict's retirement on that restoration (F-088,
"A late acknowledgement is bound before it arrives"), never an exception in the fence.

**A retained send is released where its non-transmission is PROVEN, and nowhere else.** It
has no register and no source at all (R6), so no durable pair can say whether its PUBLISH
went out, and `provenUnsentReleasableLocked` is structurally false for one. F-091's
departure property supplies the proof instead: every buffered frame is WRITTEN by a
flusher, or DETACHED and then TRANSFERRED to a same-sid replacement or ABANDONED — never
both and never neither — so `releaseRetainedSendAbandonedLocked` is the one site that may
release the pending entry. It is keyed on the frame's ALLOCATION nonce rather than its
identifier, because a disposition can arrive after a `clear()` has re-minted that
identifier under another exchange. `dropUnredeliverableRetained`, which dropped every
retained entry on resume, is DELETED: having no way to redeliver is a fact about this
broker, never evidence that the client completed, and dropping the entry freed an
identifier a QoS 2 receiver could still be holding awaiting PUBREL. Resume now reads no
retained transmission state at all, which is also what removes the window between a
flusher's `queueOutbound` and its `endRetainedSends` (F-101). **Recovery applies the same
distinction to a source that can never be re-offered**, which is TWO classifications and
not one: *Complete* — acknowledged, or authoritatively absent while its consumer still
holds interest, including a message reaped by its own Message Expiry TTL — and *Lost*,
the consumer authoritatively gone, which on an interest-retained stream took the messages
it held with it. Neither is thereby finished on the receiver's side, so both are routed
through the marker phase rather than dropped on the source alone: proven-unsent (marker
present, no recovered output token) is consumed as the lost-delete register it is, while
possibly-attempted (marker absent, or standing beside a recovered output token and kept
as deletion debt) is RESERVED — installed transmitted, its identifier held — until the
client's acknowledgement or the session's end releases it.

**The marker is the license, and the classification is not.** A confirmed marker delete
strictly precedes any write, so a marker still naming a register that carries no output
token proves the PUBLISH never went out (a holder whose token is still outstanding can
delete it and write after the read, which is why recovery's arm asks
`mqttRecoveredProvenUnsent`, F-088); the client holds nothing under that identifier, and
identifier continuity is owed
only to an exchange the client may be holding. The source classification answers the weaker
question of whether anything can re-offer the delivery, and a wrong answer to *that* costs
nothing for an exchange that stays never-transmitted — a later re-offer simply allocates a
fresh identifier with DUP=0, which is what a message that never went out is owed. It
confers no authority over a concurrent sender; that fence does not exist within a
generation, and this arm neither claims nor needs one. Extending the arm from Complete to
Lost is what gives F-102's stranded reservation a release edge: before it, a proven-unsent
pair whose consumer had gone was restored with its marker, its mapping and **no ack
subject**, and since the resume reap only scans entries that have one, nothing ever
re-examined it.

**Only *Complete* drops the source mapping.** A finished source is re-offered by nothing,
so a mapping for it would only mislead the drain and finalization paths that read
`cpending`. *Lost* is a fact about one completed consumer lookup, and a payload already
dispatched to a callback is not retracted by the consumer's deletion — with no mapping,
that callback reaches `trackPublish`, takes the new-delivery branch and mints a SECOND
identifier for one source. So a Lost reservation keeps its mapping, exactly as the live
resume reap's does and for the same reason, at the stated cost that drain enrolment can
see it. The consume arm and the mapping install therefore key on deliberately different
tests, and neither is a restatement of the other.

**The routing decision is taken at ONE site, and its position is the mechanism.** A
register is routed for source cleanup only after every exclusion above has had its chance
to divert it — a pure cancellation, an affine register its own source does not prove, a
drain-AMBIGUOUS source, a drain-OWNED record and a retirement each leave the loop first.
The recovered register therefore carries a *routed* verdict whose zero value means "not
routed", and the consume arm reads that verdict rather than re-asking the source cache.
Re-asking would preserve every ordinary case and silently delete all five exclusions —
most visibly the drain-owned one, which is excluded by nothing else.

**The resume reap is the live counterpart of that recovery arm, and it was the route that
did not ask.** `resendPendingRedelivery` reconciles the resume snapshot against
`$MQTT_msgs`, and an entry whose message is below the stream's first sequence or confirmed
absent by an exact lookup has nothing left to redeliver. It used to be untracked outright,
which released the identifier **and the Receive Maximum slot** — and the source vanishing
is a fact about what this broker can still do, never evidence about what the client holds.
Durable per-identifier occupancy does not protect that slot: a later allocation of a
DIFFERENT identifier transmits. Now the candidate is decided under one uninterrupted
`sess.mu`, in three arms. **Identity first**: an entry whose `(durable, sequence)` no
longer matches what the scan classified belongs to a delivery this pass never looked at and
is left alone, because a packet identifier is not a delivery identity. Then the predicate:
proven-unsent is released, and everything else is RESERVED — identifier and slot held, out
of the NAK set, nothing written. No durable write is issued in any arm, and the
condemnation this site used to perform is gone rather than kept beside the gate: the
predicate refuses an open send section under that same lock, so no continuation can be owed.

**Unlike recovery's reservation, the live one KEEPS its `cpending` source mapping**, and
the difference is the premise rather than the classification. Recovery runs pre-CONNACK,
before any source interest exists, so nothing can offer that source again. The reap runs
after restoration, where a callback may already hold the payload — source absence does not
retract a dispatch already in flight — and with the mapping gone `trackPublish` would take
its new-delivery branch and hand that callback a **second identifier for one source**. With
the mapping intact it takes the redelivery branch and reuses the identifier the client
already holds, carrying whatever DUP the entry's own state says. The cost is that the
retained mapping is visible to drain enrolment: the claim floor runs before `recoverDrains`
and so gets a pruning *opportunity* in the same resume, while a claim staged by a live
UNSUBSCRIBE after the reap gets none before the next one. Neither is a guarantee —
`recoverDrains` skips a barrier-unresolved durable, retains a claim on an indeterminate
lookup, and restores what it staged on a definite save failure.

**The pass's redelivery budget is read where it is used, not where the pass starts.** A
reserved entry leaves the NAK set while still holding its slot, and a PUBREC arriving
during the scan replaces a PUBLISH with a PUBREL, so `maxAck`, the not-NAK'd count and the
in-flight PUBREL count are all observed under one lock immediately before the arithmetic —
refreshing one against a stale other is worse than refreshing none. The NAK set is filtered
there too, on the same `(durable, sequence)` identity, so an entry acknowledged since the
scan is neither NAK'd as that old delivery nor charged as one. That is coherent accounting
at the capture point, not atomic admission through the sends that follow. **An oversize
refusal of a possibly-attempted exchange RETAINS it** — entry, register, source and
identifier — because refusing this attempt proves nothing about earlier ones and the
receiver may hold the identifier; it is re-offered and refused at AckWait cadence until the
client's acknowledgement or the session's end, a stuck identifier being the price of never
re-minting a held one (`oversizeDisposalAllowed`). Which observation licenses which action
is decided in exactly one operation-aware boundary, `mqttDecideMarker`, keyed by whether
the caller is deriving send state, replacing an occupant, recording intent, cleaning after
protocol evidence, or reaping — the marker's counterpart to `mqttValidateInflightShape`. On
resume the register enumeration runs first and the marker enumeration second: a marker
whose register the snapshot did not yet see loads its sibling authoritatively rather
than being read as an orphan, and an absent marker is never interpreted against the
cached register snapshot — the register's own subject is reread and that reread decides
(rows 5-9). A pass that ends in Reclassify is re-run, and the custody rewrites it landed are
not lost to the re-run: each pass's rewrite chain is seeded from every earlier pass of the
same invocation (`resumeLineage`), so a live entry left at a sequence the discarded pass
moved through is still advanced to the current one rather than aimed at a dead sequence its
own cleanup would then preserve as a stranger's. An identifier whose marker cannot be read
as present-and-ours or as authoritatively absent is held **marker-opaque**: reserved,
unsendable, its source mapping dropped and the identifier space marked incomplete until a
resume reads the pair whole. The generation teardown reaps registers then markers under one
watermark, and the orphan sweep parses marker subjects and reaps each against an
authoritative read of its sibling. Terminal cleanup removes the register **first and
provably**, then the marker: because the reap reads the register's own subject to classify
the sibling, a fire-and-forget register delete that has not yet landed is still present at
that read, classifies as a live same-exchange sibling and *preserves* the marker. So that
one delete is CONFIRMED before the reap, and a delete that cannot be confirmed reaps no
marker at all: both halves are left to the sweep rather than acted on without proof.
Recovery's drop loop is deliberately different — it keeps a fire-and-forget delete for an
unverdicted nonce and reaps opportunistically, so its marker is removed only where the
sibling reads authoritatively absent. `$MQTT_inflight` therefore requires
`AllowAtomicPublish` (the pair
is one batch), refused at startup if absent — the ten broker-owned streams are one
recreation unit (F-066), never migrated. Keyed by the identifier, so the
create-only CAS is an allocation arbitration as well as a record, and so one
incarnation is bounded at 65 535 subjects — the same bound, for the same paging
reason, as the inbound hold walk. The record carries an immutable nonce, because the
subject is reused by later exchanges on the same identifier and a stream sequence is
therefore not an identity.

It is a stream of its own for two reasons that are not preferences: `$MQTT_out` is
interest-retained, so a store with no consumer succeeds and keeps nothing, and a
register has no consumer by design; and a per-delivery write to the session record
would put every outbound QoS 1/2 message behind the record CAS and the record fence.

**A PHASE AND AN ACTION ARE TWO COLUMNS, NOT ONE** (F-098). The phase says how far the
exchange has got; the **action token** says whether a transmission is live, and it is
legal in every phase. They used to be one axis — `pubrel_sending` and
`pubrel_terminal_draining` encoded "a PUBREL write is out" as a state — and that is why a
PUBLISH transmission had no durable fence at all: there was no phase to put it in. Both
composite states are deleted; a persisted record carrying either is an unsupported shape
and is refused.

| phase | what it means | action token |
|---|---|---|
| `publish` | PUBLISH sent or about to be, not yet acknowledged | present while a PUBLISH write is out |
| `publish_terminal` | the PUBLISH phase ENDED without a PUBREL exchange: PUBACK, or a FAILED PUBREC | may survive the acknowledgement; the release waits for it |
| `pubrel_intended` | past PUBREC, canonical record **owed**. Written BEFORE the store | none — materialization needs custody, not an action |
| `pubrel_ready` | past PUBREC, the canonical record exists and the slot names it | present while a PUBREL write is out |
| `pubrel_terminal` | PUBCOMP observed; what remains is idempotent cleanup and the exact deletion | may survive PUBCOMP; the release waits for it |

`publish_terminal` exists so that **terminal authority is a fact on the record rather than
an inference from a missing PUBREL**. Without it an acknowledged QoS 1 exchange left an
ordinary `publish` slot that no peer, and no restart, had anything positive to release on
— so it would reserve its identifier forever, and at Receive Maximum 1 that stops the
session receiving anything at all.

`pubrel_intended` exists because **JetStream batches are per stream**, so the PUBREL record
on `$MQTT_out` and the slot on `$MQTT_inflight` can never be written atomically. What can
be made safe is the ORDER: the phase is written first, so a crash between them leaves a
slot that says "past PUBREC, canonical record owed" instead of a `publish` slot a peer may
legitimately reap. It is a **monotone phase, never a holder-exclusive action** — a
holder-exclusive intent would be permanently pinned by a crash between the CAS and the
store, with no other broker able to advance it.

**`Acq`, the transmission identity.** The record carries a counter incremented by every
action acquisition and **never reset** — not by a drain, not by a phase advance. An
exchange's authority identity is the triple **(slot subject, `Nonce`, `Acq`)**, and every
release, deletion and capacity free CASes on the whole triple. Nothing else could play the
role: `Nonce` is per-allocation, `Lin` per-obligation, the send nonce is process-local,
the action token is erased by a drain, and the slot's stream sequence also moves for
custody writes and retirement marks. The binding rule is what makes it sound: an
acknowledgement is stamped with the identity **already bound to that handler's exchange**,
never by fetching the slot's current counter after the packet arrives — otherwise A
receives an old acknowledgement, pauses, and stamps it with B's newer counter. A retry may
refresh the CAS *sequence*; it may never refresh the evidence identity. The acquisition
that advances the counter is fenced on the base it READ, inside the CAS: that helper
refreshes its base on every internal attempt, and a peer's acquire-and-drain in between
leaves custody unchanged and the token clear — so without the fence the write lands at a
counter the caller never saw, and its entry records an identity the slot never carried. An
acquisition ADOPTED after a lost response carries the same binding rule as a seen one: it
reconciles the landed counter into the section and its entry, because an entry left at the
pre-acquisition counter makes its own acknowledgement read as a successor's — and the
terminal cleanup it owes is then dropped rather than performed. Write-backs into the entry
are MONOTONIC and token-scoped: successive transmissions of one allocation share nonce and
subject, so an older drain resuming after a newer one completed would otherwise put the
earlier counter back.

**ONE record owns the identifier for the exchange's whole life.** That is the change.
Before it, the identifier's authority MOVED at the PUBREC handoff — from the register to
the correlated PUBREL record on `$MQTT_out` — leaving it described by two independently
changing durable sets read by two non-transactional scans, with nothing able to arbitrate
between them. F-092's whole population is a stale record meeting an identifier a later
exchange now owns, and five plan revisions tried to arbitrate the two sets before the
answer turned out to be that there must only ever be one claimant.

**Why a re-read is not a fence.** Broker A reads the slot, pauses before transmitting;
broker B performs the peer terminal release; a later exchange installs a new slot under
that identifier; A resumes and transmits the stale PUBREL. `sendsInFlight` is
process-local and fences nothing across brokers, so moving the read closer to the write
only narrows the window. A successful CAS is different in kind: it establishes an
invariant that REMAINS TRUE THROUGH the action. While an action is live, custody
transfer, slot replacement, ordinary deletion, identifier release and terminal deletion
all refuse, and only the action's own holder may drain it.

**ONE RELEASE AUTHORITY, AND IT IS A TOTAL FUNCTION** (F-098's C-IV).
`mqttSlotReleaseAuthority` is the single answer to "may this caller dispose of, or free
capacity at, this slot, under the identity it is acting for?". Recovery, the drain and
every release used each to decide that separately, and three review rounds dismantled the
contract while it was stated as an enumeration of slot shapes, because each round found a
shape that matched no row. A total function with a **reserving default** cannot fail that
way: a shape nobody enumerated falls to the last arm and holds the identifier.

The precedence is fixed:

1. **Withhold** — unreadable, an unsupported state, any indeterminate evidence, or a
   caller acting for an identity the slot no longer carries.
2. **Withhold** — **any live action token, including the caller's own.** Not symmetry: a
   broker owning a PUBLISH action whose socket write is still running could otherwise
   observe terminal evidence, disregard the token because it is "ours", and free the
   identifier while the writer can still transmit. A holder ending its own action uses the
   drain disposition, which is a different operation from a release.
3. **Terminal** — a durable terminal phase this broker WROTE, `publish_terminal` or
   `pubrel_terminal`, identity-bound. Which disposition applies is the phase's business,
   and the two owe different follow-on obligations.
4. **Proven-unsent** — a `publish` slot whose unsent marker naming THIS allocation stands
   **and no contradicting retirement**. The marker is the ONLY non-transmission evidence
   (F-088): neither the register's `Cancelled` bit nor the session's persisted cancellation
   verdict is, because a cancellation says what a teardown decided, not what reached the
   socket, and it is written over transmitted deliveries too. `Retired` dominates: a
   PUBLISH can reach the client and be successfully PUBREC'd while the slot still says
   `publish`, and retirement is backed by the client's own PUBREC, so treating it as
   unsent authority frees an outstanding exchange. Checked ABOVE this arm and separate from
   it, a positively identified pending cancellation fence (`cancel_origin:
   pending-create`, the sparse form) yields `mqttSlotPendingFenceAuthority`, which licenses
   only the fence's own disposal and says nothing about any exchange (see "One door").
5. **Reserved** — otherwise. The identifier and its Receive Maximum capacity are held.

**`Reserved` means "no release authority", not "no protocol progress".** Owed
materialization, legitimate PUBREL transmission, custody transfer and phase advance are
separate permissions and are not gated on this function; conflating them would turn a
safety default into a liveness bug.

Evidence is assembled by one loader from ONE observation — the record and the marker
(compared by nonce, so a predecessor's marker on the same subject is never borrowed) — or
it is indeterminate. The questions the
function deliberately does not answer, because they are different questions: source
classification, marker validation, affine cleanup obligations, and generation-discard
authority. None of those may independently conclude that a live incarnation's client
obligation has ended — **with one enumerated exception, stated below, which is the
experimental affine disposer.**

**THE VERDICT IS NOT RELEASE EVIDENCE** (F-088, superseding F-103's coverage rule here).
Until F-088 the loader admitted a cancellation verdict that the session record had
provably saved (membership in `cancelledRegNonces` whose insertion revision was covered),
since a merely STAGED verdict was a proof no restart could see. Since F-088 the loader
reads no verdict at all, so the question no longer arises in this function; the verdict
keeps its other readers (recovery's genuine-cancellation arm, which acts on it only while
the allocation's marker stands and no output token is outstanding on the register, and
the cancelled-reservation release paths).

**THE AUTHORITY IS SPENT, NOT MERELY CONSULTED.** Each release-class disposition names the
authority that licenses it — `mqttSlotAuthorityPermitsRelease`, total over both enums with
a refusing default — and the authority travels as a value bound to the observation that
produced it: the subject, the exchange identity and the sequence it was computed against.
A caller whose record moved beneath it therefore cannot spend an authority computed for a
different observation. That table is narrower than "destructive": replacing a PUBLISH is
bound to the transmission identity but installs a **successor** rather than freeing an
identifier, so no authority licenses it as a release. The invariant is *Reserved permits no
RELEASE*, never *Reserved permits no destructive disposition*.

**AND A DELETE THAT REMOVED NOTHING IS NOT A RELEASE** (F-104). An exact-sequence delete
reports success for an ALREADY-ABSENT sequence, so a same-identity rewrite landing between
a caller's load and its delete is indistinguishable from a removal. One extracted
confirmation re-reads the subject afterwards and partitions it four ways: **absent** (the
one answer that frees an identifier), **another occupant** (this caller's own obligation is
discharged, but the successor's identifier is not its to free), **our own record,
rewritten** (the release is unconfirmed), and **unreadable or indeterminate** (an absence
is never guessed). On this release path the cancellation verdict is retired only against
a proven absence: a retained verdict is re-derivable evidence, a forgotten one is
unrecoverable, and forgetting it over a survivor left that register permanently
unreleasable. (Recovery's acting restoration of the same allocation as possibly attempted
also retires it, as superseded rather than released: F-088, "A late acknowledgement is
bound before it arrives".)

**AND EACH ENDING NAMES ITS OWN LICENCE** (F-104's reclamation half).
`markInflightRegisterCancelled` ends five ways, and a bare `error` collapsed them into one
`nil` that both callers answered with "the tombstone is on the register itself" — true of
exactly two. `mqttRegCancelOutcome` names them, with a **refusing zero value** so an arm
added without classifying itself inherits no licence, and the two questions are kept apart
because they diverge:

| Outcome | Retires the verdict | Frees the identifier | Because |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Stored` | yes | no | the tombstone is on the record and survives a restart |
| `AlreadySet` | yes | no | the same tombstone, from an earlier attempt |
| `Absent` | yes | no | the register is gone, so the verdict describes nothing |
| `Superseded` | yes | no | `matchesRecord` compares identity, so a mismatch is a different exchange and ours is provably gone; the successor's identifier is not ours |
| `Refused` | no | no | fails closed; the caller keeps the nonce verdict |

**NO outcome frees an identifier.** That needs a captured exclusion instance and an all-bind
absence proof, which this function has neither of; it belongs to the reclamation pass.

**NO OUTCOME TURNS ON A CLAIM STAMP (F-105 7b).** An earlier `ForeignShared` outcome
retired the verdict only against a strictly newer foreign claim on a shared register.
Ordinary ownership — shared registers are ordinary since 7a — is no longer a register
claim's to decide: a cancellation is an owner-dependent decision whose tombstone is
written under the deciding connection's entitlement (see "Resume restores from the
inventory, and ownership is the entitlement's"), so a displaced connection's cancellation
is refused before it writes, and the outcome, and its boundary, are deleted.

**IDENTIFIER EXCLUSION IS NOT ENTRY RETENTION.** Preserving the identifier and preserving
the actionable, capacity-charging entry are different operations, and conflating them
breaks three contracts: the drain's cancellation handoff needs its entry REMOVED (the
cancellation records only a nonce verdict, so a retained entry lets the returning store's
confirmation admit a delivery the drain does not claim), the staged recovery release is a
real release with no replacement, and a registerless retained frame can never obtain a
durable confirmation and would hold its Receive Maximum charge forever.

So every removal site removes exactly what it removed before — actionability, source
identity, admission and capacity all unchanged — and hands the IDENTIFIER's exclusion to
`slotOwed`, the sixth liveness term on the send hold. It reserves the identifier and
charges no capacity, exactly as the acknowledged exchange's terminal hold does, and because
all six hold-deletion sites already ask the shared liveness predicate, an exclusion makes
the hold undeletable at every one of them by construction. `bumpPI` and the retained
allocator both consult that registry and never the durable register, which is why the
exclusion is effective against the allocation route that touches no durable state at all.

The exclusion is a **conjunction of binds**, each naming an exact subject — which carries
the generation, so an absence in the current generation cannot discharge one retained for
an older — and an exchange, or EMPTY where the site cannot name the occupant (a staged
recovery release, `commitRecoveryReleaseLocked`, is exactly that shape). A merge ADDS a
bind and never rewrites one, in both directions: adoption requires a unanimous,
non-empty, matching identity, so
any empty bind or two differing nonces makes the exclusion permanently un-adoptable, and a
lift requires a proven absence for EVERY bound subject at the instance the observation was
taken. Binds are a set, so an equivalent restriction is not duplicated; distinct
restrictions still accumulate, and that residual is disclosed rather than bounded away.
A recovered exchange ADOPTS its own exclusion atomically with its entry install, or it
would be refused its own transmission by a reservation it owns.

**WHAT LIFTS ONE, exhaustively.** Three routes, and only three. Terminal cleanup lifts an
exclusion whose subject it has proven EMPTY — the PUBLISH side in
`recoverPublishTerminalSlot` and the PUBREL side in `finalizeTerminalSlot`. Recovery's drop
loops lift through `settleRecoveryDropExclusion`, which is the same proof applied to a
candidate whose staged delete has just run, and which the proven-unsent disposal shares.
Recovery's adoption above is the third. **The reclamation pass is the fourth**, and it is
the subject of the section below. Every one of them captures the exclusion instance
BEFORE its confirming read, so a restriction installed or strengthened while that read was
out is not cleared by an absence that never observed it — and because a REASSERTION of an
identical bind advances that instance too, an absence observed before one cannot discharge
it. A successor
occupying the subject deliberately lifts NOTHING: that is precisely the case the exclusion
exists for.

**PROMPT RECLAMATION: THE FOURTH ROUTE IS A TRIGGER, NOT A NEW PROOF.** The first three
routes are each an edge some *other* operation happens to cross, so an exclusion no such
edge reaches again was never re-examined — and because `bumpPI` skips a reserved identifier,
accumulated exclusions eventually cover the identifier space and stop QoS 1/2 delivery to
the session outright. `exclusion_reclaim.go` re-attempts **the same proof** on a bounded
cycle while connected: `confirmSlotReleased` on each bound subject, a lift only on
`mqttReleaseEstablishedAbsent`, through the same `liftIdentifierExclusionLocked` with the
same capture-before-read instance protocol. It writes nothing durable and acquires no
authority.

**The install is the arm.** `excludeIdentifierLocked` schedules the continuation at its
single exit, so all 27 install sites are covered by construction rather than site by
site —
the same reasoning that makes `slotExclusionHeldLocked` effective at all six hold-deletion
sites. One continuation per session, never one per identifier. Under `sess.mu` the arming
touches timer state only: the server lookup and `admitWillWorker` take other locks and
happen inside the callback.

**What the absence licenses, and what it does not.** The read-to-lift window is **not**
fenced against a peer, and no claim here says otherwise. The instance counter advances only
inside this session object, and `confirmSlotReleased` observes without locking the subject
against a later creation. Two writers can create on an absent subject —
`markInflightRegisterCancelledPending`'s create-only tombstone CAS, and the allocation pair
— and neither needs to own the connection when it lands. The argument is therefore not
about **who can create** but about **what a post-absence create can describe**: a record's
existence does not put a packet identifier in the client's hands, a **transmission** does.
The tombstone is `Cancelled` by construction, so it describes a delivery that was never
transmitted; the allocation create is untransmitted at create time, and `beginSendLocked`
requires local pending state and connection ownership before anything reaches the wire.
Neither establishes an outstanding client exchange. The three routes above inherit the
identical window and are sound for the identical reason.

**Pacing, and no convergence guarantee.** A pass is bounded in **subject reads**, not in
identifiers, because distinct restrictions accumulate within one identifier. Whole entries
only — partial evidence is invalid once the instance can move — so a final entry of `k`
binds overruns the budget by at most `k-1`, and `k` itself is unbounded. The cursor is a
**packet-identifier value** with strict-successor selection and wrap, never an index into
the sorted set: an index is not stable under mutation, and churn can then starve a
persistent entry by shifting its rank away from the cursor. A pass that met its budget
re-arms at the short delay instead of the cap. The pass **polls**: it terminates when
nothing is held, when this object is no longer the live session, or when shutdown closes
the dispatch gate, and otherwise retries indefinitely with **no eventual-success proof**.
Stopping after N attempts would strand an exclusion a later outside event makes
reclaimable, which is the residual this exists to shrink.

**Nonresidency is not terminal.** A self-rescheduling timer holds the session object, so a
pass that finds `as.sessions[sess.id] != sess` disarms and stops. But the same object comes
back — the expiry fire restores it on a drain timeout, and so do the clean-disconnect and
refused-discard paths — and a restoration installs no new exclusion. `addSession`, the one
function every restoration funnels through, therefore re-enrols the continuation when
anything is still held. The predicate prevents *indefinite* self-rescheduling of a removed
object; it does not promise no timer outlives residency, since removal can happen after the
check.

Three of the five disclosed classes are reached by this route. The withheld PUBREL and the
retired source-completed register are not, and that is the correct direction in both cases:
the record stands, so no absence is provable. `docs/CONFORMANCE.md` carries what is promised
and what is not.

**A SOURCE'S COMPLETION NEVER DISCHARGES THE CLIENT'S HALF**, and recovery's retired arm is
where that bites hardest. A retired register whose source is provably complete CONVERGES —
the retirement is not re-established, or every resume would rebuild it forever — but the
register is **preserved**, not dropped. `Retired` is written on the strength of the client's
own PUBREC, so the PUBLISH provably reached the client; no proof of non-transmission can be
true of such a record, and staging a complete-delete for it produced the worst of both
outcomes: the delete refused, the durable record standing, and nothing reserving its
identifier. The occupancy obligation is therefore carried into the apply phase
**independently of any resident entry**, because a cold resume has none — which is exactly
the population that had the identifier exposed.

**A LOCAL DISPOSAL OF A PROVEN-UNSENT EXCHANGE HANDS OFF TOO.** Message Expiry may drop a
PUBLISH proven never transmitted, and a Maximum Packet Size refusal may discard one; both
exist on the plain delivery path and on the affine one, and all four are the same operation.
The delete each performs is licensed — the exchange provably never went out — but each
ignores the delete's return, because the source acknowledgement must not wait on it. So the
untrack is not the moment the identifier becomes free: the delete can be refused by the
freshness fence when a peer acquired or rewrote the slot, or it can fail. The four sites
therefore share ONE removal, `dropProvenUnsentPublishEntry`, which installs the exclusion
under the same lock as the untrack for a register-backed entry and discharges it only on a
confirmed absence. The population that arrives holding a register is the RECOVERED
never-transmitted entry, restored as a live source and disposed of on a later delivery —
which recovery's own exclusions cannot cover, because at recovery time nothing was removed.

**A DEFERRED SETTLEMENT HANDS OFF BEFORE IT UNTRACKS.** When a removal path condemns an
entry whose send section is still open, `endSendWith` performs the untrack later. For the
settlements whose durable delete may be refused by a freshness fence, fail, or never have
been issued — a subscribe denial, a recovery drop, and the retained purge-teardown arm — the
untrack would otherwise be the moment the identifier became allocatable over a slot nobody
had confirmed gone, so the exclusion is installed under the same lock first. The two
acknowledgement kinds are deliberately excluded: each already holds the identifier through
its own terminal cleanup, which is a stronger claim and carries the cleanup obligation with
it, and adding an exclusion would install a second owner for one identifier. Registerless
retained sends are exempt, tested by the entry's own JetStream backing rather than by its
nonce, because a retained send mints a nonce with no register behind it.

**THE EXPERIMENTAL AFFINE DISPOSER IS THE ONE ENUMERATED EXCEPTION**, and it is currently
only its NON-RESIDENT arm: that arm applies the phase, counter and live-action guards and
mints no release authority. The RESIDENT arm still routes through the consolidated reaper,
so the exception is not uniform across the two, and any claim that both decide their own
release would be false of this tree. The claim above that no other decision may conclude a
client obligation has ended is qualified by exactly this one arm. It is confined to a
population the supported build cannot create: the sweep selects only retired affine
registers, the affine pair is written only with the experimental gate on, and the
production command fixes that gate off. Its consolidation and its fallout belong to
`docs/ROADMAP.md` section P, which owns session-affine shared-subscription QoS 2. Naming
the exception does not make its release sound; it makes the supported-boundary claim auditable.

**THE DRAIN'S RELEASE IS A POSITIVE, IDENTITY-BOUND REQUEST** (F-098's L4). The
UNSUBSCRIBE drain used to release the register and only then open its record transaction,
so a discriminated return value died on a crash — and reversing the two does not help,
because a persisted claim *removal* is an **omission**: the serializer skips unclaimed
sequences, so the identifier and exchange metadata vanish with the entry and recovery is
back to inferring authority from an absence. So the drain's persisted entry gains a `Rel`
member naming `(subject, nonce, acq)`, written and confirmed BEFORE the delete and
captured from the record the release has already loaded and matched. Its absence means no
release is pending; it never means one happened. It is a **request, not evidence** — the
authority function must still authorize the disposition — and it is an obligation of the
drain in four places: it is not pruned with a lost source, it is serialized even when the
claim is already gone, it refuses drain retirement ahead of the save's own removal
discount, and it withholds the dependent acknowledgement. A target whose counter has moved
is **retired as superseded**, never retargeted at the newer counter.

**AN EXCLUSION OWES A CONTINUATION** (F-098). A stored PUBREL refused because a PUBLISH is
live on its slot is correctly refused — nothing may transmit a PUBREL under an identifier
whose PUBLISH is still being transmitted — but a refusal with no continuation is
indistinguishable from a stall: JetStream's AckWait is the only thing left, 30 s by
default, where a client gives up in 10. The schedule reaching it is ordinary, not exotic:
the bytes reach the client, the client answers PUBREC at once, the PUBREC handler stores
the PUBREL, and that record's own delivery callback — an independent goroutine — finds the
transmission still in progress.

So a refusal REGISTERS A WAITER and the transmission's end wakes it, by NAKing the exact
delivery that was refused. Nothing is transmitted, nothing is acknowledged and no state is
stolen: the refusal stands, only its retry clock changes, and the re-offer repeats every
admission check from the beginning.

*A transmission has two halves and admission refuses on either.* The durable half is the
slot's action token; the LOCAL half is `pubIdent`, installed on the send hold when a
PUBLISH section opens and cleared in `endSendWith` behind its exact-token match — a stale
closer clears neither, or it would report a PUBLISH still on the wire as finished. A PUBREL
opener never installs it, which is what stops "a PUBREL is going out" refusing the next
PUBREL. `pubIdent` is NOT a second reservation: `sendReservedLocked` remains the one answer
to whether an identifier is held, and this answers which KIND of transmission holds it.

*The waiter is keyed by the STORED RECORD* — its PUBREL consumer durable and its own stream
sequence — inside the identifier's bucket, with the newest delivery's reply as the value.
Several PUBREL records under one identifier is a supported stale-broker shape, so two
distinct records refused in the same window must each keep a continuation; but a record
AckWait re-offers while the blocker still stands is the SAME waiter at a new address, and
appending it would grow the set for the life of a blocked slot. Only a delivery sequence
that is not older may replace an address, so a slow callback cannot reinstate a stale one.

*Three events end a transmission and each wakes*: the end of a PUBLISH send section, after
BOTH the durable drain and the local release; the drain reconciler, which is the ONLY
remaining event when a drain could not be confirmed and the section has already ended; and
the proven-completion arms of a PUBREL action's own drain, since admission registers
against any live token and a PUBREL action outlives the section that acquired it. Every
wake is CONDITIONED on the combined check — nothing standing on either half — because a
waiter is one-shot: consuming it on a still-blocked identifier spends the very wake the
refusal was promised. The check answers "stands" on any UNPROVEN read, and only the stored
message distinguishes a present-but-unreadable record from the proven absence that has no
durable half.

**A GRACEFUL SHUTDOWN LETS EVERY RECORDED HOLDER FINISH ITS OWN DRAIN** (F-098). A PUBLISH
send section's durable action is ended by a JetStream write, and one still open when the
JSA teardown runs leaves a live token that no later start can attribute — nothing durable
says the holder's process is gone, and inferring it is the steal this design refuses. So
an ordinary restart would strand the identifier, its Receive Maximum capacity and the
session's whole outbound flow. Two mechanisms close it, both inside the window where
requests still work (after Phase 3's worker wait, before `quitCh` closes): The final pass
covers BOTH action families: a PUBREL action whose drain could not resolve after worker
admission closed is handed to the same shutdown registry as a PUBLISH one, because the
alternative is a token the next incarnation cannot tell from a peer's and may not steal.

- *A send barrier.* Both PUBLISH send sections are admitted through
  `admitPublishSend` before anything durable is taken, and release it in a defer registered
  BEFORE the section's own end, so it unwinds AFTER the drain. Shutdown closes the gate and
  joins every admitted section. A refused admission costs a redelivery.
- *An owed-drain registry.* A drain that exhausts its bounded attempts is recorded on the
  server by subject and exact token, independently of the entry maps and of the retry timer
  — the timer's admission closes at Phase 2, and an entry can change phase or vanish. After
  the barrier, shutdown makes one final attempt at each, through the ordinary identity-bound
  drain: it re-reads and re-proves the exact token, preserves phase and `Acq`, and clears
  nothing a peer holds.

Bypassing the JSA's `quitCh` refusal instead was rejected: `quitCh` also stops the
infrastructure workers, so letting a request through it does not produce a working
request/reply path. The residual below still covers abrupt termination and storage that
stays unavailable until the process ends. An acquisition whose CAS lands but whose
response is lost is covered too: the section is armed as the token's holder BEFORE the
CAS, and a reread adopts the exact identity for cleanup, so the section's drain and the
registry see it. Terminal cleanups owed at shutdown are finished in the same phase, after
the drains.

**EVERY DESTRUCTIVE EDGE GOES THROUGH ONE ADMISSION RULE** (F-098).
`mqttSlotDestructionAdmitted` is the single definition of what licenses removing a slot:
the phase must permit the disposition, a destructive disposition must name the
transmission the record carries (C-I), and ANY live action withholds it, ours included
(C-IV arm 2). Two doors apply it: the loading gate, for a caller holding only a remembered
reference, and `reapLoadedRegister`, for a caller holding the record it just read — an
exact-sequence delete is already fenced against any rewrite, which lands at a new
sequence. The gate reports a CLASSIFIED outcome, because deleted, absent and
preserved-under-another-owner are different facts and none of them means the identifier
may be freed. It applies off-session too: the orphan sweep's non-resident arm used a phase
test of its own, and the absence of a LOCAL session is exactly why that is not enough — it
does not prove the absence of an exchange, and a `publish` slot carrying a live token
belongs to a broker that may still be writing it.

**AN ACKNOWLEDGEMENT'S DURABLE HALF IS NEVER DROPPED** (F-098). The client's PUBACK — or a
failed PUBREC — frees the exchange's Receive Maximum capacity at once, but not its
IDENTIFIER: a send-hold term reserves it, from the untrack's own critical section, until
`publish -> publish_terminal -> delete` is confirmed. A step that cannot be confirmed is
handed to a continuation bound to that transmission's identity, which terminalizes an
ordinary `publish` slot only with the acknowledgement's evidence, waits out a live action,
and discharges on a successor without touching it. Recovery reserves a `publish_terminal`
record whose delete it cannot confirm with the same identity-bound hold, never an opaque
entry: an opaque entry makes the whole identifier space incomplete, and the confirmed
delete would have nothing to lift it with. The `publish -> publish_terminal` arrow an
acknowledgement drives is the one phase arrow bound to the FULL transmission identity,
checked on every CAS retry rather than only at the caller's read: a successor acquired in
between carries the same identifier, nonce and source, so an unbound arrow would record
terminal authority — and license the delete that authority permits — for a transmission
the client never answered. The identity that cleanup uses comes from ONE monotone cell per
exchange, shared by the send section and the pending entry and created before any
acquisition can resolve. An acquisition attempt marks the cell pending; only a proof
carried by our own token — a confirmed acquisition, an adopted one, or our own drain's CAS
— publishes an identity, while an absence or a foreign token resolves the attempt and
leaves the standing binding alone. The acknowledgement registers against that same cell
under the session lock, so whichever of the two completes the pair runs the continuation,
