exactly once, and an acknowledgement arriving after the section closed is no different
from one parked inside it. A confirmed release also re-reads its subject, because an
exact-sequence delete reads an already-absent sequence as success and a same-identity
rewrite looks exactly like that. The drain publishes at the moment it OBSERVES our token,
before its own clearing CAS: a CAS that lands and loses its response leaves a cleared
token behind, which is indistinguishable from a foreign one, so a publication that waited
for it would throw away proof the read already had. An unreadable or indeterminate read
publishes nothing and leaves the cell pending, and only the attempt that marked it pending
may settle it.

**A DRAINED ACKNOWLEDGEMENT WAITS FOR ITS SECTION** (F-098). A client can acknowledge a
drain's redelivery while the section that wrote it is still open. The drain's finalize
releases the same register the ordinary delete would, so it is parked on the same event
and the section's settlement runs it: run at the acknowledgement, it would first persist a
release request for a register the writer still owns — a durable obligation the
live-action veto is certain to refuse. The identifier hold is released when the handler
returns, since a drained source never runs the terminal completion that otherwise releases
it. A finalize that loses the record fence retries promptly rather than waiting for a
redelivery that the client's single acknowledgement never causes, and a persisted release
request naming another register is settled against its own identity first, then retired —
never ignored and never re-aimed. A request that survives a restart is enrolled at resume,
in its own identity-bound settlement: every other event that drives a finalize is
source-side — a redelivery, a PUBREL correlation, an in-memory retry — so an expired
source or a deleted consumer would leave the obligation with no clock at all. That
settlement finds its drain by DURABLE rather than through the delivery index, which a
restore drops when it cannot install a subscription. A settled request is consumed by the
SAME save that removes the claim and restored by that save's rollback, because a release
that retires it earlier leaves a retry whose removal was refused with nothing to bind to:
it would take whatever occupies the subject — the successor the release just preserved —
and delete it. A claim removal that DEFINITELY failed schedules its own retry once the
fence is released: "the message stays pending and is redelivered" is only true while the
source can still be delivered, and the register is already gone by then.

**A PUBREC'S INTENT OUTCOME IS CLASSIFIED** (F-098). A definitely unrecorded intent rolls
the PUBREC back to PUBLISH; a confirmed one — including a CAS that landed with its
response lost — keeps the placeholder and enrols L1's materialization; an unresolved one
takes neither continuation and leaves an identity-bound resolver. Recovery enrols a
recovered `pubrel_intended` slot after taking custody, so an owed record never waits for
traffic.

**There is no lease, no TTL and no steal**, and that is not conservatism. A broker can
pause AFTER its own expiry check, let a lease lapse, and resume into the same stale write;
and an MQTT client cannot validate a fencing token, so the external effect is not
fenceable downstream. An abandoned action therefore holds its identifier until its own
holder drains it, the generation is discarded, or an operator intervenes — stated as a
real availability cost in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md` rather than disguised as bounded failover.

The slot is the one authoritative owner; the PUBREL record is evidence and payload, not
a second identifier claimant. At terminal, cleanup performs a complete scan of the
incarnation's PUBREL subject, discharges affine proof before disposing every valid
same-nonce canonical or duplicate record, rereads the slot's freshness fence, and only
then exact-deletes it. It also requires the named source to be non-reofferable for every
terminal slot, not only one whose `Retired` bit is already set. The phase itself is durable
evidence that the payload is past PUBREC; a crash may have landed that phase but not the
later retirement mark, and deleting the slot in that window would let a live source be
sent again. `Complete` and `Lost` are distinct—the latter never licenses reaping a
POSSIBLY-ATTEMPTED PUBLISH-phase exchange, though a PROVEN-UNSENT one it does, on the
marker's evidence rather than the source's—but after PUBCOMP both mean no source can be
re-offered. A live or
unknown source, incomplete scan or failed disposal keeps `pubrel_terminal`.

**Every mutation of a slot goes through one gated path.** `casInflightSlot` loads the
record, proves the occupant is still this exchange, applies the phase gate, mutates
only the caller's own fields and CASes at the sequence the load returned. Rebuilding a
record from remembered arguments — which the mark helpers used to do — silently dropped
every field the rebuilder did not know about, and once a register carries a phase and a
canonical record identity that is a defect rather than a shortcut.

The destructive gate is phase-aware. `Retired` remains what the schema says it is: a fact
about source suppression, not a second encoding of the slot phase. An exact stored PUBREL
is what lets recovery complete `publish → pubrel_ready`; once that explicit phase lands,
delete-complete, delete-never-transmitted and same-source replacement all refuse it.
Cancellation writers load first and may set only their own bit while the current slot is
still PUBLISH; a create-only pending cancellation that loses its first CAS likewise rereads
and refuses to retarget past PUBREC. Consumer teardown uses that cancellation disposition
so a same-exchange rewrite is tombstoned rather than mistaken for another owner's completed
work. The no-resident-session affine sweep applies the same phase rule—absence of a local
object does not make an explicitly past-PUBREC owner disposable.

Deletion is **subject-addressed, identity-authorized and freshness-fenced**, and those
are three separate requirements. The subject is the address (F-034); the exchange nonce
and source authorize; and the observed sequence is a CAS-version check asking whether
the record has moved since the caller decided. A rewrite means a concurrent operation
re-targeted this exchange and reinstalled memory around it, so a stale terminal
continuation **preserves** the record — deleting it would remove the only durable
evidence needed to reconcile that memory once the source completes. F-034
mutation-tested the opposite as M26.

A DUPLICATE PUBREC — the client retransmitting because it never received the PUBREL
([MQTT-4.3.3]) — is recognised by the absence of a `pendingPublish` entry beside a live
`pendingPubRel` one, and it is ANSWERED with a NAK on that stored PUBREL's own delivery.
Two failure modes bound the handling and both were reached in review. Calling
`trackAsPubRel` again overwrites the live entry with an empty placeholder, leaving the
handler with no source and no exchange identity, refusing the store and terminating the
connection on a legitimate duplicate. Returning silently instead leaves the client waiting
for `AckWait` — a configurable interval, and at a Receive Maximum of 1 the session's whole
outbound QoS 1/2 stream stalls behind that one exchange. The NAK re-offers the record at
once so the ordinary delivery path retransmits it with its fencing, send holds and
acknowledgement debt intact, which writing a PUBREL from the read loop would bypass. In the
window before the first delivery attempt the entry has no ack subject yet, and `sendMsg`
declines an empty subject, so the placeholder needs no special case.

A stored PUBREL's headers are decoded as ONE shape, by `mqttDecodeStoredPubRel`, and no
field of it authorizes anything until every field is legal. That includes CARDINALITY and
exact parsing, because the individual header parsers are deliberately lenient for their own
callers: `mqttParsePubRelNATSHeader` discards `strconv`'s error, so `Nmqtt-PubRel:65536`
came back as 65535 — a plausible identifier that is not the one the record names — and
every one of these headers takes the first occurrence, so a record carrying two identifiers
or two source-correlation pairs was accepted with the reader silently choosing one. Both
are refused here rather than resolved by an arbitrary rule, which is the same answer a
duplicate member gets on the register. The identifier must be present
and nonzero, the exchange owner must be valid, and a source correlation may be absent — a
retained send has none — but a PARTIAL one is refused rather than read as uncorrelated,
because uncorrelated **is** the retained shape. The affine reference is deliberately not a
clause: a malformed one does not stop the record being transmitted, since the client is
owed the PUBREL, but it does stop the record being acknowledged away, so it travels as the
tri-state it is and the caller that needs it decides.

The identifier clause is there because leaving it out was a live defect. Drain recovery
indexed the stored PUBRELs by source and confirmed an intent on source plus owner, parsing
each record's identifier and then discarding it — so a record naming the right source and
the right exchange under a **foreign** identifier confirmed the intent as durable proof,
the claim was finalized and the source could be acknowledged while the client's original
exchange had no PUBREL and no evidence left to recreate one from. Recovery now requires the
record's identifier to equal the one the intent persisted; a mismatch is treated as no
record, so the exchange recreates its own.

**Both** readers of that question ask it, and the second one is not redundancy. PUBREL
delivery is asynchronous: the restore gate opens before the PUBREL consumer is installed and
before drain recovery runs, so the same record can reach the delivery callback first. With
the identifier left out of the delivery-side gate it confirmed the drain, persisted the
removal of the source claim, acknowledged that source and forwarded a PUBREL under the wrong
identifier. The gate is WITHHOLDING, not refusing-and-acking, because the record may be the
only copy of whatever it does prove and `AckWait` re-offers it.

**The resume scans the PUBREL records AFTER every batch of its initial register
enumeration, never before (F-099).** A stored PUBREL is evidence ABOUT a register, so an
absence of one may only be read against a register the pass observed EARLIER than the scan.
Read first, the scan answers "is there a record for this exchange" from a moment before
that exchange's own register was looked at, and three consumers act on the answer: route B
(a `publish` slot plus a present exact record), the completion verdict for a `pubrel_ready`
slot, and the retired-ready custody test. The consequences differ but the mistake is one.
The completion verdict is the destructive one: a peer that stored the PUBREL and re-phased
the slot in between had its record reasoned away as absent, the slot advanced to terminal
and the record deleted — the client never received its PUBREL and never sent PUBCOMP, and
nothing reported it. Route B's miss retransmits a payload the client has already answered;
the custody test's leaves predecessor custody standing, which admission refuses forever.

This is the ordering the marker phase already states for its own evidence — the register
enumeration runs first and the per-exchange evidence second, never the other way round
(N-5.6) — and the PUBREL scan was the one reader inverting it.

What the ordering does NOT establish, because a stronger reading of it is false. The scan
is a forward cursor over PRESENTLY RETAINED records, not history, so a record created and
deleted before the cursor reached it is absent from it — which is exactly the supported cut
the completion verdict exists to reap. And it excludes no FUTURE store: a body the pass
adopts LATER, from a custody contest's authoritative reread, is newer than the scan and
therefore takes no verdict from it. Positive terminal authority — a phase this broker
durably wrote — remains F-098's obligation, not this one's.

**A contest's OWNED result is routed by the body it ADOPTED, not by the bucket the walk
sorted the record into (F-099).** The claim contest's moved-and-ours arm adopts the reread
whole, and its withheld arm intercepts only action states and terminal — so a slot a peer
re-phased `publish -> pubrel_ready` between the walk and the landed CAS comes back OWNED
carrying a past-PUBREC body. Routed on the pre-contest bucket it became an ordinary PUBLISH
register: the apply install does not inspect slot state, so the exchange got a
`pendingPublish` entry, and because the source verdict was the pre-contest one a source
still able to re-offer had its `cpending` mapping restored too — re-sending the payload of
an exchange the client had already answered with PUBREC.

The rule is a property, not a site list:

> Every recovery operation that replaces a classified register with an authoritative
> returned body determines its subsequent disposition from that body's phase and
> suppression flags before allowing PUBLISH grouping, send-state derivation, or
> installation.

`mqttSplitNewlyRetired` had long stated the retirement half of this, and its comment named
the retransmission as "the finding itself"; the PHASE half was missing, and at the plain-QoS
2 site BOTH halves were. `mqttSplitAdoptedPastPubRec` supplies the phase half at the two
shared contests and the plain-QoS 2 contest, and the plain-QoS 2 contest also gained the
retirement half it never had. What each site actually routes is established by BEHAVIORAL
regression, with targeted mutation kills over the repaired routing and ordering cases; it
is not established by static inspection. Both questions are asked there because that site
selects its candidates on `publish` AND not-Retired AND not-Cancelled, so either can have
moved under the contest; a `Retired`/`publish` body takes the retirement path — a non-actionable
reservation and source suppression — and is never given an invented `pubrel_ready`
transition, while Retired-and-Cancelled goes the same way because retirement dominates
cancellation and the contest's pure-cancellation branch does not consume it. The two
past-PUBREC contests already satisfied the rule through their own retirement refresh and
explicit terminal/ready routing and are
unchanged; an AST check keeps a reviewed inventory of the five DIRECT call sites,
requires each to name a behavioral test that exists, and refuses any reference to the
contest or a wrapper that appears outside a direct call — a method value cannot be
inventoried, so it fails closed rather than being resolved. **That check is a review prompt,
not a proof**: it does not establish routing correctness, and it does not discover a route
reached through arbitrary indirection. An earlier version tried to inspect each site's
routing structure and was defeated five times running, because "no route can be added
unseen" is a dataflow property and Go indirection is not a syntactically enumerable class.

A split-off adopted body joins the POST-contest past-PUBREC reservations. It keeps its
adopted body, sequence and lineage; it gains source suppression where
`mqttInflightSourceMayReoffer` holds — live and unknown, never merely "not complete", since
a lost source can never be re-offered; it is NOT re-contested, custody being already
established and the contest having no own-claim fast path; and it takes no completion
verdict, because the only evidence available predates its adoption. A body whose record
this pass cannot ask about is OWED. The next resume observes it as `pubrel_ready` in its own
initial register load, where the scan is newer than the observation and the verdict is
legitimate — so a genuinely finished exchange is reaped there, PROVIDED its source proves
complete. A lost or unknown source retains the reservation, which is a held identifier
rather than a lost message, and is the conceding direction.

The **scan does not filter**, and that split is load-bearing. `scanPubRelRecords` returns
every record with its own decode verdict attached, because the dispositions genuinely
differ: a reader that would DERIVE something — register recovery suppressing a source as
past PUBREC, drain recovery confirming an intent — skips an unsupported record, while the
affine-proof walk and the generation teardown must SEE it, since their question is what
evidence is about to be destroyed with the consumer that retains it.

**Seeing it is not acting on it, and that distinction had to be enforced rather than
assumed.** Both affine consumers read the record's affine reference without consulting the
verdict, so an owner-less record carrying a well-formed reference could resolve an
assignment, record `PubRecProven`/`AffineDone` and reap the claim — suppressing or
retracting a real loss on evidence nothing can attribute. Each of the four consumers now
states its own disposition: register recovery and drain recovery SKIP, the proof walk
returns INCOMPLETE (the record may be the very proof it was looking for, so no loss may be
inferred either way), and the teardown reports it and destroys it with its consumer. A
guard requires every consumer of the scan to consult the verdict; it catches an absent
check, and the behavioural tests catch a disabled one. A first version
dropped refused records inside the scan and would have made the teardown destroy an affine
PUBREC proof unread while reporting nothing. For the same reason the decode fills every
field before returning its verdict: a verdict describes a record, it does not license
handing on an undescribed one.

A stored PUBREL carries a **mandatory** `Nmqtt-Q2Owner` header naming its exchange, so
it is evidence about one exchange rather than a claim on an identifier. Absent or
malformed is an unsupported persisted shape and is refused. A retained QoS 2 send has
no register at all (R6), so it mints its exchange nonce into the in-memory reservation
and carries it on the record; its authority is that reservation and nothing durable. Such
a record surviving a restart is refused and left unacknowledged because the live owner
identity died with the process.

A drain's past-PUBREC intent carries the same identity on the session record, as its
`OwnerNonce`, and it is validated before the intent is saved. An intent restored WITHOUT
one names no exchange, so nothing may act on it and nothing may take its place.

**A drain HOLDS its sid while it carries a past-PUBREC intent at all**, and the two reasons
differ only in how they end. `drainSidHoldLocked` is the one question every path that would
occupy a sid asks:

| hold | when | released by |
|---|---|---|
| unusable identity | a restored intent with no identifier or no owner nonce — a shape this broker cannot write, so it exists for records from elsewhere | an operator removing the record; no resume repairs it |
| past-PUBREC intent | any `st.intent`, unqualified | the drain's own **retirement** |

The intent hold is F-094, and it is unqualified deliberately. Adoption removes the drain
from both maps and drops its whole per-sequence state, after which the delivery callback —
which finds a drain through `drainByDur` — no longer suppresses the still-unacknowledged
source, and AckWait re-offers it as a **fresh PUBLISH of an exchange the client has already
answered**, on a different identifier because PUBREC removed the original `cpending` link.
Two narrower predicates were tried and refuted, and `drainSidHoldLocked`'s comment records
both counterexamples: qualifying the intent with `claimed || unclaimUnconfirmed` misses a
finalized intent whose source acknowledgement was lost, because `finalizeDrainDelivery`
clears that guard before the fire-and-forget ack; hoisting the same test to drain level
misses it again at the last outstanding sequence.

**The hold's release is retirement, so retirement has to be reachable.** A drain is retired
when it is DURABLY empty — no sequence `claimed` and none `unclaimUnconfirmed`, which is
strictly stronger than the old `claimedCount() == 0` and stops a teardown running on a
removal whose outcome is unknown — and ownership is proven through `sess.drains[sid]`
rather than through `drainByDur`. That last point is what makes the hold releasable at all:
`restoreDrains` deletes the `drainByDur` entry when a delivery subscription fails to
restore and keeps the sid mapping, so a `drainByDur`-keyed guard could never retire such a
drain and its filter would be refused for the life of the session. Reconciliation sweeps
for retirable drains **twice** — once before its early return, catching one that was
already empty on entry and therefore yields no pruning plan, and once after its save,
catching one its own pruning just emptied. Both keep the barrier `skip` exclusion.

**What the hold does NOT establish.** Retirement releases the sid without proving its
consumer was disposed of: `finishDrainIfEmpty` drops the maps and refunds the charge before
it unsubscribes and issues a `noWait` consumer delete that cannot report failure, and
`processUnsub` does not exclude a delivery callback already dispatched. So the same
duplicate PUBLISH is reachable through disposal with no adoption involved. F-094 closes the
**adoption** route only; the disposal route is stated in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md` and carried
by its own roadmap bullet.

**A hold refuses the whole filter, not the sid, at BOTH callers.** The preflight is
in `processSubs` and in fork repair's `applyGrantChangeLocked`; the second came a round
later for the reason the first exists: repair mutated the membership and option maps before
processing its sids and discarded `adoptDrainLocked`'s refusal, so a wildcard with a usable
main drain and a quarantined companion reported the filter applied — main adopted, companion
refused — and the accept save then persisted a live filter whose drain obligations it no
longer carried. Refusing the whole change is still the right disposition, because a
half-applied filter loses obligations PERMANENTLY while a refused one loses only the
candidate change. It is **not** a convergence: `mergeForkedGrantLocked` records the filter
as a conflict and completes, so once the accept save lands the capsule no longer authorizes
that merge and no resume retries it — the client must re-issue the operation. That cost is
stated in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`.

 A wildcard such as `foo/#` owns a
main sid and a level-up companion, each with its own consumer and its own drain, and a
per-sid refusal adopted the usable one before failing on the other — leaving an adopted
drain that the per-filter failure cleanup does not put back and that the next successful
save then dropped, obligations and durable identity together. So every sid the filter
covers is checked before any of them is touched, and a SUBSCRIBE naming a held drain is
answered with a failure code for that filter.

At fork repair the two holds refuse **different rows**, and the split is the difference
between "nothing may take its place" and "nothing may destroy it". An unusable identity
refuses every row, unchanged. A past-PUBREC intent refuses only the rows that destroy the
drain — `live`, where adoption erases it, and `absent`, where the drop does — while the two
`draining -> draining` rows preserve the survivor's drain either way and are therefore let
THROUGH the preflight — after which each keeps its existing disposition: the equal row
succeeds, and the differing row remains the conflict it already was.
Refusing every row instead would abandon repairs for a drain nothing was going to touch.
The refusal is **not retried**: `mergeForkedGrantLocked` counts it as a conflict and the
merge completes, so once the accept save lands the capsule's anchor no longer authorizes
another merge. That cost is stated in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md` rather than claimed away.

The register's `state` is mandatory and is **never defaulted**: reading an absent state
as `publish` would license a PUBLISH under an identifier already past PUBREC. Legality
is decided by one validator (`mqttValidateInflightShape`) rather than by each reader,
because every earlier attempt at this subsystem failed by classifying owner state at
the point of use, where the set of legal shapes never closed.

That validator sits behind **two** boundaries and no other code path reaches a persisted
register without crossing one of them: `storeInflightCAS` for every write, and
`mqttDecodeInflightRecord` for every read. The read boundary also closes the SCHEMA, so a
record carrying any field this broker does not define is unreadable rather than partially
interpreted. That replaced five fields the record declared purely in order to forbid them
in the one state anything writes: naming the keys to reject closes exactly the set someone
guessed in advance, where closing the schema covers the ones nobody thought of.

**`DisallowUnknownFields` is not enough to close it, and a review round proved that with
counterexamples.** `encoding/json` matches member names case-insensitively and permits
duplicates with the last value winning, so `{"state":"pubrel_ready","state":"publish"}` and
`{"STATE":"pubrel_ready","state":"publish"}` both decoded to an ordinary `publish` record
while carrying an unsupported state — the exact reading that licenses a PUBLISH under an
identifier already past PUBREC, and indistinguishable downstream from a legitimate record.
So the decoder walks the object's keys itself: each member name must be a field this broker
defines, spelled EXACTLY, and appear at most once. The permitted set is derived from the
struct's own JSON tags by reflection, because a hand-maintained list is what put three
names that do not exist into an AST guard's allow-list elsewhere in this change.

Trailing content is refused by `json.Unmarshal`, which is why the typed decode uses it
rather than a `json.Decoder`. `Decoder.More` is the wrong instrument — it answers "is there
another element in this array or object", so it returns false when the next byte is `]` or
`}`, and a record followed by a stray closing delimiter was accepted. A second trailing
check inside the key walk was deleted once a mutation showed it could never be the cause of
a refusal: two mechanisms stating one fact is how a reader and a writer come to disagree.

The read boundary is the later of the two and
the reason it is a boundary rather than a check is worth keeping. Adding the matrix to the
recovery scan alone still left `mqttSlotAdmitsDisposition` and the generation teardown
authorizing irreversible work — a delete, a claim release, a consumer removal — from a body
that was identity-valid and otherwise illegal. Enumerating the destructive readers was the
defect, so there is exactly one decoder and an AST guard
(`TestMQTTInflightRecordsAreDecodedThroughOneAPI`) keeps it the only one. An illegal shape
is UNREADABLE, which every caller already had a conservative path for: retain the record,
reserve the identifier, prove nothing from the body.

PUBREL admission, the durable action claim, route B, the terminal states and the
withheld-action recovery outcome are implemented together. Recovery refreshes custody
for quiescent, live, unretired and uncancelled QoS 2 slots, plus the narrow retired-ready
population for which a present PUBREL record names the exact exchange. The latter is still
actionable—the client is waiting for PUBREL—where a retired flag by itself is not authority.
Active actions retain the custody under which they were acquired, and terminal cleanup is
custody-agnostic.

**Custody withheld at recovery is repaired at admission, not by a background worker.**
A slot that was mid-action when a successor resumed keeps the predecessor's claim after
that action drains: the drain clears the action fields and nothing re-runs the pre-CONNACK
refresh for a connection that is already up. Admission would then refuse the exchange on
every redelivery. So when a stored PUBREL passes every admission condition EXCEPT custody,
the admitting broker moves custody itself, on that delivery, under five conditions: every
other check passed; the standing claim is non-empty and another incarnation's; the slot is
quiescent; this object is provably the current accepted incarnation bound to this
connection; and the standing claim's sequence is strictly older than the proven acceptance.
The CAS carries the exact custody tuple just observed, so a successor that transferred in
between wins. It is attempted at most once per delivery — the retry loop is the consumer's
own re-offer, since a refused PUBREL is never acknowledged and the PUBREL consumer has no
delivery limit.

**A transfer grants custody and never transmission.** The action CAS still has to be
acquired afterwards, and the acceptance fence below still has to pass.

**The transmission fence: `action CAS -> acceptance proof -> send bookkeeping -> socket
write`.** Acquiring an action proves no other holder may act on the exchange; it does not
prove the holder is still the session's current accepted incarnation, because a successor
can commit its acceptance while this broker sits between acquiring and writing. So a proof
runs after the acquisition — the head of `$MQTT_sess` must be this object's own
acknowledged write, by exact stream sequence AND write identity, with no uncertain
sequence and the connection still bound — and a non-current outcome sends nothing and
drains the action. The proof is taken BEFORE the send section, so a refusal opens no send
token, fills no acknowledgement subject and performs no ordered handoff.

That proof is three-valued on purpose. A transient read failure is INDETERMINATE, never
displacement: the fence refuses on anything but current, while the custody repair simply
declines and waits for the next re-offer, so one failed read cannot abandon a repair or
manufacture a takeover. A head record NEWER than ours is also indeterminate rather than
foreign, because a save of ours is committed before its response is adopted and carries a
freshly minted write identity in that window. The window this fence narrows is the
acquisition-to-write interval; it does not close it, and a successor accepting between the
proof and the write still transmits that exchange's own PUBREL under its own identifier,
which the client resolves with PUBCOMP.

**The claim ordering is enforced by every custody writer, before the first write.**
Recovery's contest re-compares only after a CAS fails, which covers two writers racing one
tuple but not two arriving in sequence: a newer owner can take custody, and a paused older
resumer would then overwrite it with a first CAS that meets no conflict. So a record
carrying another incarnation's claim at a strictly newer acceptance sequence is refused
before any write. Strictly newer, because accept saves are what order two owners and the
record CAS makes every accept sequence unique; equality between two different claims is a
state acceptance cannot produce. A claimless record, and a claim whose sequence is zero
(its writer had no confirmed record), are not evidence of a newer owner and are left to
the ordered contest.

**A required terminal advance that cannot be resolved refuses the resume.** Recovery
proves a past-PUBREC slot finished, reserves its identifier and advances it so the delete
becomes legal. The advance's outcome is read back and classified: terminal or provably
absent means it is done; a live action or another exchange means it was never ours; and a
failed, unreadable, unattributable or indeterminate observation is UNRESOLVED, which
returns an error through the pre-CONNACK refusal rather than accepting a connection whose
identifier stays charged with nothing left to retry it. Continuing past it turned a finite
storage failure into a permanently consumed Receive Maximum slot on a session that looked
healthy.

An acknowledgement that cannot be confirmed needs one more thing. The source may still
be pending, so JetStream will re-offer it — and its payload is past PUBREC, so sending
it again is a duplicate. The source is therefore **retired**: the next delivery attempt
of it is acknowledged (with confirmation, under that attempt's own reply subject) and
discarded rather than delivered, which both suppresses the duplicate and settles the
message.

The fact is recorded against the **source**, not against the packet identifier, and that
distinction is the whole design. Re-establishing the source's link to its identifier
would make the ordinary in-flight guard suppress the redelivery — but only until
PUBCOMP, because PUBCOMP removes the pending-PUBREL entry that guard tests. From then on
the payload of an exchange the client has already *completed* would simply be re-sent. A
fact about the source outlives the identifier's bookkeeping; this is the same shape the
affine path already uses (its claim's `AffineDone`) and for the same reason.

It is recorded in **both** places, in that order: in memory first, because the PUBREL
whose delivery is already in flight can bring a redelivery at any moment and the
suppression has to be in place before this path spends a round trip; then on the
register, as a `Retired` mark written by a CAS at its exact sequence. The durable half is
not optional. Without it the next resume sees an ordinary PUBLISH-phase register over a
still-live source — indistinguishable from a delivery that never reached PUBREC — and
re-sends a payload the client has already completed. Leaving the source deliberately
unacknowledged is precisely what makes that window reachable.

Recovery closes the crash cut before that mark: any slot whose durable phase is already
past PUBREC is itself sufficient to install the in-memory suppression before source
interest opens, and recovery then writes the missing `Retired` mark at the custody-
refreshed sequence. Terminal cleanup retains the slot while the source can still be
re-offered, so neither PUBCOMP nor recovery can erase the last durable proof first.

That mark is not best-effort either, and the reason is worth following. While the
exchange's **PUBREL record** exists a restart is safe whatever the register says, because
recovery reads register-plus-PUBREL as "past PUBREC" — and converts it into the mark it
could not write earlier. So there are two pieces of durable evidence, and the rule is
simply that the second is not destroyed before the first exists: a PUBCOMP does **not**
acknowledge its PUBREL away while the retirement it covers is not durably recorded. The
cost of withholding is a PUBREL redelivery, which [MQTT-4.4.0-1] makes legitimate and
which the client answers with another PUBCOMP — bringing the broker back to retry, paced
by AckWait. Persist before ack, the same rule a drain follows.

The source is left unacknowledged at PUBREC rather than retried best-effort: a retry that
landed would settle the message but strand its retirement, since nothing else would drain
it. One discarded redelivery settles the source, releases the retirement, and deletes the
register.

The invariants, in the order they matter:

- **Persist before send.** A PUBLISH under a new identifier goes on the wire only
  after its register is confirmed at a sequence. Between allocation and confirmation
  the entry is *unsendable by anyone*: a concurrent redelivery declines it, the resume
  NAK path skips it, and a drain does not enrol it. A definite store
  failure releases the identifier and sends nothing, which is safe precisely because
  nothing could have sent it. An ambiguous store is resolved by re-reading the subject
  and matching the nonce, never by the shape of the response. This is also what makes
  a superseded broker's late register write inert: an identifier the client can be
  holding implies a confirmed register, so it implies the next broker's scan sees it.
- **Reserve before interest.** On resume every identifier named by a register or by a
  PUBREL record is reserved *before* any source interest exists — the barrier runs
  ahead of the CONNACK, both because a client may publish the instant its CONNACK
  lands and because the drain barrier stores PUBRELs under recorded identifiers that
  must already be reserved. This also closes a pre-existing hazard: `pendingPubRel`
  was empty until the PUBREL callback replayed a record, so a fresh allocation could
  mint an identifier an unreplayed PUBREL still owned.
- **An incomplete identifier space withholds allocation, not the connection.** The
  session stops *allocating* new identifiers while everything else keeps working:
  QoS 0 flows, reserved exchanges complete, and drained PUBRELs are still recreated
  under their recorded identifiers. Allocation is the only operation an unknown space
  makes unsafe, and a withheld QoS 1/2 delivery is redelivered by AckWait exactly as
  one withheld at the in-flight cap is. Denying the CONNECT was rejected: it takes a
  whole session offline over a transient failure, and it contradicts the drain
  barrier's contract. Three conditions trigger it, and they are one condition in
  different clothes — the identifier space cannot be fully accounted for: a walk that
  could not complete (identifiers may be in use that were never seen); a register whose
  body is unreadable (the identifier is known, the delivery that owns it is not); and
  two registers naming one source on different identifiers (both identifiers are known,
  but which one the client holds is not, because a stream sequence orders the *writes*
  and not the sends). In each case reserving identifiers is necessary but not
  sufficient — what stays dangerous is issuing a new one, or re-sending a source under
  a guess. A session discard lifts the restriction along with the incarnation whose
  space it protected.
- **Absence is proven, not inferred.** A register is dropped only on positive evidence,
  of which there are two kinds and neither is an inference from a missing record. The
  SOURCE may be provably finished — acknowledged, or authoritatively absent while the
  consumer that would have delivered it still exists. Or the MARKER may prove the PUBLISH
  never went out (on a register carrying no output token; a recovered token beside it
  makes the register possibly attempted, F-088), which licenses the drop over a source
  that is merely gone as well as one
  that finished (F-102), because the client holds nothing under that identifier either
  way. A source whose *consumer* is gone is still not "complete": that delivery was lost
  rather than finished, so a POSSIBLY-ATTEMPTED exchange over it keeps its identifier
  reserved — the client may still hold it. The same rule covers a record
  whose *body* is unreadable: its subject still names an identifier this incarnation
  wrote, so the identifier is reserved and the record kept, rather than deleted as
  uninterpretable. Reading "I cannot interpret this" as "nothing is in flight" is how
  an identifier the client is holding gets handed to a second message — and because
  such a record's *source* cannot be identified either, it additionally makes the
  identifier space incomplete (above).
- **QoS 1 and pre-PUBREC terminal paths delete the register** at its exact sequence:
  PUBACK, a failed PUBREC, Message Expiry, Maximum Packet Size, and a pre-PUBREC consumer
  teardown that abandons a started delivery. A failed delete costs a stale record that the
  store path's reconcile, the next resume scan, or the orphan sweep removes; it never wedges
  an identifier. **A QoS 2 exchange PAST PUBREC is different**: the owner slot lives the
  whole exchange (F-092/F-093). The PUBREL store no longer deletes the register — it advances
  the slot to `pubrel_ready` — and a past-PUBREC teardown, an active action and an
  indeterminate terminal cleanup all deliberately PRESERVE the slot. Its one delete is at
  terminal cleanup after PUBCOMP (or a proven-finished recovery), addressed through the slot
  the exchange carried; an indeterminate cleanup keeps the identifier reserved and retries.
- **A surviving register is assumed client-held unless it proves otherwise.** Two very
  different things can leave a register behind: a delivery that really went out and
  whose consumer was later destroyed, and one this session gave up — an allocation
  withdrawn before it was ever sent, or a transmitted delivery whose consumer the
  session abandoned. The first must keep both its identifier and its Receive Maximum
  slot: that limit bounds what the *client* is holding unacknowledged, and a consumer
  disappearing proves nothing about the client, so a session stuck this way is a lost
  message being reported honestly, not an accounting bug. The second must keep neither,
  and what tells them apart is durable evidence with two homes. On the register itself:
  a **cancellation tombstone**, written when the record's deletion could not be proven.
  On the session record: a **void-register verdict**, the register's NONCE in
  `CancelledRegs`, staged by the same transaction that removes the consumer's
  membership. Since F-088 neither is non-transmission evidence on its own: recovery frees
  the identifier of a register either one names only while the allocation's unsent marker
  stands and no output token is outstanding on the register; any other such register is
  possibly attempted and is restored or reserved (and a restoration retires the verdict as
  superseded).
  A THIRD proof reaches the same conclusion by a different route: an unsent
  **marker** still naming a register whose source can never be re-offered. It
  needs no tombstone and no verdict, because the marker's confirmed delete
  precedes any write, and it is what covers the ordinary case of a consumer
  that simply went away (F-102).
- **The verdict is keyed by nonce, because a nonce is minted once and never reused.**
  Every other candidate identity is recycled: a teardown frees the packet identifier for
  immediate reuse, subjects are reused within a generation, and a shared group durable's
  name is reused for as long as its incarnation stays live, so a rejoin under a live
  incarnation returns the same name (a retirement followed by a new join changes it) — a
  verdict scoped by any of those eventually condemns a genuine later delivery, or
  resurrects an abandoned one, and both were tried and failed here. The nonce is minted
  with the ALLOCATION, one step ahead of the store that writes it, so a cancellation that
  lands while the CAS is still on the wire has something immutable to name. A verdict is
  removed only against proof: the register's confirmed deletion, its tombstone landing,
  or a cancellation settled before any CAS was ever issued — the one place absence is
  provable. Since F-088 there is a fourth: recovery's acting restoration of that allocation
  as possibly attempted, which supersedes the verdict's "never transmitted"
  (`retireSupersededVerdictLocked`). A scan that fails to FIND the register deliberately
  keeps the verdict, because scan-time absence cannot rule out a superseded broker's
  create-only CAS landing late; kept, the verdict is self-healing — the scan that
  finally sees the register deletes it and retires the verdict then, including a
  register found already TOMBSTONED, which is proof in hand rather than an absence
  question. Proof-keyed retirement is also
  what keeps `CancelledRegs` bounded across a client that subscribes and unsubscribes
  forever; the stated residual is one nonce per crash that lands between a register's
  confirmed deletion and the very next session save, since only a fence against a
  superseded broker's late CAS could license retiring that verdict on absence, and a
  time-based fence would rest a correctness invariant on a timing assumption.
- **Its durability is a tracked revision, not an assumed save.** The verdict is often
  recorded by a delivery goroutine while the UNSUBSCRIBE that caused it holds the record
  fence, and that transaction may already have marshalled its record — so the addition
  is refused its own save *and* missed by the save that does happen. A revision counter
  pairs what the set is with what the record provably carries, and every convergence
  point (the packet tail, each register store, each resume, and the settlement of an
  ambiguous save — which re-attempts the very bytes that marshalled the verdict and
  credits the revision they carried) retries until the two agree. Each verdict additionally
  carries the revision of its own insertion, because "the record carries the set" is a
  claim about a MARSHAL: a landed save proves durable exactly the verdicts recorded at
  or before the revision it captured, and a release keyed on membership alone would
  treat a verdict a concurrent teardown added mid-save as proven.
- **A consumer teardown writes the tombstone itself, and holds the identifier while it
  does.** The session record is the wrong home for this fact on the generic teardown
  paths (a QoS downgrade's deferred consumer delete, a forced shared leave, a shared
  release): each runs AFTER its packet's save, so an intent recorded there may not reach
  the record for a while. A tombstone at the register's own subject needs no fence and
  no packet, so it is durable exactly when it has to be — which is before the consumer
  that would classify the register's source is destroyed. The identifier stays RESERVED
  across the in-flight store rather than being freed at once, because a new delivery
  could otherwise take it and write its own register at the same subject, and nothing
  would then tell that record from the tombstone. The write is create-only first and a
  replacement at the exact sequence its own nonce is found at; a foreign occupant is a
  failure, never a success. And because such a tombstone can outlive its owner — where
  the teardown wins the race, the store returns without ever writing — the next
  allocation of that identifier REAPS a cancelled occupant instead of refusing it. A
  record that says "never transmitted" cannot be holding an identifier. (Since F-088 that
  tombstone is a pending fence reaped by its written provenance, `cancel_origin:
  pending-create`; any other cancelled occupant is decided by its unsent marker. See
  "One door".)
- **The cancellation goes in the write that removes the membership.** Recording it in
  the teardown instead cannot be made equivalent, and keeping the consumer does not
  redeem it: once the membership is gone there is ordinarily no subscription left to
  redeliver through, so a register that lands afterwards holds its identifier and its
  Receive Maximum slot for the life of the session whatever becomes of the durable.
  (A QoS 0 downgrade that converts its consumer into a **drain** is the one case where a
  subscription does survive the membership — the drain's — and the rule still holds
  there, because the cancelled allocations are the ones that were never transmitted and
  the drain is owed only what was. Their tombstones ride the same write either way,
  since the cancelled nonces are serialized into every record.) — under a
  Receive Maximum of 1, a session that can no longer deliver at all. So every
  transaction that removes a consumer's membership (an UNSUBSCRIBE, a QoS downgrade,
  a 3.1.1 forced shared leave, a SUBSCRIBE rollback) withdraws
  that consumer's in-flight registrations first, and its own save carries both facts.
  The drained sids are exempt because stageDrain already did it and their consumer
  survives. What the teardown itself then finds can only be a registration that arrived
  after the staging, for which the tombstone is written and the obligation is otherwise
  left to the convergence points — the consumer is deleted anyway, since keeping an
  unreferenced durable nothing reaps makes no identifier recoverable.
- **The delivery barrier comes down before the snapshot.** Staging is only a moment in
  time otherwise: the delivery callback stays live until the packet commits, so a
  message arriving after the snapshot allocates an identifier whose cancellation misses
  the write that was supposed to carry it. Marking the doomed consumer's delivery
  subscription closed first — under the same lock the snapshot is taken with, and the
  same lock the callback tests it under — is what makes the snapshot complete rather
  than current. A rollback lifts the barrier again, because a packet whose write did not
  land leaves those subscriptions the client's. Two details of that reversal are
  load-bearing: it is scoped per FILTER, because one filter of a SUBSCRIBE can fail
  while the packet succeeds and its membership then survives unchanged; and both halves
  of a multi-level filter go through the same staging helper, since the level-up
  companion is a consumer in its own right.
- **A teardown's register removals walk one durable ladder.** Most register deletes may
  be fire-and-forget, because the record left behind names a source that stays live and
  classifiable — the store's reconcile, the next resume, or the orphan sweep removes it.
  A consumer teardown breaks that premise on purpose: it is about to delete the very
  consumer that would classify those sources, after which a surviving register is
  deliberately not read as complete. So its removals run BEFORE the consumer goes and
  walk a ladder whose rungs are ordered by strength: (1) the confirmed delete, (2) the
  cancellation tombstone at the register's exact sequence, (3) the nonce verdict
  persisted with the session record. A proven rung ends the story and forgets the
  verdict; the first two rungs share a storage domain (`$MQTT_inflight`) and usually
  fail together, which is exactly when the third matters. The one exception is a
  **retired** QoS 2 source: `Retired` proves that the source crossed PUBREC, not that the
  slot reached an explicit past-PUBREC phase or that PUBCOMP arrived. Consumer teardown
  removes the now-unneeded source suppression but does not queue that slot into the raw
  never-transmitted ladder; deleting or tombstoning it would falsely license identifier
  reuse. A present exact PUBREL lets recovery complete the durable phase handoff; without
  one, recovery keeps a known, non-actionable identifier reservation without inventing
  `pubrel_ready`.
- **A withdrawn identifier is released only settled AND proven.** The reservation a
  teardown leaves on a cancelled allocation guards two different hazards, and both
  release conditions are load-bearing. Until the original store SETTLES, the identifier
  is not free even with a durable verdict: a new allocation could take the subject, reap
  what it finds, and then race the old create-only CAS onto the same subject. And until
  some rung is PROVEN, a settled identifier is not free either: released with nothing
  durable calling the register void, a crash resurrects it as an ordinary delivery
  holding a Receive Maximum slot forever. The settle points (the store's confirmation or
  abandonment) release on proof — including proof a rung established EARLIER: a securing
  tombstone retires the nonce while the store is still out, and a settle point that then
  parked the reservation pending a save would park it forever, since a retired nonce has
  nothing left to save. A settled-but-unproven reservation is released by the save that
  finally proves the verdict. Release is checked at EVERY edge with one shared
  predicate, because the proofs and the settlement race in both directions: a verdict
  durable before the settle leaves no later save to release (the settle itself must
  recognise the record's proof), and a stream-rung proof after the settle retires the
  nonce and with it the membership a save-keyed release would need (the retirement
  itself must release the settled reservations — through a small nonce-keyed index,
  since retirement runs once per voided register and a pendingPublish walk per nonce is
  quadratic teardown work). And every one of those touches is keyed by the toucher's OWN
  nonce, read under the lock that allocated it: a store can stall across its
  allocation's cancellation, release and the identifier's reuse, and the reservation it
  then finds belongs to a newer allocation whose own CAS is still on the wire — not the
  stale settler's to release.
- **Rollback withdraws verdicts on transmitted deliveries, and only those.** A packet
  whose save DEFINITELY failed keeps its subscriptions, so its transmitted deliveries are
  live and still owe their identifiers — a standing verdict would have the next restart
  free identifiers the
  client holds, the reverse of the bug and a worse one. A CANCELLED allocation is never
  reinstated: nothing was transmitted, the source simply re-offers under a fresh
  allocation, so its verdict stands on every branch.
- **A drained exchange's release accepts both "already absent" answers.** The drain
  holds its register's sequence in its own persisted state and releases it — confirmed,
  before the claim removal and the ack — in its finalizer. That retry must read BOTH
  authoritative shapes of "the sequence is already gone" as success, or a crash between
  the delete and the claim save would withhold the exchange's completion forever.
- **The drain's release is fenced against its own session being cleared, twice.** The
  finalizer captures its drain and sequence, unlocks, and does JetStream work; `clear()`
  meanwhile nils the drain maps, RE-MINTS the generation, and resets the
  packet-identifier allocator. So the incarnation identity is captured in the same
  critical section that proves the captured drain is still the session's — without that,
  a stale finalizer pairs the retired delivery's identifier with the fresh generation,
  and since the release matches on the subject's identifier plus `(Dur, Seq)`, and a
  group durable's name recurs for as long as its incarnation stays live, the FRESH
  incarnation's register is a full match and is deleted while its client may still hold
  that identifier. A **second** check runs after the release and after the record fence,
  because `clear()` can also finish during the release's own round trips, after which the
  fence opens legitimately against the new epoch while every local still names the
  retired drain: the token is released and the delivery withheld rather than undone,
  since the release itself is irreversible. Neither check arbitrates a genuinely LIVE
  owner of the same register — that stays F-036's predicate.
- **Ownership transfers explicitly, it is never assumed.** Three teardown paths take a
  register out of the ordinary terminal path's reach, and each takes the delete with it.
  A **drained** QoS 2 exchange holds its source claim until its PUBREL is proven, so
  nothing else reaches the delete: the drain records the register's sequence in its own
  state (persisted, so it survives a restart) and releases it — confirmed, before the
  claim removal and the ack — in its finalizer. A **consumer teardown** releases both the
  registers its `cpending` entries name and those of its *retired* sources, which are not
  in `cpending` at all. And an **UNSUBSCRIBE that races a first-delivery register write**
  cancels that allocation rather than skipping it, so the store's own ownership
  revalidation refuses the send instead of putting a PUBLISH on the wire whose tracking
  the UNSUBSCRIBE has just destroyed. A register left behind by any of them outlives its
  consumer, and a consumer-gone source is deliberately not read as complete — so the next
  resume would reserve that identifier. Recovery's marker-proven drop does not rescue
  these: it releases a register whose unsent MARKER still proves non-transmission (standing,
  with no output token outstanding on the register), and a
  cancelled allocation is exactly the shape where that evidence has been consumed. The
  explicit transfer is still what closes them.
- **A surviving disconnect's shared purge derives its targets from the pending state, not
  from the group membership.** The purge exists to drop this session's pending group
  deliveries without acking them, so a resume does not NAK-steal messages AckWait would
  have redelivered to other members. Neither view of the group can name what it has to
  reach. A session restored from its record has the membership but no configs — shared
  consumer configs are deliberately excluded from the persisted `Cons` and rebuilt only
  by subscription restoration, which runs later in the CONNECT than register recovery
  (and, since F-050, still before the CONNACK) — while register recovery has already
  rebuilt its pending entries under the incarnation-qualified group durable names the
  registers carry, so a config walk finds nothing. A SUBSCRIBE whose rolled-back save
  definitely failed used to leave the opposite — re-added configs live with their group
  key not back in the membership — and no longer does, because that arm now restores the
  shared membership beside `cons` (see "A SUBSCRIBE rollback restores the shared state it
  attempted"). The derivation below never rested on that shape alone and is unchanged.
  And a 3.1.1 forced leave and an UNSUBSCRIBE with no config to tear down each strand a
  TRANSMITTED delivery's entries on purpose — the staging records the verdict and leaves
  the entry "for the teardown's purge" — with NEITHER view left naming the durable, which
  is why even the union of the two is not enough. So the purge takes every durable named
  by the maps it is about to remove from (`cpending`, the withheld markers, and the
  retired sources) whose name carries the shared-group prefix. For broker-minted state
  that name IS the protocol fact "deliveries under this consumer are group deliveries":
  the shared names are minted in one place and no other durable class can collide with
  the prefix (plain consumers are hash-and-nuid, PUBREL and session-affine QoS 2 copies
  carry their own prefixes, and a drained consumer keeps its plain name). For state
  restored from a register the name is trusted rather than re-derived, the same trust
  every other restored identity gets. Re-purging an entry a removal already voided is
  idempotent end to end: a known nonce is not re-voided, the delete is at the exact
  sequence, and both release predicates key on the toucher's own nonce.
- **Both surviving closes run the purge, and the DEFERRED one runs it as a single
  classified write.** A close whose own record write was unresolved is parked and applied
  later, and that path cannot simply call the purge: the purge's third rung writes the
  session record, and an independent write of its own can land ambiguously — after which
  every later write on the session is refused, including the disconnect time's, with the
  parked action already consumed and nothing left to retry it. The record would then say
  `DisconnectedAt=0`, i.e. connected, while the deadline existed in memory only: the local
  timer fires, session expiry finds the record bumped past its stale sequence and delegates
  to the record, and the record reads as "connected, nothing due" — leaking it until a
  reconnect that may never come. So the deferred close opens the record transaction BEFORE
  its first mutation, stamps the ORIGINAL disconnect time, runs the purge in a form that
  only STAGES (the register-stream rungs, then the nonce in memory), and makes ONE
  classified save carrying both. An ambiguous save needs no continuation at all: the
  deadline and the verdicts are in the bytes it attempted, and the settlement re-attempts
  exactly those, crediting the revision they marshalled; a definite failure keeps the
  in-memory purge and the armed timer and loses only restart-survival of the deadline,
  which is the ordinary close's posture too. The Will's fate is decided on a FRESH clock
  sample rather than the one taken at entry: the branch's rungs and its save are round
  trips, and a deadline that passes during them would otherwise read as still future.
  An already-due Will enqueued into the outbox is cancellable, so a reconnect arriving
  after the deadline could suppress a Will that was already owed — precisely what the
  direct publication exists to prevent. And because the parked action is CONSUMED
  before the discharge runs, the discharge re-checks that the record state is still
  resolved — once cheaply on entry and again with its own fence held, which is the sound
  test since the fence is what serializes writers — and RE-PARKS the untouched action if
  it is not. Holding the ownership gate does not exclude an off-readLoop writer: a
  register store settling between the resolution and the fence acquisition can leave its
  own write ambiguous, and applying the close anyway would have every write refused with
  nothing left holding the original deadlines. The DEFERRED DISCARD branch cannot hold a
  fence across `clear()` — that call ends the record generation and must own its
  transaction — so `clear` performs the late refusal itself: a re-check WITH THE FENCE
  HELD, before the first deletion, releasing without ending the generation because nothing
  was mutated, and returning a distinct sentinel. The branch re-parks on that sentinel
  alone and never on "is the session uncertain now", because any other failure means a lost
  teardown claim or a half-done teardown, where re-parking would resurrect an obligation
  that is not this broker's to discharge.
- **A parked close un-jails its client ID only where it still owns the session, and takes
  `as.mu` to do it.** The flappers jail (`as.flappers`) is `as.mu` state end to end: CONNECT
  reads it, every displacement writes it, and the account manager's own cleanup timer sweeps
  it. A close whose record write is unresolved parks and then clears its client ID from the
  jail exactly as an ordinary teardown does — but it reaches the park by routes with
  different lock states, and only one of them can say what the entry it would delete IS.
  With the ownership gate held (the `mqttDeferDisconnectOwned` routes; the never-expiring
  one parks only after ending its own record transaction, so it holds no fence either)
  **neither producer can run**: `evictDecideOnce` refuses outright under a held gate, and
  `discardTakenOverClient` sits downstream of a CONNECT that would need the same gate. Any
  entry present is therefore a STALE one from an earlier displacement, and removing it is
  the ordinary teardown's behaviour. On the gate-less route nothing of the sort can be
  proven — `lockSessionForTeardown` releases `as.mu` between attempts and samples ownership
  in a separate critical section, so the holder it lost to can release and let
  `evictDecideOnce` jail this client ID in the interval before the park — so
  `mqttDeferDisconnectUngated` leaves the jail alone. The two entry points exist so the
  precondition is visible at the call: one boolean silently carrying both "must still be
  uncertain" and "may delete a jail entry" is what would let a future ungated caller
  compile into a wrong deletion. Deleting there would cancel a live displacement's jail;
  leaving it
  costs at most one `mqttSessJailDur` of reconnect *enforcement* on an entry that may
  have been stale — CONNECT compares the stored timestamp against that duration, and the
  cleanup timer runs on its own longer interval, so an expired entry can sit in the map
  well past the window in which it jails anything — which is the fail-closed direction.
  The lock is taken at the park rather than
  inherited (the gated callers hold the session gate, not `as.mu`) and taken BARE —
  `sess.mu` is released inside the park's own critical section — so it adds no edge to the
  `as.mu` → `sess.mu` order, and the section holds one map delete and waits on nothing, so
  it has no outward edge that could close a cycle with the gate, the record fence or `c.mu`.
  No `docs/CONFORMANCE.md` entry: the jail is an inherited anti-flap heuristic, not an MQTT
  surface.
- **`clear()` always refuses before its first deletion on an unclassified sequence.** That
  is the delivered invariant, and it is unconditional: both refusals — at entry and with the
  fence held — always carry the sentinel. What each caller then does is NOT uniform, and
  is enumerated below rather than summarized: the shared recovery can decline, so this
  section deliberately asserts no universal recovery.
  The refusal was once opt-in for the deferred discharge alone, because no other caller
  could act on it; four more now can — five of the seven call sites in all — so the flag
  was a mechanism reading
  "true" at every site it could reach. The refusal alone is not enough either:
  "never tear down on an unclassified sequence" would otherwise become "strand the object
  while its record, its consumers and the shared group durables it owed a release all
  survive", because those callers evict before clearing. The ORDINARY CLEAN CLOSE and
  SESSION EXPIRY share one helper
  (`reparkRefusedDiscard`): it parks a discard-only obligation — `expiryInterval` 0, so the
  discharge takes the deferred discard branch above — and then RESTORES RESIDENCY, which is
  what every resolver needs, since the retry pass and CONNECT both scan the resident
  sessions and the expiry sweep looks at no `ExpiryInterval == 0` record at all. Park
  first, publish second: the obligation must exist before the object is reachable. The WILL
  is deliberately NOT parked — a parked Will is memory-only, so a CRASH in that window drops
  it, regressing a Will the broker delivers today — so the close falls through to
  `mqttHandleWill`, which publishes immediately for the expiry-0 session a discard always
  is; expiry has no Will, its own was discharged by the close that started the deadline.
  The helper ARBITRATES NOTHING against an obligation already parked: it accepts only the
  shape it would have written itself (ends at disconnect, no Will), never mutating or
  replacing it, and declines every other shape back to the caller's historical
  evict-and-log, because a parked action carries no owner identity and nothing there can
  prove whose deadline or whose Will a retarget would overwrite. CONNECT's clean start
  instead REJECTS WITHOUT EVICTING, the same answer its early path gives: it has a client
  waiting for a CONNACK, not an obligation, and the retry's own uncertainty check resolves
  the session. Session expiry also stops reading a higher record sequence as a remote owner
  while its own write is unresolved — an ambiguous write that LANDED with its response lost
  produces exactly that shape, and evicting there would discard the only object that can
  classify it — so the decision is deferred to the digest classifier, and it is made inside
  ONE record transaction spanning the load, the `sess.seq` read and the decision, since a
  mutex sample alone is check-then-act and arming uncertainty requires the fence. The two
  callers built from a record just read (the record-based expiry, the restore path's
  overdue discard) cannot reach the sentinel at all: nothing writes through those transient
  objects before the discard, so no save can have armed uncertainty. They keep the
  unconditional refusal as a fail-closed invariant and carry the proof as a comment. What
  the recovery does NOT make durable is stated in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`: the obligation is
  memory-only, so a CRASH in that window drops it. **A remote takeover no longer does**: as
  this was written, a record-observation eviction consumed a parked action and discarded it;
  since F-084 that route EXTRACTS the action and discharges its Will against the original
  deadline (`dischargeDeferredWill`), so the surviving loss is the crash window alone.
- **Every landed record write credits the verdicts it marshalled.** Durability of a
  verdict is a property of the write that carried it, not of the intent of whoever was
  persisting, so the credit lives at the write: `save` samples the void-register revision
  in the same critical section that marshals the record, and a CONFIRMED store advances
  the saved-revision watermark to that sample and releases the reservations it frees. The
  same sample travels with the attempt's identity, so every settlement that PROVES those
  exact bytes durable credits it — a read finding them at a newer sequence, the resolver's
  own re-attempt landing them, and each landed classification of the contention retry —
  none of which passes through the confirmed-store path. Never on an unresolved,
  definitely-failed or FOREIGN outcome: a record that is not ours
  carries nothing of ours. Crediting only at the paths that set out to record a verdict
  left the other half open — a reconnect's accept save inherits the staged verdicts and is
  not a verdict path at all, so it made the fact durable while its identifier stayed
  reserved in memory with nothing due to look again. The one deliberate exemption is the
  accept ROLLBACK's raw write: its snapshot is built inside the rollback, so a nonce staged
  after it is not in the bytes that land, and crediting the then-current revision would
  claim exactly that nonce durable (`docs/CONFORMANCE.md` states what happens to it).
- **A lock release is what re-checks a verdict staged behind somebody else's lock.** The
  stager and the writer are not the same thread of control: a register store settling
  off-readLoop stages its nonce and finds its own persistence refused, because at that
  instant the record fence — or the ownership gate a resolver needs — is either held by
  somebody else, or free but RESERVED for an announced blocking writer under waiter
  priority. The second cause needs nobody to hold anything: a blocker announces itself,
  stalls before `sess.mu`, and every non-blocking acquisition refuses meanwhile — with that
  waiter's eventual release as the retry edge. A BOUND session
  converges through its own packet tails; an UNBOUND one has no traffic, and a
  never-expiring one no timer, so the identifier could stay reserved for the life of the
  session. So both canonical releases re-check: the RECORD FENCE release, sampling the
  decision inside its existing critical section (after the fence is cleared, before the
  unlock — a decision made after the unlock does not compose atomically with staging), and
  the OWNERSHIP GATE release, at both forms — `unlockSession` and CONNECT's own inline
  delete, since a CONNECT does not release through the former. The re-check fires only for
  a session that is resident, unbound, not uncertain (the uncertainty machinery owns that
  retry, and its resolver's releases re-check afterwards), not mid-transaction, and whose
  revision is above the HANDOFF WATERMARK. "Not mid-transaction" is also where waiter
  priority applies: an ANNOUNCED blocking writer suppresses the trigger outright, because
  the attempt's own acquisition is a non-blocking one and taking the fence there would be
  exactly the barge waiter priority refuses — while an announce landing after the
  release-time load produces a trigger whose inline re-check then defers instead. Either
  way the deferral is a handoff, not a strand: that waiter's own release re-checks, and
  provided blocking arrivals are finite the chain reaches a release with none announced.
  That watermark advances when an attempt ACQUIRES the fence, never when a release merely
  decides to try: a trigger that lost the fence to a waiter it just signalled stored
  nothing, and burning the watermark on it would strand the very nonce it fired for — the
  fence winner's own release is the next re-check. One attempt per newly staged revision
  makes the sequence of attempts finite; keeping it to one STACK FRAME is a separate
  property, and a LOOP is what provides it. The releases inside an attempt would otherwise
  re-enter the decision in their own frames — once per late staging, each frame holding a
  JetStream round trip, so a session with many outstanding register stores could build a
  stack proportional to them. So an attempt marks the session as having a handoff in
  progress, the releases route work to that loop instead of recursing, and the flag is
  cleared only in the same critical section that finds nothing left pending, which is what
  keeps a staging racing the exit from being dropped between the two. A loop that gives up
  on GATE contention hands that ownership back inside the gate's own critical section, for
  the mirror-image reason: a gate owner deletes its entry under the manager lock and only
  then asks whether a loop is running, so a hand-back made after that lock was released
  could be seen as still running — the owner suppresses itself, the loop exits, and the
  staged revision has no successor at all. **The releases alone are not the whole liveness
  argument**, and the gap is the watermark's own doing: a DEFINITE store failure leaves
  the revision AT the watermark, so no release triggers again, and an unbound
  never-expiring session may never stage another nonce to lift it. So the periodic pass
  carries a BACKSTOP — for a resident, unbound, resolved session with an unsaved revision
  it puts the watermark back below it and runs the ordinary attempt. Re-arming rather than
  bypassing keeps one path to the store, and the sweep interval is the retry cadence,
  which is the right one for a failure that did not look transient. The backstop re-arms
  WITHOUT regard to the waiter count, deliberately: the attempt it drives still refuses
  while a blocking writer is announced, and the re-armed watermark is precisely what lets
  that waiter's own release trigger the store instead of waiting a whole further sweep
  interval. So the backstop is a liveness carrier past a definite failure, not an
  unconditional one: while blocking writers keep arriving, each attempt defers again. The
  attempt itself runs UNDER the ownership gate, taken fail-fast and skipped on contention:
  gated, any ambiguity it creates exists only while the gate is held, so a CONNECT that
  ever holds the gate sees it at its own uncertainty check and resolves it — ungated, an
  ambiguity landing just after that check would have the CONNECT bind, find its accept
  save refused, and evict the object holding the continuation. The unbound scoping is
  equally deliberate: fired at CONNECT's accept-transaction release it could inject
  uncertainty right behind a success CONNACK, with the gate held and no packet tail yet to
  resolve it.
- **A resume claims the shared registers it recovers before installing them.** A
  cross-broker takeover constructs a new session object but preserves the session
  incarnation generation, so that generation correctly finds the durable state but cannot
  distinguish the two owners. Each object therefore has an unpersisted register claim.
  Every register write stamps it, and recovery CAS-rewrites each readable live or retired
  shared register with its claim at the exact sequence it loaded — before the
  duplicate-source grouping, so that even the members of a group that fails closed have
  moved: a reservation protects nothing while the registers behind it still sit at
  sequences a stale close knows, and deleting one would let the next resume install the
  survivor as authoritative, resolving by deletion the ambiguity the group refused to
  guess about. A live member whose claim fails — a concurrent resumer owns it, or it is
  unreadable — keeps its source identity and fails its whole group closed for the same
  reason: installing the sibling as a singleton would resolve the duplicate by the same
  guess through the split-claim door. The single-slot subject
  moves, invalidating every sequence a stale close knows. If the stale close deleted first,
  or its matching-nonce cancellation tombstone won, recovery consumes that durable close
  decision and does not install the identifier. The negative dispositions also reconcile
  a REUSED object's memory, because "in-memory state wins" holds only for records
  recovery would re-install: a consumed close decision retires the live entry it backed,
  and a poisoned group demotes a live member's entry to a bare reservation and removes
  its source mapping — each touch guarded by the record's own nonce, so an entry a newer
  allocation owns is never disturbed. A reservation left by a LOST arbitration is marked
  foreign: its sequence may be the rival's, and no terminal path settles a record this
  object does not own — the completion path's register delete carries no nonce or claim
  check, so the mark is what keeps a stale object's late acknowledgement off the rival's
  only durable identity. The acknowledgement paths decline a foreign reservation before
  any state moves: a successful PUBREC would otherwise store an uncorrelated PUBREL from
  a bodyless entry, and a later resume would then hold an identifier-first record against
  the rival's still-live register. The reservation stands, nothing durable is written,
  and the owner the client ends up bound to answers the retransmission. A READABLE live
  record under an active rival's claim, observed mid-barrier, is stronger than any of
  this: the rival claims only after its own accept save, so it is durable displacement
  proof, and the RESUME IS REFUSED — nothing installs, the CONNECT aborts, and the
  client's retry binds to the authoritative owner. A dead rival's standing claim never
  reaches that re-read (the ordinary CAS at the loaded sequence re-claims it), so
  foreign reservations arise only from unreadable records, which prove nothing and stay
  fail-closed. There is no own-claim fast path: every shared register is rewritten on
  every barrier run, because the moved sequence is what turns a terminal path's paused
  register delete into a no-op — a same-object rebind between an acknowledgement's two
  halves legitimately reinstalls the entry, and the paused durable half must not then
  complete the exchange invisibly. Registers dropped on proof of completion reconcile
  memory exactly as consumed closes do (cancelled reservations exempt), so such an entry
  is released at the next barrier run rather than counting against Receive Maximum
  forever. An own-claim re-read is adopted only when the sequence has MOVED from the
  attempted one: without a fast path the loaded record was own-claimed already, so an
  unmoved re-read proves nothing about the write and is retried — the move is the
  fence — and both exhausting those retries and an INDETERMINATE re-read after a failed
  CAS refuse the resume rather than reserving at an unproven sequence. Every contest
  therefore ends owned-with-a-moved-sequence, consumed as a close decision, opaque from
  an unreadable (and therefore rewritten) record, or refused; no outcome leaves an
  installed entry at a sequence a paused terminal path still holds. Claims are ordered
  by their accept save's record sequence — unique by
  record CAS — so a contest between two live resumers has exactly one newer side: the
  newer takes over an older claim by re-targeting its CAS, the older reads displacement,
  and the mutual-refusal loop two unordered claimants could otherwise enter cannot
  happen. The contest budget is generous and exhausts to displacement, never to an
  opaque reservation: a fixed budget cannot bound unbounded contenders, and the newest
  owner stranded behind a chain of older claims would otherwise complete CONNECT with
  its allocation withheld. Every
  nonce-keyed reconcile on a shared
  durable — ambiguous first store, retirement, cancellation and pending cancellation —
  must also match the current claim before it may adopt a sequence or rewrite the record,
  and so must the store's same-delivery replacement, the one reconcile whose occupant
