  carries the OTHER writer's nonce and which no nonce gate can therefore cover. A
  mismatch abandons the stale operation without producing a competing session-record
  verdict. The complete-source reap is deliberately claim-independent: a provably
  complete source means the exchange terminated, and continuity protects only
  incomplete exchanges. Plain registers are not claimed and therefore not claim-gated;
  applying one side without the other would turn a resumed owner's own plain records
  into foreign state.
  The ordinary exact-sequence delete needs no added read: the claim rewrite is the fence,
  and a delete holding the pre-claim sequence removes nothing. Thus each shared register's
  close-versus-resume decision is durable and consumed once at its own subject sequence.
- **Registered if and only if transmitted.** A delivery withheld by the in-flight cap
  was never sent, so it is never registered. A retained-message send has no JetStream
  backing at all, so it has no register and no post-restart redelivery.
- **A retargeted CAS rebuilds from the record it just read.** Several writers of
  `$MQTT_inflight` build a body once and, when their CAS is rejected, re-read the subject
  only to learn the SEQUENCE — then re-target with the original body, silently erasing
  whatever a concurrent writer proved in between. The alpha-blocking instance was the
  resume claim contest re-proposing a pre-retirement snapshot over a `Retired` mark, which
  puts a completed exchange back in the live bucket and re-sends its payload after the
  client's PUBCOMP. The rule is one rule over the whole writer set: a re-targeted CAS
  starts from the reread and mutates only the fields the operation OWNS. Monotonic facts
  (`Retired`, `Cancelled`) merge forward; identity facts (nonce, identifier, source, QoS,
  the affine pair) never change under one exchange — the same-delivery takeover replaces
  them as a SET, which is a new exchange identity taking the slot rather than a mutation
  of the old one; and the arbitration fields (`Claim`/`ClaimSeq`) belong to the contest
  alone. A body proposed at the caller's OWN cached sequence is exempt and stays sparse:
  the CAS is itself the proof, because any intervening writer moved the sequence. What
  those writers may not do is re-propose that body after a reread.
- **`Retired` dominates `Cancelled`.** Rebuilding makes the two bits coexist durably for
  the first time, whenever a cancellation races a retirement. One precedence rule decides
  the shape at every reader — recovery's classification, the contest's close arm, the
  store's tombstone reap, and the affine sweep's settle gate: a retirement is backed by
  the client's own PUBREC, so the transmission provably happened, while a cancellation
  over a transmitted delivery is F-088's known-false write. Freeing an identifier the
  client holds is the catastrophic direction; holding one that was actually free costs a
  slot. So a record carrying both is never consumed as a close and never frees its
  identifier: it reinstates the suppression, exactly as a pure retirement does.
- **A register delete whose caller can name the NONCE and reach the VERDICT routes
  through one helper.**
  Three separate reviews each found one more delete site that stranded a cancellation
  verdict, which is the signal that enumerating sites is itself the defect. The boundary
  is a decision procedure rather than a list: a caller that holds or can recover the
  exchange nonce owes the verdict a proof, so its delete is confirmed and the verdict
  released against that proof, while a caller whose own semantics already require
  confirmation keeps it. THREE shapes are outside it: a site that cannot name a nonce at
  all; a site that runs the SAME discipline through a stronger ladder of its own —
  confirmed delete, else a tombstone on the register, else the nonce verdict — which is
  the full version of what the helper does in one step rather than a bypass; and a site
  that can name the nonce but cannot REACH the verdict, which lives on a session. The
  orphan sweep's affine arm is the third: with no identity-fenced session resident it
  retains a register that CARRIES a cancellation, but a verdict held only in that
  session's persisted `CancelledRegs` is invisible to a walk that reads registers rather
  than records, so such a register is still deleted and its verdict stranded — F-090,
  filed under `docs/ROADMAP.md` §P, pre-existing, and not an alpha blocker because the
  stranding arm needs a register carrying both an affine claim and its copy subject, which
  the supported default never creates. The residue is one nonce per occurrence and
  CUMULATIVE over a generation, not bounded in aggregate. An AST guard parses every production
  file in the package and fails on any register delete outside that allow-list, so a new
  site cannot silently rejoin the stranding class. The forget's persistence stays
  opportunistic, riding the existing
  revision machinery — the same standard, and the same one-nonce crash window, the
  committed recovery path already accepts.
- **A sequence is applied to a live entry by LINEAGE, not by base.** A resume's operation
  may legitimately re-target through several sequences, so it carries the chain it
  authoritatively held the record at, and a live entry's register sequence is advanced to
  the chain's end only when it names a link in that chain. Admitting only the base leaves
  an entry aimed at a sequence that no longer exists when memory sits at an intermediate
  link; admitting anything overwrites a fact this operation never saw. A record nothing
  contested carries a one-element chain, which makes the rule exactly "unchanged since
  the walk".
- **A same-delivery takeover disposes of the occupant by what it IS.** When an
  allocation's create-only CAS meets a register naming the same source under another
  writer's nonce, the disposition follows what the occupant records. A RETIRED occupant
  is adopted, not replaced: it proves this identifier's exchange
  for this very source is past PUBREC, so the retirement is reinstated (behind a
  generation fence, since a discard may have re-minted the incarnation while the
  reconcile was outside the lock) and this allocation settles through the post-CAS ladder
  without transmitting. A pure CANCELLED occupant is reaped and the create retried, which
  is why that arm is ordered ABOVE the takeover: our allocation IS the fresh first
  transmission the tombstone's freeing licensed. A LIVE occupant is replaced at its exact
  sequence, and no claim is compared (F-105 7b): on the authority-backed admission route,
  which every supported QoS 1/2 delivery takes, the replacement batch compares the
  connection's accepted entitlement, while the experimental affine route (chapter P) writes
  with the standalone CAS. Two outcomes other than a landed replacement are distinct. A
  replacement whose write fails or is refused gives the allocation up, and its identifier
  passes to identifier exclusion. A replacement whose occupant marker reads as neither the
  occupant's nor authoritatively absent is WITHHELD: the allocation becomes a marker-opaque
  reservation over the occupant (`docs/CONFORMANCE.md`, "An unaccountable identifier space
  withholds new QoS 1/2 deliveries").
- **The resume's release is STAGED by the walk and COMMITTED once the resume succeeds.**
  What it releases is a RECOVERY reservation — opaque, demoted, marker-opaque or
  placeholder — captured before the walk enumerates. Recovery runs long before the success
  CONNACK, and every refusal after it — the CONNACK write, the lifetime grant, subscription
  restoration, consumer reconciliation, the 3.1.1 forced leave — preserves the session
  object and its maps, so releasing at the walk would free an identifier on a resume that
  never completed. The walk therefore only STAGES a release, and only when the custody
  census and the identifier space are both complete, the identifier is absent from the
  register and the PUBREL observations alike, and the capture is still current. It appends
  to a FRAME-LOCAL list, and the commit runs past every refusal return, immediately before
  the restore verdict opens, re-fencing the whole condition: the same client binding,
  generation, stream epoch and walk, completed-apply provenance, a complete identifier
  space, a custody ledger that is not withholding allocation, no custody or disposal hold
  on the identifier, and the same reservation entries at the same captured register
  sequences with no send section. A committed release hands the identifier to exclusion
  rather than freeing it outright, so its reclaim proves the absence. A fence miss keeps the
  reservation; a later resume can reconsider it and stage an eligible absence. The list is
  frame-local rather than session state because session-resident staging would let an
  aborted resume's decision be committed by a later resume whose own walk never observed
  the absence. Staging is not the only way a recovery reservation ends: recovery may also
  replace or reactivate it into an actionable entry, or hand it to terminal or exclusion
  ownership.
- **A transmission holds its identifier until it is no longer owed.** `queueOutbound`
  is a synchronous socket write, bounded by `mqttWriteDeadline` but not by anything
  shorter, so between the tracking decision and
  its return a teardown, a subscribe denial, a recovery apply, a terminal
  acknowledgement or a session discard could free the identifier and the allocator could
  re-mint it — two packets under one identifier, in order, on one socket. Every
  JETSTREAM-BACKED QoS 1/2 **PUBLISH** transmission and every **PUBREL** transmission
  therefore runs inside a SEND SECTION, and a **retained** QoS 1/2 message — which has no
  section, because it allocates in `serializeRetainedMsgsForSub`, frames itself, and is
  written by a later `queueOutbound` — carries an equivalent reservation in the same
  registry instead (F-091, below).
  The authority is a session-level registry of identifier-to-hold rather than the entry:
  a successful PUBREC replaces the PUBLISH entry with a PUBREL one while the write may
  still be blocked, and a PUBCOMP untracks the PUBREL entry while a duplicate copy is
  still unanswered, so per-entry state alone would strand the identifier. The registry
  deliberately survives a session discard — `clear()` resets the identifier counter to
  zero while the displaced connection's write is still in the socket.
- **A hold has THREE release conditions, and PRESENCE IN THE REGISTRY IS NOT A
  RESERVATION.** A *write that has not returned* is the only fact available on the
  PUBLISH side, because at that point no acknowledgement has been asked for yet. On the
  PUBREL side the real event is available and it is the one [MQTT-2.3.1-4] names: the
  identifier is free once the corresponding acknowledgement has been processed, which
  for a PUBREL is its PUBCOMP. So a hold also counts the PUBRELs transmitted under that
  identifier whose PUBCOMP has not arrived, and releasing on the write's return alone
  leaves the *second-order* case open — the client answers the duplicate later, and that
  stray PUBCOMP acknowledges away a re-minted exchange's PUBREL record, destroying the
  evidence that it is past PUBREC (F-089, the same severity class as F-088).
  The two halves differ across a connection change, which is why one hold carries both:
  the write drains at `endSend` on the transmitting goroutine and survives every
  transition, while a PUBCOMP is only ever processed on the session's CURRENT connection,
  so a debt owed to any other connection can never be answered.
- **A retained send's reservation is the third condition, and it is fenced by the session
  INCARNATION rather than by the write.** A retained QoS 1/2 message has no JetStream
  backing, so it has no register (R6) and never had a send section: it allocates in
  `serializeRetainedMsgsForSub`, is buffered on `sub.mqtt.prm`, and is written by a later
  flush — the SUBACK tail's, or the first live delivery to that subscription. Across that
  span its only other reservation is the `pendingPublish` entry, and `clear()` destroys
  exactly that while resetting the counter, so the identifier was handed straight back out
  while the displaced connection's write was still in the socket. The reservation is
  therefore taken in the same `sess.mu` acquisition as the allocation — under
  `asm.sessLocked[sess.id]`, so no successor can rebind between the two — and each buffered
  frame carries the identifier it was framed under.
  **Written completion ends it only while the allocating generation is still current.**
  Then `pendingPublish` is still there to carry custody on to the PUBACK, or a PUBACK for
  this very frame removed it and the identifier is genuinely free. Past a `clear()` neither
  is true, so the write returning does NOT free it: releasing there put a second PUBLISH
  under that identifier on the same socket, because `clear()` does not rebind `sess.c` and
  the still-bound connection's own delivery callbacks pass every gate. `sess.gen` is the
  fence because `clear()` re-mints it and an acknowledgement does not, and it never errs
  toward releasing — no path nils `pendingPublish` without re-minting.
  **A subscription leaving `c.subs` must not take an owed retained frame with it**, and the
  two dispositions differ. Its frames are detached while the connection lock is held, and
  then either TRANSFERRED to a reachable replacement or ABANDONED with their reservations
  released. Abandonment is UNFENCED — no bytes reached the client, so there is nothing for
  a re-minted identifier to collide with, and holding on would reserve the identifier against
  reallocation for the session's life while nothing will ever write the frame.
  **The same-sid replacement TRANSFERS rather than abandons**, and that distinction is
  load-bearing: a v5 SUBSCRIBE may legitimately carry one filter twice with the first entry
  asking for the replay, so releasing the displaced frames would silently discard a retained
  delivery the client is owed. Moving them onto the replacement — the entry every later flush
  and every later teardown finds — also keeps the replacement out of the reservation
  vocabulary entirely: the ordinary written and abandoned paths dispose of the supplemental
  RESERVATION. Neither releases the identifier itself — the `pendingPublish` entry goes on
  reserving that until the client acknowledges, or until the session's next resume drops an
  abandoned frame's entry.
  The three direct mutation sites are `processUnsub`'s delete, `processSub`'s replacement
  and `closeConnection`'s map swap; the last is for totality rather than correctness,
  since `mqttHandleClosedClient` nils `sess.c` first.
  A structural test holds those three to a frozen predicate — the mutation must be inside
  the connection lock with an unconsumed detach between the lock and the mutation. That test
  is a bounded regression tripwire, deliberately not a proof: it recognises only direct
  mutations through a signature-declared `*client` identifier, and does not resolve local
  aliases or helper-mediated mutation. The invariant above is universal; only the test's
  reach is bounded, and that boundary is fixed rather than open — see its res-judicata note.
  Once ownership moves the term is inert, and soundly so: no additional identifier-bearing
  PUBLISH *under that identifier* can reach the orphan's socket, because every route that
  could frame one opens a reservation refused on `sess.c != cc`.
  **PUBREL ADMISSION IS NOW A DURABLE GATE.** No SLOT-BACKED PUBREL bytes are transmitted
  without first ATOMICALLY ACQUIRING AN ACTION TOKEN on the slot that owns the identifier,
  and that acquisition is what permits the write — not the nonce, and not the callback
  having been reached. The one exception is a live retained exchange, which has no slot
  (R6) and is authorized instead by the live in-memory owner identity of its incarnation,
  refused once that identity is gone. The stated invariant is deliberately NOT "the slot
  must already say
  `pubrel_ready`": the store is what makes a record deliverable, and JetStream delivers it
  before the PUBREC handler's own phase CAS can run, so requiring `pubrel_ready` refused
  the very PUBREL the PUBREC had just created and every exchange waited out AckWait. A
  valid same-nonce record on a `publish` slot is therefore admitted through a **direct
  arrow to `pubrel_ready`** that installs the canonical record identity and the action
  token in ONE CAS. That is sound because a stored PUBREL cannot exist without a
  PUBREC: the ordinary producer stores only on the successful-PUBREC path, the only other
  producer is route-B recreation from a persisted past-PUBREC intent, and the builder
  refuses an absent or invalid owner nonce.

  Exactly ONE shape is authorized without a slot: a **retained** exchange has no register
  at all (R6) and is authorized by the exact live in-memory owner identity of this
  incarnation, which is why a retained record surviving a restart is refused rather than
  transmitted. A **drained** past-PUBREC exchange is NOT slot-less: §10.5 keeps its owner
  slot for the exchange's whole life (the drain does not release the register pre-forward),
  so its PUBREL transmits under an action acquired on that slot like every other slot-backed
  PUBREL. Its
  persisted drain intent is recovery EVIDENCE, not transmission authority — it authorizes
  recreating the record under the exchange's own owner nonce and gates the recovery-time
  reconciliation, but transmission still binds to the slot's durable action. The intent,
  the record and the slot all carry the register's own `regNonce`, so they name one
  exchange; a record whose nonce differs from the slot's is a different exchange, refused.

  `beginPubRelSendLocked`
  refuses an active transmission token, as it always did, and NOT a retained-only hold —
  so a PUBREL token and PUBCOMP debt may sit beside a retained term on one hold, which is
  coherent because the owner matches and both `endSend` and `consumePubRelAckLocked` ask
  the shared predicate, so each term is discharged only by its own event. Three refusals
  were tried here and all three refuted: a retained-term refusal blocks the retained QoS 2
  exchange's OWN PUBREL (the flusher holds the term live until after the triggering live
  PUBLISH is written, so the record waited out AckWait); a refusal on any live
  `pendingPublish` entry breaks a drain, which legitimately recreates a
  correlated PUBREL under a recovered entry's identifier; and one on a source-less entry
  starves an abandoned frame's record for the connection's life. The stale-PUBREL
  multiplexing hazard is owned wholly by F-092, whose fence admits a stored slot-backed
  PUBREL only under an action atomically acquired on the DURABLE OWNER SLOT that owns the
  identifier — never a correlation inferred against whatever in-memory entry holds it. A
  live retained exchange is the one slot-less admission: no register and so no slot (R6),
  authorized instead by the live in-memory owner identity of its incarnation and refused
  once that identity is gone. A
  successful PUBREC is ordinary successor custody: it replaces the PUBLISH entry with a
  `pendingPubRel` one, and the retained term is untouched by it. That is deliberately not
  the stronger "every transmission passes a send gate" — QoS 0 has no gate — nor "no
  additional identifier-bearing PUBLISH at all", since a multi-frame retained buffer holds
  several, each under its own identifier.
- **The acknowledgement debt is OWNED by a connection identity and read through
  `sess.c`, not dropped at named transition sites.** The identity is the connection's
  `cid`, a monotonic never-reused scalar — deliberately not a client pointer, because an
  inert hold outlives its connection by design and a pointer would keep the departed
  client's whole object graph reachable from a resident session for as long as that
  session lives, which for a never-expiring one is forever. A ZERO identity is refused
  rather than recorded, so no hold can carry one: zero means uninitialized, and two
  uninitialized connections would be indistinguishable to every ownership comparison.
  The sites cannot be enumerated safely: `clear()`
  never assigns `sess.c` at all, a persistent-session disconnect nils `sess.c` and never
  calls `clear()`, and the clean-start path runs `clear()` while the displaced client is
  still bound. A debt dropped at `clear()` would therefore leak forever on a
  never-expiring session and free an identifier the client still holds on a clean start.
  Read through `sess.c` instead, a debt stops reserving at exactly the moment its
  PUBCOMP stops being processable, at any of the seven `sess.c` writers. A retransmission
  on the next connection RESETS a dead predecessor's count rather than adding to it, or
  the one PUBCOMP the client owes could never clear a count of two.
  Because presence is not a reservation, an *inert* hold — no write out, no debt of ours
  — reserves nothing, and a reader that met one and refused would strand the identifier,
  its register and a Receive Maximum slot for the session's life. Such a hold is TAKEN
  OVER, never refused, and dropping it loses nothing precisely because it reserved
  nothing. The sweep is bounded-memory hygiene on that basis and nothing rests on it; it
  runs at `clear()` and again immediately after the CONNECT rebind assigns `sess.c`, which
  is the only point a hold's owner changes and therefore the only point the predicate turns
  a predecessor's owner-scoped term inert. A live write token is owner-independent and
  survives both. That is not the "dropped at a named transition site" the debt rule
  forbids: the rule is about a LIVE debt, and the sweep deletes only what the predicate has
  already proved reserves nothing. The rule is enforced as an ownership boundary rather
  than a habit: the registry is touched only by the liveness predicate and the helpers that
  mutate a hold, and every other reader asks `sendReservedLocked`.
  Adding a term to that predicate is NOT additive — it changes what every reader and
  mutator means. The ones that ask the predicate adapt for free; the ones that re-spell the
  condition do not — and when the retained term arrived, `consumePubRelAckLocked` was the
  one that had to change, switching to the shared predicate so a PUBCOMP could no longer
  delete a hold carrying a live retained reservation. `beginPubRelSendLocked` was given a
  retained-term refusal too and it was DELETED again: see the PUBREL-admission paragraph
  above for why, and do not reinstate it.
- **A removal path that meets an active section CONDEMNS the entry** instead of deleting
  it, parking the continuation it owes; the first parked disposition wins, because every
  continuation is idempotent against another remover's durable work, with ONE exception
  (F-097 D4, witnessed by W6b): the client's ANSWER replaces a parked non-answer. An
  acknowledgement kind (`AckComplete`, `PubRecFailed`; `mqttSendSettleIsAnswer`) parked
  after a teardown, deny or recovery drop takes the section's end, because that
  acknowledgement was already consumed from the wire and the client never sends it again;
  left behind a deny's `DenyRelease` it completed nothing and the exchange stayed at
  `Publish`. The reverse never happens: once an answer is parked, no later non-answer
  replaces it. Terminal
  acknowledgements park their identifier-freeing half (their protocol answer is
  unaffected), while a successful PUBREC needs no transfer machinery at all, the registry
  holding the identifier however the entries move. F-089 originally required no PUBCOMP
  park because the register was then deleted at PUBREC. F-092 replaced that handoff: the
  same slot now survives through the PUBREL states, PUBCOMP terminalizes it, and terminal
  cleanup disposes the matching PUBREL records before deleting the slot.

A session discard removes the retiring incarnation's registers with a **bounded reap**
rather than arbitrating each one as the inbound hold walk does: on the discarding broker
nothing is competing for a register — no claim record, no marker — though a resuming
session does read one as durable authority and rewrite it to take ownership. Its
enumeration filter names a generation `clear()` has already re-minted, so it cannot reach
the next incarnation. That is the extent of the claim. A resume preserves the generation,
so a peer may still be serving this incarnation; whether removing a register costs anything
there is `$MQTT_inflight`'s own consequence question, and **F-034 answered it on
2026-08-22**.

Until F-034 this was a blind FILTER PURGE, and that is why the remedy `$MQTT_qos2in` had
already received could not simply be copied: **F-062** bounded every hold purge to a proven
cutoff, and a filter purge enumerates nothing, so it has no watermark to be bounded by.
Giving `$MQTT_inflight` one was F-034's work and is done — `reapIncarnationRegisters`
enumerates, loads, classifies and deletes only at or below the sequence its own enumeration
returned, and only a record whose identity and subject agree. **No filter purge of this
stream remains anywhere in the broker**, which is also why `DenyPurge` moved from a fatal
prerequisite to a waiver in the table above.

**Cost, stated plainly.** One create-only CAS round trip per *first* transmission of
every outbound QoS 1/2 message, one delete per completion, and on QoS 2 a confirmed
rather than fire-and-forget source ack. Redeliveries and recovered deliveries pay
nothing. Batching the *writes* was rejected because it would delay first transmissions
behind a batch, and registering *after* sending is not a cheaper version of this design
but a reintroduction of the deviation as a narrower window.

**Resume reads are batched, and that is a correctness-adjacent property.** The barrier
runs before the CONNACK, and a session may legitimately hold up to 65 535 in-flight
identifiers, so one request per record would put tens of thousands of serial round trips
in front of every reconnect — pushing restart recovery past ordinary client timeouts and
making failover impractical for exactly the sessions that need it most. Instead the
registers are enumerated by subject in one request (the identifier's 16 bits bound the
filter below JetStream's subject-detail truncation point, which is why this enumeration
is safe here although the account-wide orphan sweep refuses it) and loaded in bounded
batches; sources are then classified once per *source*, with one consumer lookup per
durable and batched message reads. Shared-register claim writes are likewise pipelined in
a bounded concurrent window; their subjects are distinct and carry no ordering dependency,
so serializing them would restore the same pre-CONNACK latency problem. Every uncertainty
is preserved exactly as the one-at-a-time path preserved it: a missing response, an
unreadable consumer and a
consumer that is gone are all "unknown", never "complete".

An unreadable register cannot participate in claim arbitration: its body cannot be
rewritten while preserving the allocation identity, so a stale object may still know its
sequence. It remains in the existing loud, fail-closed opaque state — the identifier is
reserved and new allocation is withheld — rather than being guessed owned or closed.

### An exchange's LINEAGE is carried, where its nonce is deliberately re-minted

A register's `Nonce` identifies the **allocation**. The same-delivery replacement arm
re-mints it on purpose — "take the slot over at its exact sequence so the record carries
OUR nonce" — so that the previous writer's cleanup is fenced off the new record and
cannot tear what this writer just installed.

That same arm can **inherit a client-facing obligation**, and it says so in its own
terms. When the occupant's unsent marker is authoritatively **absent**, the register
alone is rewritten, "with no marker minted for an exchange the client may already hold",
and the occupant's QoS is preserved because it "is evidence about what the CLIENT may
already be holding". After that write the record is a **new allocation for an old
obligation**, and until now no field named the obligation.

`Lin` names it. It is **mandatory**, and it is a second identity beside the nonce rather
than a reuse of it, because the two answer different questions: *whose write is this*
and *whose message is this*.

**The value is decided by each attempt's WRITE MODE**, never once per call:

| Write mode | `Lin` |
|---|---|
| create-only pair — a fresh allocation, and every retry that falls back to one | this attempt's own `Nonce` |
| replacement, marker present and naming the occupant (**proven-unsent**) | a fresh `Nonce` |
| replacement, marker authoritatively absent (**possibly-attempted**) | the occupant's `Lin` — **inherited** |
| cancellation tombstone, create-only body | its own allocation's nonce |
| every whole-record rebuild — custody rewrite, phase CAS, `Retired`/`Cancelled` mark, action install | carried by the copy |

The write-mode rule is not a stylistic choice. The admission ladder
(`runInflightAdmission`, behind both `admitInflightPublish` and the affine
`storeInflightRegister`) builds its record once and its retry loop resets the mode to a
create-only pair **without rebuilding that record**, so a lineage chosen for a
replacement and then carried into the retry would durably stamp a genuinely new exchange
with an obligation the client had already discharged. The reset therefore lives beside
the mode reset, and the two replacement arms assign it where the marker boundary has just
partitioned the occupant.

**One derivation, frozen once per attempt.** The table's first three rows are ONE
function, `mqttLineageForWrite(mode, occupant, nonce)` (`outbound_replace_compose.go`):
a create or a pair replacement yields `(nonce, 0)`, a register-only replacement the
occupant's `(Lin, Acq)`, and anything else an empty lineage every caller refuses. The
ladder applies its `Lin` before each attempt (the reset arm with no occupant, since the
previous attempt's read is stale there); the orchestrator hands that same value to
custody as the attempt's charge, the ambiguous-attempt record stores it, and the landed
settlement installs it. The ladder applies the `Lin` only: nothing on the ladder or
settlement path reads `Acq`, and the affine writer stores the ladder's record verbatim,
so its bytes are unchanged. The writers that build the batch derive it AGAIN and refuse
on disagreement rather than correct it: the replacement composer
(`mqttReplacePublishTransition`) refuses a displacing register whose `Lin` is not the
derived one and then applies both `Lin` and `Acq`, and refuses a pair replacement's
fresh exchange unless `opReplacePublish` named it by the derived lineage;
`opAdmitPublish` refuses a create whose register's
`Lin` is not its own `Nonce`, a rule that before was enforced only incidentally by the
exchange's create-only collision. So a batch that would write one obligation while
custody charges another is never submitted. Two definitions of this mapping used to
agree only by coincidence of code.

"Marker absent" is deliberately **not** read as "transmitted": send intent deletes the
marker **before** the bytes leave, so absence means *possibly-attempted*. That is
precisely the state that carries an obligation forward, which is why it is the
inheriting arm.

A custody rewrite preserves the lineage with **no code of its own**: every rewrite
rebuilds from the record it read, and `casInflightSlot` copies the loaded record before
mutating selected fields. `TestMQTTLineageWriterCensus` holds that closed — it **scans
the source** for every call that persists a register body and requires a disposition for
each discovered site, with no restriction to functions already named, so a writer added
later fails it rather than escaping it.

In memory the lineage rides beside `qos` on the pending entry, installed from the
**landed** record at confirmation for the same reason `qos` is: the replacement arm may
have inherited the occupant's, so the value an attempt proposed is not authoritative.

A register with no lineage, or a malformed one, is an **unsupported persisted shape and
is refused** — never defaulted to the nonce, which is the value a *fresh* exchange gets
and would read an inherited obligation as a new one. Refusal is what the compatibility
boundary requires; such a record means the development store predates this design and
must be recreated.

The lineage is what custody charges and releases ("Capacity and identifier custody
belong to the exchange"), what an exchange is named by, and the identity F-097's
terminal-completion evidence is keyed on.

### An exchange's QoS is carried, not recomputed

**Shipping scope, stated first because the rule below is stated universally.** What ships
is **QoS 1 ↔ QoS 2**. A QoS 1/2 → **QoS 0** re-SUBSCRIBE is a different mechanism —
teardown rather than transmission — and is **not** covered by this rule; it is covered
instead by converting the consumer into a drain, under "UNSUBSCRIBE drain", with its own
residuals for a stream-imposed inactivity limit and the CONNECT restore path. The
**shared-affine** route is not covered either: an
effective-QoS-2 shared delivery branches into the affine move before the identifier is
allocated, and shared subscriptions are capped at granted QoS 1 for the alpha.

A subscription's maximum QoS is an input to a message's **first** transmission and to
nothing else. `sub.mqtt.qos` is mutable — the existing-consumer refresh arm writes the
new granted QoS onto the live delivery subscription on any re-SUBSCRIBE — while
[MQTT-3.8.4-3] requires the replacement to be accepted *without interrupting the flow of
publications*. Recomputing the wire QoS per delivery therefore re-derived a started
exchange's QoS from whatever the subscription said at that instant.

So the exchange's QoS lives on its pending entry, and the delivery callback reads it
there:

- **Sourced only from per-exchange evidence, and the list is exhaustive:** the QoS the
  register actually landed holding, the register's own QoS on recovery
  (`mqttRecoveredPending`, which is where it used to be dropped), or — for a retained
  send, which has no register at all — the QoS selected when the identifier was
  allocated.
- **Subscription- and drain-level QoS are not evidence about an individual exchange.**
  Delivery QoS is `min(published, granted)`, so a QoS 1 publication through a QoS 2
  subscription is transmitted at QoS 1: one drain routinely holds both, and a drain's
  own `qos` is a copy of whatever the subscription said at staging time.
- **The read is in the send section**, under the same `sess.mu` acquisition that admits
  the send, and it is **unconditional** — there is no branch on whether the delivery is a
  retransmission. It has to be after any register store has settled, because a
  replacement can make the record adopt a QoS the caller never supplied; and the
  no-evidence case is tested *before* the send is reserved, so the fail-closed return
  leaks no reservation.
- **Zero means no evidence, and is a withhold rather than a default.** It is not a phase
  or history discriminator: some PUBREL reservations are built through the same recovery
  helper and carry a non-zero value. And it is not a claim that a transmission happened —
  an admitted replacement donates its occupant's QoS to an allocation that may never have
  been transmitted. F-072 since gave the broker a durable transmission fact — the register's
  `unsent` marker, present for proven-unsent and absent for possibly-attempted (or present
  beside a recovered output token, F-088) — but this
  field is not derived from it and still asserts nothing about transmission.

**The same-source replacement preserves the occupant's QoS.** Where a register for this
exact delivery already exists, written elsewhere, the replacing writer takes the slot
over at its exact sequence so the record carries its own nonce — but it cannot prove the
occupant was never transmitted, because a cancellation may live only as a nonce in the
session record rather than in the record body. A live PUBLISH-phase occupant is therefore
evidence about what the client may already be holding, and its QoS is the only durable
trace of it. The replacement is assigned in the arm rather than at the store's argument,
because the record is built once before the retry loop. Successful confirmation then
threads the QoS **as landed** back onto the pending entry, on both the successful-CAS and
the lost-response reconciliation path, so the wire and the register cannot disagree; the
reconciliation path reads the record that actually exists, since a nonce identifies the
*allocation* and never an immutable body.

**What this does not do is keep the inherited exchange alive.** A concurrent cancellation
or a failed store still destroys or abandons it, because `regPending` is still read as
evidence of never-transmitted at several sites. Those are pre-existing lifecycle defects
of the replacement arm, consolidated into **F-088**'s roadmap bullet, which owns
cancellation proof together with continuous custody; the
acknowledgement guard that declines a PUBACK/PUBREC for an unconfirmed allocation stays
in place for that reason — the handler below it cannot advance such an entry safely —
though for an inherited allocation the client's acknowledgement may be entirely
legitimate, and nothing replays a discarded one.

**A drain owes PUBREL handling on per-exchange evidence, not on its own QoS.** Because a
re-SUBSCRIBE can lower a drain's `qos` below the QoS of exchanges already started under
it, gating PUBREL recreation, PUBREL-delivery establishment and the withhold-on-failure
set on `d.qos` alone meant a QoS 2 exchange past PUBREC inside a QoS 1 drain never had
its PUBREL recreated — loss, not a wrong header byte. One predicate answers all three:
the drain's own QoS, **or** a persisted past-PUBREC intent on any sequence (only a QoS 2
exchange can be past PUBREC), **or** a recovered PUBLISH entry whose register says QoS 2,
identity-matched on durable and sequence. The third term is what covers an exchange
transmitted but not yet past PUBREC, which carries no intent; it is sourceable because
register recovery runs, and aborts CONNECT on failure, before any of the three gates.

## Session incarnations and teardown

A client ID hashes to a stable token, and a session's JetStream resources used to
be named from that hash alone. But the hash is reused: a clean start, a session
expiry and a takeover-discard each destroy one session and let a later one adopt
the same hash. A deterministic name is therefore **not an identity**, and a
teardown issued by a superseded broker could delete a resource a fresh session had
just created.

**Incarnation generations** (`internal/mqtt/sess_incarnation.go`) fix that
structurally. Each session carries a persisted generation (record field `gen`) that
scopes every otherwise-hash-only name: the PUBREL durable, its `$MQTT_out` subject
and its delivery subject; the `$MQTT_qos2in` hold subjects and the filters a
discard purges; and each `$MQTT_willq` outbox record. It is minted when a session
is first created and re-minted by `clear()` — which every discard path runs,
including the two that *reuse* the session object as a fresh session — while a
plain reconnect or resume **preserves** it, because a resumed session must still
find its own PUBRELs, QoS 2 holds and Will. The invariant this buys is exactly one
thing: a late delete from a retired incarnation cannot name a FRESH incarnation's
resources. It does not establish that no live resource exists under the retiring
generation — a resume preserves the generation, so a peer may still be serving it. Where a
late removal had to be made safe against that peer, the bound came from the removal rather
than the name: on `$MQTT_qos2in` every hold purge carries the highest sequence its remover
could prove it was entitled to destroy (F-062). What that premise costs on
`$MQTT_inflight` was audited by F-034 (2026-08-22), and the answer is the same in kind: the
teardown's register pass carries the watermark its own enumeration returned, and conditions
each delete on the identity it loaded at the sequence it loaded.

This is the same conclusion the QoS 2 move protocol and the affine delivery path
reached independently, and it is why the fix is naming rather than a lock: a nonce
re-check before each delete is a check-then-act, and no in-process lock arbitrates
anything against another broker.

**The teardown claim** (`internal/mqtt/sess_teardown.go`) covers what naming
cannot: two brokers tearing down and resuming the same record at once. Before
deleting anything, a discard CASes a `Teardown{Origin, Nonce, StartedAt}` marker
onto the record at the sequence it resolved against, preserving the record's
content so any broker can finish the job and so the orphan sweep still reads its
durables as referenced. Losing that CAS means the claim is not ours, and the loser
deletes **nothing** — a complete outcome, not a failure. Releasing is a
sequence-targeted delete whose result is classified by **re-reading**, because
`MaxMsgsPer: 1` may already have removed that sequence on a peer's behalf: absent
means done, our own nonce means retry, and a foreign nonce or no marker means the
release is not ours to make. The release is always confirmed even on the no-wait discard
path, since an unclassifiable release is not a release.

Nobody resumes a marked record. Every CONNECT that can interpret the record (and the
record-driven expiry path) **finishes** the teardown when it finds a marker —
repeating the generation-scoped deletions and releasing the record — and
only then starts a fresh session with a fresh generation and Session Present false.
Repetition is safe for names nothing can re-occupy. The inbound QoS 2 hold walk purges by
subject, so a repeat can name a subject re-occupied since: what makes it safe is the bound
each call carries, per walk, which naming alone never gave — see **F-062** for what that
bounds and what it deliberately does not. It is **not** claimed for the deletion set as a
whole on naming alone — but the other unbounded member is gone: the same teardown used to
purge `$MQTT_inflight` by filter with no bound at all, and **F-034** replaced that with an
enumerate-load-classify pass carrying its own watermark.
That also makes a crashed teardown self-healing instead of leaking until the orphan
sweep. The exception is a record the restore boundary refuses outright — a subscription
in the reserved `$MQTT.>` namespace, or a missing or malformed generation: the CONNECT
is refused without adopting the marker. What finishes it then depends on which refusal
it was, and only one of the two is recoverable:

- **Reserved namespace, generation valid**: the expiry path and the orphan sweep's
  adoption both still act on the record — the deletions they issue are
  generation-scoped and the record's generation is sound — so the marker is finished
  and the state is reclaimed without a CONNECT.
- **No valid generation**: nothing adopts it. `expireSessionFromRecord` refuses to act
  on a record it cannot validate, `mqttValidateTeardownTargets` rejects it through
  `mqttValidateSessionRecord`, and the orphaned-consumer sweep counts the consumers the
  record names as *referenced*, so they are not reaped either. The record, its
  consumers and its marker persist until an operator resets the ten-stream `$MQTT_*`
  bundle.
  That is the pre-existing consequence of the generation refusal — there is no
  generation to scope a safe deletion by — and it is why both refusals prescribe
  recreating the streams rather than offering a way to work around the record.

Shared group durables stay outside all of this: they are not owned by one session. The
teardown seals this generation's acquisition ledger, releases every acquisition it lists
(retiring the incarnation whose last acquisition it was), and only then — behind a gate
that requires the sealed ledger to be empty — releases the record. See "A group durable
is held by arbitration, not counted by a scan".

### The incarnation completion lease

Re-minting a generation protects the NEXT incarnation from the retiring one's late
writes, and for years the clean-start discard did it **while the displaced client was
still bound and still admitted**. That was F-036's own defect, and its cost was not
theoretical: a displaced PUBREL derives its hold subject from `sess.gen` at handler
time, so once the generation moved it looked under the FRESH incarnation's subject,
found nothing, and answered a success-shaped PUBCOMP — telling a client an
exactly-once exchange had completed for a payload the same teardown then destroyed.
One broker, no crash, no peer.

The property that has to hold is **P**: *a session object's incarnation generation
changes only while no client is bound to it*. What makes P enforceable rather than
asserted is a per-incarnation ownership ledger (`internal/mqtt/sess_lease.go`).

**The tracker, and why identity is the object.** Each incarnation gets a fresh
`mqttIncarnationTracker` — `open → closing → retired`, an owner count, and three
per-close-cycle channels. Every owner CAPTURES the tracker it was admitted by, so a
late release lands on the incarnation that admitted it and can never decrement the
fresh one's count. The channels are recreated by `reopen()`, so a closed channel from
an aborted transition can never satisfy a later transition's drain.

**A lease is a capability, not a bit.** `mqttLease` is a pointer with a released
flag, checked and changed under the same mutex as the count, so a retained copy cannot
resurrect ownership once the drain proof exists. `promote()` converts a self-retiring
caller's own lease into tracker-only debt — so a caller performing the retirement never
waits on itself — and revokes it in the same operation.

**The boundary is local execution, not the transport.** There is deliberately no way to
hand ownership to a QUEUED effect. What the lease owns is execution that can outlive the
retirement and then observe the re-minted session, mutate the reused object, derive a
name from the fresh incarnation, or emit the old route's protocol result. A JetStream
entry whose subject, reply, headers and body were fully captured while the parent lease
was held is none of those: its safety is a property of its TARGET, and those rules are
authoritative and unchanged —

- an **incarnation-scoped or per-consumer-unique** target cannot reach a successor: a
  plain durable is `idHash + "_" + nuid.Next()`, and both the plain and the drain
  consumer deletions are restricted to such names;
- an **exact stream sequence** is never reused;
- a **session-record write** that times out leaves the write UNCERTAIN, and
  `prepareClear` refuses the retirement until a readback classifies it — which is why
  an ambiguous record write blocks a discard rather than racing it;
- a **shared-group** target is arbitrated by the group record: a group ack names a
  physical incarnation, and a `CONSUMER.DELETE` is issued only for an incarnation the
  record has moved into `retiring`, whose name a successor incarnation never reuses — the
  group-scoped arbitration the lease was never the instrument for;
- a **user subject** — the derived Sparkplug publication — is a session-independent
  application publication that a takeover may legitimately not retract.

So a JSA timeout abandons the WAITER, not necessarily the already-queued operation, and
the retirement owes no wait beyond the synchronous owner's return.

**Where ownership is acquired.** Not a list of sites — three structural boundaries:

- **Per packet**, at the single pre-dispatch point in `mqttParse`, against
  `c.mqtt.tracker`: the incarnation this CONNECTION was bound to, captured at both
  bind sites and never cleared. That is the whole discrimination — after a re-mint the
  displaced connection still names the RETIRED tracker and is refused, while the
  replacement names the fresh one. The read loop holds no standing lease, so a quiet
  displaced connection cannot hold a takeover off, and the DISCONNECT route releases
  its own lease before entering the teardown that drains it.
- **Per delivery**, inside `sess.processSub` — the one wrapper every session-scoped
  delivery callback reaches its NATS subscription through, so the boundary covers the
  class by construction. This is what closes the class three earlier attempts died on:
  an ordinary QoS 1/2 delivery passing its own `sess.c == cc` check and then lazily
  RECREATING a map `clear()` had nilled. A refusal skips without acking, so JetStream
  re-offers to whoever owns the consumer next.
- **Per timer fire**, never per timer delay. A pending expiry timer holds nothing —
  otherwise a ten-minute deadline would hold every clean-start reconnect off for ten
  minutes — and acquires when it fires, BEFORE it takes the client-ID gate, so a fire
  against a retiring incarnation returns without ever holding the gate a retirement
  needs. Each timer carries an immutable install token, so a callback that fired and
  then lost `as.mu` to a cancel-and-re-arm cannot consume the replacement's entry and
  expire a session it never named; and a fire that finds its incarnation retiring
  re-arms **only if its own view is still current** — same resident object, same
  tracker, no timer already installed. An unconditional re-arm there is a fresh
  session's data loss rather than a nicety: a callback descheduled across a re-mint
  would replace the new incarnation's deadline with a one-second retry, and the retry
  would expire a session that had just connected. Where the check refuses, the sweep
  re-arms a finite expiry from the record.

An in-route bounded wait is cancelled by the retirement too. Both QoS 1/2 waits — the
transmission gates and the phase gate — select on the tracker's per-cycle closing
signal, because their cap is up to thirty seconds, far past the drain ceiling: a
delivery admitted just before a takeover would otherwise hold its lease long enough to
make the takeover refuse, repeatedly, for a reason unrelated to the contender. The
answer on that arm is the one an armed gate already gives — WITHHELD, recorded without
acking, so the redelivery is still a first transmission.

A parked retirement obligation is watched by a worker admitted **eagerly, when the
obligation is armed** — never spawned later by whichever release happens to drain the
tracker. A release does nothing but close the cycle's drained channel; the worker was
already inside the server's shutdown lifecycle before it could run. Where admission is
refused because shutdown has begun, the discard completes SYNCHRONOUSLY on the arming
goroutine rather than being left in memory: a clean session's record carries expiry
interval zero and the expiry sweep skips exactly those, so there is no recovery anchor
to defer to.

The obligation's identity is the pair **{session object, its tracker}**, not the client
ID. While a finisher waits, an uncertainty resolver can evict its object and a CONNECT
can install a replacement under the same ID; a client-ID claim would then delete the
replacement's map entries and leave its live connection bound to a session no lookup
finds. Both manager indexes must still name that object, and the object must still
carry that tracker, before the claim is taken — and the eviction that completes it is
`removeSessionIfCurrent`.

**Two-phase retirement.** `clear()` is split: `prepareClear` (both uncertainty
refusals and the record fence — nothing mutated on any path through it), then the
permit, then `destroy` (today's destructive body). Every caller closes the tracker and
drains it under a wall-clock ceiling before preparing, and `setIncarnationLocked`
REQUIRES a permit that only `retireIncarnationLocked` mints, over `sess.c == nil` and
a drained tracker. On the one caller with a client bound, the order is: close, drain,
capture, prepare, **detach**, mint, destroy, bind.

**The capsule.** The detach takes the displaced client and its parked
deferred-disconnect action into a `mqttRetiredBinding`, atomically, because after it
`sess.c` is nil and every later arm would otherwise rediscover nothing: the fourth
attempt showed a bare early detach silently drops the connection's close, its
notification, its Will, its disconnect stamp and its expiry. The success, superseded
and teardown-incomplete arms all consume the capsule; nothing reads `sess.c` after the
detach. The `sess.c`-reading form of the superseded disposal was deleted rather than
kept beside the capsule one.

**Failure is refusal, never disposal under a live owner.** A drain ceiling or an
unresolved-state refusal REOPENS the tracker, wakes the parked routes, leaves the
incumbent bound with its Will, socket, expiry and disconnect state untouched, and
refuses the contending CONNECT. That is the disposition the fourth attempt could not
supply. `destroy` arms the retirement resolution by defer at entry, so every
destructive outcome — success, superseded, teardown-incomplete, any post-reset error —
releases parked ingress exactly once.

**A clean session's discard is owed even when it cannot run.** `[MQTT-3.1.2-6]`
requires it, and the expiry sweep skips expiry-zero records, so the close path may not
simply leave the object resident: on a ceiling it parks a **retirement-pending**
obligation (the tracker stays closing, which is what makes the session
non-resumable), restores residency for reachability, and completes the discard either
from the drain trigger — scheduled off the tracker mutex, because the finisher
reacquires the client-ID gate — or from a CONNECT that finds the mark, JOINS the
existing cycle rather than closing a second one, and claims the obligation under the
gate it already holds. The claim is the arbitration; the loser finds it gone.

**The record epoch is not a substitute for the drain.** It invalidates transactions
opened before the generation ended. The completion drain additionally prevents an
already-admitted continuation from resuming after the reset, opening a NEW transaction
at the new epoch, recreating cleared state, or deriving a target from the re-minted
object — which is why every discard path drains, not only the two that hand the object
back as a fresh session.

**What it does not subsume.** `sess.c != c` still discriminates the wrong CLIENT on a
live incarnation; the lease discriminates the wrong INCARNATION. The record fence still
serializes record writers and classifies ambiguity — it does not cover pre-fence map
mutation, which is precisely why the lease exists. The inbound-release and affine
fences still serialize their own in-flight windows for all six callers. Send
reservations still hold identifier custody, and F-089's rule that a displaced
connection's PUBCOMP debt survives the discard is preserved by making that connection
the authority for its own holds while nothing is bound in its place — self-clearing at
the rebind, which is the event that retires the debt.

### A deleted record is retired under a licence, not under its absence

The session-record watch converges every MOVED record, bound sessions included. A
DELETED one on a BOUND session is the shape it could not finish, and it was site 1 of
F-036. `reconcileResidentOwnership` already recognises it — a resident session holding a
non-zero sequence whose subject is authoritatively empty — and ARMS the ownership marker,
because absence IS an ownership fact: only a party that first CLAIMED the record at the
sequence it believed current can remove it.

Nothing consumed that marker for a bound, silent client. The settlement's bound half runs
PRE-DISPATCH on the connection's own read loop, because a QoS 1 PUBLISH served from a
displaced connection is acked and unretractable; its unbound half claims the client-ID
gate as NOBODY and so is refused while a client is attached. A client that negotiated Keep
Alive 0 and then went quiet satisfies neither, and held a session another broker had torn
down for the whole remaining life of the connection — the split-brain
`[MQTT-3.1.4-3]` forbids.

**The licence, and it needs no new durable state**
(`internal/mqtt/sess_gone_retire.go`): a valid retirement watermark whose `mseq` exceeds
this session's acknowledged sequence, PLUS the record authoritatively absent, PLUS a full
in-fence revalidation. Each conjunct earns its place — a claim marker is a CAS against the
sequence the claiming party believed current; a failed `recordGenRetirement` aborts before
any deletion and leaves the record MARKED rather than absent; a landed local write moves
`sess.seq` while an ambiguous one arms `seqUncertain`; and an apply-time watermark
regression can only cause a false NEGATIVE. **Absence alone is NOT the licence** — that
inference is what F-036's site 3 is a finding about.

**The ordering**, and the reason it cannot be the obvious one: the proof must run BEFORE
the detach, because afterwards `sess.c` is nil and the permit is already minted, so there
is no binding left to check. `retireBoundIncarnationChecked` therefore takes a PRE-DETACH
callback and pauses after `prepareClear` has opened the record transaction. An off-gate
prefilter refuses the ordinary case without ever contending for the gate; the gate is then
claimed as the exact resident object AND the exact bound client — **both** manager
indexes, which is the identity set `finishPendingDiscard` already requires, because a
CONNECT looks up through `as.sessions` while the record watch's eviction worker resolves
through `as.sessByHash`, and checking one would let this route and that worker each
believe it owns the object. Inside the callback the durable reads run with neither manager
nor session mutex held, the watermark is read BEFORE the final record-absence read so the
last fallible observation is the one establishing absence, and the in-memory identity —
both indexes, the owner, the sequence, the generation, the armed marker, the uncertainty
flag — is then re-checked under `as.mu` with `sess.mu` nested, as ONE observation.

**Failure is refusal, never disposal under a live owner.** Every arm before the detach
aborts the transaction, reopens the tracker and leaves the incumbent bound with its Will,
socket, expiry and disconnect state untouched; the marker stays armed and a later pass
asks again. The unwind guard lives inside the helper rather than in the caller, because at
that point the caller has not received the prepared clear, so a panic or `runtime.Goexit`
escaping the callback would otherwise leave an open record transaction and a closed
tracker with nothing holding a reference to either — a session that refuses every write
and every packet for the rest of the process's life.

Because the record is gone, `destroy` normally returns the superseded error after
resetting the incarnation: its own claim cannot land against an absent record, which is
the very fact that licensed the retirement. **That is the expected outcome here**, and it
reports `ownership unsettled` — never a takeover, because no record shape demonstrates a
successor (F-084). **The Will is not suppressed**: the disposal is unlicensed, so a
retirement watermark proves a TEARDOWN and not a successor connection, and the remote
teardown owned the durable session retirement rather than this broker's TCP connection or
its connection-local Will. A successful retirement here also captures no parked action,
and that is an invariant rather than a hope: parking consumes the connection's Will and
nils `sess.c`, so the pre-detach owner check refuses a parked session outright.

Everything owed after the detach is armed by DEFERRED wrappers over mutable variables
before `destroy` runs, and read at execution time — the construction `mqttProcessConnect`
already uses. Straight-line code was wrong there and the failure was silent: an abnormal
exit escaping `destroy` or the Will phase let `destroy`'s own defers close the record
transaction and retire the tracker, and the caller's defer release the gate, while the
disposition, the Will, the notification and the socket close were all skipped — leaving
the client connected against a RETIRED tracker. The connection tail is armed BEFORE the
Will runs, so an exit from inside the Will phase still closes the socket; and because
closing alone is not enough, a **Will BACKSTOP** retries the discharge.

**The backstop's claim is exactly one thing: recovery from an exit BEFORE
`mqttTakeWillLocked` has consumed the live Will.** It is not general recovery from a
partial application, and it is worth being precise because the imprecise version invited a
mechanism this design deliberately does not have. Before the take, a retry discharges the
Will normally — which matters because a detached connection's own teardown takes the
rebound path through `mqttPublishOwedWill`, which publishes only an IMMEDIATE Will, so a
Will carrying a nonzero Will Delay Interval would otherwise be neither published nor
enqueued and would be lost silently. AFTER the take, the retry is harmless but recovers
nothing: the take is exactly-once under the client lock, so the retry simply finds no Will.
The window between the take and the durable handoff is therefore a **stated residual**, not
something the backstop closes, and `docs/CONFORMANCE.md` records it as one. Production has
no post-take abnormal-exit source on this route, and a genuine uncaught panic terminates
the process. Closing it properly would need a claimed/completed handoff with a stable
outbox identity — a fourth variant of this mechanism, refused as disproportionate for a
window no comparable route in this broker survives either.

**What this does not close**, both stated in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`: a record GONE with an
absent, corrupt, indeterminate or insufficient watermark has no licence, so the marker
stays armed and the client may strand until it sends traffic — which then drives the
pre-dispatch settlement exactly as before; and the take-to-durable-handoff window above,
where an abnormal exit loses the Will the backstop cannot recover.

For the same reason this route exists at all, the periodic pass sends a BOUND armed
session to the ownership backstop instead of the unbound settlement. Otherwise the first
refusal would be final: from the moment the marker is armed that branch owns the session,
and the backstop that re-reads the record would be unreachable.

### The generation-retirement watermark

The claim licenses the deletions, and the release that says whether the claim is
still ours runs *after* them — it has to, because it proves absence rather than
authorship, and moving it earlier only lets an already-admitted proposal recreate the
same shape one step later. So while the deletions run, the marker is the only durable
record of the retirement, and the marker lives on the record's own subject. An
UNCONDITIONAL foreign write can land after it did — a CAS excludes a competing
conditional write off that base but not one carrying no expectation (see the
same-base boundary in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`) — and `MaxMsgsPer: 1` then **evicts**
it. What survives is a record naming
exactly the resources the winner deleted, with no marker for an adopter or the sweep
to find: a **hollow survivor** that a reconnect resumes with Session Present 1 for
consumers, holds and in-flight registers that no longer exist.

The fix keeps the retirement fact **off the replaceable subject**. Every teardown that
wins its claim first records a permanent per-client watermark on `$MQTT_teardown`
(`{id, gen, mseq, nonce, origin, started}`, one subject per client,
`MaxMsgsPer: 1`), and only then deletes. It is written on both writers — `clear()` and
`finishAdoptedTeardown`, which deletes the same resources under a marker just as
evictable — always confirmed, even on a no-wait discard: a fence that only reached a
send queue is not a fence. There are two direct writers and a **third initiating
path**: the CONNECT rollback's zero-lifetime branch, which routes through `clear()`
rather than fencing on its own (see "Two frontends taking over one session from the
same base"), so nothing else can record a retirement without holding the base. A write
that cannot be confirmed **aborts the teardown with nothing deleted**, leaving the record
marked, which is the already-handled self-healing state.

**A generation whose retirement was ever recorded is retired, and stays fenced.**
`mseq` — the `$MQTT_sess` sequence the claim marker landed at — is the ordering field,
and replacement is decided by it *alone*: a standing watermark at or above ours is
already at least as new, a lower one is CAS-replaced at the sequence we read, and a
rejection is resolved by re-reading rather than classified. The generation plays no
part in that decision, because a generation-equality early return would let a newer
same-generation retirement be skipped and leave a paused older writer's write final.
The monotonicity is **decision-time** monotonicity; an admitted CAS that applies after
a leader transition can still regress the single slot, which is a stated residual.

**The watermark carried an `rwid` naming the record the deletion removed, and that field
was REMOVED** by `docs/ROADMAP.md`'s vanished-record item, which is the box that decided
its fate. The reasoning is the item's product and is recorded here so it is not
re-derived:

A record's write identity names its BYTES, not one OCCURRENCE of them. `storeFramedSessionMsg`
replays acknowledged bytes verbatim and the readback adopts the new, higher sequence with
the original `WID`; restore adopts `WID`/`PWID` from record JSON without validating
provenance. So one identity can stand at two sequences, and a reader asking "did a
teardown retire the record I hold?" cannot tell which occurrence a retirement removed.
`mseq` bounds the removed occurrence below the marker but does not say WHICH occurrence it
was, so no conjunction of surviving fields is occurrence-exact either. The field therefore
never acquired the reader it was retained for, and could not.

**What an exact reader would need instead**, if one is ever wanted: the claimed
PREDECESSOR SEQUENCE, stored on the marker where `claimTeardown` knows it and copied into
the watermark, compared for equality with the reader's own `sess.seq`. That is two new
required fields on two permanent shapes; the route is analyzable — `$MQTT_teardown` is
already epoch-coupled to `$MQTT_sess` — and it was refused as DISPROPORTIONATE to what it
buys, which was a more specific DISCONNECT Reason String. Disproportionate, not blocked.

**What the field also did, and what replaced it.** Being required, it made a teardown of a
record carrying no `WID` **fail closed** with the record left marked, rather than retiring
a record on a name nothing can attribute. Nothing else in the teardown path checks `WID`
or `PWID`, so that refusal is now an explicit precondition in `recordGenRetirement`,
checked before the watermark is built and before any deletion.

Readers consume the fence — the three destructive ones below, the record-absent create
(deleted with the create-parent inheritance, and now reading it only to refuse a corrupt
one), and two added by **F-036 unit 2**: the inbound QoS 2 **release classifier** and the
orphan sweep's **destruction licence**, both described after this list. Each applies
the same validation
(`mqttValidateGenRetirement`: decodable, the client ID hashes back to the subject
token, a valid generation, a nonzero `mseq`) with the same
fail-closed disposition — a watermark that is unreadable or malformed in any field is
never repaired in place, because it may name a retirement newer than the reader's own:

- **The winner's release-superseded arm.** The release now hands back the record it
  classified against; when that record carries the generation just retired and no
  marker, it is the hollow survivor and is condemned with a fresh teardown claim. A
  record carrying a DIFFERENT generation is left alone — outside this retirement's
  reach, which is a statement about the generation and not about who holds it.
  **Mark only** — no deletions, no release — because a marked record is already the
  fully-handled state: the survivor's broker observes the move on its session-record
  watch (or the committed-read backstop) and evicts, its client's reconnect adopts the
  marker and starts fresh with Session Present false, and with no client the expiry
  path or the sweep finishes it. A *different* generation is a legitimate successor and
  is left alone; a record already marked by a foreign teardown belongs to that
  teardown's finisher. `finishAdoptedTeardown` carries the identical arm, because its
  deletions ran on the same licence.
- **The CONNECT restore.** One exact-subject read per record-restoring CONNECT: a
  record whose generation the watermark names is routed into the *existing*
  overdue-discard shape rather than resumed, so there is one discard path and not two,
  and the client gets Session Present false — the truthful answer. This is the only
  prompt reader for a winner that crashed after recording the retirement; without it
  every reconnect resumes the same hollow record until the sweep runs.
- **The orphan sweep**, for a client that never comes back. See "Orphan
  reconciliation".
- **The record-absent CREATE**, which is the only non-destructive reader and now reads
  the watermark for ONE outcome: **corrupt REFUSES the CONNECT**, because admitting a
  session over a watermark this broker cannot read leaves its own later teardown unable
  to record a retirement — `recordGenRetirement` refuses to replace a corrupt standing
  watermark — so the record would stay marked for every future finisher. **Valid, absent
  and indeterminate all ADMIT, and none of them supplies a parent**: the create is
  parentless whatever the watermark says.

  It used to take `rwid` from the valid arm as the identity its first write descended
  from, which is what the write-lineage audit deleted; the field itself has since been
  removed, so there is no longer any record identity here to inherit. A valid watermark is
  still read on this arm and deliberately draws nothing from it — an inheritance restored
  here would reintroduce the false-fork routes `docs/CONFORMANCE.md` records, not close a
  gap.
  The read's PLACEMENT after the proof of absence is likewise no longer load-bearing for
  ancestry; what remains of it is that the refusal decides on a watermark at least as new
  as the deletion that emptied the subject.

Two things a marker means constrain the three DESTRUCTIVE readers: it licenses its
adopters to delete every durable the record names, and the CONNECT discard deletes them
itself. So each
of them validates the record with `mqttValidateTeardownTargets` before it acts — the
CONNECT *refuses* rather than discarding — and a record whose names are not this
session's is condemned by nobody. The create-side reader names no target and deletes
nothing, so it has none to validate.

**F-036 unit 2 added two readers, and both are non-destructive in themselves.**

- **The inbound QoS 2 release classifier** (`internal/mqtt/qos2_retire_classify.go`). A
  PUBREL reads the watermark between its hold proof and its onward store, and refuses the
  fan-out when the watermark is valid AND either it names this incarnation OR its `mseq`
  exceeds the sequence this broker is acknowledged for. The classification is
  **two-dimensional** because one dimension alone is wrong in both directions: refusing on
  a bare generation MISMATCH is wrong since the single slot is replaced by increasing
  `mseq` alone — retire G1, then create and retire G2, and a broker still serving G1 reads
  "a different generation" and fans out — and refusing only on a MATCH loses the same case
  from the other side. `mseq == sess.seq` is unreachable for a bound session and has no
  arm: every `sess.seq` adoption takes a store response for this broker's own bytes or a
  digest-matched readback, and a marked record is never restored into a bound session. A
  valid MATCHING observation is memoized per (client, generation) — it is monotone, and
  the slot can lose the fact's discoverability but not the fact — while absent,
  different-generation, corrupt and indeterminate are never cached, because each can be
  invalidated by a retirement landing afterwards.
- **The orphan sweep's destruction licence** (`internal/mqtt/orphan_retire_proof.go`).
  Every sweep arm that can still destroy live session-generation state requires a valid
  watermark whose generation EQUALS the candidate's; without it the state is RETAINED.
  `mseq` supplies no second dimension there, and the reason is structural rather than
  conservative: the candidate generation belongs to a REMOTE party, so this pass has no
  `sess.seq` of its own to compare a marker against, and comparing `mseq` with a
  `$MQTT_qos2in`, `$MQTT_inflight` or consumer sequence crosses incomparable sequence
  spaces. See "Orphan reconciliation".

Nothing ever reaps a watermark. Storage is bounded by the client-ID population, and
permanence is what keeps the residual from being widened by a GC choice. Because
`mseq` is a `$MQTT_sess` sequence, `$MQTT_teardown` is only comparable within the
incarnation that issued those sequences — which is now a property of the whole
bundle rather than of this pair: every broker-owned stream carries the account's
recovery epoch and a mismatch is **refused at startup**, and no stream may be
recreated without the other eight. See "The ten streams are one recreation unit".

The deliberate exception to the fence is a crash *between* the won claim and the
watermark write. It is non-destructive by construction, since the write precedes every
deletion, so that generation has lost nothing and is legitimately resumable until an
adopter fences it.

**Every session carries a generation.** A record without one is **rejected** at the
boundary rather than resumed on hash-only names: it predates this design, and under
the compatibility boundary above the development store is recreated. Accommodating
it would not be a smaller version of the same safety — a hash-only session has no
identity to scope an arbitration with, so the inbound QoS 2 release claim could not
be arbitrated for it and the discard would fall back to a blind hash-wide purge,
which destroys a held payload whose releaser claimed it and then died. A
partially-arbitrated path is worse than a rejected one.

What this leaves open is stated in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`: the fence names only the
latest retirement, and the single slot can itself be regressed by a cross-term apply.

## The outbound obligation authority (F-105, integrated and accepted)

**Status: integrated, and accepted with F-106 on 2026-10-08 by the integrated gate.**
The record classes, transitions and rules below are implemented, tested and
mutation-checked, and the
supported outbound classes - ordinary QoS 1/2, shared-group QoS 1 (7a) and retained QoS
1/2 (7c) - run through the authority in production:

- An accepted CONNECT drives the ownership protocol to a SERVING authority inside its
  accept transaction (`driveAcceptToServingAuthority`): reserve or prepare, the fenced
  metadata commit `saveAcceptWithOwnership` (acceptance fact, COMMITTED receipt and
  session record in one batch, replacing the two-member accept save), then finalize. One
  ownership budget anchored at F-051's stop covers every request and re-drive; a standing
  proposal is settled before anything is destroyed, and an own aborted proposal refuses
  the CONNECT and is abandoned (8a); the connection holds one tenure and one closing
  driver (8b).
- A QoS 1/2 delivery is ADMITTED (`admitInflightPublish` → `opAdmitPublish`), co-creating
  the register, its unsent marker, the exchange, the resource edges and the obligation's
  duty ordinal in one batch; a same-delivery replacement is composed by the replacement
  composer under the one lineage derivation ("An exchange's LINEAGE is carried").
- A supported obligation's frame leaves only through `writeAuthorizedFrame`, which
  consumes the acquisition for its live holder; the remaining bypass set is the two
  mixed emitter sites under "Boundaries and stated limits".
- The client's PUBACK, PUBREC (refused or successful) and PUBCOMP advance the exchange in
  the batch that re-phases its slot (`opAdvanceExchangeAck`), a drain completion advances
  it (`opCompleteExchangeDrain`), and an obligation destroyed untransmitted is ended
  durably (`opWithdrawUnsent`).
- Capacity and identifier custody are the exchange's (the custody ledger;
  `capacityAvailableLocked`), and a resume restores from the duty inventory (7b).
- A SUBSCRIBE claims its source consumer's name before the create
  (`opProvisionResource`); a name is never reused, use is arbitrated by name, and
  deletion is keyed by incarnation (7c-lc). A discarding teardown transfers its
  consumers to the recovery executor (7d), an acquisition is released only through the
  release fence (7e), a serving generation settles its displaced tenures (7f), and a
  closure certificate outlives its process and clears a dead holder's token (8c).

Only the experimental **affine** route stays on the pre-F-105 `storeInflightRegister`
writer, and its conversion is chapter P's. What is documented for that route is a
component guarantee, not the integrated one.

Every accepted connection is given an immutable output binding at construction, and
`writeSocket` consults that binding's gate under `wmu`. The gate is sealed on every close
and on a refused CONNECT by `mqttCertifyClosed`, and by a torn `writeAuthorizedFrame`
through `sealOutput` before it releases `wmu`. `finishAdoptedTeardown` asks the
metadata-release gate before it releases a session record.

That gate decides real generations: admission creates the generation's inventory ledger,
and every discarding close writes a closure and a recovery root. It reads the closure
(with its discard disposition), the ledger, the root's reachability and the completion
certificate, and is vacuous only for a generation with neither a ledger nor a closure,
which admitted nothing. It never asks the caller for facts the caller cannot have.

### What it is for

A resume **preserves the generation**, so two brokers may legitimately operate one session's
subjects, and within a generation there is no fence. A teardown therefore destroys backing
resources that an obligation admitted before it still needs. Before 7d,
`deleteTeardownTargets` removed the ordinary source consumers and then the PUBREL consumer,
and because `$MQTT_out` is interest-retained, deleting that consumer dropped the records it
carried - the only evidence the client answered PUBREC. The register could survive and
prove nothing. That was the defect F-105 was filed for. Since 7d a discarding teardown
TRANSFERS those consumers to the recovery executor (`transferLogical`); only a vacuous
generation (nothing admitted, no closure) and a preserving one take the raw delete.

The invariant is:

> Retirement must not destroy the durable representation, or the completion route, of an
> obligation that was admitted before it.

It is **not** a sequence comparison, and nothing in it reopens a retired generation. An
earlier design that compared an admitting sequence against the retirement watermark was
withdrawn: `sess.seq` is mutable, `ActionClaimSeq` is an ordering rather than an acceptance
sequence, the session object is not the tenure because resident reconnects rebind it, and
a
