tenure-relative reader would contradict the six existing readers of the watermark, which
treat retirement as generation-wide and irreversible.

### The records

All live on `$MQTT_inflight`, because a JetStream atomic batch is **per stream** and the
authority must commit together with the exchange mutation it authorizes. They are kept out
of
the register machinery's reach by a leading `f105` class token, which can satisfy neither
the
client-hash nor the generation validator; closure and outcome subjects also carry a token
count the register parser refuses. The authority subject carries the same count as a
register, so **token validation alone excludes it**, and a test pins that.

| Record (class token) | Meaning | Lifetime in the recovery epoch |
|---|---|---|
| authority (`auth`) | per client: which tenure may create outbound obligations, its revision, its state | permanent, CAS-rewritten in place |
| generation closure (`closed`) | this generation is closed to new admission | permanent, create-only |
| transition outcome (`txn`) | one attempted transition's verdict | permanent, create-only |
| exchange (`xch`) | the client-facing obligation, identified by a nonce; the packet identifier is an ALLOCATION belonging to it, never its identity | permanent |
| action (`act`) | one acquired operation, carrying the ORIGINAL run, connection and tenure | permanent |
| resource (`res`) | a backing resource and the obligations still depending on it, by role | permanent |
| ledger (`led`), duty (`duty`) | a generation's inventory high-water and its predeclared duties | permanent |
| name ownership (`own`) | a physical consumer name: absent → LIVE → RETIRED, never reused | permanent |
| closure certificate (`cert`) | one connection, of one broker run, can emit nothing more | permanent, create-only |
| completion certificate (`done`) | a generation's retirement completed | permanent, create-only |
| directory shard (`shard`), readiness (`rdy`) | recovery directory position; affine readiness | permanent |
| recovery root (`root`) | a closed generation enrolled for recovery | deleted at its exact sequence after its completion certificate |
| manifest (`pay`), chunk (`chunk`), retained `rel` | retained replay material and its PUBREL record | deleted at exact sequences by the named removal functions |

A third top-level subject space, `$MQTT.handoff.`, was added to `$MQTT_sess` for the handoff's
metadata receipt. Top-level rather than under `sess.` for the reason the acceptance facts
are:
every session walk filters `sess.<domainTk>>` and decodes what it gets as a session record.

### Admission is arbitrated, not observed

Every transition that creates an obligation, acquires an action, transfers ownership or
closes admission contends on the authority record, and the exchange mutation commits **in
the
same batch**. An exchange installed without a winning authority transition would be an
obligation nothing authorized; an authority advanced without its exchange landing would be
an
authority that admitted nothing.

Each transition kind carries its own rule, and a kind with no rule fails closed at the
default. A first admission may not write a closure — otherwise it installs a SERVING authority
and a permanent closure for the same generation in one batch, after which an ordinary
admission passes the serving check while closure says the generation is closed.
`dispose-resource` is the only OBLIGATION/RESOURCE transition exempt from requiring serving
authority, because old-generation cleanup runs after closure; it is exempt from nothing
else, and it may address a resource of an EARLIER generation while a successor serves. The
ownership transitions naturally have other predecessor states — a finalization requires a
preparing or reserving one, a readmission a closed one.

### One metadata protocol, two proposal shapes

An accepted CONNECT commits the metadata half of an **ownership proposal**, and there are
exactly two shapes. A **handoff** displaces a named predecessor in full — generation, tenure,
ownership token, session write identity and session-record sequence — and that binding is
what stops a delayed acceptance retargeting a successor. A **first creation** displaces
nothing, because there is nothing there.

They share ONE create-only permanent slot per proposal, deliberately. Splitting the slot by
shape would give a creation and a handoff of the same identity two independent verdicts over
one client's ownership, and the create-only mutual exclusion between commit and abort is the
whole fence. The receipt therefore carries a mandatory closed `kind`, and the members it is
required to carry are computed from `(kind, verdict)`: a creation receipt naming a
predecessor describes a displacement that never happened and is refused; a handoff receipt
naming none has lost its binding and is refused. The kind is compared **before** anything
else when deciding whether a standing receipt answers a proposal.

One executor settles a proposal, and it is the same one whether the proposal is the
acceptance's own or another claimant's: **resolve, abort create-only only over an unresolved
slot, then re-resolve and return that**. A failed abort establishes only that the slot is
occupied; by what is a question only a validated readback answers.

### An abandoned proposal is settled, never deleted

A claimant that stops between writing its create-only reservation and resolving its metadata
half would otherwise leave the client permanently unservable: no arbitration record is ever
deleted, so no later create-only write can succeed against it. Another acceptance may
**settle** that proposal — take its permanent metadata slot, which the original
claimant's own commit member is racing for.

This is not a liveness claim and needs no lease, timer or proof of death. It is a race the
slot arbitrates, and a live claimant may legitimately lose it — in which case it is
*told* it lost rather than discovering it from an absence. What the settled verdict licenses:

| standing authority | settled verdict | continuation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| reserving | aborted | close the reserved generation, then claim a **fresh** one over the closure |
| preparing | aborted | cancel the intent, **restoring** the predecessor — a failed handoff retires nothing |
| either | committed | finalize **exactly** the original proposal, on its behalf |

An on-behalf finalization installs the proposal's own generation and tenure and grants the
helper nothing: it takes its own tenure by an ordinary handoff afterwards, and gains no right
to adopt, rewrite, transmit or drain another connection's action.

Two bounds keep this from becoming an abort war. **One acceptance settles at most one foreign
proposal** — it may finish settling that target across CAS retries, but never chases a second.
And **an acceptance whose own proposal was aborted loses**: it closes its generation and then
refuses the CONNECT, rather than minting a replacement proposal in a retry loop. The decision
function is stateless and cannot tell a fresh acceptance from the loser re-entering, so the
second bound is owed by the caller. Sustained competing CONNECTs still have no starvation
guarantee; the slot decides the winner and elapsed time does not.

### A claim serves nothing until its metadata half commits

`reserve-creation` installs a RESERVING authority over either an **absent** predecessor, at
revision 1 and create-only by virtue of that, or a **CLOSED** one proposing a fresh
generation. Both are one fact, and together they are the ONLY route to a serving authority.

There is deliberately no kind that installs SERVING outright. Two once existed —
`admit-tenure` at revision 1 and `readmit-tenure` over a closure — and both were the
bootstrap gap itself: ownership entitled to serve a client with no reservation behind it and
no committed metadata half. Deleting only the first would have left the gap reachable one
kind name away on the SECOND attempt, after an abandoned first creation, which is exactly
when a broker is there. Every route to SERVING is now reserve-creation, a metadata commit,
and finalize-creation, whose verdict check reads the permanent receipt.

### The exchange phase is a durable, arbitrated fact

An exchange moves along its protocol by a transition, never by a handler assigning to a
field. The relation is **enumerated per QoS** rather than derived from the phase
ordering: an ordering check admits a QoS 2 exchange going from its publish straight to a
successful completion, which
discards the release the client is still owed, and admits a QoS 1 exchange recording a PUBREC
it never received. It is acyclic and strictly forward, so an ended obligation cannot be
resurrected to re-charge Receive Maximum and re-authorize output for a message the
client has finished with.

**An exchange ends in one of two ways, and they are different facts.** A QoS 2 exchange whose
PUBREC carries a reason code `>= 0x80` was REFUSED: per [MQTT-4.3.3] the sender must not send
a PUBREL and the exchange is over, with no ownership transferred and no release ever owed.
That is `rejected`, reachable only from `publish` and nowhere else — a successful PUBREC can
never be talked back into a refusal — and it is an ending on the same terms as `terminal`:
releasable, absorbing, and the phase at which a dependency may be released. Routing a
refusal through PUBREC-observed instead would put a permanent record on the store claiming
the client holds a message it declined, and would oblige a release nothing may emit. Each
ending has a pending-drain form for the same reason the completion does: the evidence is
durable at once, and the release still waits for the output to stop.

The advance CASes the exchange at the sequence it was read, so two brokers observing the same
acknowledgement produce one advance, and it contends on the authority in the same batch. Both
the phase-only guarantee and the successor relation are enforced at the **write boundary**,
against the exchange as it durably stands — not only in the helper that composes the
transition. A guarantee that lived only in a builder would be a caller convention: every
check a transition can make about itself still passes for a body substituted after it was
built, and the CAS would succeed.

That boundary rule is keyed on the **member**, not the kind. An exchange member at a nonzero
expectation IS an advance whichever transition carries it, so scoping the check to
`advance-exchange` would leave the identical bypass one kind name away — `admit-exchange`
and `acquire-action` confine their members by nothing at all. An **action** member is
subject to the matching rule in its simplest form: it must always be create-only, because
an action is never rewritten. Its `Run`, `Conn` and `Tenure` are the original binding a
captured completion handler resolves against, and a retransmission is a new acquisition
counter rather than a replacement of the attempt that may still be executing.

Like resource disposal it does **not** require a serving authority, for the same reason: a
closed generation's obligation must still be able to END — its PUBCOMP arrives on the old
connection while the successor serves, and only the current authority's CAS can succeed. A
kind that
demanded SERVING would leave that generation permanently unfinished, its charge held and its
identifier unreclaimable. It is confined to exactly that: it carries exchange members and
nothing else, never create-only, and it preserves the authority's state, generation, tenure,
ownership and both pending proposals exactly.

### A caller states intent; the mechanism composes the conclusion

Every operation this mechanism supports — claim, finalize, prepare, cancel, close, admit,
advance, release an edge, authorize a deletion, complete a cleanup — is an entry point that
takes the operation's own arguments, **loads the state it reasons about**, derives the
successor records, composes the whole atomic batch and commits it. A caller supplies
identities, a payload and the evidence its request rests on. It does not supply the
authority record that results, the predecessor it was derived from, the generation closure,
the metadata receipt, or a batch member of its own choosing.

The reason is empirical rather than aesthetic. Four consecutive review rounds produced one
finding each, and every instance had the same shape: a caller composed a durable
conclusion, and the rule about what it was allowed to say lived in the optional helper that
built it rather than in the writer. Moving each rule to the write boundary fixed each
instance; it does not end the class, because the boundary was still proving a caller's
conclusion permissible rather than deriving it.

Two layers, with different jobs, and both are kept:

- the **operations** own composition, so a caller cannot state a conclusion about stored
  state at all;
- the **write boundary** owns enforcement, and still re-derives every such fact from the
  store, so a composition bug cannot land either.

The metadata half follows the same rule. Its operation reads the proposal from the client's
STANDING authority — a reservation or a preparation — reads the expectation from the record
that stands, derives the receipt from both, and freezes the attempt internally. A metadata
commit for a proposal no authority carries is refused at the write boundary too, and the
comparison is over the WHOLE proposal rather than what it proposes: a receipt naming a
predecessor the standing intent does not carry would pass the session-record check — which
compares the write identity and the generation — take the permanent COMMITTED slot, and
then be read as FOREIGN by every later resolution, leaving admission frozen with nothing
able to finalize or cancel. Otherwise a caller could invent a creation proposal and commit
over a live session having reserved nothing, since a creation displaces nothing and the
predecessor check never reaches it. The
frozen attempt is returned to the caller, including when the send fails, because a RETRY
RESENDS IT UNCHANGED: the slot is create-only, so a recomposed attempt would be a second
commit racing the first.

Every operation returns the HANDLE for the attempt it sent, frozen before the send. An
operation composes its own transition, so without it a lost acknowledgement leaves the caller
holding neither the transition nor its digest — and calling the operation again is not a
retry: it reloads the state, composes a different revision, and may be refused because what
it asks for already stands.

An operation also takes the ENTITLEMENT ITS CALLER CAPTURED — the generation and tenure it
decided under, the proposal identity it means, the whole ownership it intends to close — and
compares it with what it loaded. The generation alone does not identify an ownership: a RESUME
preserves the generation and changes only the tenure, so a closure captured under one tenure
and delayed past a resume would otherwise match and end the generation its successor is
serving. Reading the current state says what is there; it does not
say which owner the request belongs to. A closure composed for G1 and delayed until G2 serves
would otherwise load G2 and end it, with every boundary check passing because the operation
itself had substituted the target.

### Every claim about stored state is checked at the write boundary

The rule is INVARIANT PRESERVATION, not member validation: given the state that stands and
the mutations a batch proposes, what must hold is the state the batch RESULTS IN. Checking
members one at a time is not the same thing, in two directions.

A batch is ATOMIC, so members that could never coexist can be written together — two
obligations on one identifier, two registers for one lineage, an action for an exchange the
same batch ends.

And a batch is not the WHOLE STATE, so a member that is legal against its own subject can
still contradict a record nobody touched: two registerless admissions, committed one after
the other, each carrying a single exchange, leave two obligations outstanding at one
identifier with nothing within either batch to object.

Where this is enforced by reading standing state, an UNREADABLE record refuses. A record this
broker cannot interpret may be the one holding what the batch is claiming, and treating it
as absent is the inference the whole mechanism exists to remove.

**What the boundary enforces is relations between DURABLE RECORDS**, and that is not
everything. Three facts have no record to check them against and are the caller's: whether
another action for an exchange may still emit (`Outstanding`), which phase an acknowledgement
establishes, and whether output has actually drained — the difference between terminal and
terminal-pending-drain is a fact about a socket and a scheduler. The operation surface
documents these as preconditions; the conversion rows own the evidence that makes them true,
along with serialized output acquisition, closure evidence, complete backing-resource
selection and the physical cleanup result. Immutable action records cannot establish any of
them: an acquired action that has finished looks exactly like one still executing.

This is the rule for every record F-105 introduces — the authority, the exchange, the action,
the resource and the metadata receipt. **The register and its unsent marker are the named
exception, and it is deliberate**: the register's transition rules are HEAD's own slot state
machine (`inflight_slot_state.go`), applied by its existing writers, and F-105's boundary
does not reimplement them. What it does enforce on that pair is what is entirely its own —
the marker is validated through the one marker decoder and is always create-only, so a hand-built
member cannot write an unattributed marker or describe a transmitted allocation as unsent
again — and a register member at a NONZERO expectation is REFUSED outright, whatever kind
carries it.

That was the deliberate restriction on admission: F-105 **creates** a register and never
replaces one. Which occupant may be displaced by which allocation is the slot machine's
decision, and validating a nonzero expectation here would be a second definition of a
legal register step — while not validating it would let a hand-composed admission
overwrite a live past-PUBREC register, because an absent unsent marker is normal after
transmission and is not evidence that an identifier is free. Full REPLACEMENT (a fresh
obligation over a proven-unsent occupant) is still refused — `opReplacePublish`'s pair
mode is unbuilt — and becomes supported when it REUSES the slot machine's decision inside
this batch rather than calling an existing writer first and admitting afterwards.

**The row-3 acknowledgement re-phase is the one nonzero-expectation register member now
admitted, and it is not a replacement.** A client acknowledgement that ends a PUBLISH must
move the durable exchange off PUBLISH AND re-phase its slot in ONE batch, or recovery
would resend an already-answered payload under a fresh identifier — the exact at-most-once
break the exchange exists to close. So `opAdvanceExchangeAck` appends a register member at
the slot's current sequence carrying ONLY a state move: `mqttIsAckPhaseAdvance` recognises
it — the member equals the occupant in every field except `State`, moved along one of the
arrows `mqttAckSlotArrow` names, which is keyed on the slot's ORIGIN as well as the
acknowledgement's phase:

| slot origin | exchange phase recorded | slot result | acknowledgement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `publish` | `Terminal`, `Rejected` | `publish_terminal` | PUBACK, refused PUBREC |
| `publish` | `PubRecObserved` | `pubrel_intended` | successful PUBREC |
| `pubrel_ready` | `Terminal`, `TerminalPendingDrain` | `pubrel_terminal` | PUBCOMP |

`checkAckPhaseAdvanceMembers` binds the member to the batch's exchange by lineage,
packet identifier and generation, AND to the exchange's validated standing phase
(`checkExchangeOverwrites` returns it; `mqttAckExchangeOrigin` names the phase each slot
origin requires — `publish` beside `Publish`, `pubrel_ready` beside `PubRecObserved`),
because the successor table admits two routes into Terminal and only the origin says
which arrow a member is. The coarse kind gate and the token-installation gate name the
three slot states an advance may carry through one helper, `mqttAdvanceKindSlotState`.
It is not a replacement because it re-mints no identity: same nonce, same lineage, same
allocation, one field moved along the slot machine's own arrows. A PUBLISH pending-drain
ending carries the exchange ALONE (a live action token IS the outstanding output, so the
PUBLISH slot cannot terminalise yet). The PUBREL branch differs on purpose: a PUBCOMP
over a live PUBREL action records `TerminalPendingDrain` AND moves the slot to
`pubrel_terminal` with the token, custody and `Acq` kept, because `pubrel_terminal` with
a token is already the gated shape (`finalizeTerminalSlot` refuses disposal while it
stands); the boundary requires the pending phase exactly when a token stands.

**One class gate for every acknowledgement arrow.** `ackExchangeFor` answers, once, what
an acknowledgement of a slot must advance, and both entry points ask it. An experimental
affine slot (its source durable carries `mqttQ2AffineConsumerDurablePrefix`) has no
exchange — its conversion is chapter P's — so it is slot-only and no exchange is read.
Every other slot, a shared-group QoS 1 slot included since 7a, is ORDINARY. An ORDINARY
slot is admitted beside its exchange in one `opAdmitPublish` batch, so its acknowledgement
advances both records atomically — and an ordinary slot whose exchange is absent,
unreadable, or names another obligation is REFUSED: nothing is written, and the caller
keeps its own continuation. There is no legacy route. The only non-test writer of an
exchange-less register is the experimental affine admission, prefix-classified (the shared
one was too, until 7a); an ordinary slot without its exchange is either a transient read
failure or a shape this broker does not write, and completing it slot-only would leave the
obligation's durable record saying nothing about the answer (consult 20, which superseded
the row-3 checkpoint's "explicit absence means a pre-F-105 register" route and migrated
the test fixtures that relied on it to admit through the authority).

**Every acknowledgement arrow of an ordinary exchange is wired.** The terminal arm
(`attemptTerminalRegisterRelease`'s `case mqttInflightPublish:`) carries a PUBACK to
Terminal and a refused PUBREC to Rejected; on refusal it returns false and its scheduled
continuation re-attempts at the capped delay. A SUCCESSFUL PUBREC goes through
`intendPubRelSlot`, which for an ordinary obligation now commits `publish ->
pubrel_intended` on the slot and `Publish -> PubRecObserved` on the exchange in the same
batch, the phase derived by `mqttPhaseForAck` rather than chosen. A PUBCOMP goes through
`mqttTerminalizeOnPubComp`, which for an ordinary obligation commits `pubrel_ready ->
pubrel_terminal` with `PubRecObserved -> Terminal` (no PUBREL action live) or `->
TerminalPendingDrain` (a live PUBREL action) — PUBCOMP ends the exchange whatever its
reason code, and the slot token is the LEASE a live PUBREL output holds — an ordinary
PUBREL acquisition now writes its action record in the same batch as the token (row 2,
below), but the record is immutable and says nothing about whether output is still
executing, so a live token is what makes the ending pending-drain; no PUBLISH action can
be live at `pubrel_ready`. All three callers reach the batch
through one route, `advanceExchangeAck`. PUBCOMP's loop is bounded by
`mqttInflightStoreAttempts` and ends in one resolving read, because a failed final
attempt may hide a landed batch; its exhaustion closes nothing, so PUBREC's longer
budget is not imported.

**The exchange carries no separate "PUBREL owed" phase.** Phase value 3 is RESERVED: it
named a PUBREL-owed phase that stated nothing PUBREC-observed does not — every consumer
treated the two alike, and the canonical PUBREL's identity is the SLOT's fact, bound by
the rebind's readback proof — and nothing ever wrote it. `mqttValidExchangePhase`
refuses a persisted 3 as an unsupported shape (never read as PUBREC-observed, never
renumbered away); the successor table's QoS 2 release arrow is `PubRecObserved ->
Terminal | TerminalPendingDrain`.

**The PUBREL drain completes a pending-drain completion.** When the exact holder of a
`pubrel_terminal` slot's token drains it, `opCompleteExchangeDrain` clears the token and
advances `TerminalPendingDrain -> Terminal` in ONE batch (standing authority, like the
acknowledgement). Split, a lost response on the clearance would hit the drain's "token
already gone" early return and leave the exchange reading "drain owed" for ever. The
boundary admits the clearance member (`mqttIsDrainTokenClearance`: only the token and its
custody cleared, state and `Acq` kept) only beside an exchange whose standing phase is
`TerminalPendingDrain`. The token clearance is sufficient evidence HERE because it is the
settlement of the PUBREL's output lease, fenced at the slot and authority sequences, and
no execution can still be running under it: the write entry requires the live token, and
no drain of a holder can begin while its frame is being written (the next section); it is
not the identifier-release conjunction, which is the allocator's (row 5: no scheduling
entry, no custody-ledger charge and no live send hold). After an acknowledged batch the
drain reads the slot back for
its own sequence (the op returns the authority's), and a landed-but-lost batch is
recognised by the re-read (the token gone from THIS exchange's `pubrel_terminal`) and
finalized, not dropped.

**No canonical PUBREL is acknowledged before its completion is recorded.** At HEAD the
PUBCOMP handler acknowledged the canonical PUBREL whatever the terminal step concluded;
on interest-retained `$MQTT_out` that removed the one record a retry, a redelivery or a
restart needs. Now `mqttTerminalizeOnPubComp` reports whether the completion is durably
recorded (`mqttPubCompResult.recorded`; false means UNCONFIRMED, not absent), and an
unrecorded completion WITHHOLDS the ack and hands it to the completion worker
(`pubcomp_completion.go`). The worker owns its record alone (`sess.pubCompOwed`, keyed
by identifier and exchange nonce): AckWait can re-admit the PUBREL from `pubrel_ready`
meanwhile, and the delivery callback replaces the pending entry, so nothing may be carried
there. It retries at the capped delay, sends every withheld ack once the completion is
recorded, and detaches (acks taken and record removed in ONE critical section, so a
concurrent install either joins before or starts a new record) while keeping its cleanup
ownership until the outcome settles. A closed worker gate retires it with its acks
unsent: an unconfirmed completion's record is still unacked (it redelivers after the
resume, or — if the batch landed — recovery finalizes the terminal slot), and a recorded
cleanup's continuation is the terminal slot recovery finalizes. It never consumes a
delivered entry's acknowledgement debt, never frees its capacity, and never deletes
under a stale transmission binding: a redelivery's acquisition advances `Acq`, and a
reference captured before an acquisition may not release after it, so that delivery's
own PUBCOMP finishes the cleanup.

**One owner for every unsettled cleanup of an ordinary completion.** Every path that
cannot settle an ordinary exchange's terminal finalize inline — the drain's (post-batch
read failed, indeterminate finalize, landed-lost batch), the PUBCOMP handler's
recorded-but-indeterminate outcome and its NONLOCAL `HeldByAction`, and recovery's
indeterminate finalize — goes to the completion worker through `ownTerminalCleanup`,
never to `retainAndReconcileTerminal`, which refuses to enrol over a delivered entry;
affine slots keep that helper (the class is `mqttDurIsSlotOnlyClass`'s,
stated once, so an unreadable exchange never selects a slot-only route). Settlement is
per outcome: `Done` releases only the nonce-bound placeholder; `RetainedReoffer` hands
the identifier exclusion on (`releaseRetainedTerminalReservation`) and, in the same
critical section, enrolls the slot's retained-cleanup owner (below); `HeldByAction` is
settled only when THIS process's live action holds exactly the durable token finalize
saw (`localActionHoldsLocked` — an exclusion or an older action reserves the identifier
but proves nothing about which drain clears the token); otherwise the placeholder stays
and the worker keeps re-checking. A permanently dead holder is not settled by retrying:
its exchange reads `TerminalPendingDrain` (drain owed) and its identifier stays held.

**A retained terminal slot is owned until its cleanup completes.** Every
`RetainedReoffer` arm — the PUBCOMP handler, the completion worker, the retry worker,
recovery and the holder's drain — installs the identifier exclusion and enrolls ONE owner
per exact slot identity (subject, allocation nonce, source durable and sequence, store
epoch) in the same critical section (`retained_terminal_cleanup.go`). The owner re-runs
the terminal finalizer under the register's fresh sequence with capped backoff and no
lifetime cutoff: an attempt count paces it and never retires the obligation. A matching
register not at `pubrel_terminal` ends the owner, because source settlement never
manufactures a PUBCOMP. Every confirmed source settlement — the disposal continuation,
a cleared or resolved retirement, recovery's fresh retirement pass and the successful
PUBREC confirmation — wakes the owner of the same allocation BEFORE the settler drops its
own ownership, so the slot's exit follows the settlement rather than a poll. A retained
arm that runs late, after another owner already finished the slot, re-installs an
exclusion over an empty subject; the finalizer's first-read absence lifts it, fenced by
the instance captured before that read, the same rule its confirmed-delete arm applies.
An owner refused worker admission at shutdown gets one last attempt in Phase 3b
(`finishOwedRetainedCleanups`); what it cannot finish stays durable for the next resume.

**The recovered PUBREC.** A drained QoS 2 delivery's PUBREC persists its drain intent
before its exchange advance (`recordPubRelIntent` precedes `intendPubRelSlot`), so a
crash or takeover in between leaves durable PUBREC evidence beside an exchange at
PUBLISH. Every route that interprets such evidence records that PUBREC through the one
PUBREC arrow (`recordRecoveredPubRec`: slot `publish -> pubrel_intended` with `Publish
-> PubRecObserved`, identity-bound, re-read on a lost response, no packet fabricated, no
materialization enrolled) before it lets a PUBREL reach the client: recovery's route B
(`phaseRecoveredPublishSlotToReady`, then the ordinary canonical rebind from
`pubrel_intended`; a crash between the two is the ordinary owed-materialization shape),
the drain resume (`recoverDrainPubRels`, before both its confirm and its recreate
branch; unresolved withholds that drain for this resume), and PUBREL admission, which
records it from the delivered record itself and then takes the direct arrow from
`pubrel_intended`, so the live connection makes progress on the next re-offer. The
direct arrow's `publish` origin is refused for an ordinary slot
(`acquireActionFromPublish`); affine keeps it (a shared delivery is QoS 1 and has no PUBREL).

**Recovery finishes an ordinary slot only on its exchange's word.** Recovery's
"finished" proof for a `pubrel_ready` slot — no canonical PUBREL and a complete source —
is an ABSENCE, and since the source is acked at PUBREC it reduces to "no record". It now
serves only the slot-only classes. An ordinary `pubrel_ready` slot is finished when its
exchange, read for the exact obligation (epoch, generation, lineage, identifier, QoS),
durably reads `Terminal`: positive evidence the PUBCOMP was recorded, which is the shape
a store that revives a limit-evicted register version leaves (MAXMSGSPER-REVIVAL,
`docs/known-upstream-issues.md`, reproduced on a clean shutdown). Recovery then only
reflects that fact into the slot and finalizes it; it writes no exchange.
`PubRecObserved` and `TerminalPendingDrain` keep the reservation.

The PUBREC path has no scheduled continuation of its own — a "not recorded" outcome rolls
the PUBREC back and closes the connection — so it re-attempts IN LINE: after any error the
next attempt re-reads the slot and the authority and submits again. It has its own budget,
`mqttPubRecAdvanceAttempts` (8), spaced by an independently jittered 10-25 ms wait taken
before each fresh read and never between a read and its batch, with no lock held (consult
22). The budget differs from the acquisition and provisioning loops'
`mqttInflightStoreAttempts` (3) for a reason: a successful PUBREC records a monotone
acknowledgement under the STANDING authority, valid across a handoff, so it may
legitimately outlast a burst — the send's own token drain, a resuming CONNECT's successive
ownership writes — where an acquisition authorizes new work under a pinned tenure a
handoff should defeat, and its exhaustion leaves the delivery pending rather than erroring
the connection. Nothing in the loop establishes that a failed attempt was refused rather
than lost: a batch that landed behind a lost response is found by the next attempt's read
as past PUBREC and resolved as Confirmed. Eight spaced attempts mitigate a contention
burst and guarantee nothing against sustained contention. An acknowledged batch is itself
the proof that the intent is durable, so `Confirmed` is returned without a readback (a
failed read there would turn a durable intent into a closed connection); the slot sequence
is refreshed best-effort because no later CAS uses it as a base. Exhausted attempts
conclude nothing — a timed-out attempt may have committed — and the resolving re-read
decides between Confirmed, NotRecorded and Unresolved. The extra reads, the larger batch
and any backoff (70-175 ms at most, none on a first-attempt success) add latency before
the PUBREL store while the identifier stays held throughout, so they open no
identifier-reuse window and carry no residual.

After this, the only ordinary QoS 2 exchanges left at PUBLISH are the ones the client has
not answered, a completed exchange reads a durable ending (`classifyExchangeDuty`:
MayResolve), and one whose PUBREL output is still live reads "drain owed". The capacity
and identifier release is the custody ledger's (row 5). What a release executor still
lacks is re-materialization
of a PUBREL whose canonical record vanished for a reason other than PUBCOMP (rows 6/7b;
`docs/CONFORMANCE.md`).

**Authority contention is re-attempted under a pinned entitlement, not classified.** The
acknowledgement advance rewrites the authority (Rev+1) on every ending, so the authority
is now a frequent writer on a live session. Every OTHER authority writer that a concurrent
acknowledgement can lose a CAS to must re-attempt rather than treat the rejection as a
decision. The two live-session writers on this path — the SUBSCRIBE source-name claim
(`opProvisionResource`) and the send-path output acquisition (`opAcquireAction`) — adopt
the admission ladder's contract exactly: a **bounded re-attempt on ANY error** after an
authoritative re-read of the authority (each op re-reads it internally) and the register.
There is deliberately no predicate that enumerates which pre-submit check a concurrent
commit tripped — the sequence check, the inventory ledger (`checkInventoryMembers`), and
the batch CAS itself are all just "the store moved", and a predicate that had to name each
one is the seam a review keeps re-cutting (holistic rounds 2-3; the class is closed by
adopting the ladder, not by growing the list).

Ownership is what makes a blind re-attempt safe, and it is **pinned outside the loop**:
the entitlement (`Gen`/`Tenure`) is captured ONCE and passed on every attempt, never
re-read per attempt. For the output acquisition it is not even read from the store: it is
the **connection's own accepted entitlement** (`c.outboundEntitlement`), recorded once by
the CONNECT accept loop from the pair `driveAcceptToServingAuthority` made servable. A
per-call read of the serving authority pins nothing across calls — the next redelivery,
or admission's own outer loop, would read the successor's tenure — so a displaced
connection whose session object still believes it serves would acquire under a tenure
that is not its own. With the connection's pair, `opAcquireAction`'s guard refuses every
acquisition that connection makes after a takeover, reported as `errMQTTEntitlementEnded`,
which is TERMINAL for the delivery (admission returns without redispatching). A
connection with no accepted entitlement acquires nothing. A takeover always bumps the
generation — a reserve-creation over a closure must propose a FRESH generation
(readmit-tenure at the same generation was deleted), so there is no same-generation tenure
change to worry about.
With the entitlement pinned, a takeover mid-loop fails the op's own captured-entitlement
guard ("an entitlement that has moved on") on every attempt, so the loop exhausts its
budget and resolves rather than acquiring output for a displaced binding under the
successor; a mere sequence bump keeps the same entitlement and re-CAS's to success. That
distinction — a takeover ends the attempt, contention retries it — is the op guard's, not
an error string's. An AMBIGUOUS outcome (a lost response whose write in fact landed) is
left to the resolver and the orphan sweep: the acquisition's landed token is seen by the
premise re-read and routed to `resolveUnacquiredPublishAction`; a late-landing provision
leaves a PENDING resource its readiness gate withholds and the sweep reclaims. The advance
itself does NOT re-attempt: on a CAS rejection its arm returns false and the terminal
continuation re-runs it.

**The CONNECT ownership steps reconcile rather than re-attempt blindly.** A resuming
CONNECT's authority steps (claim, prepare-handoff, finalize, cancel, close) contend with
the old connection's acknowledgement advances too, and a lost CAS there used to refuse the
CONNECT. A blind loop would be wrong for them: the ownership operations are not idempotent
retries — a claim or a preparation refuses the very state its own landed success creates,
a finalize or cancel loses its target once it has acted. So `reconcileOwnershipStep`
resolves a failed attempt from the handle `commitOp` froze before sending: landed, or
landed and since superseded, is a transition that HAPPENED and the executor continues from
the durable state; an unresolved attempt is settled by taking its outcome subject
(`abortTransition`, create-only, which loses to a batch that committed) and resolved
again; only a positively never-landed attempt — the pre-submit refusal a concurrent writer
causes sent no batch — is repeated. An operation that refused before composing a
transition returns no handle and its error stands. The episode's identity is pinned: the
run's own proposal, gen and tenure; the finalize or cancel target discovered once per
step; the close's gen, tenure and owning transition read once; the landed claim's
transaction for the metadata-loss cleanup; and a preparation read back after a prepare
must be this acceptance's own (`Intent.ID`), or the step refuses without entering the
metadata commit. The fenced metadata commit (`saveAcceptWithOwnership`) stays outside,
with its frozen-attempt resend, record fence and settlement unchanged. Re-attempts draw on
one allowance per CONNECT (`mqttOwnershipStepReattempts`, 4), constructed above the
`restoreSession` label so no re-drive replenishes it, and on the absolute ownership
deadline; the deadline bounds starting another attempt, while the resolution, abort and
store calls already running are bounded by the JetStream request timeout. Historical
success authorizes nothing: after every step the driver re-decides from the current
authority. The `testTransitionCommit` seam on `mqttJSA` wraps the store comparisons and
the send, which is where a test lands the racing write or loses the response.

Three separate rules had the same shape and the same defect: the exchange's phase-only
guarantee, the authority **predecessor** every kind rule reasons about, and the **zero
dependency count** a deletion authorization rests on. Each was enforced by the helper that
COMPOSED the transition, and a helper is optional. Every check a transition can make about
itself still passes for a body substituted after it was built, and the CAS passes because
the sequence is right — so each guarantee held only for callers that chose to use the
builder.

`commitAuthorityTransition` therefore compares, after every self-contained check and before
it composes the batch:

- the **predecessor** against the standing authority at `PrevSeq`, by byte equality over the
  marshalled bodies — a field-by-field comparison would silently stop covering whatever is
  added next, which is how a pending proposal would become erasable again. Without it a caller
  copies the standing SERVING authority, calls it CLOSED at its real sequence, and reserves
  a generation over live ownership with no handoff and no permanent closure.
- every **exchange** member that overwrites, as described above.
- every **action** member, against the exchange it emits for AS THIS BATCH LEAVES IT: that
  exchange must exist, its resulting phase must admit this packet, and the identifier the
  bytes will carry must be the one the exchange holds. Reading the store would be reading
  the state BEFORE the batch, and a batch is atomic — so one batch could otherwise acquire
  emitting output beside the very advance that ended its obligation, each half legal alone.
  The operation surface derives all three, which makes the surface correct and says nothing
  about a member composed some other way.
- WHICH KIND may carry a member that creates one. The kind rules confine members for every
  kind that has a member rule, and the ownership kinds have none — so a closure, including
  the one an abandoned claim must make, could carry a fresh exchange and its action and
  acquire emitting output in the transaction that ends the generation. New work is admitted
  by an admission and acquired by an acquisition, and by nothing else.
- that a **register** says what its subject names. A slot is NAMED by its subject and SAYS
  what it is in its body; a record stored under one identifier while claiming another is one
  nobody can use, because recovery treats the disagreement as unreadable and retirement
  declines to delete what it cannot interpret — so the allocation is stranded for the whole
  recovery epoch.
- that an admitted exchange and the register it is admitted WITH describe ONE obligation:
  the exchange's nonce is the register's lineage, and the two agree on the identifier and
  the QoS. Change only the exchange's identifier and both records still pass their own checks,
  and the batch installs an obligation whose allocation disagrees with the register recovery
  will read — an acquisition takes its identifier from the exchange, recovery takes the slot
  from the register, and one obligation holds two. A registerless admission has nothing to
  disagree with and is still supported; the rule binds what is present. The pair must also
  START together: an admission is an obligation's beginning, so the register beside it sits
  at its publish — one already terminal is a slot recovery treats as done and eligible for
  cleanup while this mechanism would still permit another PUBLISH, and one at a PUBREL
  state describes an ownership transfer an admission has not made. One obligation holds
  ONE allocation within a batch: two registers carrying a single lineage at different
  identifiers are two recovery allocations for an exchange ledger that knows about one, and
  that is reached by ADDING a member rather than substituting one.
- that a **marker** is minted WITH the register it names, never on its own, and names that
  register's own allocation nonce. A marker's presence means nothing has been transmitted
  under this pair identity, and a transmission records itself by DELETING it — so its subject
  is then free, and a create-only write alone would succeed and claim an allocation is unsent
  that has already been sent. Recovery would read the matching marker, call the delivery a
  first transmission, and put DUP=0 on a retransmission, which is the one direction
  [MQTT-3.3.1-1] forbids.
- that an identifier a batch claims is held by NOTHING ELSE still outstanding, including
  records the batch does not touch, for EVERY admission — and that the enumeration which
  establishes it was COMPLETE. The server pages a stream-info subject list at 100,000 and
  reports the true total beside it; a generation retains its exchange records after they
  end, so that size is reachable while the 16-bit identifier space is not. The walk
  (`streamSubjectsComplete`) therefore reads page after page until a validated page
  reaches the total it reported, and is incomplete, and the claim refused, on any page it
  cannot vouch for: an echoed offset that differs from the request, a non-positive page
  size, a page shorter than `min(Limit, Total - Offset)`, or a subject outside the filter.
  Reading only the first page and refusing past it made 100,000 retained exchanges a
  ceiling on how long a generation could keep admitting work (the F-105 integrated gate,
  round 2). The walk is sound without a snapshot because NO EXCHANGE SUBJECT IS EVER
  DELETED: each page is recomputed by the server over a sorted set that only grows, so a
  subject created between pages can shift a later one onto a second read but cannot hide
  one that already existed, and the creator itself is excluded by this admission's
  authority CAS. Any future reclamation of exchange records (F-112) must bring its own
  admission fence or a stable enumeration; an equal total before and after a walk is not
  one. A create-only member excludes another writer at ITS OWN KEY and says nothing about
  a different key describing the same thing: a registerless obligation never occupies a
  register subject, so a later registered admission on that identifier writes create-only
  and succeeds, and both stand.
- that one identifier carries ONE OUTSTANDING obligation per batch, computed from the
  state the batch RESULTS IN. Two obligations left outstanding at one identifier are two
  messages a client can only answer ambiguously, because an acknowledgement names the
  identifier and nothing else — and a registerless admission has no register to collide
  with, which is the shape that reaches it. An ADVANCE counts: a batch moving one
  exchange along its protocol while admitting another at its identifier is the same
  collision through two kinds of member, and only an ENDING gives an identifier up.
- that one obligation acquires ONE action per batch. Two actions for a single exchange land
  together and are therefore executable together, which is exactly the serialization the
  acquisition rules impose — another transmission waits while an acquired action may still
  emit. Their subjects differ, because the acquisition counter is part of the name, so
  nothing about the members themselves objects.
- an **action**'s acquiring transition and tenure, which are immutable evidence a captured
  completion handler resolves against and which the decoder only checks the SHAPE of. An
  action naming the tenure a resume displaced would be permanent evidence attributed to
  ownership that never authorized it.
- every member that CREATES a record, which was the longest-standing hole: "nothing to
  compare against" is not the same as nothing to check. An exchange is admitted at its
  PUBLISH, naming this transition and this tenure — otherwise an admission whose body says
  TERMINAL simply commits, because the successor relation is only consulted for an advance,
  and a dependency release then accepts that fabricated ending. A resource is provisioned
  LIVE, owing nothing and authorizing nothing, and only by the kind whose rule requires a
  serving authority — otherwise a disposal, which is deliberately permitted after closure,
  becomes a way to provision under a closed generation.
- the **generation** a claim or a clean start proposes, against its PERMANENT CLOSURE. The
  kind rules compare with the immediate predecessor, and a closure outlives every predecessor
  it had: after G1 is closed, G2 served and G2 closed, nothing local to a claim notices that
  G1 was ever used. A generation is claimed ONCE, and an unreadable closure refuses, because
  the claim rests on the ABSENCE of one.
- every **resource** member that overwrites, against the resource's own state machine:
  identity never moves, **at most one** named edge is added or removed — an authorization
  and a cleanup completion change none — an added edge
  must name an
  exchange this same batch creates, a removed edge must name an exchange standing at an
  ENDING, completed or refused,
  an authorization requires the list to be empty when that CAS wins, and nothing may be added
  or resurrected afterwards. Without it a caller supplies `DELETE_AUTHORIZED` with no
  dependents over a resource several obligations still need.
- the **metadata verdict** of the proposal an ownership move answers. The kind rules establish
  that a finalization names its predecessor's pending proposal and nothing more; they cannot
  tell a proposal that COMMITTED from one that was ABORTED, because that fact lives on
  `$MQTT_sess`. Without it a caller reserves, aborts its own metadata slot, and finalizes
  anyway — installing SERVING over a permanent ABORTED verdict — or cancels a proposal whose
  metadata half had committed. Reading across streams is safe here because the slot is
  create-only and its verdict permanent, so it cannot change between the read and the CAS.
  UNRESOLVED and FOREIGN both refuse.

The metadata half is checked the same way, and at the same place: `commitMetadataAttempt`
validates the WHOLE frozen attempt before it reads anything or composes the batch, because
a frozen attempt is a mutable struct and its freezer is a helper. The receipt is **derived**
from the proposal and the write identity the session record actually installs, and the
caller's receipt must equal those bytes — so no member of the outcome can be substituted
after freezing, and a member added to the outcome later cannot stop being covered. The
session record must be this client's, at the proposed generation, and a handoff's must not
reinstall the write identity it claims to displace. The acceptance fact goes through its own
decoder against the subject the batch will publish it on. Without this an attempt naming
proposal P could carry the PREDECESSOR's session body and still publish a permanent COMMITTED
receipt saying P installed a new one, which is what every later ownership move reads.

And the metadata half's own write is bound to the predecessor it names: a handoff's session
expectation must BE `PrevSessSeq` — enforced at the write, not only at composition — and the
record standing there must carry the proposal's
`PrevSessWID` and `PrevGen`. Otherwise a delayed handoff naming session A commits against
whatever stands now — session B — overwrites it, and publishes a permanent receipt
claiming it
displaced A, which the resolver accepts because it compares the proposal's fields and
not the
record actually replaced. A sequence is a position, not an identity. A creation displaces
nothing and is deliberately unconstrained.

### An ambiguous transition is decided by a record that EXISTS

The authority is a single-slot record, so a later transition overwrites the body an earlier
one wrote and a caller holding a lost acknowledgement would be reading an absence. Each
attempt therefore has its own permanent outcome subject, and its commit batch carries a
**create-only** `COMMITTED` member. A caller that cannot decide publishes `ABORTED`
create-only to that same subject, racing the original batch: whichever lands first, the other
is refused in its entirety. The answer is always a record that exists.

The receipt is bound to the mutation by a digest over the attempt, the authority body and
expectation, and every member's subject, expectation and body — so a receipt cannot answer
for
a different batch that happened to share a transition id. A caller that has restarted
holds a
**handle** carrying the immutable attempt identity and the expected digest; there is
deliberately no constructor that builds one from an outcome, because a handle built by reading
a receipt would agree with every receipt.

### Completion does not require serving authority

Completing an obligation that was already admitted does **not** need the current serving
tenure. Beginning new work does. If completion required it, transfer and closure would
themselves destroy the completion route of everything admitted before them, which is the
defect this mechanism exists to remove. So preparing, transferred and closed authorities all
still permit an admitted exchange to finish.

Terminal evidence observed while output is still outstanding yields
`terminal_pending_drain`, not release: an action acquired earlier may still be executing,
and
releasing there would let a late first transmission escape after its own release boundary.

### The socket effect cannot be fenced, and is not pretended otherwise

Bytes handed to a transport are beyond any CAS. An action acquired before a retirement may
execute afterwards, on its **original** connection, with its original exchange and identifier
binding; it is never redirected through a rebound one. What is reachable is a positive
statement that a connection can emit nothing more: seal a one-way output gate, close the
socket **outside** the write lock so a blocked writer returns, cross the writer barrier, then
record a closure certificate. That certificate is not `c.closed`, not a write deadline, not
read EOF, and not disappearance from a registry — and only the process owning the connection
can produce one. Where none is obtainable the obligation stays outstanding, which is a leak
and the correct trade against destroying a live exchange.

### An acquisition executes once, and only for its live holder

Row 2 of the cutover wires the output boundary to both ordinary emitters. Every ordinary QoS
1/2 PUBLISH — first transmission and retransmission alike, since a retransmission is a new
acquisition — and every ordinary PUBREL is written through `writeAuthorizedFrame` as the
execution of the acquisition that authorized it.

**One acquisition is two carriers in one batch.** `opAcquireAction` installs the
register's output-custody token and creates the action record
`act.<hash>.<gen>.<lineage>.<acq>` in ONE authority batch, CASing the authority and the
register at their read sequences; there is no standalone register CAS for an ordinary slot
and no fallback to one. The PUBREL direct arrow rides the same member: from
`pubrel_intended` it also moves the slot to `pubrel_ready` and installs the canonical
PUBREL tuple the delivered record proved, so the evidence and the authorization still land
together. The write boundary enforces the pairing in both directions — a token member with
no action record is refused, and so is an action record with no token member, because
without the register CAS nothing excludes a second acquisition while the first is
outstanding — and binds the packet to the register step through one function,
`mqttActionKindRegisterState` (a PUBLISH action rides `publish -> publish`, a PUBREL
action `pubrel_ready -> pubrel_ready` or the direct arrow's `pubrel_intended ->
pubrel_ready`). Recognition is MANDATORY for an acquire-action register member: one that
is not a recognised token acquisition is refused, never reconsidered as a replacement.
Affine slots (`mqttDurIsSlotOnlyClass`, the same class gate every acknowledgement arrow asks)
keep the slot machine's own CAS and write no action record; that is chapter P's scope
boundary, not a fallback. A shared-group QoS 1 slot acquires through the authority since 7a.

**Only the holder ends live custody.** `checkLiveCustodyPreserved` holds for every
register member of every authority transition: over an exact predecessor carrying a live
token, the member carries the same token and custody, unless it is the holder's own drain
clearance on an advance-exchange (`mqttIsDrainTokenClearance`). An acknowledgement
re-phase preserves the token by construction and an acquisition's predecessor carries
none; a replacement that would clear or substitute live custody — admit-exchange's
register-only replacement included — is refused. The slot machine's own exact-token drains
are not authority writes and are not judged there.

**Consumption is not the holder check.** An acquisition given up before output still has an
immutable, unconsumed record, and a saved request for it would pass consumption. So the
boundary also asks the acquisition's holder, and the two atomicities it needs are taken under
two locks, in order and never nested:

1. the holder's decision is atomic against the DRAIN that gives the acquisition up, under
   the session lock. For a PUBREL that is `enterPubRelWriteLocked`, which moves the holder
   `acquired -> writing` only if it is acquired, not released, not drained, still holds
   its live token and is still the identifier's registered holder — and, for an ordinary
   holder, still holds the exact action record it landed, acquired for this connection. It
   returns an ENTRY TICKET private to that one synchronous execution; a slot-only PUBREL
   takes the same conditional entry without an authority record, and an ordinary holder
   without its record writes nothing;
2. consumption and the gate are atomic against the SOCKET, under `wmu`. There the writer
   reads only execution-private state: the ticket (the request's action and the writing
   connection must be the ones entry captured, and it is single-use), or the PUBLISH
   section's shared output object (`*mqttPublishOutput`, one per section, pointed to by
   every value copy of its token and closed by the section's first drain).

Nothing needs both in one critical section because **no first drain of a holder can run while
its frame is being written**. This is a property of the control flow, not something row 2
added: every entry into the drain is the acquiring goroutine before it hands the holder off,
the delivery callback's deferred drain after the synchronous write returned, or a
reconcile/shutdown pass that only a drain which already ran can enrol.
`TestF105DrainEntriesCannotRunDuringAWrite` records that call-site set, method values
included; an unchanged count cannot prove an unchanged ordering, which the token-retention
test carries. The durable token therefore stands for the whole write, and a peer's
acquisition of the same exchange is refused for as long as the bytes may be going out.

**The consume-once record lives on the holder, not the connection.** Each acquisition has
exactly one holder object — a PUBLISH send section's output (`mqttPublishOutput`, created
once by `beginSendLocked`) or a PUBREL action holder (`mqttSendAction`, freshly allocated
by both acquisition constructors; the identifier's `mqttSendHold` merges a new holder in
but never reuses one) — and that holder carries the acquisition's EXECUTION CELL
(`mqttExecCell`). Every value copy of the holder and every PUBREL entry ticket it issues
points to the same cell; the cell names the connection the holder was acquired for, and
its state moves only from unset to EXECUTING (then FINISHED) or to ABANDONED, and is never
reset. The writer consumes through the request's holder, so the fact lives exactly as long
as anything can still present the acquisition: when the holder is gone, nothing can
execute under it and its cell goes with it. No connection or session structure records
executed acquisitions; an earlier per-connection map did, and grew by one entry per
transmission for the life of the connection (the F-105 integrated gate, round 1). That
claim is about execution-history bookkeeping only: a PUBREL attempt that entered its write
and was then prevented still leaves its PUBCOMP debt on the identifier's send hold (F-116,
open).

**Abandonment is local evidence, recorded where ownership is proven.** The execution cell
has ABANDONED beside EXECUTING and FINISHED: an acquisition that will never execute on
its connection. It is recorded, naming `(gen, lineage, acq)` — the lineage, not the
allocation nonce, which a register-only replacement re-mints — only where this holder's
ownership of that exact acquisition is proven: a holder given up before write entry; an
entry that ended without consuming, on any exit including a panic, through a `relinquish`
deferred immediately after entry; and an ownership discovered late (a lost response, an
unreadable resolution, the reconcile and shutdown passes), named by the counter read
beside the exact token and recorded before that token is cleared. The exact token is what
proves the acquisition the holder's own, so the read counter is not compared with the
holder's executable identity, which an adopted acquisition never publishes; the late pass
reaches the same holder object, and therefore the same cell and connection, as the
section that acquired. A failed attempt's candidate counter is never abandoned — a peer
may own it — and an EXECUTING or FINISHED cell is never overwritten. An ABANDONED
acquisition is refused by the frame's consume-once check, so a saved request can never
execute it. This is not a release and does not replace the durable token drain, and the
cell is process-local. The PUBREL
drain that makes such a late discovery carries the token it just proved present as its own
CAS authority; before row 2 it carried the holder's captured copy, which a holder whose
acquisition landed behind a lost response and an unreadable resolution never had, so every
reconcile was refused and the identifier stayed held for the life of the session.

### An unsent obligation is ended, not forgotten

An ordinary obligation can be destroyed without ever having been transmitted: its message
expires, it exceeds the client's Maximum Packet Size, its allocation is cancelled by a
teardown or a takeover, a drain finalizes it, or recovery drops it on its marker's proof.
Every such route used to delete the register and its unsent marker and write nothing to the
exchange, which then read `Publish` for ever — an obligation no client can ever answer, and,
once the exchange owns the Receive Maximum charge (row 5), a slot held for the life of the
generation. The destruction now ENDS the obligation first, durably.

**The evidence is whole-exchange, and it is the store's.** An ordinary PUBLISH is written
only by the holder of an output token acquired through the authority, and only after the
allocation's unsent marker is durably gone — the section's own confirmed intent delete, or
an earlier one whose absence it inherits (an ambiguous delete writes nothing and is
re-attempted). A marker is created only by an admission's pair write for a fresh
allocation, naming that allocation's nonce. So a register at `publish` carrying no token,
with the marker naming its allocation still standing when read after the register, proves
that no PUBLISH of it ever reached the client: any acquisition since the register read
rewrote the register. Cancellation, a completed source and register absence are not
substitutes (F-088, F-100, F-102 each paid for one of those inferences).

**A known-false cancellation is cleared, at the write boundary, never trusted.** Because a
cancellation is written over transmitted deliveries too, a register can carry `Cancelled`
while its exchange is live and answered. Two recognisers may clear it: the ACK re-phase
and the output-token acquisition. The shape half is `mqttClearsCancellation`: the occupant
is an unretired `publish` record carrying `Cancelled` with `cancel_origin: occupant`, and
the member carries neither. The evidence half is `mqttRefutedCancellation`: the
allocation's unsent marker reads AUTHORITATIVELY absent, read by the write boundary in the
same attempt. A standing marker means the cancellation is genuine, and an unreadable read
proves nothing; both refuse. A pending fence is never cleared, advanced or acquired, and
the same-delivery register-only replacement, which may land over an `occupant`
cancellation under its existing checks, clears both members too. The cost is one marker
read per boundary evaluation that needs it, paid again on each retry.

**The transition.** `opWithdrawUnsent` (kind `withdraw-unsent`) is handed the allocation
and the obligation its caller validated for disposal — never just the subject, which is
reused — and ends that obligation or nothing: a different occupant standing on the subject
(a successor admitted after the caller looked) is no evidence about the allocation being
disposed of. It reads the standing authority, the register, the exchange and then the
marker, and commits ONE batch: the
authority at its sequence (its revision only), the register rewritten at its exact sequence
as the existing cancellation tombstone — the loaded record with `Cancelled` set and nothing
else changed, custody and the acquisition counter included — and the exchange
`Publish -> WithdrawnUnsent`. `WithdrawnUnsent` (phase 9) is an absorbing ending of its own,
the standalone sibling of `SupersededUnsent`: no acknowledgement was observed, so recording
completion or rejection would fabricate one, and nothing may be acquired at it. Like the
acknowledgement advance it needs no serving authority — ending work already authorised
authorises no output — so it lands under a closed authority and for an earlier generation's
obligation while a later one serves, changing nothing on the authority but its revision
(`mqttCheckEndingPreservesAuthority`, shared with the advance).

**The write boundary checks the evidence itself.** Under the withdraw-unsent kind the
register member is recognised first and judged only by the withdrawal rule
(`checkWithdrawalRegister`): its predecessor at the member's expectation is at `publish`
with no token and names the paired exchange's obligation, identifier and QoS; its body is
that predecessor with `Cancelled` set and nothing else; and the marker naming the
predecessor's allocation stands, read after the predecessor. The kind carries exactly one
register and one exchange of one obligation and nothing else. Under every other kind a
`WithdrawnUnsent` exchange member, or a register member that turns a `publish` occupant into
a tombstone, is refused — so the acquire-action boundary keeps its mandatory acquisition
rule.

**One door.** The ending is written where the destruction happens: inside the gated
destructive door, at both of its entrances (`reapLoadedRegister`, which the drain finalizer
and admission's reaps use directly, and `reapRegisterGatedOutcome`, behind
`reapRegisterWithVerdictGated` and `deleteInflightRegisterFor`), after the door has admitted
the destruction and before the delete (`endUnsentBeforeDestroy`). For an ordinary `publish`
register destroyed as never transmitted:

- an exchange already ended (a re-run after a crash or a lost response) — proceed;
- the evidence standing — withdraw, then delete the TOMBSTONE, re-read by identity, so a
  landed-but-lost or superseded withdrawal never licenses deleting a successor that has since
  taken the subject;
- no marker evidence (`mqttWithdrawNoMarker`: the marker the door admitted on is gone, so
  the PUBLISH may now be on the wire), or an exchange MISSING: REFUSE (F-088). The door
  admits a never-transmitted destruction only on the standing marker, and a cancellation
  or a nonce verdict is not that evidence; the register is the only durable carrier of
  what a late acknowledgement completes, and an UNATTRIBUTED ordinary register without its
  exchange is a shape admission never writes, refused rather than interpreted (a
  positively identified pending fence never reaches this row: see the rule below). The
  exchange stays at
  `Publish`, still refusing a competing durable admission on its identifier
  (`checkIdentifierExclusivity`), and its Receive Maximum charge is the custody ledger's to
  hold (row 5), not this step's. The tombstone-first fallback that used to destroy here
  (`tombstoneBeforeDestroy`) is deleted. An exchange that is UNREADABLE (the read could not
  be completed, or the record did not decode) is not missing and is likewise REFUSED; a
  void falls to its own entitlement-fenced tombstone rung while recovery keeps the pair. A
  RETIRED register (past PUBREC) owes no ending and is destroyed as before; a pure
  cancellation tombstone is withdrawn like any register when its evidence stands, and
  refused otherwise;
- a withdrawal whose landing is unknown: refuse, and record the withdrawal as OWED
  (`mqttWithdrawOwed`, `outbound_withdraw_owed.go`) under the deciding licence: the custody
  dispatcher retries it, one `withdrawUnsent` per unit, retiring the record when it lands,
  when the licence no longer serves (the successor's recovery classifies the register
  under its own licence: it withdraws an unsent obligation whose source is gone, and
  restores an unsent acting entry over a live source), when the
  marker is gone, or, finding no evidence, when its exchange owes no further delivery or
  its register no longer names the allocation (the dispatcher paragraph below), and
  re-reading a moved register rather than erasing the record. A
  register whose ending may or may not have landed is never deleted. A positively aborted
  attempt is re-read and tried once more.

**The pending-fence disposal rule goes through the same door.** A cancellation of an
allocation whose store is still in flight writes a create-only sparse fence on the empty
subject (`markInflightRegisterCancelledPending`), carrying the written provenance
`cancel_origin: pending-create`; every other cancellation is a CAS over an occupant and
carries `occupant`. The provenance is written, never inferred: a fresh register's body can
carry every other field of the sparse form. Only two writers may create a `pending-create`
body, both create-only (the ordinary classes' tombstone-register member, and
`storePendingFenceCAS` for the experimental slot-only class); the generic register sinks
refuse it, and a fence is never advanced, acquired, replaced or withdrawn. A validated
fence (`mqttValidPendingFence`) yields its own release authority,
`mqttSlotPendingFenceAuthority`, checked above arm 4 and separate from it, which licenses
exactly one disposition, `mqttSlotDeletePendingFence`, and nothing else; a door asked to
destroy a never-transmitted register that finds a fence applies that disposition instead
(`mqttDoorDisposition`). `endUnsentBeforeDestroy` does not apply to it: the door deletes
exactly the observed fence, always CONFIRMED, preserves a moved or different occupant, ends
no exchange, writes no `WithdrawnUnsent`, releases no ledger charge and lifts no exclusion
by itself. The rule is used by the admission classifier (`ReapPendingFenceThenRetry`), by
the door, by `confirmInflightRegister` for our own fence, and by recovery, which diverts a
fence right after its shape validation, before the shared-record validation and the affine
claim pass, straight to its drop list; a fence is never restored. A fence that disposal
left standing after a finite failure is retried by the exclusion-reclaim continuation
(`exclusion_reclaim.go`), the owner of the identifier's exclusion: when a bound subject's
base read finds a fence, the pass takes a fence step THROUGH THE DOOR
(`reapLoadedRegister` with `mqttSlotDeletePendingFence` and the pass's `mqttDoorGate`)
followed by a confirmation, and only confirmed absence counts toward the lift. Every
request the step adds is charged to the pass's 64-request budget as issued, at most
`mqttExclusionReclaimFenceStepMax` (six) per step; the dispatch gate is asked before each
added request, so a shutdown issues nothing further; a pass stops on budget only before
STARTING a fence step after it has completed one; and a per-exclusion `fenceCursor`,
scheduling state only, rotates the steps over the exclusion's subjects by value, so a
fence that keeps failing recurs once per traversal of its exclusion and starves nothing.

**An ordinary fence of the serving generation goes only behind a confirmed authority
advance (F-119, `pending_fence_disposal.go`).** Provenance says what may be disposed of, not
when: a fence is the only thing between a cancelled allocation and its late landing, since
an attempt of that nonce that meets it loses its register create-only CAS. So at BOTH door
entrances, immediately before the delete, `fenceBeforePendingFenceDisposal` decides from
the STORE. A SERVING authority at another generation, or a CLOSED one, needs nothing: an
admission requires a serving authority at its own generation, a generation is never
re-proposed, and every attempt prepared while the fence's generation served CASes a
sequence the change has moved past. PREPARING, RESERVING, absent or unreadable keep the
fence (a cancelled intent restores its predecessor's generation). At the fence's own
serving generation three things must hold, in order: the deciding connection's licence
names the serving generation and tenure (a displaced connection, on any broker, deletes
nothing); QUIESCENCE — the session's custody ledger is that generation's and holds no
admission of the fence's nonce whose ladder has not returned (`admissionLadderLive`:
liveness from the LADDER, because a drain removes the scheduling entry while its store is
in flight, and a ledger of another generation refuses, because a local generation mismatch
is never retirement); and a CONFIRMED `fence-pending-disposal` transition (revision +1,
nothing else, under that licence, settled resolve-abort-resolve; landed or superseded).
The advance kills every attempt of the nonce already prepared, quiescence proves no ladder
can prepare another (a nonce is allocated once and `ladderDone` never reverts), and the
licence leaves every other tenure to the entitlement compare admission already makes.
Anything else returns refused and the fence stays, with its identifier excluded, for the
next disposer. The cancelling ladder's own disposal (the adopt arm, the cancelled
confirmation) is therefore refused while it runs and falls back as it always did; the
exclusion-reclaim continuation disposes of the fence once the ladder has returned, under
the licence of the session's current connection — the sole current-binding exception to the
licence-provenance rule, stated beside it (a connectionless object keeps the fence:
it cannot tell whether another broker now serves the session), with the advance admitted
as a background authority attempt and run on a JSA view that asks the pass's dispatch
gate, and charges its budget, once per actual store request (`withRequestGate`: the
authority load, the commit's predecessor readback and batch, and every read and write of the
resolution and abort). The slot-only class has no authority to advance
and keeps the plain disposal; its cancellation durability is chapter P's.

Only the generation-level deletes stay outside the door — the incarnation reap of a
discarded generation, the orphan sweep of generations no session references, and the
settled affine register (slot-only, chapter P) — and a structural check pins that set. A
cancellation's own fallback tombstone, for an ordinary obligation with its evidence
standing, is the withdrawal's too.

**Readers.** A tombstone beside an ended exchange is reaped through the door by recovery's
cancellation routing and by admission's reap-and-retry; nothing transmits it
(`beginSendLocked` refuses a cancelled register, acquisition refuses the phase). A
cancelled `publish` occupant of any class is decided by its unsent marker: recovery
routes it as a genuine cancellation only while the marker stands and, for an ordinary
register, no output token is outstanding at the read ("A late acknowledgement is bound
before it arrives"), and otherwise treats it like any
possibly-attempted register, and the admission classifier probes that marker
once before it classifies (standing: reap, then retry; authoritatively absent and the same
delivery: the register-only replacement, whose body clears both `Cancelled` and
`cancel_origin`; absent and another delivery: the different-source arm; indeterminate:
the allocation is abandoned with its identifier excluded). A pending fence takes no probe
and is classified by its provenance (the rule above). Recovery restores an ordinary
register only beside the exchange its complete inventory census reached, and no
cancellation is exempt from that: the pending fence was diverted earlier by its
provenance, so an OCCUPANT cancellation whose exchange the census did not reach is an
unattributed shape, reserved like any other register (its identifier quarantined,
nothing acting on the record), never restored or dropped on the strength of its bit. A
tombstone
carrying OUR OWN nonce while our allocation is NOT cancelled — our admission landed, its
response was lost, and a withdrawal ended it before the ladder re-read — is no longer
adopted: the tombstone is reaped through the door, the allocation is abandoned with its
identifier excluded until a confirmed absence, and the source re-offers under a fresh
lineage. Our own pending fence (our allocation cancelled) is still adopted, so the
confirmation's cancelled arm disposes of it under the pending-fence rule. Where that arm
instead finds a landed register-only replacement, which inherited an occupant that may
already be on the wire, it destroys and tombstones nothing: our cancelled placeholder
goes, the identifier stays excluded and the custody ledger keeps the exchange's charge;
a resume restores the register as a possibly-attempted delivery. No live entry is rebuilt
for it on this connection.

**The admission's register sequence.** The ladder records the REGISTER's own sequence on
the entry, read back by nonce after the batch lands. An authority batch acknowledges on its
commit member — the authority — and recording that sequence as the register's made every
later exact-sequence reference to the slot read as a moved record, so the gated door's
freshness fence preserved registers it was asked to destroy (the proven-unsent disposals
among them) while reporting the continuation unblocked. A read-back that finds our own
register already TOMBSTONED — a withdrawal landed between the batch and the read — is not
a settlement: it is reported as a write the ladder re-reads, and its adopt arm abandons the
allocation exactly as for a lost response.

**Admission is pinned to the connection's own entitlement.** `admitInflightPublish` captures
the entitlement the CONNECT accept loop recorded on the connection, once, and every attempt
of the ladder — create and both replacement modes — composes under it; it never reads the
serving authority. A displaced connection's delivery therefore meets the commit-time
comparison with the standing authority and is refused, instead of admitting under its
successor's tenure.

### Capacity and identifier custody belong to the exchange

An ordinary QoS 1/2 exchange holds one Receive Maximum charge and its packet identifier
from its admission's reservation until the EXCHANGE durably ends. The scheduling maps
(`pendingPublish`, `pendingPubRel`) used to own both: removing an entry freed the slot,
