identifier the ledger holds), and that fact is carried forward by the allocation's FENCE —
generation, connection, ledger and the ledger's `holderEpoch`, which
`ensureExchangeLocked`, the only place a holder is created, advances. An unchanged fence
proves no lineage became a holder in between, so none can have been released; any change
refuses. A refusal is local cleanup of the attempt's own allocation and mapping. The
incomplete identifier space is marked in the same critical section as the reservation, so
a mark cannot land after a resume that already read the pair whole. An occupant
reservation's lifetime is HEAD's: a resume reading the pair whole may replace it; it is
not claimed to end then.

**The enforcement set.** The selectors that grant an action consult the kind:
`beginSendLocked`, the `trackPublish` resident arm, `mqttPendingRedeliverable`, the
resume's PUBREL re-offer, the duplicate-PUBREC NAK, `drainClaimEligibleLocked` (which lets
an ALLOCATION Hold through only to its cancel disposition), the PUBREL write entry,
retained PUBREL admission (exactly Retained — authority never inferred from shape), and
the PUBACK/PUBREC handler's settlement inferred from the resident entry. The
evidence-backed routes — the abandoned-ACK binding, a captured slot's terminal settlement,
the cancelled-reservation and terminal-reservation releases, disposal, recovery release —
act on evidence the client or the store supplies and are not kind-controlled; a Hold is
counted by the scheduling-map term of `receiveMaxOccupancyLocked`, as before.

**Structural closure.** `pending_entry_structure_test.go` type-checks the package against
export data and fails closed on any load or type error, scanning every function body and
every package-level initializer. It refuses a map write outside `setPendingLocked`, a
whole-map assignment other than `make`/`nil`, an expectation that is not a direct
expectation call, ANY outside its recorded sites, kind, evidence or identity fields
written outside a constructor, an evidence literal outside a producer, a field pointer, a
pointer-receiver method on a pending field, an interface conversion, a function-value or
channel escape, and a `reflect`/`unsafe` reach; it records every other field write (by
function, field and class: constructor-internal, detached snapshot or resident), escape
and kind reference, so a new one fails until it is justified. Its engine is self-tested
over a fixture declaring one function per bypass form.

**Not covered, stated.** An UNPROMOTED lineage-less placeholder whose exchange completes
elsewhere stays a Hold (it acts for nothing) until the nonce-keyed terminal release or the
gate-driven pass removes it, as before. Affine behaviour is unchanged (chapter P).
Retained QoS 1/2 is converted by 7c ("Retained delivery through the manifest", below): its
acting kind `Retained` is custody-gated exactly as `Ordinary`, and before its admission
the allocation is a Hold.

### Recovery: a bounded sweep with a two-part cursor

Any broker serving the account may resume a duty. There is no owner election, because an
election is an availability dependency on exactly the state being recovered. A claim on a
duty entry coordinates work and authorizes nothing: an expired claim proves nothing, a
held claim never authorizes deletion, and neither proves completion. Every duty execution
is therefore written to be safe under CONCURRENT execution, because a paused claimant
resuming after its lease expired cannot be excluded — only made rarer.

Generations are enrolled in a sharded directory, PAGED: a header carrying the shard's
high-water and traversal position, plus one entry per root. A root is ENROLLED only when
its shard has a header and its ordinal falls within that high-water — a root record
outside it is a record at an address no traversal reaches. A single record per shard would
grow with the account until the enrolment batch no longer fit, and reading it whole would
multiply the work budget by the number of roots it found.

#### Closure commits with a reachable root

The root is allocated by the CLOSING BATCH: the permanent transition outcome, the
generation
closure, the enrolment's resource and duty members, the SEALED ledger, the directory shard
header
taking the next ordinal, the root at that ordinal, and the authority record last. Every
F-105
class lives on `$MQTT_inflight` and a JetStream atomic batch is per stream, so all of it
commits
together or not at all.

A second write after the closure would leave a crash window in which a sealed, enrolled,
CLOSED
generation has no root — which the release gate refuses for ever, and which could only be
repaired
by discovering unrooted closed generations, the enumeration the paged directory exists to
avoid.

The invariant is therefore stated exactly: **closure commits with a reachable root, and
thereafter
recovery ownership stands as that root or as a valid completion certificate.** Not "a
closed
generation always has a root" — retirement removes it.

The closure RECORDS that root's address, and the release gate reads it there. An
enumeration of a
shard's roots can come back short — the server caps a subject listing — and a root it
missed would
read as "no reachable root", making the gate's answer depend on how many subjects the
filter
happened to match. An exact address cannot be short.

The rules are keyed on the CLOSURE rather than on the members a batch happens to carry,
because
the bypasses they exclude are omissions: a closure carrying no ledger member over a
generation
whose ledger stands open, a first enrolment that seals directly and allocates no root, a
closure
whose recorded address names an ordinal nothing writes. A transition that writes a closure
must
seal that generation's inventory and allocate exactly one root for it; a transition that
writes no
closure may carry neither.

What the boundary does NOT establish is that the enrolment is COMPLETE — that every
durable the
retiring session held is named. It cannot: the membership lives in a session record the
accepted
batch has already displaced, and `$MQTT_sess` carries `MaxMsgsPer: 1`, so the
predecessor's body
is evicted by the write that displaces it. Completeness is the closing caller's assertion,
and the
handoff intent carries the targets so they survive that eviction. See "The trusted
producer set".

#### Which durables a closure enrols, and the selector is the DISPOSITION

The shared group durables of the retiring membership are NOT enrolled: they are not
resources of this authority. Their release is the shared closing's — the generation's
acquisition ledger is sealed and every acquisition it lists released against the group
record, before the record goes on the teardown routes and by the recovery executor under the
discarding closure for a clean-start handoff ("A group durable is held by arbitration, not
counted by a scan"; "A discarded generation retires through its recovery owner"). Until
the shared-group lifecycle transfer they were enrolled whatever the disposition, on the
ground that their cleanup duty outlived the record that named them; that duty no longer
exists.

The AFFINE consumer is enrolled only when the closure DISCARDS. A closure that preserves
the
session's obligations leaves its affine consumer to the incarnation that continues — the
affine
generation outlives incarnations, which is why no session-generation fact could ever
authorize
deleting one (F-036 course E). A `close-admit` cannot carry a discard at all, so the
enrolment
rides the discarding FINALIZATION.

Ownership is therefore per TARGET, and the selector is the closure's own immutable
`Discard`
member: exactly one mechanism owns each durable, and which one is a durable fact rather
than a
property of whichever code path runs. A discarding closure REQUIRES the enrolment and its
teardown
refuses without it; a non-discarding one enrols no affine target and refuses nothing.

The affine resource carries the PUBREL durable as a FIELD. Securing the PUBREC proofs
reads the
records that consumer carries, so the readiness work needs its name after every transient
teardown
object is gone. Enrolling it as a resource would have given it provisioning and cleanup
duties
nothing here performs, and a generation carrying one could never certify. A name is data;
nothing
has to finish a field.

The affine target is therefore named WHOLE OR NOT AT ALL: the affine durable, its affine
generation and the PUBREL durable that carries its proofs, or none of them. Every producer
of a retirement's descriptor — the clean start's discarding handoff request and both session-end
teardown receipts — projects through `mqttAffineRetireDescriptor` (`outbound_authority.go`),
which drops the PUBREL name when the retiring generation holds no affine consumer, and
`mqttValidateAffineDescriptor` stays strict: a PUBREL durable named alone is refused. An
ordinary QoS 2 session's PUBREL consumer is not an affine target at all; it is a provisioned
resource enrolled when it was created and retired by the recovery executor from that record.
Naming it alone was F-113: every clean start over an ordinary QoS 2 session was refused before
CONNACK. The clean start's TEARDOWN target still carries the PUBREL durable, because the
post-finalize classification partitions it; only the retirement's descriptor is projected.

#### The cursor, the cycle and the horizon

The sweep cursor is four fields — where this sweep began, the next ordinal to examine, the
bound
captured when the sweep started, and THIS sweep's accumulator of unresolved ordinals. The
accumulator is kept apart from the restart point and reset when the next sweep begins. A
single
accumulated minimum can only fall: an ordinal unresolved once would hold the cursor
forever and
the generation would never retire.

A sweep completes at `bound + 1`, because the resume position names the NEXT ordinal to
examine.
Retirement then needs all four of: everything below the sweep's start previously
established
terminal and unable to reopen, every ordinal from there through the bound examined, an
empty
accumulator, and a SEALED ledger whose sealed high-water EQUALS the captured bound.

The shard header carries a CYCLE and a HORIZON beside its high-water. A cycle walks
ordinals
`1..Horizon`, where the horizon was the high-water when the cycle began, so an allocation
during
the cycle does not move the wrap: without it a busy shard could advance for ever and never
revisit
ordinal 1. The transition table is total:

| the walker holds | the stored header says | what it writes |
|---|---|---|
| a position in cycle `C` | cycle `C` | `Next = max(stored, local)`, keeping the stored `Hi` and horizon |
| a completed walk of `C` | cycle `C`, its position past the horizon | CAS `C -> C+1`, horizon = `Hi` as re-read, position 1 |
| a completed walk of `C` | cycle `C`, position NOT past the horizon | merge only: a cycle ends when the HEADER's progress reaches the horizon, not when one worker personally visited it |
| anything from `C` | cycle `C+1` or later | discard the local position entirely and adopt what stands |

A walker's own cycle is only ever one it read from a COMMITTED header, so a stored cycle
below it
is unreachable rather than merely unhandled.

#### Bounded work, with capacity reserved for progress

One budget covers the work a pass does, counted in UNITS rather than in raw store
operations: counting invocations bounded nothing, because one classification can read
several records, so a unit is charged where work is DISPATCHED and its price is set by
what that dispatch costs at worst. What a unit is NOT is one round trip. An authorization
spends two units and then calls `opAuthorizeDeletion`, which reads twice and whose
`commitAuthorityTransition` performs further predecessor and resource validation reads
before publishing its batch; a cleanup completion and a provisioning seal likewise carry
nested reads their caller does not itemise. So **`mqttRecoveryOpBudget` is 512 work units,
not 512 store calls**, and the operation count is that figure multiplied by a bounded
per-unit constant. The bound is still a bound — every helper a unit dispatches performs a
fixed, statically known number of reads and at most one batch — but it is work-unit
accounting, and describing it as a store-operation limit would claim a precision the code
does not enforce at the store-call boundary. The readiness walk is exempt from even this,
for the reason stated below. A RESERVE is held back for the progress writes
and is
sized for what they cost under contention: the cursor CAS, its re-read after a lost CAS,
and a
bounded number of such conflicts. A pass begins only with enough budget for one complete
unit.

Three ordinal states are distinguished, because two of them are not "unresolved": examined
and
unresolved enters this sweep's accumulator, below `Resume`; read but DEFERRED does not
advance
`Resume`; not read at all is the same. An OVERSIZED unit — one whose classification and
execution
cannot fit a minimum pass — is examined and unresolved on EVERY sweep that passes it,
atomically
with the advance. Not "recorded once": rolling a sweep RESETS the accumulator, so a
once-recorded
ordinal would be skipped by the next sweep and the root could finish with an empty
accumulator and
certify while that duty was still pending.

Fairness is scheduled rather than assumed. The shard walk RESUMES where it stopped rather
than
restarting at shard 0, which a per-pass budget would otherwise starve; within a shard the
walk
always advances past a root it visited, whatever that visit concluded, so a permanently
withheld
or unreadable root is revisited on the next cycle rather than consuming every pass; and a
per-root
budget stops one large generation spending the whole pass.

**The readiness walk is exempt from the operation budget, and the exemption is the only
way it converges.** The walk it performs — securing an affine generation's PUBREC proofs
and discarding its assignment claims — is account-wide and cannot be filtered: assignment
claims are keyed by GROUP DURABLE, not by client, so there is no subject a narrower scan
could use. Charging that walk per record would not bound it, it would STARVE it. A claim
population stably larger than one pass's budget means the budget expires before the end,
every pass re-reads the same prefix and readiness is never published for any generation,
so the seal never happens and the consumer is never reclaimed. The bound is therefore a
COUNT — ONE attempt per pass, run to completion — and what protects the sweep goroutine is
CANCELLATION rather than accounting.

The cancellation granularity is stated exactly, because the useful contract is narrower
than "every store operation". The shutdown check runs between the enumeration's own reads
and before each record's PROCESSING UNIT begins. A unit already entered runs to its end:
it performs nested reads, up to `mqttQ2AffClaimAttempts` load/CAS rounds, and its
mutations — and on the discard side one reap, which re-reads the claim and may itself
perform another bounded advance and a delete. So cancellation is a stop between units, not
a transactional prohibition on writes the unit in progress has already licensed, and the
elapsed wait is that unit's bounded operations at their own timeouts. That is what the
sweep goroutine needs: shutdown waits for one bounded unit rather than for the whole
account. It is also distinct from the pass's own shutdown, which still performs its
bounded progress bookkeeping. An interrupted walk leaves exactly the durable facts it
already committed; those are repeatable, so the next pass walks from the start and loses
nothing but the work.

**The assignment walk carries a FINITE HORIZON, and that is what makes it terminate
at all.** Bounding how many walks a pass performs bounds nothing if one walk never
returns, and the unbounded form reads from sequence 1 until a read reports no next
message — so concurrent writers arriving ahead of the reader keep it running, and the
one-attempt cap and the pass-end rule are both powerless because neither is reached
again until the helper returns. On the shared maintenance goroutine that is not a slow
pass; it is session expiry and both orphan sweeps stopped with it.

A fixed horizon alone would be WRONG, and the reason is the stream's own shape.
`$MQTT_Q2AFF` is `MaxMsgsPer: 1`, so advancing a claim REWRITES it at a higher sequence,
and `confirmSourceAckAndRecord` advances a claim with no owner scoping at all. A claim of
the generation being discarded can therefore be moved ABOVE a fixed horizon by an
unrelated contender, and a walk that stopped there would report completion having never
seen it — licensing the seal, the consumer's deletion, and a started delivery being
redistributed instead of dying with its session ([MQTT-4.8.2-5]).

So the walk takes an authoritative horizon, walks strictly increasing sequences within
it, and then READS THE END AGAIN. Completion is asserted only when that later read finds
the tail exactly where the segment ended, in the same stream incarnation. Reaching the
horizon does not establish it alone, an initially empty stream included: it leads to the
verification read. "No next message" does not lead there at all — it is INDETERMINATE and
fails the segment, because the pinned server answers a failed store read the same way
(F-108), and a read that asks whether the tail MOVED cannot tell an enumeration that
finished from one that gave up. A tail that moved is followed into a new fixed segment
beginning at the old horizon plus one, for at most **two extensions**; two is a policy
choice rather than a correctness threshold, because what correctness this walk has comes
from the verification read rather than from the number of tries — and that read is not
authoritative today either (F-108), so the number is not load-bearing in either
direction. Records a next-message read returns from ABOVE the current segment are
neither processed nor
advanced past. Horizon reads are cancellable like any other store operation, and a failed
or unusable read, a horizon that went backwards, a recreated stream, an enumeration error
or exhausted extensions all WITHHOLD readiness rather than assert it.

What that argument reaches for — CONDITIONALLY, see below — is the MONOTONE DISCARD
PREDICATE, not an atomic inventory snapshot. A
rewrite lands at a higher sequence, never behind the cursor, so an owned claim rewritten
during a segment landed at or below the horizon read after it and the next segment visits
it; when the final read shows no movement, every surviving owned claim was either visited
here or carries a discard an earlier visit wrote, because the `SourceAcked` update
preserves `Discarded` and a claim already reaped need not still exist. The conclusion
rests on the closed generation admitting no fresh undiscarded claim — the stable-tail
check supplies no admission fence of its own.

**THAT ADMISSION PREMISE DOES NOT HOLD AT HEAD, and the proof above is therefore
CONDITIONAL.** `beginQ2AffOp` admits a shared QoS 2 move against LOCAL session state, and
the claim it creates is a subject-only CAS that never contends with the generation's
durable closure. A mover admitted before the closure and paused can resume after this
walk's final verification read and install a fresh undiscarded claim — reachable
cross-broker, where a successor closes the generation remotely and the old owner's
in-memory closing flag is never set. So what this section documents is the EXECUTOR:
given an admission closure that accounts for every previously admitted producer, the pass
establishes readiness and completes the cleanup from persisted evidence alone, without an
owner teardown. The missing half is **F-107** in `docs/ROADMAP.md`, which lives in
**chapter P**: it was relocated there on 2026-09-20, unresolved, because session-affine
shared-subscription QoS 2
is not an alpha release feature and the premise F-107 supplies is consumed only by this
AFFINE half. It is therefore a prerequisite of EXPERIMENTAL affine recovery, not of F-105's
cutover step 2. Until it lands, this mechanism is a non-shipping checkpoint and not an
independently safe production cleanup transfer.

**A SECOND premise is missing too, and it is independent of the first: the walk has no
authoritative completeness evidence.** The horizon comes from a `STREAM.INFO` whose `State`
and `Cluster.Leader` are sampled INDEPENDENTLY, so an election between the two samples
returns a lagging follower's state carrying the new leader's name; refusing a leaderless
answer does not close that. And the forward reads cannot tell an empty suffix from a FAILED
STORE READ, because the pinned server maps every error from `LoadMsg`, `LoadNextMsg` and
`LoadLastMsg` to `JSNoMessageFoundErr` — so this walk now treats a no-message response as
INDETERMINATE and withholds, which is safe and costs it availability on a sparse or empty
suffix that it can afford only because it does not run in production.

**The repair this section used to name has been DISPROVED, and the correction is recorded
here rather than left standing.** An acknowledged control marker whose sequence bounds each
segment and which the forward walk must ENCOUNTER does **not** establish that the walk
examined every matching record below it. `fileStore.firstMatching` `continue`s past any
`cacheLookup` error that is not `errPartialCache` or `errNoCache`, block indexing defers
checksum validation to the individual lookup, and a checksum mismatch produces `errBadMsg`.
So a corrupt record is SILENTLY SKIPPED and a later record — the marker included — is
returned SUCCESSFULLY, with no error and no no-message response anywhere. The walk then
encounters its marker having never visited the record, and declares completion. Adding
further markers cannot repair this: the omission happens below the API boundary the marker
protocol reasons about. What a marker establishes is that the responder's store applied that
sequence; it establishes nothing about which records between were successfully read.

**There is therefore no established repair to name here.** The requirement is a read
contract in which an unreadable candidate cannot silently disappear from a successful
enumeration while genuine exhaustion stays distinguishable. **No client-side protocol
satisfying that has been ESTABLISHED under the present constraints** — which is not a claim
that none can exist, and this document does not make the stronger one. Two narrower
error-reporting paths exist and neither is an approved enumeration primitive: a direct
multi-last get terminates a
resolved candidate's load failure with an error rather than a successful EOB, but returns
only the last message per subject, and its HISTORICAL selection — where `UpToSeq` puts the
ceiling below the stream's end — enters a backward search that ignores lookup errors, a
request without `UpToSeq` taking a last-block fast path instead; and a direct ordinary
batch keeps a pending count that a skip can
leave nonzero, but its count has partial-range branches that undercount, an EOB can mean a
byte or batch limit rather than exhaustion, and it needs freshness, incarnation, retention
and pagination arguments it does not have. See **F-108**, which carries the evidence and is
an upstream data-layer defect tracked in `docs/known-upstream-issues.md`, filed as
nats-server#8632.

What is demonstrated here is therefore execution over the exercised fixture populations,
conditional on BOTH premises — not affine recovery.

The residual is a LATENCY one and it is stated plainly: sustained movement of the
assignment stream postpones readiness indefinitely, and a single write inside every
verification interval is enough — the writers need not outpace the reader. While readiness
is withheld the physical cleanup is delayed and the recovery state is retained; no MQTT
client observes an error for it. The bound is finite for the horizons it captured, given
that store calls terminate, but it is not a population-independent operation or wall-clock
bound: the attempt occupies the shared maintenance goroutine for its whole duration and
may delay that goroutine's other work substantially. Cancellation still waits only for an
entered bounded unit plus the pass's own progress bookkeeping. This applies to the
RECOVERY PASS's charged walk only; the uncharged callers — the owner teardown, resume and
the orphan inventory — keep the behaviour they had, where an incomplete result means
something different. That leaves a known limit: **this does not establish that the
maintenance goroutine as a whole cannot hang**, because its pre-existing orphan scan walks
the same stream unbounded and can still keep recovery from being reached.

**The single attempt is made FAIR by ending the pass with it.** The attempt is spent before
either helper can succeed, so a root whose proof resolution fails permanently would take it
on every pass, and because roots are visited in ordinal order the sibling visited after it
would never get one — a stable starvation rather than an incidental one. The pass therefore
ends after the root that spends the attempt: that root finishes its bounded visit, the
shard's traversal position is advanced past it and PERSISTED, and no further root or shard
is visited. The readiness quantum is the traversal quantum. The shard then resumes at the
sibling, which meets a fresh attempt, and the failing root comes back on the next cycle.
This uses the existing `Next`/`Cycle` state and its existing CAS — no new persisted shape,
no separate fairness record — and costs only root throughput in a pass that attempts
readiness. The cost is honest and pre-existing: this
is the same walk the owner's teardown already performs inline for the same generation, so
the pass takes on no cost the broker was not already paying, only a different actor.

There is **no progress guarantee** to claim. A duty blocked on external evidence stays
unresolved
across arbitrarily many sweeps, and under unrestricted growth of the root population there
is no
latency bound, only eventual visitation. What the mechanism guarantees is bounded work per
pass
and no permanent skip.

#### What a pass may DO, named rather than inferred

The classifier says what a duty owes; it says nothing about whether this actor may do it.
The set
a background pass performs is therefore written down, and everything else is withheld by a
stated
rule:

| verdict | the pass |
|---|---|
| `authorize-deletion` / `cleanup`, for an AFFINE resource | performs it: the physical delete, then the completion and the duty's resolution in ONE batch |
| `may-resolve` | continues the entry to terminal |
| the readiness work and the provisioning SEAL of an affine resource | performs both. The seal is one unit under the budget; the readiness WALK is bounded by a count instead, for the reason given under Bounded work above |
| `authorize-deletion` / `cleanup`, any other kind | WITHHELD. `source`, `pubrel` and `payload` are deleted by paths not converted here; a shared group durable is not a resource of this authority (its deletion is the group record's, "A group durable is held by arbitration, not counted by a scan") |
| `deliver`, `release` | WITHHELD: both need an action acquired under a SERVING authority, which the pass holds none of |
| `drain` | WITHHELD by rule. Acquisition fences delivery and release; it does not by itself prove a background drain impossible |
| `provision` | WITHHELD: the materialization half is not built |

A retired generation's disposal runs under the CLOSED authority the client still carries:
`dispose-resource` is permitted under any authority state and may name an EARLIER
generation,
which is the whole reason that kind exists. Nothing deletes the authority record; an
ABSENT one
WITHHOLDS every duty rather than licensing anything.

The cleanup outcome is derived from the delete call's own result — `removed` when it
succeeded,
`gone` when it reported not-found — and an AMBIGUOUS delete records nothing at all. The
next pass
re-acts, which is safe here because the affine durable's name carries the affine
generation: a
late or duplicated delete names a consumer no live session can hold, since a fresh session
mints a
new affine generation and a new name. That property is what makes the affine transfer
separable
from the shared one.

#### The affine cleanup's prerequisites, and who performs them

Deleting the affine consumer destroys the records that carry the only evidence a client
answered
PUBREC. So the consumer's cleanup is not authorizable until two acts are done — the proofs
are
secured into their assignments, and the assignments' discard disposition is established —
and the
mechanism that says so is the PROVISIONING AXIS, which already states exactly this: a
resource
whose provisioning is unsealed may not have its deletion authorized, because a delayed
create may
still land under its name.

The affine resource is therefore enrolled PENDING, and the seal is gated on a READINESS
record: a
create-only assertion naming the client, the account recovery epoch, the generation, the
affine
generation and the durable. The write boundary admits `PENDING -> SEALED` for an affine
resource
only against one that matches exactly.

**Readiness is a TRUSTED ASSERTION, not a fence**, and both halves of that matter. The
boundary
establishes WHOM the assertion is about and that a seal cannot be written without one; it
cannot
establish that the acts ran, because matching identifiers are not evidence of work. A
premature
record written by a producer that skipped them would satisfy the rule. It also does not
prevent a
delayed JetStream create: a creator that read the record as absent and then paused can
still land
its create afterwards, because a read cannot invalidate a request already in flight.

Two producers may write it — the teardown, which is the fast path, and the RECOVERY PASS,
which is
the finisher for the window where no teardown ever runs. A discarding finalization
replaces the
predecessor's metadata, so no marked record anchors a teardown for it, and "the
successor's
acceptance will do it" names a live caller rather than a restartable one. Both write the
same
create-only record, so whichever arrives second reads it as done; a conflicting one is an
error,
because one generation has one affine consumer.

#### Retirement: the certificate, then the root

A generation whose four conditions hold is retired by writing its completion certificate
FIRST and
deleting its root second. The certificate is what satisfies the release gate after the
root is
gone, so writing it first is the fence: a crash between the two leaves both, which
converges — the
next pass re-derives retirement, validates the standing certificate and deletes the root
again.
The other order would leave a generation with neither.

An ABSENT read after a timeout is not proof the certificate never landed: the original
publication
may still commit, so absence means retry the IDENTICAL certificate, and only a present,
validated,
matching one settles success. A standing certificate is validated rather than overwritten;
a
conflicting bound is an error, because one sealed inventory has one bound.

A HOLE at an ordinal within the high-water is an empty traversal slot and never evidence
that a
generation retired — `Hi` never decreases, so a retired root leaves its ordinal behind,
and the
certificate is the only claim.

#### The trusted producer set

Three assertions in this mechanism are trusted rather than enforced, and they are listed
together
so the three stay distinct and none drifts into being described as proof:

| assertion | producers | what the boundary enforces |
|---|---|---|
| a cleanup OUTCOME | the duty executor's two composers, which derive it from the delete call's own result | the value is legal, the resource stands DELETE_AUTHORIZED, the member is a legal step at its CAS expectation, and the duty's ending is judged against the state the batch RESULTS IN. NOT the physical fact |
| affine READINESS | the teardown routes and the recovery pass | the record decodes, every member is present and non-null, and it names exactly this client, epoch, generation, affine generation and durable. NOT that the acts ran |
| target-set COMPLETENESS | the closing caller, carrying the targets in the handoff intent | every member is attributed, decodes and carries its duty; shapes match; nothing outside the declared set. NOT that the set is the whole set |

An arbitrary batch cannot forge STATE-MACHINE SUPPORT — an unrelated or invalid member, a
wrong
CAS expectation, a duty ending no member and no record supports. A batch that IS
structurally
legal can still assert a physical result that did not happen. That is a trust boundary,
not a
proof, and it is named rather than implied.

### Retained replay material is immutable and separately identified

Retained QoS 1/2 has no register bypass since 7c. Before it, a retained send built its
frames from the LIVE retained slot, so the material an obligation replayed was whatever
that slot happened to hold later — which is not the material the client was promised.

Material becomes a **manifest** plus create-only **chunks**, under a payload identity
minted per materialization and never shared with the retained topic slot. The manifest
carries the MQTT 5 properties, the absolute expiry deadline and the authenticated No Local
origin marker as well as the topic and QoS — material without them replays a DIFFERENT
message once the slot has changed, losing a Response Topic or a Correlation Data and
outliving the Message Expiry Interval its publisher set. The deadline is stored absolute
rather than as an interval, because an interval would restart at every materialization.

The manifest also names the resource incarnation that OWNS its cleanup, and that owner
must already exist or be created by the same batch. Naming an owner does not reserve
one: material whose owner never existed is material the duty sweep never discovers,
because discovery runs through the owner's predeclared entries. The naming runs BOTH
WAYS: the owner must be a payload resource whose own name is this materialization's
payload token, and it must not be SEALED. Material landing after a seal is material the
seal already said would not exist, and the agreement in both directions is what makes
the seal answerable at all — a resource whose name did not address its manifest could
be sealed while material stood under it, because the boundary would be reading an
address nothing occupies. The chunk fence is an atomic
manifest CAS together with the chunk creation in ONE batch: reading the manifest and then
publishing a chunk leaves a window in which the manifest is sealed or closed, and the
chunk lands against a payload already declared whole or already being deleted.

The manifest's written count rises by exactly the chunks its batch carries, so it is a
durable trace rather than an assertion, and READY requires every chunk to have landed
through the fence.

**Material is written by a kind of its own.** `materialize-payload` carries manifests and
chunks and nothing else, and is governed like provisioning: NEW
WORK under a SERVING authority. The RESERVATION is the one exception, and it is
provisioning's: the batch that provisions a copy's owner resource also creates its
manifest, empty and PROVISIONING (7c), because an owner and the material it owns are
created together or not at all. Every chunk and the seal after it are
`materialize-payload`'s. Disposal cannot either: disposal is permitted under a CLOSED
authority because
cleanup must outlive closure, and writing bytes must not. Material landing in a closed
generation is material nothing may admit against and nothing will finish.

**The SEAL verifies the material, inside the transaction.** `Written == Chunks` proves
every chunk landed through the fence; it proves nothing about the bytes, and READY is what
an ADMISSION relies on. So reaching READY reads the payload's chunks and checks them
against the manifest being sealed: the length and the digest, over the material as the
CAS fences it. There is no evidence RECORD, because a record that says "I verified" is a
claim rather than a verification — an earlier design carried a caller-supplied witness and
a review showed it could be fabricated from the manifest's own numbers while the stored
bytes were something else entirely.

The cost is proportional and it is paid once: an ADMISSION reads the manifest and nothing
else, while a SEAL happens once per materialization, immediately after the material was
written chunk by chunk. Replay verifies again before emitting a byte, because material can
rot after it was sealed.

**Only the kinds that are ABOUT their members may carry any.** Six transition kinds
provision, materialize, dispose, admit or advance, and their members are their purpose.
The rest install, freeze, cancel or close OWNERSHIP, and carry nothing: a closure that
could carry an inventory allocation would take an ordinal in the generation it is
ending, in an inventory about to be sealed shut behind it, and no rule about allocation
asks which kind is taking the ordinal. The set is closed and stated once, so a kind
added later is refused by default rather than inheriting the permission by being
forgotten.

**The enrolment rides in the transition that CLOSES the generation, and that is the one
permission a closing kind has over members.** The enrolment must outlive the session
record, because the record is what names the durables and the metadata release is what
deletes it; what outlives it is a cleanup duty, a duty needs an ordinal, and only the
ledger allocates one — which the seal forbids after. Closure is the last act able to
take one, so the enrolment rides in the batch that closes or it cannot exist at all.
That batch SEALS as it allocates, in one act, which is what makes the enrolment's
completeness a fact rather than a snapshot: after it no further ordinal can be taken.
The permission is narrow in every direction. The generation is the one the CLOSURE names
— not the transition's own, since a discarding finalization installs its successor
while closing its predecessor — and the cross-generation exception is reachable only by
a transition that actually writes that closure. The resource must be the affine
consumer. Every duty the batch allocates must name a resource the same batch enrolled,
which is the reverse of the coverage rule and closes the same hole from the other side.
Anything else is refused: an exchange would admit work into a generation that is ending,
a source consumer would provision under an authority about to stop serving, and a
continuation would advance an entry whose sweep may already have passed it.

**The closing batch carries the SEALED ledger, and the boundary requires it.** The
enrolment's claim to completeness is that the act which allocates is the act which
seals, so no further ordinal can be taken afterwards. Checking only the ledger member's
generation would leave that to whoever composed the batch: an otherwise valid enrolment
beside a ledger body still OPEN closes the generation with its inventory unsealed, and a
later disposal — which may legitimately name an earlier generation — then allocates into
an inventory the closure was supposed to have shut. What the release gate reads off that
generation would be a snapshot again.

**An allocation never starts TERMINAL, and a closed generation takes no further
ordinal.** The first is the write boundary's own rule and not the composer's: the thing
a duty is predeclared for is created by the same batch, so it cannot already have ended,
and an entry that arrives terminal is one the bounded sweep advances past forever while
the obligation is still owed — the same defect as asserting an ending later, reached by
allocating it instead. The rule that requires an ending to be EARNED cannot catch it,
because that one runs only where a duty is being continued. The second closes the case
the seal cannot: a seal speaks only for a generation that HAS a ledger, and one closed
before it ever allocated anything has none, so the allocation path reads the permanent
closure and refuses — and refuses equally when that read fails, because what licenses an
allocation is the ABSENCE of a closure and a failed read establishes no absence.

**A shared group durable is not a resource of the authority at all.** It used to be
ENROLLED here, its cleanup CONDITIONAL on a last-holder question re-asked where the
deletion executed, because its name was derived from the subscription key and several
generations held it at once. That kind, its enrolment, its classifier and the walk they
rested on are deleted: a group durable is held by acquisitions counted in its GROUP record
on `$MQTT_inflight`, its name carries a physical incarnation no successor reuses, and its
deletion is authorized by the release of the group's last acquisition — "A group durable is
held by arbitration, not counted by a scan". The teardown seals the generation's acquisition
ledger, releases what it lists and gates the record's release on the empty seal, before the
authority's own metadata-release gate is consulted, so the two gates ask different
questions of different records and neither rides on the other's vacuous arm.

**The enrolment makes a duty DISCOVERABLE; it does not by itself make the release
PERMITTED.** The metadata-release gate asks two different questions — what this
generation holds, and who will come back for it — and the enrolment answers only the
first. The second is answered by a reachable recovery root or a completion certificate,
and neither is a thing a transition can carry: root and shard are deliberately not
obligation classes, because a sweep cursor authorizes nothing and belongs to no
authority's batch, and a certificate is written by the sweep that COMPLETES rather than
by the act that enrols.
So a generation may be fully enrolled and still be refused release on durable recovery
ownership, which is the fail-closed direction and the honest answer while no broker can
be shown to be coming back for the duty. Until a recovery pass exists to enrol a root
and walk it, that refusal is the state of an enrolled generation. Shared group durables
are outside this: they are released by the shared closing above, never enrolled.

**A RESERVATION IS AN ACT OF MATERIALIZING, so only a materializing kind performs one.**
The chunk rule — material is written under a serving authority, and the kind is what
says so — applies equally to the act that brings a payload into existence. A disposal
legitimately carries manifests, because closing one precedes deleting its material and
cleanup must outlive closure; it never CREATES one. Without that rule a disposal could
reserve material in the same batch that sealed its owner's provisioning, and each half
of the seal, reading the other's record from the store, would have seen nothing to
refuse.

**A payload resource's provisioning seal is ANSWERABLE, so it is answered.** A seal says
nothing can materialize this resource any more, and a deletion authorization rests on
it. For a consumer that fact settles in the JetStream API and the caller is the only one
who can state it. For replay material it does not: the manifest is in this stream, at
the address the resource names, so a seal taken while it is still PROVISIONING is a
claim the store refutes. Left unchecked it authorizes deleting a name that is not free,
and the material is then refused removal forever, because removal requires a manifest
that reached CLOSED. The read is by identity: a record standing at that address under
ANOTHER materialization is refused rather than interpreted, because reading another
materialization's record as this one's is the class this protocol keeps closing. And it
reads the STORED material, never the material the sealing batch is itself writing: a
seal rests on a cessation that is ALREADY ESTABLISHED, and one act that closed the
manifest and sealed the resource would be consuming its own closure as the seal's
evidence. The recovery order is therefore CLOSE THE MANIFEST, THEN SEAL THE RESOURCE,
which is always available: a manifest may go from provisioning to closed, so a
materialization that crashed mid-write strands nothing.

**Cleanup seals before it deletes.** A delayed chunk writer arriving afterwards finds a CLOSED
manifest and its batch fails, so it cannot recreate material already removed. Closing is terminal.

**Removal requires two facts and announces itself first.** Deleting material needs the
EXACT cleanup owner's deletion authorization AND the manifest's closure — they answer
different questions, and neither implies the other. Without the authorization a deleter
destroys material an obligation still needs; without the closure a delayed writer
resurrects material after an apparently completed cleanup.

Reading a chunk therefore comes in two named forms. One requires the materialization the
record must belong to and refuses a blank identity; the other reads WHATEVER stands at
an address, for the two cleanup callers whose question is exactly that — a re-delete of
an announced interval and a confirmation establishing that its own chunks are gone, both
of which may legitimately meet a later materialization's record. A single reader taking
an empty token to mean "do not check" would make the permissive read an accident of a
blank argument rather than a deliberate call.

Every chunk records the MATERIALIZATION it belongs to, because a subject can be reused
and a record cannot be un-deleted. Without it a paused cleanup resuming after a
replacement materialization reserved the same payload token would delete the newcomer's
material by subject. Each delete loads the record anyway, to learn its sequence, so
identifying it costs nothing.

A JetStream delete cannot ride in the atomic batch, so a removal is TWO counts and three
acts. The manifest's ANNOUNCED count rises first, in bounded intervals; the chunks that
interval covers are then deleted; only then does the CONFIRMED count rise to meet it. One
count was not enough: advanced before the deletes, a crash between the announcement and the
first delete left a manifest saying the work was done, so the resume found nothing to do.
A resumed cleanup re-deletes everything announced and not confirmed — deleting an absent
chunk is the one operation that is safe to repeat — and only then confirms.

A CONFIRMATION IS EVIDENCE, not arithmetic: accepting one reads the interval and refuses
while a chunk of this materialization still stands, because two counters agreeing say
nothing about whether anything was deleted.

The manifest goes LAST and goes by its exact SEQUENCE. While it stands an interrupted
cleanup can be resumed from it; and deleting whatever currently occupies the address would
let a paused worker destroy a LATER materialization's record, one with a live cleanup owner
and obligations already admitted against it.

### Two tagged unions, because a fabricated value is believed

An ordinary delivery has a source consumer and a sequence; a retained send has neither.
Satisfying one shape for both means FABRICATING a durable and a sequence, and those values
then flow into every reader that believes it is looking at a delivery — a
source-completion classifier asks the consumer about a sequence that was never delivered.

A missing value refuses; a fabricated one is believed. So the source is a union whose
retained arm FORBIDS the delivery coordinates rather than leaving them empty by
convention. The ordinary arm carries the source consumer's INCARNATION as well as its
stream, durable and sequence, because a consumer NAME can be recreated: coordinates alone
cannot distinguish the source an obligation was delivered from and a successor occupying
the same address. The canonical PUBREL reference is a union for the same reason: an
ordinary exchange's release lives on a consumer at a sequence, a retained one at an
exchange-specific subject — different KINDS, not different values — and the in-flight arm
carries an IDENTITY beside the subject, because a subject locates an address and a record
read back from a rewritten subject is a different record.

### The ownership protocol's deadline

F-051's deadline does not cover this. `mqttAdmitConnectLocked` STOPS that timer before
authorization and ownership processing, so the interval between the stop and a servable
authority had no deadline at all — a CONNECT could sit in the ownership protocol
indefinitely while the client waited for a CONNACK.

The ownership budget is anchored at exactly that stop. It is ONE absolute budget, never
reset by a retry, and the remaining amount is derived from the anchor rather than
decremented as steps report back — a decremented counter measures work that came back, and
the client is waiting on the wall clock, so a step that hangs must still spend it. Steps
are gated before they begin, and since F-105 8a the budget also caps every REQUEST the
protocol makes: its deadline (anchor plus total) is carried by the JetStream assistant
VIEW the protocol runs on (`mqttJSA.withDeadline`, `outbound_connect_deadline.go`), so the
settlement, the reservation or preparation, the metadata commit, the finalization and every
resolution, abort and re-attempt nested in them wait at most until that instant. One
instant, not a duration per call: N requests each handed "the remaining budget" would spend
N times it. A request after the deadline is refused before it is queued (certain: nothing
was sent); a reply wait the deadline cuts off is ambiguous exactly as a per-request timeout
was, and is resolved from durable state like one. What the deadline does NOT cut off, and
the budget only spends: the restore, the uncertain-record resolution and the incarnation
retirement, which keep their own bounds (the per-request timeout, the re-drive cycle
admission, the drain ceiling).

Expiry has **three** dispositions and two of them look alike:

| state at expiry | this connection | the generation | the proposal |
|---|---|---|---|
| ABORTED | refused | **abandoned**: a reservation closed, a preparation cancelled | lost; no replacement is minted |
| COMMITTED, not finalized | refused | untouched | **stands, settleable by the next acceptance** |
| UNRESOLVED | refused | untouched | **stands, settleable** |

The verdicts are LATCHED from everything the run established, before the budget is asked:
the latest read, and the executor's observation of its own proposal
(`mqttOwnObservation`), which the executor writes the moment it establishes a fact — so a
verdict read inside a step that then fails at the deadline (a cleanup cut off after the slot
read ABORTED, an adoption readback cut off after it read COMMITTED) is disposed by that
verdict, not as UNRESOLVED. An executor error at or past the deadline is an expiry.

A committed slot is never aborted — that is the one act the create-only fence forbids, and
another acceptance finalizes the proposal exactly as proposed before taking its own tenure
by an ordinary handoff. UNRESOLVED is a third class and not a synonym for aborted: absence
of a committed verdict is not proof of non-commitment. No disposition deletes an
arbitration record, so an expired attempt leaves the client servable by the next
acceptance — which is **not** a promise that the next acceptance succeeds.

### A standing proposal is settled before anything is destroyed (F-105 8a)

An acceptance that crashed — or one still running on another broker — can leave its
reservation or preparation standing, with its metadata half committed, aborted or
unresolved. Before 8a every later CONNECT read that proposal as ITS OWN
(`loadConnectOwnershipInput` took the identity from whatever the authority carried): an
unresolved one was refused forever, an aborted one made the new acceptance a "loser", a
committed creation was finalized under the wrong id; and the clean-start block and the
restore's overdue discard destroyed over it before anything settled it.

**Own versus foreign is the acceptance's own record, never the authority's.** A CONNECT
knows the intent ids its drives proposed (`mqttConnectOwnershipState.ownIntents`, declared
above the re-entry label with the budget). The current proposal's verdict is read from ITS
OWN slot, whatever the authority now carries — a peer that aborted it and closed the
authority over it leaves `CLOSED + own + ABORTED`, which is what the loser bound turns on.
Any other standing proposal is SETTLED: `settleProposal` (resolve, abort if unresolved, read
again — the abort's own error is never the verdict), then the continuation its permanent
verdict licenses (`mqttForeignRecoveryContinuation`): finalize a committed one exactly as
proposed (the acceptance then takes its own tenure by an ordinary handoff), cancel an
aborted preparation back to its predecessor, close an aborted reservation's generation.
Every act names its proposal: one whose target no longer stands (another settler acted
first) returns `errMQTTOwnershipTargetMoved` with a fresh read, and the driver decides
again — it never acts on what replaced it. ONE foreign target per CONNECT, across every
drive and re-drive; a proposal an earlier drive of the same CONNECT left is its own residue
and spends no bound.

**Two places settle, and both before destruction.** The CONNECT settles at the top of
`restoreSession`, before the restore, the uncertain-record resolution, the retirement and
the clean-start block, in a settle-only run of the same driver and arms (never a
reservation, preparation, metadata commit or record adoption). If the settled authority
then serves a generation other than a RESIDENT object's — a committed proposal moved the
record past it, whoever finalized it — the object is disposed with the existing foreign
disposal (`disposeForeignSessionLocked`, unlicensed: the Will is consumed or discharged,
never discarded, F-084) and the restore runs on the moved record; an object whose
retirement is pending is left to the CONNECT's existing join, which drains its owners and
finishes its discard (whose claim the moved record supersedes). The CONNECT's read is not
a fence, so EVERY discard settles again at its own boundary: `prepareClear`, the existing
pre-mutation phase of the restore's discard, the clean-start retirement, disconnect,
expiry, record expiry, gone-retirement and the pending-discard finisher. It makes one
authority read there and, if a proposal stands, settles it (bounded by one request
timeout, no client-ID gate: it touches no binding or local state, and the receipt slot and
the authority CAS arbitrate). The FINAL load rides on `mqttPreparedClear.auth`;
`destroy`'s retirement receipt and the clean-start handoff-versus-destroy choice read that
load and no later one. So every discard sees only states its callers already handle:
SERVING at its generation (a receipted discard), ABSENT or CLOSED (receiptless), or a
record a committed proposal already moved (the claim supersedes) — it never refuses. A
proposal appearing AFTER the boundary's read is arbitrated by the session record: the
teardown claim and the proposal's metadata commit CAS the same sequence, so exactly one
wins; a receipt-marked record whose close cannot land while the proposal stands waits for
the adopter. The boundary's RESIDUE — a store that cannot answer within the bound — is a
receiptless claim, after which the closing driver finds no licence and withholds the
record's release until an adopter settles the proposal and continues it (F-105 8b, "One
tenure and one closing driver"), stated in `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`.

**Who aborted it decides whether the CONNECT may propose again.** When a metadata commit
fails, the acceptance settles its own proposal's slot. The ONLY proof that the resulting
abort is its own settlement of a lost record race (a rival's record, a moved predecessor)
is its own create-only abort write positively succeeding — an empty or unreadable read
proves nothing, since a peer can abort in between. With that proof and a confirmed
cleanup, the CONNECT re-drives against the winner: re-drive arbitration against a settled
authority (consult 10), not a loser proposing again. Without it — another party's abort,
an unconfirmed one, a cleanup that failed, or a slot that cannot be read at all — the
handler returns a fresh error wrapping nothing retryable. And the decision does not rest
on that: the accept loop decides whether the CONNECT may drive again from what the drive
ESTABLISHED, never from the identity of the error it returned (consult 120). Before the
success arm and every retry arm, a CONNECT whose own proposal may stand — recorded the
moment its reservation or preparation landed, or when that transition could not be
resolved and so may have landed — and is neither COMMITTED nor provably aborted and
abandoned by this acceptance itself (`mqttOwnObservation.forbidsRedrive`) refuses. A
re-drive is therefore licensed only when no own proposal may stand, when it COMMITTED (the
next drive finalizes it exactly as proposed), or after the proven self-abort above. An
unknown verdict stays unknown: refusing does not license abandoning it, and it stands for
the next acceptance to settle.

**An own aborted proposal is abandoned on one path.** The executor's in-place cleanup
closes or cancels it; when that does not confirm — it failed, or the deadline cut it off —
every terminal refusal carrying that evidence launches the owed-abandonment worker after
the refusal is certified and the CONNECT holds nothing: one attempt under its own deadline,
on the CAPTURED proposal only, and only while that exact proposal still stands with an
ABORTED verdict. Its durable fallback is the next acceptance, which meets the proposal as
foreign and settles it the same way.

**A refused acceptance never activates.** Every refusal that wrote no success CONNACK
certifies its connection closed through the external protocol — seal the gate, close the
transport outside the writer lock, cross the writer barrier, record the certificate — after
whatever failure CONNACK it wrote; a finalization another acceptance completes later cannot
make that socket emit. A failure after the success CONNACK is left to its caller, which
owes the client a v5 DISCONNECT with the reason, and is certified by `closeConnection`,
which since 8a certifies every teardown instead of closing the transport bare. Since 8c a
connection that attempted an acquisition also persists its certificate ("A closure
certificate outlives its process"). A
pending-discard finisher that finds its object evicted (a foreign record resolved before
any join ran) resolves the drained tracker itself, since that object will never reach
`destroy`.

### Retained delivery through the manifest (F-105 7c)

A retained QoS 1/2 delivery is an exchange like any other since 7c: a register, an
exchange, an action, an acknowledgement advance, a terminal cleanup. What it has that an
ordinary one does not is its MATERIAL — a per-subscriber copy in a manifest and chunks —
in place of a source delivery, so the register is a union: the retained arm (`payload`,
`digest`) or the source arm (`dur`, `seq`), never both. Every ordinary-source sink (the
source cache, source state, completion, terminal settlement, restoration matching) refuses
the retained arm at its entry and counts the refusal (`outbound_retained_sink_guard.go`);
the dispatch routes every retained register away first, and the behavioural tests assert
the count stays zero.

**Snapshot under the SUBSCRIBE locks, execution after SUBACK.** The SUBSCRIBE takes its
snapshot where it always did and allocates each QoS 1/2 item an identifier as a Hold (it
acts for nothing). The items are staged on the subscription's replay object, whose GATE
holds the raw QoS 0 subscription's live deliveries until the replay is done, so a live QoS
0 message never overtakes a retained frame of that subscription (QoS 1/2 live deliveries
ride the durable consumer and are not gated, `docs/CONFORMANCE.md`). After the SUBACK the
staged items are transferred to the session's REPLAY worker, off the read loop. A same-sid
replacement INHERITS the object — nothing departs — and adds its own snapshot behind the
inherited items; an UNSUBSCRIBE, its connection's close or a takeover DEPARTS it, which
also drops any live QoS 0 delivery parked on its gate rather than leaving it parked until
the worker retires the object.

**Materialization, admission, transmission.** For each item the worker reserves the copy
(the provisioning batch creates the owner resource and the manifest, bound to the
producing tenure), writes its chunk batches through the manifest's fence, seals it READY
(the boundary re-reads and verifies the chunks), and ADMITS it in one batch: the exchange,
the retained register and its unsent marker, the owner's `retained-material` edge, the
exchange's duty, and the manifest's `admitted` — so an admission and a close arbitrate on
the manifest's sequence. An admission whose create-only register meets an occupied subject
re-allocates the identifier under the session lock, only once every earlier attempt is
proven never landed (consult 102). The send section then judges the frame BEFORE
acquiring: the subscribe deny over the copy's topic, then the Maximum Packet Size on the
frame as built. An acquisition under this connection's tenure would make the delivery this
connection's quota, which no abandonment may then release. The first send writes the
snapshot's bytes already in memory; no acquired action ever reads material. A copy that
cannot be acquired has no source redelivery to retry it, so the worker re-attempts while
the connection serves and closes the connection after the budget (the reconnect's resume
replays it).

**One exit door (consult 106).** Every retained obligation this connection created,
observed or possibly landed — a PUBLISH, a PUBREL, a withdrawal, a PUBREL installation, a
copy's material — stays OWNED, its allocation's identity kept, until its own durable
settlement is confirmed, the session serves another connection (whose resume restores it
from the records), or its connection is effectively closed with the records intact. A path
that can show none of the three hands the obligation to the continuation worker
(`oweRetained`, keyed by the allocation's identifier and nonce), whose only exits are
those three: it re-attempts with capped backoff and, exhausted, requests the connection's
close and keeps the obligation until the close has taken effect. A refusal, a missing
local entry, an unreadable record, an indeterminate verdict or an exhausted retry is none
of the three, so none of them ends an obligation; a write the connection refused while it
stays open wrote nothing. An abandonment decision past the same budget closes its
connection and is still stepped. A materialization step whose attempt stays unresolved
past the bound may have landed a copy: the copy is the reclaimer's and the connection is
closed, so the next CONNECT's discovery finds it. ONE named exception (consult 107): the
POSITIVE-STORE-ANSWER RECOVERY QUARANTINE. A resume may be accepted with a retained
exchange unowned only when answered reads, after the consistency re-reads, establish a
specifically enumerated unusable or contradictory persisted condition — its exchange
absent or naming another identifier, a phase the register contradicts, its copy absent,
contradicting or not verifying, its marker another allocation's, its canonical PUBREL
absent or mismatched, its abandonment fact contradicted — recorded with its reason against
that exact register and allocation; or when the register's own persisted shape is one this
broker refuses (the walk's unreadable-register reservation). The identifier stays
reserved, and the quarantine authorizes no replay, completion, abandonment or cleanup.
Every surviving continuation stands down for it — an owed obligation, an abandonment
decision, and a PUBREL installation, which is also fenced on the serving connection so a
previous connection's intent resolver never installs over a resume — and on a same-object
resume a resident retained entry over a register of a refused shape is demoted. An
unanswered read, an exhausted reclassification, an incomplete walk or a refused
installation is never the exception: each refuses the resume before CONNACK.

**Acknowledgements.** A PUBACK advances the exchange to Terminal and the register to
`publish_terminal` with no source settlement, and wakes the copy's reclamation. A
successful PUBREC is ONE advance: the exchange to PubRecObserved, the register `publish ->
pubrel_ready` carrying `rel_subj`/`rel_id`, the create-only CANONICAL PUBREL
(`f105.rel.<idHash>.<gen>.<nonce>`, class `rel`) on `$MQTT_inflight`, and the manifest at
its read sequence, unchanged and READY — so a copy cleanup has closed forbids a late
`rel`. The PUBREL is acquired on the register and written directly; nothing is stored on
`$MQTT_out`. A duplicate PUBREC acquires a new PUBREL action and re-emits it; a PUBREL
that could not be acquired is the continuation worker's to re-attempt. PUBCOMP
terminalizes as an ordinary exchange does, and the terminal finalization removes `rel`. A
PUBREC with a failure code rejects the exchange. The advance stays tenure-agnostic — a
client's answer crosses tenures — but its boundary admits a retained slot's arrow only
when the standing register and the exchange's predecessor, read whole at the member's
expected sequence, agree by the same consistency definition (a PUBREC validates the
predecessor without the canonical it creates; a PUBCOMP requires the standing canonical),
so an advance already in flight cannot carry a contradiction a resume quarantines.

**An unservable replay is withdrawn or abandoned, by what the marker proves.** Proven
unsent (the allocation's marker stands): withdrawn, WithdrawnUnsent, through the RETAINED
door (`outbound_retained_withdraw.go`), which is also the departure's. It captures the
allocation and EXCLUDES its identifier before the first attempt — the custody observer
removes the entry the moment the landed withdrawal ends the exchange — then withdraws
before it deletes the register, re-reading the register on every attempt so a retry
consumes OUR cancellation tombstone at its own sequence. The obligation is the register,
not the entry: a refused delete is owned by the continuation worker, and the exclusion is
lifted only by a subject-confirmed release. The ordinary proven-unsent door, which
untracks first and ignores the delete's outcome because a source redelivery repairs it,
is never used for a retained exchange. Possibly sent: ABANDONED, through the retained
arm of the abandonment fact — `{reason, tenure, alloc, acq, payload}`, reasons `acl-deny`
and `packet-too-large`, no source coordinate, no source settled; the charge goes, the
identifier stays until a valid completion or the generation's discard. An indeterminate
deny verdict decides nothing and is OWED: the PUBLISH is judged again by the continuation
worker, and a verdict still indeterminate after the budget closes the connection. A late
PUBREC on an abandoned retained exchange takes the
material-free ABANDONED arrow: the same `rel`-creating advance without the manifest
member, fenced instead by the generation's closure — a boundary read of it, itself fenced
by the authority CAS, since a Discard rewrites the authority (consult 103). The
abandonment is the CONTINUATION worker's until it stands in memory: an unresolved attempt
is settled before anything is re-submitted, the durable abandonment is applied only once
it reads back, and a decision whose captured entitlement no longer serves is passed on.

**Reclamation is material-only, and one protocol.** `reclaimRetainedPayloadStep` performs
one bounded step and is re-entrant from any landed predecessor: close the manifest,
release the edge, seal the owner's provisioning (the seal requires the manifest CLOSED),
authorize deletion, purge the chunks and the manifest, then record CleanupComplete and
resolve both duties. The close's boundary arm decides eligibility, never an earlier read:
an admitted copy closes only when its exchange ended, carries the retained abandonment
fact, or its generation was discarded — the first two only when the allocation's own
register agrees with the exchange by the ONE consistency definition recovery restores
pairs with (`retainedPairVerdict`: identity and identifier, the legal pairs of register
state and exchange phase, the abandonment fact, the canonical PUBREL), read in the same
batch. The register is located by the copy's ADMISSION ADDRESS (`admitted_pi`, written
with `admitted` by the admission batch, bound there to the exchange, the register and its
subject, and immutable), and the exchange's PI must equal it before an absent register —
legitimate only for an ended exchange, whose cleanup deletes it — or another allocation's
occupant counts; a register present in a shape this broker refuses agrees with nothing, so
a contradiction a resume quarantines never authorizes a close (consults 107, 108); an
unadmitted one under a successor serving tenure, a standing closure, or the producer's own
entitlement — "not serving" and an unreadable authority refuse (`retainedCloseArm`). No
drain proof is needed: no acquired action reads material. The exchange's own records — the
register and `rel` — are not this protocol's; they go with the exchange, and on a
discarded generation the recovery executor's discard census deletes them (7d). The
reclaimer is a worker of its own, woken
by every retained PUBACK, PUBCOMP, withdrawal and abandonment. It drops a copy only on a
POSITIVE answer: after the bound, a copy whose close boundary says its exchange may still
need it (`errMQTTRetainedMaterialNeeded`), whose exchange's ending is the wake that brings
it back — every wake restarts the count, so an answer older than the copy's last wake
never reaches the bound; a step that failed on the store keeps the copy while this session
object is resident, and a payload wake whose manifest cannot be read is read again rather
than dropped. The recovery executor dispatches a payload's duties to the same step BEFORE
classification; and CONNECT's inventory traversal collects the payloads its resource
duties name (and an uncertain duty's later resolution enrols its payload) so a copy whose
producer died is reclaimed at the next CONNECT or closure.

**Recovery replays from verified bytes.** The resume dispatches a retained register before
every ordinary-source route, reads the exchange FRESH with its sequence (the census
decides membership only), and for a PUBLISH reads and verifies the copy's chunks before
any acquisition, holding the bytes on the restored entry; `pubrel_ready` restores the
PUBREL from `rel`; `delivery_abandoned` restores the ACK-only identity with no material
read, seeding custody provisionally when the inventory could not decide the exchange (as
every restored entry does), so a late PUBREC's PUBREL entry is not refused for want of the
lineage; OUR cancellation tombstone over an ended exchange — a withdrawal whose delete did
not land — is consumed like a terminal register. Terminal cleanup the resume continues is
retried while the session object serves the generation. A material failure is reclassified
before it withholds: if the register or the exchange moved the pass re-runs and dispatches
on the fresh phase, and if both are unchanged the exchange is withheld, deterministically.
Withholding is reserved for a POSITIVE answer (an absent or contradicting record, material
that does not verify): a read the store did not answer — the exchange, the manifest, a
chunk, the marker or `rel` — refuses the resume before CONNACK instead, since a withheld
exchange has no owner and its client would be owed its PUBLISH or PUBREL; the reconnect
classifies again with the records intact. So does a consistency re-read that goes
unanswered (it is not a move). And EVERY success of the walk that installed nothing is
checked, not each exit that produces one: the conservative successes — the identifier
space withheld after an enumeration, a batch, a marker or a PUBREL scan failed, or an
exhausted reclassification — apply nothing, which is sound for a source-backed delivery
its consumer re-offers and would leave a retained exchange owned by nothing. Such a
success is refused unless the inventory rules a retained exchange out: a complete, certain
census, no live exchange carrying the retained abandonment fact, and no retained copy
still standing among the resources it names (`retainedObligationsUnexcluded`). A copy that
VERIFIES is not a fresh phase either: an answer on another broker after the pass's reads
(a PUBREC) leaves the copy intact, so the pair is re-read once more after verification and
a moved pair re-runs the pass. The pass re-checks the entitlement before its exhaustion
fallback, for both arms (a pre-existing gap for ordinary registers too).

**Foreground priority over the retained workers (consults 104, 105).** Every outbound
authority transition of a session CASes its one authority record, so this broker's own
writers serialize on it, and the retained workers (replay, continuation, reclaimer)
produce bursts of such writes right after a SUBSCRIBE and after every retained
acknowledgement. A foreground operation — the SUBSCRIBE's source-consumer name claim, the
PUBREC, PUBACK and PUBCOMP advances — ANNOUNCES itself before its first relevant read and
stays announced across every attempt; every background authority-transition ATTEMPT is
admitted on its own and waits while any is announced (`outbound_foreground_priority.go`).
An attempt admitted just before an announcement may still commit, so with the three
workers a continuously announced foreground operation loses at most three attempts to
them; the SUBSCRIBE claim's budget is eight, spaced by the shared authority-contention
wait before each re-attempt's fresh reads. Writes outside the handshake (another broker,
the recovery pass, the ordinary delivery paths) are not covered, and continuous foreground
traffic can delay background work without bound.

### The source consumer's lifecycle: ending release, disposal and retirement (F-105 7c-lc)

A plain subscription's `$MQTT_msgs` source consumer is a resource an admitted obligation
holds: its replay depends on that physical name. 7c-lc makes the consumer's END the same
kind of fact as its beginning — arbitrated on the resource record, never inferred from a
session record or a timer. Four rules, each enforced at the write boundary rather than by
its callers.

**An ending releases its holds in its own batch.** An exchange carries `holds`, the
reverse index of the source-replay and canonical-PUBREL edges its admission took (written
once by the admitting batch, equal to exactly those edges in both directions, never
rewritten). The batch that moves an exchange INTO an ending — terminal, rejected,
superseded unsent, withdrawn unsent — must carry, for every hold, the resource member
removing exactly that edge; and a hold edge is released by nothing else: no stored-ended
release door exists, so a lost response leaves both or neither and the caller resolves it
by reading the exchange. The boundary judges these removals against the ONE set of
exchanges the batch ends (`endedHere`, S-xor-Delta), for these two roles only; the
retained-material role keeps its own rules. An abandonment is not an ending and releases
nothing; a pending-drain phase releases nothing until its drain completes. The ending
kinds (advance, withdraw) may carry a resource member only as such a release, including
for an earlier generation's resource when a G1 obligation ends under G2; and more
generally, outside a dispose-resource transition every resource overwrite is an edge
change and nothing else (holistic H-2/H-3, stated as one property): sealing, authorizing,
completing and disposing are that kind's alone, so no separate resource change can ride an
admission, a pair replacement or an ending; and a dispose batch overwrites at most one
resource, so none can ride a disposal step either (consult 112). A pair
supersession merges the predecessor's release into the member that adds the replacement's
edge. Holds are released with the ending, not in a later continuation: every authority op
already CASes the client's authority record, so the release adds no serialization point
and removes the crash window a continuation would have had to bridge. Before 7c-lc no
source or PUBREL edge was ever released, which made every such resource that admitted
anything permanently unauthorizable — a prior-row omission this unit closes first.

**A logical-use consumer is retired only on a route's DISPOSAL decision.** Zero edges is
also what an idle subscription looks like between two messages, so it is never the
decision that a consumer is ended. The resource carries `disposal` — `{txn, reason, gen,
tenure}`, reasons unsubscribed, downgraded, rolled-back, drain-retired,
provisioning-failed, repair-undone — written once by the route that decided, never cleared
or changed. An edge is never admitted against a disposed resource (the disposal and the
admission CAS the same record, so whichever lands second meets the other) and readiness
refuses it; `LIVE -> DELETE_AUTHORIZED` of a source or PUBREL resource requires it; the
cleanup duty of a serving consumer is WITHHELD. The decision is licensed by the
entitlement the route decided under: the batch that introduces it must displace an
authority SERVING at exactly that generation and tenure, so a route paused across a
takeover cannot mark the successor's consumer disposable. A resource is
never CREATED carrying a decision (holistic H-1): that would bypass both rules.

**The authorization retires the name in the same batch, both directions.** A logical-use
resource's `DELETE_AUTHORIZED` member rides only beside the `LIVE -> RETIRED` ownership
member naming exactly it, and a RETIRED member only beside that authorization (Codex
consult 14 finding 1). The sweeps read the ownership half alone, so the pairing is what
lets them trust it.

**One owner performs the retirement, outside every fence.** The routes — UNSUBSCRIBE, the
live and restored QoS 0 downgrades, the SUBSCRIBE rollback and the failed filter, a fresh
consumer's failed CREATE or local subscription, the drain's retirement, the resume
repair's failed CREATE and undo — no longer delete. Each hands its decision (consumer name
or claimed incarnation, reason, captured entitlement) to the session's retirement owner,
the same live owner that reclaims retained copies, and returns: several run under the
record transaction, which must not block on a JetStream request. The owner's step for a
source item, one bounded step per call: settle the claims of a failed provisioning
(below); resolve the name's incarnation from its ownership (a missing or foreign owner
WITHHOLDS the delete and drops the item — never a raw delete); write the disposal
(idempotent: a lost response or another route's decision is found standing; an entitlement
that moved on drops the item); wait while holds remain (an ending's commit wakes it; a
hold whose exchange already ended is a contradiction this broker does not write, withheld
and reported, never repaired); authorize (resource and name, one batch); delete and
classify (removed, gone, or unresolved — which records nothing and repeats, safe because
the name is RETIRED and never reused); record the cleanup outcome and resolve both duties.
A restored subscription's consumer is never disposed of by a local failure: it is the
persisted subscription's durable, and the CONNECT that cannot restore it refuses instead.

**A failed provisioning is settled by arbitration, never by a read.** A SUBSCRIBE's claim
